News.title: Woman jailed after falsely accusing multiple men of rape over seven years
News.content:
Woman jailed after falsely accusing multiple men of rape over seven years

Khloe Simmonds, 26, has been jailed after spending hundreds of hours with police officers making false allegations of serious sexual assault and claiming to be a victim

View 2 Images Khloe Simmonds falsely accused multiple men of rape over seven-year period

A woman who falsely claimed she had been raped by multiple different men over a seven-year period has been jailed.

Khloe Simmonds, 26, was sentenced for eight counts of perverting the course of justice over allegations made against the victims between 2018 and 2026.

Harrow Crown Court heard that Simmonds spent hundreds of hours with police officers bolstering false allegations of serious sexual assault.

At the height of the offending, Simmonds was responsible for 2.5% of all rape and serious sexual assault allegations in Harrow. Several of the men accused of rape were arrested and detained for a short period of time before being released, the court heard.

Sentencing Simmonds to seven and a half years in prison, His Honour Judge John Lodge said: “You repeatedly made false allegations of rape between July 2018 and January 2026. This was a sustained pattern of conduct, not isolated incidents.”

View 2 Images Khloe Simmonds has been jailed

More than 3,500 Next shop workers suffer blow in Next equal pay victory READ MORE :

The judge said Simmonds’ conduct had an impact on the number of resources that should have been available to investigate cases involving “genuine victims of serious crime”.

Simmonds is a pre-operative trans woman, the court heard, and was referred to using female pronouns throughout the hearing. Simmonds initially attended the sentencing via video link from HMP Wormwood Scrubs, west London, but subsequently returned to a cell and refused to observe.

Prosecutor Ben Temple told the court that in the summer of 2018, Simmonds claimed an Afghan national had held a knife to her throat and orally raped her.

The man was identified, arrested, detained and spent 88 days under police investigation, the court heard. He denied the allegation and instead stated that it was Simmonds who had made advances towards him which he had rejected.

In February 2022, Simmonds met a chef on the LGBT dating site Grindr and invited him to her flat. The court heard that after drinking with the defendant, he decided to leave because he felt uncomfortable.

After he left, Simmonds called 999 alleging she had been raped and implied that he had drugged her by placing something in her drink. The man was arrested outside his home address and told police that while at her flat, he went to the lavatory and upon returning, found that his beer smelt of whisky.

In his victim impact statement, he described the arrest process as “humiliating”, adding that he spent 20 hours at the police station. The court heard that the following month, Simmonds had spent the evening on a date and subsequently caught a taxi home.

Upon arriving home she called 999 and alleged she had been raped by the cab driver. However the police obtained data from the vehicle and found that it had never travelled less than 25 miles per hour and had not stopped.

Mr Temple said this data “annihilated the allegation” and Simmonds was arrested on suspicion of perverting the course of public justice. It was heard she admitted the allegations were false. In a victim impact statement, the taxi driver said he found the ordeal “traumatic”.

In June of that year, Simmonds matched with a musician on the LGBT dating site and the pair subsequently drank alcohol and ended up at Simmonds’ home address.

He felt tired and asked if he could rest on Simmonds’ sofa. The court heard there was no sexual contact between them and he fell asleep.

While he rested, Simmonds called the police and claimed that the man had orally raped her. He was arrested but insisted there had been no sexual contact, telling police: “I am an innocent man.”

In a victim impact statement, he said: “I find it deeply distressing that an innocent person could be subjected to such a traumatic process because of a deliberate lie.”

Simmonds claimed that she had been raped by an unknown male on three occasions in November last year. She also falsely claimed she had been raped on three separate occasions by an unknown male between December 2018 and February 2022.

In January, Simmonds claimed she had been raped on a bench by a man she had met that evening.

Article continues below

The court heard that she had approached a group of strangers to say that she was in an “abusive situation” and asked for “help”. However, the man was quickly exonerated as footage showed no such assault had happened, the court heard.

The defendant also claimed she had been raped by her ex-partner in November last year.

Dominic Benthall, mitigating, said Simmonds has been diagnosed with autism, ADHD, and suffered longstanding issues of alcohol dependency. “There is plainly, or was plainly, at the time an underlying mental health difficulty,” he said. Simmonds previously pleaded guilty to eight counts of tending and intending to pervert the course of public justice.

News.title: Brits face ‘major risk’ heat alerts in Spain as tourists told ‘be prepared’
News.content:
Brits face ‘major risk’ heat alerts in Spain as tourists told ‘be prepared’

Spain's weather agency as issued several amber and yellow weather warnings across the country with temperatures hitting as high as 40C in some holiday hotspots

View 2 Images Brits have been warned to expect temperatures in the high 30C range (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

Holidaymakers have been warned of extreme temperatures across Spain with the mercury reaching 40C in coming days.

‌



Weather warnings are in place across Spain for extreme heat following weeks of scorching summer temperatures across Europe and the UK.

‌



Spain's weather agency AEMET (State Meteorological Agency) has issued several amber and yellow weather warnings across the country, the Liverpool Echo reports.

‌



An orange warning poses a more serious risk, referred to as an "important hazard". AEMET says an orange, or amber, alert signifies a "major risk", with people advised to "be prepared", take precautions and follow the latest weather information.

Popular tourist areas including Gran Canaria, Andalucía and Cataluña have been placed under an orange warning. Meanwhile yellow warnings are in place for Aragon, the Balearic Islands, Castile and León, Castile-La Mancha, Extremadura, Madrid, Murcia, Navarre and Valencia.

View 2 Images The warnings cover a wide swathe of Spain (Image: aemet)

‌



The yellow warnings are "low risk", but temperatures could reach 36C which is hotter than average for September in Spain.

The warnings remain in place throughout Monday (September 7), with temperatures looking to remain high throughout the week.

Spain is a popular holiday destination for millions of British tourists every year. Many people will still be jetting off to resorts across Spain over the next few weeks to make the most of the final summer sunshine.

‌



In the BBC's forecast for Seville this week, temperatures will remain in the high 30s. There will be a high of 39C on Tuesday (September 8) before a slight decrease to 35C on Wednesday (September 9).

Ibiza is cooler, with a high of 31C on Tuesday (September 8) and 29C on Wednesday (September 9).

While large parts of Europe continue to experience extreme heat, temperatures have dropped in the UK compared to the blistering sunshine we experienced over the summer.

‌



In its outlook for the UK this week, the Met Office said: "Drier and brighter on Wednesday with spells of sunshine. Another band of rain then moves in for Thursday, before drier and brighter weather returns on Friday. Temperatures likely around average."

Temperatures remain around 17C and 18C this week, with drizzly spells and sunny interludes.

September is officially underway, which marks the start of autumn for many. The beginning of a new season often brings about some unsettled conditions.

Article continues below

Some signs that autumn has arrived include the changing colour of the leaves, a fall in temperatures and the arrival of cooler mornings.

According to the Met Office, meteorological autumn always begins on September, 1 and ends on November 30.

However, astronomical autumn begins with the autumn equinox, which usually falls on September 22 or 23 each year.

News.title: King Charles issues letter making clear Prince Harry and Meghan are still not working royals
News.content:
King Charles issues letter making clear Prince Harry and Meghan are still not working royals

King Charles has issued a letter to "senior stakeholders" today where he has made it clear that despite being back in the UK, Prince Harry and Meghan should be considered "private citizens"

View 4 Images Prince Harry and Meghan with King Charles and Prince William (Image: POOL/AFP via Getty Images)

The King has made it clear that Prince Harry and Meghan will remain private citizens and are "on their own" despite their bombshell move back to the UK. .

‌



In a firm letter issued on behalf of the King today, it states that the Sussexes' should not use their HRH styles, which are still in abeyance, and that they "do not represent the sovereign" while out making public appearances.

‌



The guidance was sent under the King's instruction by his most senior official, the Lord Chamberlain, to offer clarity over Harry and Meghan's royal status after requests for guidance. It has been issued to those in government, the military and lord lieutenants up and down the country.

‌



View 4 Images Prince Harry pictured at Tower Bridge Studios in London on Friday (Image: Tower Bridge Studios)

A royal source said: "Timing is everything. Harry and Meghan have only been in the country a matter of days but this important line has been drawn early, leaving no one in any doubt where his feelings lie on the matter.

"Undoubtedly there will be clashes in the future with the Sussexes, no one expects them to give the royal households the courtesy of their plans, and even less so now. But the King could not be clearer. You may have come back to the UK, but you are on your own."

‌



In the run up to the Sussexes' return to Britain, the King was said to be glad to be able to spend more time with the family, but remained adamant they would not be working royals and there was no half-in, half-out option.

Andthe letter issued today on behalf of the KIng sets out: "Following the decision by the Duke and Duchess of Sussex to relocate to the UK, we have received a number of requests for guidance. To help avoid doubt or confusion, the King has directed that the following information be shared.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of The Royal Family.

‌



"This position, distinct from the state and royal duties undertaken by the working Royal Family, and with the personal latitude it brings the couple in respect of financial independence and protection of their privacy as they would wish, will continue to be fully respected.

View 4 Images Harry with his father, the King (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

"It follows that there is no change to the current status of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex. Their styles as His and Her Royal Highness remain in abeyance and are not used.

‌



"The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity. In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests."

It came as the first picture of Harry since his move back to the UK also emerged today, showing him at Tower Bridge Studios on Friday, where he signed a wall and posed alongside his signature.

The central London studios is where several high-profile TV shows and podcasts are filmed, including Steven Bartlett's Diary of a CEO and BBC's The Apprentice. It is unclear why he was visiting.

‌



The Sussexes stepped down as working royals in 2020 for personal and financial reasons but returned to the UK last month, with rumours rife as to the reason behind the unexpected development.

Previously, Harry had said he "could not see a world" in which he brought his wife and children back to the UK after they lost their automatic right to taxpayer-funded police protection while in the UK.

View 4 Images Harry and Meghan with their children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet (Image: @meghan/Instagram)

‌



It is understood that the letter has been issued to the Sussexes’ team and officials have made it clear the guidance has been sent with Harry and Meghan’s wishes to “remain private citizens while in the UK”.

It has been stressed that there is nothing new in the letter and the agreement reached at the Sandringham Summit in January 2020, after Harry and Meghan dramatically said they would not longer be working royals, still stands. It is also said that any security provision for Harry and Meghan remains an issue for RAVEC ( Executive Committee for the Protection of Royalty and Public Figures).

The letter added: “Any specific questions from official and state organisations about the courtesies which should be extended to the Duke and Duchess, and particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace.

‌



“Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities.” The letter is in the name of Lord Benyon, whose office is responsible for organising the King’s ceremonial and public-facing events.

Content cannot be displayed without consent

The letter at the King's request comes after reports that Meghan is expected to carry out some public charity work in the UK in the coming weeks with Harry expected to start his public appearances a lot sooner.

Article continues below

Later this month, he is due to appear at the annual WellChild Awards and events for the Invictus Games and he will also carry out a skydive for military charities after making a promise to 102-year-old veteran Ed Marshall during a visit to Toronto, Canada, last November.

The couple’s children Prince Archie and Princess Lilibet are expected to be starting school in the UK near to the family’s reported countryside retreat in the Cotswolds.

News.title: Minister condemns disorder at Portsmouth anti-migrant protest after police officers hurt
News.content:
Council leader Steve Pitt said the decision had caused "needless disruption".

Around 200 people, some wearing masks, confronted police in riot gear after they descended on the Eastney Landing ferry port area, where the migrants were landed.

Police protected a number of coaches parked on a road leading away from Eastney Marina as protesters blocked traffic. A dispersal order was put in place, meaning anyone failing to comply with police could be arrested.

In a statement, Hampshire and Isle of Wight Constabulary said a handful of officers were treated at the scene for injuries, none of which were serious.

It said: "Violence and criminal damage have no part in peaceful protest.

"No arrests have been made at this time, however an investigation to identify offenders responsible for any assaults to officers, criminal damage to vehicles or other criminal offences has been launched."

Spencer Wragg, chair of Hampshire Police Federation, said: "I've seen footage of officers being pushed off their motorbikes, I've seen pictures of police vehicles damaged. It appears that the police last night became the target for some of the protest."

Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo - an associate of far-right activist Tommy Robinson - was livestreaming from the scene - where he called for his supporters to "get down to Eastney" and stop the migrants being transported.

The coaches carrying the migrants were able to leave in the early hours of Monday and the Border Force confirmed "individuals from the boat have been transported outside of Hampshire for processing".

News.title: What we know about anti-migrant protests and organiser Danny Thomas
News.content:
Hundreds of demonstrators gathered in Dover and Portsmouth over the weekend in protests against small boat crossings.

But what is the connection between the two protests?

The answer is one man - Danny Thomas, more often known as Danny Tommo.

UK correspondent Daniel Sandford looks into the background of Danny Tommo and how he has galvanised these protests through social media and local support.

News.title: Jaguar Land Rover to cut 4,000 jobs over next two years
News.content:
Jaguar Land Rover (JLR) is to cut 4,000 jobs as the carmaker struggles with Chinese competition, US tariffs, and the transition to electric vehicles.

The cuts will happen over the next two years and will mostly affect the head office, which is based in the UK.

JLR's long-term issues were made worse after a cyber-attack last year caused the firm, which employs 43,000 people globally, to shut down production for more than a month.

Chief executive PB Balaji said the firm was "committed to supporting everyone with care, fairness and respect" through the redundancy process.

"The automotive industry faces significant challenges, with technological change amidst intense competition and ongoing geo-political uncertainty," he added.

JLR is hoping to achieve the cuts through voluntary redundancy, with a window open until 4 October, but said it would make compulsory redundancies with less generous terms if necessary. Affected staff will receive an email in the coming days.

The redundancies are being made in an attempt to save Â£1.7bn over the next two years.

JLR is "as strategically important as it gets for the UK economy", according to David Bailey, business and economics professor at Birmingham University.

He said many UK jobs were dependent on its supply chain and the economy as a whole took a hit when the firm closed down production because of last year's cyberattack.

"It's the centre of our automotive industry," he added.

Yet, the car maker has been losing sales to rivals from China, a country which JLR initially saw as a market for growth rather than a source of competition.

In addition, US President Donald Trump's tariffs have hurt the company, which unlike many of its rivals does not have a factory in the US.

In its results for the year to the end of March, JLR said US tariffs and the cyberattack were the main reasons why its sales had slumped by a fifth to Â£22.9bn from Â£29bn in the previous two years.

Ian Robertson, former director at BMW, told the BBC's Today programme that JLR should have copied its rivals and started manufacturing in the US.

"The biggest operation for BMW in the world is in Spartanburg, South Carolina. Mercedes have their plant further south in Tuscaloosa. JLR didn't take that decision early enough in my view," he said.

He also said JLR had been "somewhat late to the party" in terms of electric vehicles.

Jaguar launched the I-PACE, a fully-electric SUV, in 2018. But the electric Range Rover announced last week will be its first electric vehicle launch since then.

Robertson added that Brexit had hurt the firm, despite its factory in Slovakia giving it "some flexibility".

News.title: King makes clear Harry and Meghan remain non-working royals
News.content:
The King's letter has been sent to Prince Harry's team, government departments, military officials and Lord Lieutenants, according to Palace sources.

Lord Lieutenants, who are the monarch's local representatives, and government staff are often involved in royal visits and engagements.

This letter makes clear that any engagements carried out by the Sussexes will be in a private capacity and they will not be representing the Royal Family.

It seems to be something of a shot across the bows, making clear that any Prince Harry and Meghan visits should not be treated as royal engagements.

This comes ahead of what are likely to be public appearances by the Sussexes this autumn, as they settle in the UK and support their charities.

The couple have kept a low profile, but the first picture of Prince Harry since coming back to the UK appears to have been posted on the social media account of Tower Bridge Studios in London.

The message from the King emphasises that the position agreed in 2020 when the Sussexes left the UK - the so-called Sandringham Agreement - is still in place.

This ruled out any "half-in and half-out" status, so Harry and Meghan could not pursue their own commercial interests while continuing to be working royals.

"It is well known that in January 2020 the Duke and Duchess stepped down from undertaking representative duties on behalf of the Sovereign, and are no longer working members of the Royal Family," the letter says.

The letter sent on behalf of the King makes it clear that this remains the case.

"The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," it adds.

The King's message says that any questions from organisations about the reception to be given to the Sussexes, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".

Prince Harry and Meghan faced an acrimonious departure from the UK in 2020, which they chronicled in their Netflix documentary.

They established their financial independence in California, including Prince Harry writing a best-selling memoir Spare and Meghan creating an online food range, As Ever.

This summer the couple made a surprise return to the UK, where their children will be going to school.

It's expected that Prince Harry will be supporting his charities, including the Invictus Games, which are due to be held in Birmingham next year.

There have been reports that Meghan is considering a return to acting.

Disputes about Prince Harry and Meghan's security in the UK remain unresolved and the letter spells out: "Any operational security issues should continue to be directed to the relevant police authorities."

Prince Harry has complained about a lack of adequate police protection in the UK, but the Palace says that has to be addressed by the Royal and VIP Executive Committee - known as Ravec - which decides security for royals and public figures.

Palace sources have suggested it was better to make the Lord Chamberlain's letter public, in a spirit of transparency, rather than risk it emerging in leaks.

Prince Harry and Meghan's representatives have been contacted for a response.

News.title: Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises
News.content:
The chancellor may have thought about shifting the venue of his first major speech this morning.

It was an absolute and total coincidence that he chose to make it in the Coventry Manufacturing and Technology Centre (MTC), just a few minutes' drive from the city's totemic HQ of Jaguar Land Rover (JLR).

In the event, no one was pulling punches. The 4,000 office-based job losses at JLR were confirmed as John Healey answered questions a few miles away.

Healey chose to lean into it as an example of the global turbulence against which the UK needs more resilience.

The difference between this chancellor and his predecessor was he also feels that stressing fiscal discipline should instil confidence in consumers, businesses and investors, and not sap it away amid rolling fears of tax hikes.

So the prime minister and his chancellor have been engaged in a conscious attempt to boost the economic vibes - "a new story", as he called it.

In his speech, and in a BBC interview afterwards, this was clear. There are some positive underlying signs from consumer, business and recruiter confidence measures that indicate this message has been heard, although the hot weather and World Cup have also been factors.

The Downing Street duo are trying to maintain this precious commodity of confidence and the promotion of economic animal spirits that have been suppressed by years of political and economic chaos.

"Borrowing costs are too high," Healey acknowledged at the start of his speech. The global rise in bond yields is like a boa constrictor squeezing the Budget maths, slowly and relentlessly, occasionally loosening its grip, but never actually slithering away entirely.

It raises some reasonable questions therefore about how to balance reining in borrowing with protecting mildly better confidence?

The speech did not seem to me to prepare the ground - a "pitch roll" - for significant tax rises, as I heard at the equivalent Budget "scene setters" for the past two years.

"Am I right?" I asked the chancellor on this point. A pause as he sought precisely the right word formulation. "I won't comment. I can't comment. No chancellor can ahead of a Budget I will take and announce on October 28th".

OK, what about the advice from one of the PM's favourite economists Lord O'Neill that the rise in borrowing rates is a golden opportunity to scrap the triple lock?

This lock guarantees the state pension rising each year in line with either inflation, wage increases or 2.5% - whichever is the highest - but some have argued it is unaffordable.

"The prime minister has said, like I have, that we must bring down welfare costs, but we are also responding to the extreme pressure that is there in wider markets," Healey said.

Neither answer was a denial, but nor were they any type of confirmation. Like a stubborn batsman, the chancellor is going to stay at the crease, giving little away, in his case, about next month's Budget.

News.title: Self-described 'genocidal racist monster' jailed after BBC investigation
News.content:
Warwick Crown Court heard Webster had been referred four times to the UK Government-led Prevent programme, a scheme aimed to stop people becoming terrorists.

The court also heard police found a crossbow in the attic of his property, which was still in its wrapping.

Jamie Scott, prosecuting, told the court that the CPS took a "proportionate approach" to charging him with 12 offences - but asked it be noted that there was "a raft" of similar material posted online by Webster.

His defence lawyer Susan Guest said Webster had a long-standing difficulty around social interaction and anxiety and said he became "more isolated" where his views were "reinforced rather than challenged" by people online.

"He almost lived in a bubble and this online community reinforced his views," Guest told the court.

"That bubble subsequently popped and he now has to take responsibility for those actions."

Sentencing Webster to two years, Judge Anthony Potter said he had been given numerous opportunities to show remorse and change his behaviour.

"Talk is very very cheap," he told Webster. "It has allowed you to escalate your offending and propagate the most harmful views.

"I cannot accept that there is a realistic prospect of rehabilitation in the community. I'd be failing in my public duty if I didn't sent you to custody."

Frank Ferguson, the Chief Crown Prosecutor for the CPS, said inciting racial hatred was a "very serious offence" which went "beyond any debate about freedom of speech."

"Expressing a wish for people to be killedâ¦ Jewish people, Muslim people, black people, south-asian people, immigrants and LGBTQ+ community as wellâ¦ and encouraging other people to express similar views.

"It's not just about what he might do, it's what he might be encouraging others to do by his words," he said.

Det Ch Supt Alison Hurst, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing for the West Midlands, said Webster had been investigated previously for racially aggravated offences and thanked BBC Wales for bringing him to their attention again.

"Parts of the evidence from that documentary has been presented to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which has led to the prosecution and sentencing," she said.

Webster was given a two-year sentence, where he'll serve half in prison and a year on licence.

If you or someone you know has been affected by the issues raised in this story, information about available help and support can be found via BBC Action Line.

News.title: 'I have chronic cancer but I'm not going to die' - BBC presenter Maryam Moshiri
News.content:
BBC News presenter Maryam Moshiri has shared more detail about her two years living with cancer, and the way the chronic disease will affect the rest of her life.

She was diagnosed in November 2024 with polycythaemia vera (PV) - a rare, treatable blood cancer. Although it cannot be cured, it can be managed effectively.

Speaking to her colleague Lucy Hockings, Moshiri said she was lucky her GP caught the cancer early and reflected on how she felt in the aftermath of her diagnosis.

Read more on this story.

News.title: Next wins key appeal to overturn £30m equal pay ruling
News.content:
Next has won an appeal allowing it to keep paying warehouse workers a higher hourly rate than shop floor staff in a long running battle over equal pay.

The Employment Appeal Tribunal has overturned a key part of a landmark ruling in 2024 which found the retailer was wrong to pay its warehouse staff higher basic pay than shop floor workers for jobs of equal value.

More than 3,500 current and former employees, mainly women, had been set to share potentially more than Â£30m in back pay as a result of that judgement.

After Next's appeal, the law firm Leigh Day, which represents store workers, described the conclusion on basic pay as "disappointing" and said it will appeal the decision.

The tribunal accepted that Next was justified in paying higher rates because of recruitment and retention pressures for warehouse workers.

Next described the decision as a "landmark victory" succeeding on the "key issue of basic pay".

In a statement, it said: "The importance of this decision is that the Appeal Tribunal has confirmed that it was justifiable for Next to rely on market forces to distinguish between different groups of employees, where there was a good rationale to pay one group more than the other.

"In this case, Next had to pay a higher market rate to warehouse operatives because of recruitment and retention pressures, which did not apply to the workforce in its stores. Next believes this element of the judgment is not only correct in law, but also a victory for common sense.

"The judgment affirms a principle at the heart of any effective employment market - that employers must be able to pay what is necessary to recruit the people they need; and that doing so does not oblige them to raise the pay of other employees where there is no reason to do so."

Leigh Day said judges did uphold 2024 findings on night-time premiums, overtime premiums and paid rest breaks.

Next said it will now seek permission to appeal these decisions.

Both the original Employment Tribunal and the Appeal Tribunal found there was no direct sex discrimination in Next's pay rates. Shop floor staff are predominantly women while warehouse workers are predominantly male.

Questions are now being asked about if this result could set a precedent across the industry. Tesco, Asda, Morrisons, and Sainbury's are all involved in similar long running claims and will be studying the findings closely.

Last year, thousands of female workers at Birmingham City Council heard how much money they will receive in a long-awaited equal pay settlement. Brighton and Hove City Council is also facing over 1,000 equal pay cases.

News.title: Chancellor calls for 'confidence about Britain' despite 'historic high' borrowing costs
News.content:
Asked about the impact of higher borrowing costs, which have surged this month, the Chancellor said that the government was responding to "extreme pressures in the wider market," and reiterated that he wanted to "bring down welfare costs."

Earlier, in his first major speech as chancellor, Healey said his mission was to "make Great Britain growth Britain" again.

Speaking at the Manufacturing Technology Centre (MTC) in Coventry, he said,

"My defining mission as chancellor is growth, good growth in every postcode. And I've set out today the way this government will set about it: more devolution, more public leadership and control, more investment, more innovation, more jobs."

Healey said he is in "lockstep" with Prime Minister Andy Burnham about the need for fiscal discipline and having a buffer in the government's spending plans "against the sort of uncertainty that the JLR decision locally has shown".

It came as Healey offered an upbeat view of the state of the UK economy ahead of the Budget, building on a recent uptick in consumer and business confidence.

Speaking in Coventry, he set out a "new story" of the economy not just turning a corner but being resilient, optimistic and "ready to seize the opportunities of new technologies and ideas".

With seven weeks until the Budget, Healey said the government will stick to Labour's manifesto pledge, made under Sir Keir Starmer and former Chancellor Rachel Reeves, to not "increase taxes on working people".

He repeatedly refused to comment on possible tax rises or spending cuts ahead of 28 October, stating only: "Staying true to our values means being honest about the need to control government spending."

Conservative Shadow Chancellor Andrew Griffith, said: "Healey failed to end uncertainty by ruling out more tax rises."

He added that Healey "sounds increasingly like continuity Rachel Reeves".

In his speech from the Manufacturing Technology Centre in the Midlands, Healey described the UK as "turning the corner" and said greater devolution would spread economic growth more evenly across the UK.

But recent ructions in government debt markets have piled fresh pressure on already-stretched public finances, with the Treasury needing to fill possible multi-billion pound gaps caused by rising borrowing costs and the need to fund higher defence spending.

News.title: Murder arrests over baby girl's death in woodland
News.content:
Four people have been arrested on suspicion of murder after a baby was found dead while camping with her family in Staffordshire.

The three-month-old girl died after emergency services were called to reports of a child in cardiac arrest in woodland off Strawberry Lane, near Cheslyn Hay, at 08:45 BST on Saturday.

The people arrested were a 42-year-old man and 30-year-old woman from south Staffordshire, a 20-year-old woman from Wolverhampton and an 18-year-old man from Walsall.

All four were detained at the scene and have since been bailed while inquiries continue, Staffordshire Police said.

Det Insp Josh Lee said officers were working to gather further evidence around the circumstances of the girl's death and were "keeping an open mind".

He said it was being treated as an isolated incident and urged people not to share "unconfirmed and speculative" claims online.

News.title: Money offered by SoS does not go far enough, parties say
News.content:
Alliance Party leader Naomi Long said the meeting has been a "positive starting point" adding she would not "get ahead of myself in terms of deciding whether something is adequate or not".

"I want to see our finances put on a sustainable footing and I believe part of that is putting these institutions on a sustainable footing," she said.

"So I think we have to take those conversations in parallel."

She added Northern Ireland's unmet need has to be covered in the financial settlement and said this has not been met yet.

On reform, she said it was a "major step forward" that this was on the agenda, adding this was something her party had been wanting for years.

UUP leader Jon Burrows said the meeting was "the opening gambit"but said there is still a "significant short fall" of the money that was asked for.

"There's going to have to be a meeting of minds between His Majesty's government and the political parties," he said.

"We certainly accept the premise that we need to come to this with credibility ....so we don't keep asking for more."

"We need a fair settlement but then we need to spend more wisely and govern more prudently."

The SDLP - Stormont's official opposition - was not part of the executive discussions on the budget, but a delegation of its politicians is meeting the secretary of state to discuss another issue on Monday - potential reform of the institutions.

Alliance and the SDLP have long called for the power-sharing institutions to be reformed to prevent them from collapsing again.

Leader Claire Hanna said there did not need to be a "long period of diagnosis".

"We don't need months and months of negotiation in a stately home, everybody knows what needs to be done.

"If they're not done we're going to be right back here and if we fail to put these mechanisms in place ahead of the next election we're facing into more lost years."

Taoiseach (Irish prime minister) MicheÃ¡l Martin said that "no party should have a veto in the Assembly coming together after an election".

"Sinn FÃ©in have now agreed and come forward with proposals to reform strand one. DUP are not as enthusiastic right now, but, to enable the better working of the Executive, those reforms are needed."

News.title: Plans for major overhaul of councils halted
News.content:
Plans for a major shake-up of local government are on hold, after the government launched a review in light of new legal advice.

Proposals to merge smaller councils to form larger authorities in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk have been withdrawn.

Meanwhile, plans for 14 other areas will also be reviewed and paused.

Reorganisation in Surrey, where councillors for two new unitary authorities were elected in May, will not be affected by the review.

The government confirmed local elections in May 2027 would go ahead on existing council boundaries.

Confirming the review in Parliament, Local Government Secretary Angela Rayner told MPs that "in light of legal advice, I want to satisfy myself firstly that the right process is in place, that it is robust, and of course complies with the law".

She added: "And secondly, I want to fully test whether our proposals for local government reorganisation meet the priorities of a new administration and a new prime minister and any additional considerations."

Rayner acknowledged the announcement was "disappointing" but insisted the government was "determined more than ever to devolve power closer to the people we represent" - a key priority of new PM Andy Burnham.

The plans originated under Sir Keir Starmer's government, when Rayner was also local government secretary, before she was replaced by Steve Reed.

The government was already facing legal challenges over proposals to reorganise councils in Essex, Hampshire, Norfolk and Suffolk.

In June, Reform-led councils in Essex, Norfolk and Suffolk launched judicial reviews against the plans, while the Conservative-led administration in Hampshire did the same.

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said: "Reform UK not only argued that this government's plans for local government reorganisation were an unmitigated disaster, but we once again put our money where our mouth is."

He added: "Thanks to our judicial reviews in affected Reform-led councils, the government has backed down on their plans yet again."

Conservative shadow local government minister David Simmonds said it was a "humiliation" for the government.

He said: "Ministers are only backing off because they have been found out in the face of relentless Conservative opposition to their gerrymandering."

Liberal Democrat local government spokeswoman ZÃ¶e Franklin said: "This is an embarrassing and chaotic climbdown, which has resulted in already cash-strapped councils wasting huge sums on plans the government told them were legally watertight."

Sean Matthews, from the County Councils Network, welcomed the move, adding: "Many of our members will be relieved that the decisions they viewed as damaging to local services and financially unsustainable have been withdrawn or are being reviewed."

A spokesperson for the Local Government Association, which represents councils, said that while local authorities hold different views on the reorganisation plans "there is no excuse for the government's mishandling of this process".

The spokesperson added that Rayner's announcement "will have caused significant uncertainty, after councils have invested scarce public money and countless hours" in the reorganisation programme.

Local government in England is currently covered by a complicated patchwork of arrangements.

In some places, responsibility for local services is shared between county councils, which manage areas including social care and education; and district councils, which cover smaller areas and are responsible for services such as bin collections.

Some areas, particularly larger towns and some cities, have "unitary" authorities responsible for both - while the regions surrounding big cities are increasingly covered by regional mayors and multi-council "combined" authorities, with greater powers in areas such as transport policy, planning and housing.

In late 2024, as local government secretary, Rayner announced plans to move towards unitary councils across all of England, with council boundaries redrawn and smaller district councils abolished.

The government argued the proposals would make the system simpler and produce savings by making the delivery of services more efficient, while also handing new powers from Westminster to regions across the country.

However, critics said the plans would not save money, while diverting resources from front-line services and leaving councils more remote from their communities.

Under Sir Keir, the government had been pushing ahead with the proposals.

In July â just days before Burnham became prime minister â Rayner's successor as secretary of state, Reed, had announced plans for new councils in 14 areas.

News.title: Jorja Smith, Chase & Status and Sam Smith to head up Radio 1's Live Lounge month
News.content:
Sam Smith, Chase & Status and Jorja Smith are among the artists who have been revealed for BBC Radio 1's Live Lounge month.

Indie band Blossoms, singer-songwriter Rachel Chinouriri and US rappers Anderson .Paak and Cordae will also take to the studio in October.

Each Live Lounge guest traditionally performs an acoustic version of one of their own songs, plus a cover of a track by a different artist.

The sessions will air on Radio 1's Live Lounge show, which will now be fronted by Charlie Hedges and Jeremiah Asiamah.

The recordings will go out throughout October on Mondays, Wednesdays and Fridays at midday on the pair's new show.

A performance from Stockport-formed band Blossoms on 5 October will kick off the run.

Rock band Nothing But Thieves, US rising star Stella Lefty, Brit-nominated singer Beabadoobee and London-based artist Odeal are also among the artists on the line-up.

Brighton duo Royal Blood will close out this year's sessions on 30 October, but a surprise artist, who will perform just before them, is still to be announced.

West Midlands superstar Jorja Smith will be performing following on from the release of her third album, What Are The Odds.

The Brit Award winner's latest album received largely positive reviews, with Rolling Stone UK describing it as her "best album yet". , external

Electronic heavyweights Chase & Status will also take to the studio after they headlined Reading and Leeds Festival last month.

And Oscar-winner Sam Smith will be rolling out their vocals following on from the release of their fifth album, Hazel Eyes, last month.

News.title: 'Super-university' created amid funding squeeze
News.content:
The universities of Kent and Greenwich have merged to form the UK's first "super-university" amid sector-wide financial pressures.

The new London and South East University Group (LASE) becomes the UK's third largest, with more than 50,000 students across four campuses in south-east London and Kent.

Leaders say the institutions are "much stronger" together as higher education providers face mounting economic strain, but the University and College Union previously raised concerns that the merger signalled a "broader problem for the sector".

The two universities, which legally merged last month, will still operate as distinct academic divisions within the group, retaining their current names.

Students will still apply to the institution they choose and degrees will be awarded in the name of Kent or Greenwich.

But the group will now be able to offer subjects that they could not before when they were separate entities, and students will be able to use libraries and access wellbeing services across the campuses in Greenwich, Medway and Canterbury.

Chief executive Prof Jane Harrington said the merger had made the universities financially stronger.

She said the combined group would also be better placed to help tackle regional youth unemployment.

"If I was to look through south-east London going out we've got areas of urban deprivation, then you go out into Medway and Kent you've got areas of rural deprivation and then we've got areas of coastal deprivation," she said.

"It's a real opportunity for us to address the very people that the government's worried about."

News.title: Rapist serving life may face more assault charges
News.content:
A convicted serial rapist described by police as "one of the most prolific predators" in the UK could face further charges after fresh allegations involving seven more women were passed to prosecutors.

Chinese national Zhenhao Zou is serving a life sentence with a minimum term of 24 years after he was found guilty of drugging and raping 10 women in London and China between September 2019 and May 2023.

Believing Zou had committed further crimes, police appealed for more potential victim-survivors to come forward.

The Metropolitan Police has sent a file containing the new allegations of sexual crimes to the Crown Prosecution Service (CPS), which will decide whether to bring further charges.

According to the Met Police, the file contains evidence relating to several alleged offences, including rape and administering a substance with intent to commit a sexual offence.

It relates to reports made by five women who contacted police following the appeal, as well as the alleged rape of two women who remain unidentified, the force said.

A total of 23 women contacted police following the appeal, but most of them did not want to pursue criminal charges, the force added.

The Met said separate inquiries were ongoing into allegations involving women who were allegedly assaulted by Zou in China, with officers working to obtain evidence from the Chinese authorities.

News.title: Schools close early again for A66 crash funeral
News.content:
A number of schools will again close early on the day of the funeral for one of the men who died in a crash which killed seven, including two police officers.

Theo Rae, 17, was among the five in a car which went the wrong way down the A66 near Middlesbrough in the early hours of 22 August and hit an oncoming Cleveland Police vehicle.

Middlesbrough Council said some schools had chosen to close ahead of Monday's funeral, including a primary school which claimed the move would "ensure safe transit home for all our families".

Schools in neighbouring South Bank closed early on Friday for Jakub Matusiak's funeral, which police said "passed without issue" and with "very minimal traffic disruption".

Rae's funeral is to take place at Teesside Crematorium, Acklam, Middlesbrough, on Monday afternoon.

The funeral cortege is expected to travel around Middlesbrough before going to St Bede's Chapel on Acklam Road.

Cleveland Police said Ladgate Lane, Ormesby Road, Cargo Fleet Lane and Acklam Road will all be affected.

News.title: The West’s firewall against the far right is going up in smoke
News.content:

Mainstream politics received two wake-up calls this weekend. One was the emphatic victory of the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) in the Saxony-Anhalt state election. The other came from Dover, where black balaclava-wearing protesters lined the streets to demonstrate against the boat crossings.

There were other concerning images, too. In Portsmouth, where thugs turned out, in less-organised fashion but still in force, to blockade migrants arriving from France – and from the Reform UK conference, as hecklers were brutally ejected, with one picture showing a woman being dragged by her hair and struck with a walking stick. When the footage was played to Robert Jenrick, the Reform Treasury spokesperson said “boohoo” and told her to “get a life”.

Clearly something deeply worrying is afoot. The AfD celebrated in a country which, since the Second World War, has avowedly moved to prevent organisations on the right acceding to power. Yet the momentum of politics and power has lurched in that direction. In Britain, as protests against illegal immigration escalate and take one sinister turn after another, it is indefensible that a party with representatives in parliament, including Mr Jenrick, does not condone violence and instead adopts a boorish, nasty stance.

Nor are Germany and Britain outliers. In France, Marine Le Pen and her acolytes are in the ascendant – among them Reform’s party conference guest of honour Jordan Bardella, who signed a pact with leader Nigel Farage to send the migrants back to France. In other nations, too, not least the US, ICE continues to hunt down and deport undocumented immigrants.

What is doubly troubling is that anti-migration parties stand for a destabilising reordering of global politics. The victorious AfD is no supporter of Ukraine, Nato or indeed the EU, and if one incumbent ruler was delighted at the German result, it was Vladimir Putin. Should the AfD go on to replicate its march in an eastern corner across Germany as a whole, the foundation of the long-standing defensive alliance would seem very shaky. Trump is also no fan of Nato, and Europe’s ability to protect itself against attack, possibly from Russia, would undoubtedly weaken.

There is another aspect to these developments which is telling – whatever the mainstream says, fewer and fewer are listening. The AfD has been labelled an extremist organisation by the German security service, a tag usually reserved for the most hard-line groups, those that commit acts of aggression and terrorism. Yet that description did not prevent voters from indicating support in their droves.

Here in the UK, the government says Channel crossings have almost halved this year, thanks, at last, to France’s commitment to intervene and prevent their departure. But, as with Germany, that official account is simply not believed. It is noticeable how many of those basking in the AfD’s triumph are young. They are apparently not bothered about attempts to liken the party to the Nazis. In the UK, ministers can say what they like but their entreaties are equally falling on deaf ears.

It highlights an increasing distrust, a breakdown in faith between government and citizens. Carry on much further along this path, and momentum takes over. Only a very dark future awaits.

Migration is the lightning rod that governments nevertheless need to grasp. The widely held perception is that policies to date have not worked, or at least they have not succeeded in changing views, and frequently, they have been held up as making a bad situation worse. A rethink is urgently required, one that is accompanied by visible action, producing tangible results, not mere words. There is nothing wrong per se with a strong migration policy that is firm but fair. More must be done to show that illegal migration is a global concern, but it is not going to be solved by a patriotic front or minor right-wing demagogues.

There will always be those holding abhorrent, extreme views. What is happening now, however, is that groups previously consigned to the fringe are collecting voters, many of whom would not have dreamt of supporting them in the past. They are becoming ever more popular, and that growing populism, as it gathers swing voters, is capable of determining the outcome of national ballots, changing the tide of history – and not for the better.

The established parties, which have often enjoyed lengthy periods in charge, underestimate this shift at their peril. If they choose to discount and downplay, they will soon regret their folly, realising too late that their sensible, historic values have been rejected and in their place is a new set of rules that run counter to a civilised society, one in which justice, the rule of law and order and accountability, responsibility and decency prevail.

After what we have just witnessed in the past few days, it is a real and ever-looming danger. The terrible warning of the past is transparently clear. Established parties have received two wake-up calls. How many more must they receive?

Qinwen Zheng continued her extraordinary US Open run as she produced a comeback from 0-5 down in a set for the second match in a row to knock out six-time grand slam champion Iga Swiatek and reach the quarter-finals.

Former Olympic champion Zheng, who defeated Swiatek in the gold medal match in Paris two years ago, had to qualify to reach the main draw of the US Open. The Chinese star missed long stretches of the 2025 season due to an elbow injury and had fallen to No 121 in the rankings.

After qualifying for the main draw and reaching the third round, Zheng trailed former Australian Open champion Madison Keys 0-5 and was match point down in the third set before winning seven consecutive games to win 1-6 7-6 (7-3) 7-5 against the American 22nd seed.

open image in gallery Including her third-round win over Keys, Zheng won successive sets from 0-5 down ( Reuters )

Two days later against the eighth seed and former US Open champion Swiatek, Zheng trailed 0-5 in the first yet produced the same trick, winning seven games in a row to clinch the set. She then converted the only break of serve in the second set to win 7-5 6-3 and reach the quarter-finals of the US Open for the third time.

Zheng fell onto her back after converting her fourth match point. She has now won seven matches in a row in New York. “Well, honestly, I have to say, I started the match not so well,” she said. “Little by little I found my rhythm on the center court because it's been a long, long time. I just really appreciate it to be here in the Ashe Stadium.

”I just focused point by point and little by little I start to play better tennis, I start to find my game and in one moment I even forgot the score in the first set at 4-5. That shows how I'm focused. I guess to come back 0-5 yesterday is not lucky, that's all I can say.

”I'm just really happy to win this match cause it's not easy and it's been a while really. I didn't beat any top 10 player. I just really, really appreciated this win for me, and I want to say thank you for all the fans who come to support me today.”

For Swiatek, defeat to Zheng brought a familiar story and the former Wimbledon champion left Arthur Ashe Stadium in tears. The Pole’s error count spiralled, finishing with 28 in total. Swiatek’s last five exits from the grand slams since winning Wimbledon in 2025 have also come in straight-sets.

open image in gallery ( Getty )

Zheng will play either second seed Elena Rybakina or 13th seed Naomi Osaka, the two-time US Open champion, in the quarter-finals. Earlier, French Open champion Mirra Andreeva produced her own comeback to defeat Anastasia Potapova 5-7 6-4 6-3 and reach her first US Open quarter-final.

Potopova was also in floods of tears as her stay in New York came to an end. The 25-year-old, who represents Austria, won the first set against fifth seed Andreeva, but, at 5-3 down in the third she badly twisted her knee chasing a forehand down.

Potopova had the knee heavily strapped up and bravely finished the match, but did not win another point. “Anastasia is a good friend, and seeing what a battle we have and then seeing her fall is not easy,” said Russian teenager Andreeva. “It’s not the way you want to finish the match. I just told her she is playing amazing and I’m sure she’ll come back even stronger, she’s a warrior.”

A school teacher accidentally revealed his YouTube search history, including “teen bikini haul”, to pupils during a geography lesson at an all-girls’ boarding school, a teaching conduct panel heard.

James Hindson, teacher at Moreton Hall School in Shropshire, was searching for a clip to illustrate global trade based on a song when students caught sight of his previous searches on the video-sharing platform.

They reported they had seen a search term “teen bikini haul”, and another term which they recalled to be either “teens in thongs” or “girls in thongs”.

One pupil even managed to take a photograph of the screen, which was taken into account as part of the school investigation which resulted in Mr Hindson being sacked.

Ahead of a Teaching Regulaton Agency (TRA) meeting, Mr Hindson admitted displaying at least one of the YouTube search terms to pupils during the class in May, 2025, and that the searches were of a sexual nature.

The panel found, on the balance of proabilities, that the search term "teen bikini haul" and at least one of the search terms "teens in thongs" or "girls in thongs" were displayed to pupils. In a written submission to the panel, Mr Hindson said the searches had been made whilst at home.

When school investigators reviewed, they found Mr Hindson’s search history linked to the term “teen” came up with results for teenagers in little clothing or engaging in athletic activity, the panel was told.

A “long list of inappropriate videos” had also been searched for, the school found.

The TRA conduct panel concluded: “[The panel] noted that the searches had been carried out over a prolonged period and that many of the search terms shared common themes of a sexual nature. The panel carefully considered whether there was any innocent explanation for the conduct but found none on the evidence before it.

“The panel concluded that on the balance of probabilities, there was sufficient evidence that Mr Hindson’s conduct was sexually motivated.”

Reflecting on teaching standards, the panel found Mr Hindson had breached several, including upholding public trust by treating pupils with dignity and having regard for the need to safeguard pupils’ well-being.

Pupils’ attitudes toward the teacher had changed following the incident, the panel said, and it would have caused embarrassment to the pupils.

The panel, however, noted that the police determined that the conduct fell below the threshold of criminality. It also concluded that there was insufficient evidence to establish that Mr Hindson had viewed any indecent image or photograph of a child.

Mr Hindson was found guilty of unacceptable professional conduct by Marc Cavey, decision-maker on behalf of the education secretary, and banned from teaching indefinitely.

News.content:

A man arrested in connection with the notorious “Putney pusher” case has been released under investigation, the Metropolitan Police have said.

The 44-year-old man was arrested at his home in west London on 15 June on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm following a decade-long manhunt. He was then rearrested over allegations of drug offences.

It comes after a female pedestrian, who has never been named, was shoved into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge in 2017.

The woman, who was 33 at the time, sustained a few minor injuries after the bus driver’s quick reaction meant he missed her head by inches.

At the time, police interviewed more than 50 men and arrested three suspects, but the case was closed in 2018, and no one was ever charged.

A Met spokesperson said: “On Monday, 15 June, a 44-year-old man was arrested on suspicion of attempted grievous bodily harm.

“The arrest relates to an incident on 5 May 2017, where a woman was pushed into the path of a bus on Putney Bridge in Putney.

The Met Police had closed the case in 2018 ( Metropolitan Police )

“Once in police custody, he was also arrested on suspicion of possession of Class A and Class B drugs.

“He has since been released under investigation while enquiries continue.”

The initial incident took place during rush hour at 7.40am when the woman was crossing Putney Bridge, in southwest London, towards a nearby Tube station.

CCTV footage that went viral at the time shows a jogger forcefully shoving the woman to his right with both of his hands into the path of a double-decker bus.

Around 15 minutes later, he passed the victim as she was receiving help on the bridge and ignored her calls for him to stop.

The Met Police described him as being a white man in his early to mid-30s, with short brown hair and a stocky build. He was wearing dark blue shorts, trainers and a grey T-shirt.

Bus driver Oliver Salbris, who swerved at the last minute, told the Sunday Times: “If I hadn’t swerved, I would have smashed her head.

“It was reflex. The consequences would have been terrible for her – and for me.”

Sergeant Matt Knowles, the investigating officer from Putney Safer Neighbourhood Team, said at the time: “The victim was put in extreme danger when she was knocked into the road.

“It was only due to the superb quick reactions of the bus driver that she was not hit by the vehicle.”

Pope Leo XIV returned Monday to a sanctuary where he prayed just after his election and revealed a permanent sign of his devotion to the place: a fresco depicting him praying that now adorns an upper cornice of the basilica.

Leo unveiled the portrait before celebrating Mass with his fellow Augustinian brothers at the Sanctuary of Our Mother of Good Counsel in the medieval village of Genazzano south of Rome. He joins a handful of past popes whose visits to the sanctuary were commemorated with portraits that adorn its walls, going back to Pope Urban VIII in 1630.

Leo visited the sanctuary on May 10, 2025, just two days after his election and in his first outing as pope. The former Robert Prevost had been there many times before, since the place has special significance for the pope's Augustinian religious order.

The sanctuary is managed by Augustinian friars and has been a place of pilgrimage since the 15th century. Leo’s namesake, Pope Leo XIII, elevated it to a minor basilica and expanded the adjacent convent in the early 1900s.

Leo referred to that 2025 outing during his homily at the basilica Monday, which commemorates the birth of Mary. Leo recalled what he wrote then in the sanctuary's guest book.

The new pope wrote at the time that he felt the “need and profound desire” to come to the sanctuary after his election to pray before the Madonna of Good Counsel “who has accompanied me all my life with her maternal presence, with her wisdom and example of love for her son who is always the center of my faith.”

Leo and the Vatican are stepping up activities now that summer lull is coming to a close. The Holy See’s typically busy autumn conferences and audiences are taking shape, and Leo is gearing up for a trip to France at the end of the month and his much-awaited trip to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru in November.

___

Winfield reported from Rome.

Prime Minister Andy Burnham and US President Donald Trump agreed on the need to "continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life" following a fresh wave of talks, Downing Street said.

Mr Burnham spoke with Mr Trump on Monday afternoon.

It follows a visit to Kyiv on Sunday by US envoys, who held talks in an effort to end the conflict with Russia.

A Downing Street spokesperson said: “On Ukraine, the two leaders agreed on the need to continue working towards a ceasefire that prevented more loss of life.

“The Prime Minister reiterated the UK’s support for Ukraine and for recent US-led peace negotiations.

“On the Middle East, the Prime Minister set out the UK’s commitment to working towards peace and security in the region, stressing the importance of the Two-State Solution, the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz, and ensuring that Iran never acquires a nuclear weapon.”

Mr Burnham began the call by wishing Mr Trump a happy Labour Day and congratulated him on recent US employment statistics.

“(Mr Burnham) noted the positive signs of growth within the UK’s own economy,” the Downing Street spokesperson added.

“The Prime Minister said the Government was building more positivity about the UK and that he was making progress, but with more still to do.”

US envoys Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner held “encouraging” talks in Kyiv on Sunday following a meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin in Moscow on Saturday in a push to end the fighting, the Associated Press reported.

Mr Burnham’s first international trip in office was to Kyiv in a show of support for the country.

Last week, in reference to an attempted drone strike on a German airport that allies including the UK blamed on Russia, Mr Burnham said: “Russian attempts to undermine our united resolve and our willingness to support Ukraine are futile and doomed to fail.”

The British Government, last week, summoned a senior Russian diplomat to protest at last month’s “egregious and reckless attack” at Leipzig airport.

A drone laden with explosives found near a Ukrainian plane was subsequently defused.

The airport is a major international freight hub used for providing support to the Kyiv government, which has been battling invading Russian forces for more than four years.

Moscow denied involvement.

Mr Trump said Mr Putin is “not looking to attack Nato territory” when pressed over the incident last week.

Mauricio Pochettino has promised to overhaul the culture and standards within the United States men’s national team at the start of his second stint, in comments that seemed aimed at star Christian Pulisic’s choice to opt out of the 2025 Concacaf Gold Cup.

"It was difficult to make the roster for the Gold Cup one year before because the mindset was different," Pochettino said Monday during an online question-and-answer session with reporters. "You say, 'If I play, I have not holidays. I cannot arrive fresh for the World Cup.' ... You know now that is bull----."

The manager noted that his ultimate objective "is to change this type of idea that are not right."

Pulisic, widely regarded as the top player in the American squad, removed himself from selection for the 2025 Gold Cup, citing the necessity of rest following his season with AC Milan and a desire to remain fresh for the 2026 World Cup. He failed to find the net during four World Cup appearances this year, sitting out one group-stage match due to a calf issue before leaving the Americans’ round of 16 defeat to Belgium on July 6 with a fractured right tibia and fibula.

open image in gallery Pochettino appeared to hit out at Pulisic's decision to not play in last year's Gold Cup ( Getty )

After netting 10 goals across his opening 15 matches for AC Milan last term, he went without a goal in 19 subsequent club fixtures after December 28. He has remained an unused substitute in AC Milan’s opening three games of the current campaign.

Pochettino succeeded Gregg Berhalter in the fall of 2024 and was handed a four-year agreement in a deal announced last month.

The head coach intends to name his squad on September 17 for the initial fixtures of his second tenure, a double window featuring friendlies against Peru (Sept. 26 in Orlando, Florida), Chile (Sept. 29 in St. Louis), Mexico (Oct. 3 in Glendale, Arizona) and Canada (Oct. 6 in St. Paul, Minnesota). In their first competitive fixtures since the World Cup, the Americans play Concacaf Nations League quarterfinals in November.

"A new process, new project, new rules, new principles," he said, addressing media from London. "I think that the headline needs to be that (it) is a new start, a fresh start. And I think we need to change habits."

"We need to create a group of players that (are) really being professional and compete in the way that we expect that they need to compete," he added.

Several players left off the World Cup squad, including midfielders Diego Luna, Tanner Tessmann and Aidan Morris, could earn recalls. Emerging talent like 16-year-old Philadelphia midfielder Cavan Sullivan could also be brought into the team for potential senior debuts.

open image in gallery Cavan Sullivan could get his US debut soon ( Getty )

Others, such as 19-year-old Crystal Palace winger Zavier Gozo, might be left off to grant them time to adapt to new clubs following summer transfers. Pochettino also expressed uncertainty regarding midfielder Sebastian Berhalter and defender Max Arfsten, who transferred to Middlesbrough.

Pochettino indicated that prospects might receive national team debuts prior to shifting focus toward the under-23 team, which will be managed by former US defender Steve Cherundolo heading toward the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics. He emphasized a "need to be careful" with young players.

"You need to (have) confidence. You need to have the trust in yourself and belief that you can perform and do well," he said. "Sometimes if you play well and you are 17, 16 or 18 and you play well and people start to talk, about you are (Lionel) Messi or you are a big star in the world because you do some good things. If after you are confused and you don’t manage well, that can be dangerous for your career and that is what we don’t want.

"You only are entitled to talk a little bit out of order if you are Messi, if you win. If you won, you can talk with certain arrogance."

Among the attitudes Pochettino intends to alter are those of club coaches who would rather keep their young players back during international breaks.

"Sometimes the coaches say no. I have a 17-year-old guy that play in the MLS but when the (under) 19 national team called, say no because they need to rest," Pochettino said. "If (you are) 17, you need to rest, aye yai, yai. We have a big problem."

open image in gallery Pochettino has vowed to support Folarin Balogun following his failed move to Everton ( Getty )

Banks decision pending Augsburg defender Noahkai Banks still hasn’t decided whether to represent the U.S. or Germany.

"Noki is still in the same situation that (he) was before the World Cup," Pochettino said. "We are in contact with all the potential duel nationals. I think it’s important for us to see. That is the connection, the human connection, that is so important."

Focus on Balogun Pochettino intends to phone striker Folarin Balogun, whose proposed move from Monaco to Everton fell through last week.

"I want to know from him what happened but always offering our support," he said. "He’s an important player for us, was an important player in the World Cup and (I) hope that he can find being in Monaco, in another place, his best place to perform."

Police officers were injured and vehicles damaged when a second major anti-migrant protest turned violent as fears grow over further far-right unrest and disorder across the UK.

Less than 48 hours after masked vigilantes blockaded roads in Dover, around 200 black-clad activists descended on Portsmouth, where a small boat with 140 asylum seekers on board was intercepted off the coast.

In an ensuing standoff with police, some of the protesters, who were trying to stop the newly arrived migrants from being driven away, attacked officers and vehicles.

On Monday, the Home Office strongly condemned the “intimidating and thuggish behaviour”. However, politicians and campaigners raised fears of further unrest across the UK, particularly along the southern coast, with 625 people crossing the English Channel illegally over the past seven days.

Concerns have also been raised that traffickers could be shifting their desired destinations across England’s coast.

Local Patriot groups, thought to be part of a national Patriot Platform network led by Tommy Robinson associate Daniel Thomas, urged their members to be on standby to react to more migrant boats arriving at ports such as Bournemouth, Poole and Portsmouth.

But crime and policing minister Sarah Jones vowed “disorder of any kind will never be tolerated”, warning that crossing the line from a “peaceful protest into illegality will face the full force of the law”.

Giving a statement in the Commons on Monday afternoon, she said: “Peaceful protest is a fundamental part of our democracy, and it must be defended. But so too is the right of other citizens to go about their lives without undue interference, and there can be no excuse for threatening behaviour or serious disruption.

“Let me therefore make clear to the House and to the country that disorder of any kind will never be tolerated ... illegality will face the full force of the law.”

open image in gallery A standoff between police and protesters in Portsmouth after more than 100 migrants were rescued from the English Channel and landed nearby ( PA )

But she added: “None of this is to in any way minimise the very valid concerns that people have when they see vile criminal gangs exploiting our nation's generosity and people making illegal and unnecessary journeys to reach this country.”

It comes after Nick Lowles, chief executive of anti-racism charity HOPE, said any failings to act on threats of mobilisation could mean “things will only get worse from here”. The group later warned that the events should be a “wake-up call for authorities to take this type of threat seriously”.

Lord Walney, who was Keir Starmer’s Independent Adviser on Political Violence and Disruption, told The Independent that the protest in Portsmouth highlighted the need for police and political leaders to “respond firmly”. He said: “Politicians who excuse extreme protestors of either right or left because they sympathise with the cause risk fanning a wave of unrest and disorder across the UK.”

Reform UK leader Nigel Farage said the country was “on the edge of serious civil disturbance”, warning the movement of small boats across the Channel was getting out of control. “I predicted an invasion, and boy is it happening,” he said.

However, he said protesters dressed in paramilitary-style uniforms were not going to solve the issue.

open image in gallery Daniel Thomas, known as Danny Tommo, live streams during the operation to rescue the migrants in Portsmouth ( PA )

So far this year, 16,513 people have been detected crossing the English Channel in small boats, which is the lowest for five years, when the same figure at this point in 2021 was 12,647.

On Monday afternoon, a press conference arranged by Reform UK home affairs spokesperson Zia Yusuf on the coast in Portsmouth was interrupted by Mr Thomas, a leading figure behind the protest in Dover.

Mr Thomas said there was no violence in Dover and, when questioned about his Patriot Platform group’s masks and attire being intimidating, said: “The reason people felt potentially intimidated was because of the faces covered. I’ve made that point very clear. The only reason they’ve done that is because no one wants to be labelled far right.”

He claimed the group members were creating an “infrastructure of men” to create a voting bloc to back “the most suitable party that is able to bring this country back into order”.

Across both incidents in Dover and Portsmouth at the weekend, neither Kent nor Hampshire and Isle of Wight forces made any arrests. However, an investigation has been launched to identify those who attacked officers and vehicles in Portsmouth.

open image in gallery Daniel Thomas interrupts Reform UK home affairs spokesman Zia Yusuf’s press conference ( PA )

Footage shared on social media from Sunday night showed protesters blocking roads in an attempt to stop the migrants being taken by coach to Kent. Mr Thomas, also known as Danny Tommo, livestreamed himself running on the beach toward the coaches, threatening those preparing to help the migrants: “If you don’t stop right now I’m calling 1,000 men to come to this place.”

The migrants’ dinghy was met by lifeboats from the Isle of Wight when it reached UK waters, having set off from the Cherbourg area. It is thought to have made one of the longest journeys of any small boat, and landings as far west as Hampshire are rare.

It is understood that the government currently has no evidence to suggest there has been a change in people smuggler tactics.

However, Mihnea Cuibus, senior researcher at the University of Oxford’s Migration Observatory, said people traffickers could change targeted landings along England’s southern coast to avoid the patrolled Calais to Dover route.

open image in gallery Local resident Sue Dewey, 68, collects some of the discarded life jackets following Sunday night's operation in Portsmouth. Local leaders say the city is not suited for such landings. ( PA )

“It’s much harder to leave by boat from around the Calais area because of all of the patrols, drones in the air, and more boots on the ground, so they're just trying to find ways to avoid that,” he told The Independent.

Donna Jones, Conservative police and crime commissioner for Hampshire and Isle of Wight, said that places such as Portsmouth are “not set up” for the arrival of migrants. Portsmouth’s Liberal Democrat council leader Steve Pitt said the city was an “unsuitable” disembarking location for the boats.

A Home Office spokesperson said: “The right to peaceful protest is fundamental to our democracy, but it must never cross a line into disorder. We thank the emergency services who safely managed this situation.

“This government is doing the hard and necessary work of bearing down on small boat crossings, with the lowest number of June to August arrivals since 2020.”

News.title: The Chancellor’s speech, as it happened
News.content:
John Healey failed to rule out tax rises at next month’s Budget in his first major speech as Chancellor.

Mr Healey also sought to blame Liz Truss and her mini-Budget in 2022 for the high borrowing costs being paid by the Treasury.

During a speech in Coventry, the Chancellor said he would be “honest” about the need to control public spending during his time in Number 11.

He was speaking days after the cost of government borrowing hit its highest level since 2007.

It was also overshadowed by Jaguar Land Rover announcing plans to cut 4,000 jobs in the face of “intense competition and ongoing geopolitical uncertainty”.
