Sports.title: Putellas outshone by Cascarino on debut but is spine of London City's success
Sports.content:
Sky Sports columnist Laura Hunter analyses the big talking points from the first round of Women's Super League matches, bringing you closer to the key stories at the heart of the women's game.

Putellas only part of London City's style meets substance persona

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Women's Super League match between London City Lionesses and Manchester United

Michele Kang rolled out the red carpet in Bromley for London City Lionesses' season opener under the lights, where the Sky Sports cameras were in attendance to watch a dominant win over Manchester United. Kang herself was among the spectators in a sell-out crowd.

Alexia Putellas inevitably made all the headlines. The two-time Ballon d'Or winner commands that kind of attention. But the real standouts from such a positive opening night, in footballing terms, were Delphine Cascarino and Danielle van de Donk. Neither part of this summer's spending spree but the two most influential players on the park.

Datawrapper Datawrapper , which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enable Datawrapper cookies or to allow those cookies just once. You can change your settings at any time via the This content is provided by, which may be using cookies and other technologies. To show you this content, we need your permission to use cookies. You can use the buttons below to amend your preferences to enablecookies or to allow those cookies just once. You can change your settings at any time via the Privacy Options Unfortunately we have been unable to verify if you have consented to Datawrapper cookies. To view this content you can use the button below to allow Datawrapper cookies for this session only. Enable Cookies Allow Cookies Once

London City gave a good account of themselves in most departments, actually. A performance far more complete than the majority of last season, or even the sum of all their individual parts suggested.

Putellas was sound, if not as spectacular. It will take time for her to acclimatise to new surroundings, or perhaps more appropriately, take patience for those surroundings to adapt to her. It has always been that way around for La Reina. Team-mates must reach her wavelength.

What was clear is that the Spain superstar will be the nucleus of Eder Maestre's plan. Of the eight chances London City created, she claimed two and Cascarino was responsible for four. The restless Putellas hype will no doubt carry through the season, her standards acting as the spine and soul of this group of newcomers.

Image: Alexia Putellas celebrates London City's second goal against Man Utd with scorer Danielle van de Donk

But Maestre's side look to have gelled fairly well on first glance. No doubt they will face sterner tests in future weeks. London City and Man Utd were actually the perfect antithesis for opening night, a side on their way up passing one in obvious decline. London City barely stopped to say hello.

Kang's empire has consumed Bromley and will continue to dominate WSL chatter for as long as their results match their endeavour. There is no denying the pull of Putellas. Or Cascarino. Or Mary Earps, who did not feature on Friday but was still a major fan attraction. But buying footballers is really the easy part. Creating a consistent team out of them much more difficult.

Are Man City too reliant on Hemp?

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of Manchester City against Birmingham in the Women's Super League

It's only week one and Khadija 'Bunny' Shaw has reaffirmed her position as the best the Women's Super League has to offer, her 11 shots yielding two goals as Man City beat Birmingham.

Nothing about that victory was especially experimental, though still impressive. Shaw scored two carbon-copy goals, both from corners, both delivered from the left. Her movement for each was similar except the angle of the second header was far more difficult to guide on target. She made it look easy.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Bunny Shaw scored Manchester City's second goal of the game against Birmingham City

City scored 15 times from corners last season, a seasonal record, and such a superpower will no doubt come in handy again as they look to defend their crown. They were the only side to score from a set-piece across opening weekend. Last term, they scored from a set-play in all but seven games.

But what struck me was how lop-sided their attacking phase was from open play. Almost everything went through Lauren Hemp. Loading on the left is not necessarily a new tactic, but to such an extent surely misses an opportunity.

Hemp is an exceptional outlet, with pace to burn and superb crossing accuracy, which is why the centre-backs often look left when playing out from the back. Gracie Prior found Hemp 11 times against Birmingham. Opponents know to expect this.

Where City might profit this term is by exploiting that expectancy to unlock different pockets of space. Use the threat of Hemp to attract numbers and play elsewhere. Andree Jeglertz has spoken plenty about wanting City to have fresh, innovative ways of creating goals. He likes central rotations, utilising the ball-playing skill of Yui Hasegawa. City should lean into her passing range more.

Perhaps that will be helped by Vivianne Miedema's return from injury, whenever that might be. But before then, they can also afford to mix it up a bit more. Becoming even more versatile than they are now could propel them from being a very good team to an unbeatable one.

Chelsea's goal-shy streak persists

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the Women's Super League match between Chelsea and Aston Villa

New season, same problem for Chelsea. Their creators are crying out for a finisher.

Lauren James cannot be expected to shoulder the scoring burden on her own. So, how can Chelsea combat a flaw that has been plaguing them since Sonia Bompastor took charge?

Stylistically, Chelsea are doing most things right. A statistical reading of their 1-1 draw with Aston Villa will tell you that final-third entries were plentiful. The Blues created five big chances, missing four.

Essentially, James has been left to do the job of a winger and striker. She created the joint-most chances for others (4) while taking the most shots herself (11). Aggie Beever-Jones accumulated the highest expected goals total but debutant goalkeeper Akane Okuma was equal to both of her two efforts on target, neither particularly taxing.

The speed at which Chelsea arrive in the box remains an issue. It allows enough retreating defenders to make blocks; Villa made six of them. Okuma also made a remarkable nine saves. "We have to speed up the game," reflected Bompastor.

Chelsea's 35 shots were their most ever in a league game they failed to win. Bompastor added: "If you analyse the statistics, you would say it's crazy that we didn't win." The club's succession line of attackers looks too thin given what they are up against. They have Melvine Malard and Mayra Ramirez to return. But they need firepower now.

Sports.title: Fitter, happier, more productive: Arsenal could hardly have started better | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Three league games played, three games won. For Arsenal this season could only have started better if Manchester City, who look like being one of their two most serious challengers, had dropped points. But it’s not just about results: Arsenal have been comfortably the better side in each of those three games, approaching each of them in very different ways.

After the controlled victory over Coventry City and the tight game against Aston Villa that was won thanks to ratcheting up the pressure in the 15 minutes after half-time, came success in a far more open game in which they conceded for the first time this season. Chelsea tested Arsenal on Sunday, went ahead, and yet Mikel Arteta’s side still always looked like they would win – even if it did take a superb late save from David Raya to keep out an Estevão shot. But the goalkeeper too is part of their strength; even if an opposing team can work a shooting opportunity, Raya has the capacity for spectacular saves that can dispirit opponents.

Arsenal threatened from set-pieces but also from open play; they can beat opponents in multiple different ways, even when Declan Rice, probably their player of the season last year, has an off day (his unpunished late trip on Morgan Rogers was cynical and nasty, one of those deliberate offences miles from the ball that the game would benefit from treating as a red card offence).

The uplift may simply be confidence, the pressure of not having won the title, of those three successive second-place finishes, now lifted. But there are also individuals who look sharper, livelier, fresher than they did at any point last season. Martin Ødegaard is perhaps the most obvious. He struggled with injuries last season and scored only one goal; already this season he has two in the league and one in the Community Shield. Some players return from the World Cup and look exhausted or find the readaptation to the grind of the domestic game difficult; Ødegaard seems reinvigorated.

There is an imagination to his play, a lightness, and he took his goal against Chelsea superbly. His link-ups with Kai Havertz, another at times mercurial presence, were often delightful, conjuring space and angles where none seemed to exist and bringing the winner. In a team that last season developed a reputation for uncompromising physicality, there is something almost otherworldly about seeing two such ephemeral talents combining, sprites glimmering on a castle wall.

But it’s not just Ødegaard. For Bukayo Saka, last season felt like chickens coming home to roost. He is only 25 but Sunday brought what was already his 205th league start, while playing regularly for England as well. Fatigue had been stored up, which is always a worry for players who emerge as early as he did. Thomas Tuchel didn’t use him in the World Cup semi-final for reasons of tiredness or injury that remain opaque (the situation was promptly confused when he scored a hat-trick in the third-place game). But he seems back to something like his best in the early weeks of this season, fizzing in from the right-hand side and delivering dangerous corners on demand.

The other standout in the early weeks of the season is Riccardo Calafiori, who has already developed a very promising relationship going forward with Christos Tzolis, even if a few issues remain to be resolved defensively on that flank. The Italian, who scored Arsenal’s opener in the Community Shield, is not only a threat from set-plays but is very good at breaking through the lines, making him a real weapon against low blocks.

Chelsea are improving. Xabi Alonso’s side were far less open through midfield than they had been against Fulham and Brighton – easier as that can sometimes be to manage against sides who don’t instinctively cede possession. It may be, especially as the attrition of European fixtures strikes others later in the season, that they emerge as a very serious force. Arsenal, though, are very, very good now, and that means they could be several points clear by the time that putative Chelsea challenge emerges.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Twice weekly Sign up to Soccer Desk Jonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer. Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Arteta’s side are not merely playing with great authority; the fixtures have also fallen well for them, getting Villa away and Chelsea at home while both sides are still finding their patterns of play. It’s still very early. We haven’t even got to the first international break yet. Pitfalls are always waiting, and football is not a sport that reacts well to being taken for granted. But for Arsenal, their title defence could hardly have started better. Things could change but, at this moment, it seems more likely that they’ll have it won with several games still to play than that their grasp on the title will have slipped.

Sports.title: Chelsea’s midfield a headache for Alonso after Arsenal press advantage | Jacob Steinberg
Sports.content:
There have been seasons when Chelsea have turned up at the Emirates Stadium and parked the bus. “You know, I think 10 years without a title is boring,” José Mourinho said in response to criticism from Arsenal fans after a stultifying 0-0 draw in April 2015. On Sunday, though, there was no holding back from Chelsea. “I want to compete in the best possible way to win,” Xabi Alonso said after seeing his new side edged out by Arsenal in a breathless encounter. “Today we didn’t want to sit deep from the first minute. We wanted to be active.”

The plan worked at times. Chelsea maintained their habit of scoring early goals, going ahead through Morgan Rogers, and created further openings. But they were facing the champions and do not have Arsenal’s completeness. Shortcomings were exploited, particularly in midfield. Declan Rice romped through the middle at one point and the winning goal owed much to Reece James losing track of Martin Ødegaard as Arsenal’s captain strode through to fire past Emiliano Martínez.

It was expected to be a key battleground, and the way Arsenal went 2-1 up was felt keenly by Chelsea given their difficulties on deadline day, when Enzo Fernández got his £125m move to Manchester City and no one was signed to replace the Argentinian. However, it is worth remembering Chelsea were short not only of Fernández’s offensive skills as they fell to their first defeat under Alonso. It was also significant that Moisés Caicedo was out again, an unspecified issue proving a nuisance, and it is a concern that Alonso lacks a suitable stand‑in for the Ecuador international whose ability to cover ground, snap into challenges and shield his defence would have come in handy against a midfield as powerful as Arsenal’s.

There is much to like about Alonso’s vision. Chelsea are not obsessed with possession and are speeding forward on the counterattack. Yet while they look menacing with every attack there is a cost to the chaos. Alonso has found balance elusive. Chelsea have conceded seven goals in three games, are without a clean sheet in the league since January and need the oomph provided by Caicedo if they are to make this full-throttle style work.

Caicedo, such an important presence since joining for £115m in 2023, is yet to start this season. He missed the 3-2 win against Fulham and was replaced 14 minutes after coming on during the 4-3 victory against Brighton. Alonso is erring on the side of caution. He stressed there was no long-term problem after the Arsenal game and admitted Caicedo was rushed back against Brighton. “I don’t want to make the same mistake again,” Alonso said, keeping the wider picture in mind. It is a long season, even with no European football, and the physical demands of the league means there is no point Caicedo playing through pain when doing so would surely cause more problems down the line.

As it stands, though, Chelsea are too open and cannot strengthen until January. Compromises are necessary but the jury is out on some fixes.Alonso is a believer in James, whose shift from right‑back to central midfielder started under Enzo Maresca, but the captain is learning the role and his lack of feel for the position was exposed by Ødegaard.

View image in fullscreen Reece James carries the ball forward, trying to avoid the attentions of Ben White. Photograph: John Walton/PA

Arsenal found the gaps. Roméo Lavia started alongside James but is yet to complete 90 minutes since joining Chelsea three years ago. The Belgian has struggled with injuries and ran out of steam against Arsenal after an hour, at which point Alonso looked to his bench and replaced Lavia with Malo Gusto, leaving his expensively assembled side to play out the closing stages with two repurposed right-backs in the middle.

This was never the plan. Chelsea looked at replacements for Fernández. They wanted Alex Scott but Bournemouth would not sell. Crystal Palace’s Adam Wharton has admirers, there was interest in Roma’s Manu Koné, whilea move for Monaco’s Lamine Camara, which collapsed as the summer window closed, left Chelsea fuming.

In January Chelsea will hope to find a player more suited to Alonso’s system than Fernández, who is not the most mobile. They are not missing him in an attacking sense. Chelsea are scoring and the bigger headache is what to do out of possession. They do not have another player with Caicedo’s skillset.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

Dário Essugo was billed as Caicedo’s deputy when he joined last year but does not have Alonso’s trust and has been loaned to Strasbourg. Jordan Henderson is recovering from a broken wrist and is 36, and sending on Gusto over Valentín Barco was an early pointer. Barco, signed from Strasbourg this summer, is promising but the 22-year-old is inexperienced and, in any case, is more passer than destroyer.

Arsenal started with Rice, Ødegaard and Myles Lewis‑Skelly in midfield. They kept the £75m Bruno Guimarães in reserve and brought on two Spanish World Cup winners in Mikel Merino and Martín Zubimendi, another player wanted by Chelsea.

The gulf in midfield resources told and it was the absence of Caicedo that mattered most for Chelsea. Perhaps Alonso could have adjusted and fallen back. If Chelsea continue to look so vulnerable at the back in the big games the tactics will be called naive. Yet Alonso will trust that sticking to his ideals will be rewarded in the long run. This is the start of a process. He is introducing a new system and accepts it comes with risks. The problem is that he does not have a midfielder to put out fires if Caicedo is out.

Sports.title: Joey Barton to remain in custody until trial after bail application turned down
Sports.content:
The former footballer Joey Barton will remain in custody until his trial next year after a bail application was refused.

The 44-year-old had been due to stand trial at Liverpool crown court last week accused of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to Kevin Lynch, 51, at Fairway, Huyton, on 8 March. But on Wednesday the case was adjourned and put back to March next year.

Barton, wearing a grey zip-up fleece, appeared over video link from HMP Liverpool at a hearing on Monday, when the judge David Potter refused a renewed bail application. Barton nodded as the judge remanded him in custody in advance of a pre-trial hearing on 11 December.

His trial will take place exactly a year after the alleged assault, meaning the defendant, who was arrested shortly after the incident, will have spent 12 months on remand.

Barton is accused of carrying out the attack on Lynch after they had been drinking together at Huyton and Prescot golf club. Lynch, a former non-league football manager and founder of the special education school NexGen Academy, was said to have sustained serious injuries to an eye.

Barton, the former Manchester City and QPR midfielder, of Widnes, Cheshire, won one England cap and also played for Newcastle, Rangers, Burnley and Marseille. After stopping playing he moved into coaching and had managerial spells at Fleetwood and Bristol Rovers.

Sports.title: WSL talking points: Palace result in doubt after substitution nightmare, Arsenal signings shine
Sports.content:
Threat of punishment ruins Palace’s big day

Kirsty Howat’s 60-second cameo deep into injury time could ruin what was a memorable day for Crystal Palace on their return to the top flight. An impressive 1-0 victory over Everton was celebrated emphatically by Jo Potter and her players but that joy would have been replaced by concern and frustration not long after. On Sunday evening WSL Football revealed that there had been a breach of the rules – the Eagles used four different substitute windows rather than the regulated three – which had not been picked up by either the coaching staff or the match officials. An investigation has now been launched with punishment to be decided (there is a potential for the result to be overturned). The needless error has put a dampener on what should have been a positive afternoon thanks to England Under-23s forward Lexi Lloyd-Smith’s winner on her WSL debut. Sophie Downey

Chelsea must sharpen their claws

It was not the first time Chelsea have struggled to kill off games under Sonia Bompastor and, on the basis of Saturday’s 1-1 draw with Aston Villa after an almost excessively dominant performance, it seems the issues of last season have not been put to bed. “I think in a few games we had last season we were in the same scenarios,” said Bompastor. “So, yeah, if you analyse the performance today and the statistics of the game you can say that it’s crazy we couldn’t win the game.” It felt all too familiar, with last season’s 1-0 defeat to Everton in December, which ended a 585-day unbeaten run in the WSL, particularly springing to mind. Then, Chelsea accrued 79% possession, had 30 shots and hit the woodwork three times but came away with a loss. The fear for Chelsea fans will be that, in the 10 months since that defeat, the issues that were becoming increasingly evident have not been resolved. Suzanne Wrack

Match report: Chelsea 1-1 Aston Villa

View image in fullscreen Sjoeke Nüsken (left) shields the ball in Chelsea’s game against Aston Villa at Stamford Bridge. Photograph: Jermaine Addo-Yeboah/SPP/Shutterstock

Signings shine on competitive debut for Arsenal

Much has been made of Arsenal’s recruitment over the summer with many believing that Renée Slegers now has a team primed to challenge for the title. Four of their new signings started in the 1-0 win over Brighton, with two standing out. Recognition of Lisa Baum’s potential came to the fore with a series of impressive showings in pre-season. The 19-year-old caught the eye on her WSL debut on Sunday not just for her well-taken goal but for her direct, positive style of play. Meanwhile, Georgia Stanway showed exactly why Slegers was so keen to bring her in. The England international has added balance to the midfield, allowing Mariona Caldentey to operate more creatively. Stanway controlled the middle of the park, ranking first for touches – at 131, she had 25 more than anyone else – joint top for accurate passes (86%), first for passes into the final third (23) and second for chances created (2). SD

Role model Hemp brings up double century

“Just give her the ball and then something happens!” Andrée Jeglertz said of Lauren Hemp after her 200th appearance for Manchester City. The England winger was on typically strong form during the 3-1 victory over Birmingham City and became only the fourth Manchester City player to reach that landmark of appearances. Jeglertz was full of praise for the 26-year-old and continued: “One thing that is fascinating with Lauren is, if you come and watch one of our training sessions, she has the same joy for playing football. It’s also shown in the games. Our job is to put her in situations where she can show how good she is. [She] shows young players what it’s about. They need to love to go to work and love to go to the football field. It’s not just a job. It’s also an identity.” Tom Garry

Maestre masters the melting pot

Many believe the biggest challenges faced by the London City Lionesses manager, Eder Maestre, is integrating a squad that has experienced a high turnover of players and balancing the demands of an expectant cast of superstars. There have been eight arrivals this summer and seven players have departed. Teams that have experienced a high turnover of players after a strong WSL season have previously struggled. On Friday night, however, Maestre’s team showed signs they could buck that trend with a 2-1 win over Manchester United. It wasn’t always the prettiest of performances but fledgling connections were forming in Bromley, with the individual quality of players helping to cut across any lack of cohesion. Gelling players is not easy though. “I think it’s one of the most challenging situations for any coach,” said Maestre. “We have talented players, but we have a clash of cultures. I’m trying to align everybody in the same place, trying to create something big where everybody can feel represented … I’m very happy with the performance.” SW

Match report: London City Lionesses 2-1 Manchester United

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

View image in fullscreen Daniëlle Van De Donk (centre) peels away after scoring London City Lionesses’ winner against Manchester United. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Are Charlton strong enough to stay up?

It was a worrying start to the season for Charlton Athletic fans, as the newly promoted side were convincingly beaten on home turf by the club that finished second from bottom in the WSL last season. Not only that, Charlton failed to register a shot on target during Liverpool’s 4-0 victory and the hosts could only manage two efforts off target, as Gareth Taylor’s visitors’ enjoyed 76% of the possession. It had been a much closer-fought affair when the two sides met on the same ground on April in the Women’s FA Cup quarter-finals, when Liverpool eventually squeezed through after extra-time, but the Merseyside club appear to have strengthened significantly over the summer whereas Charlton clearly have significant work to do. TG

Hanson makes instant impact for Spurs with debut double

Kirsty Hanson wasted no time making her mark at Tottenham, scoring twice on her debut to secure a 3-1 victory over West Ham after joining from Aston Villa this summer. The forward opened her account with a first-time finish after an assist from Signe Gaupset and then produced a superb left-footed strike into the top corner. Hanson was the third-highest scorer in the WSL last season, behind Bunny Shaw and Alessia Russo, with 12 goals in 22 matches. She was one of several key transfers made during the window with the club believing she will add a new dimension to their attack. Speaking to Spurs Women social media about her performance, the manager, Martin Ho, said: “The movement for her first one was outstanding, and the second was a wonderful strike. When she’s in those positions with that quality and control, she’s really hard to play against. There’s lots more to come from Kirsty.” Réshma Rao

Sports.title: Premier League: 10 talking points from the weekend’s action
Sports.content:
1 Everton need Grealish’s energy

With 25 minutes to go against Manchester United, the Everton supporters had something to roar about as Jack Grealish made his return after rejoining on loan. The attacking midfielder remains universally popular thanks to his desire to entertain, getting the hosts back on their feet by creating dangerous situations within seconds of his arrival. Everton were limited in the final third for long periods as Thierno Barry sat on the periphery. If David Moyes is to keep his side pushing for a top-half finish, he will need Grealish to be a creative focal point. Will Unwin

Match report: Everton 2-2 Manchester United

2 Tzolis stands out among new faces

There was no shortage of highlights from the new arrivals as Arsenal battled back to beat Chelsea, Morgan Rogers setting the tone with a well-taken goal within two minutes. Emi Martínez got a hostile reception on his return to the Emirates but, while he may feel disappointed not to have kept out Kai Havertz’s opener, he made a handful of excellent saves, a diving stretch to deny Bukayo Saka the best of the bunch. Ezri Konsa, on his first start for Arsenal, had the home fans on their feet after a thunderous slide tackle to stop Rogers early in the second half, the standout moment of a solid performance. It was Christos Tzolis who really took the game by the scruff of the neck, however, harrying Chelsea’s defence with mazy dribbles and driving runs forward. He also provided the diagonal ball which, via Havertz’s audacious dummy, set up Martin Ødegaard to score the winner, earning a first Premier League assist. Will Magee

Match report: Arsenal 2-1 Chelsea

View image in fullscreen Arsenal’s Riccardo Calafiori (left) and Christos Tzolis team up to thwart Chelsea’s Pedro Neto. Photograph: John Walton/PA

3 Scott showcases England potential

If Thomas Tuchel required a reminder of precisely how good Alex Scott is, the Bournemouth midfielder provided it at St James’ Park. The 23-year-old reads the game a little faster and a little better than those around him and his stellar passing range raised the tone in a game Marco Rose’s side really should have won after cantering into a 2-0 lead, with Scott helping to create both goals. While Newcastle’s manager, Matthias Jaissle, can be heartened by his team’s refusal to surrender and, courtesy of goals from Harvey Barnes and Jacob Ramsey, their ultimate collection of a point, for long periods his players found no answers to Scott’s questions. Surely a first senior England cap beckons. The forthcoming Nations League fixtures against Spain, Croatia and Czechia offer ideal openings for Tuchel to put Scott on the international stage his talent demands. Louise Taylor

Match report: Newcastle 2-2 Bournemouth

4 Arbeloa already seeking solutions

The omens don’t look good for Álvaro Arbeloa. Only twice before have Fulham started a top-flight season with three successive defeats and it ended with relegation on both occasions: in 1951-52 and in 2020-21 under Scott Parker. Arbeloa tried to concentrate on the positives after throwing away the lead twice against Crystal Palace and ending up losing to Ben Chilwell’s winner. His side looked dangerous in attack, with Josh King having already developed an understanding with the summer signing Gonzalo García, even if the Spaniard played a comical role in Tyrick Mitchell’s second equaliser. Fulham’s defending is another matter entirely: Joachim Anderson’s lack of pace was repeatedly exposed by the high line they deployed against Palace and Arbeloa must find a solution before facing his former club Liverpool and then Manchester United. “We knew that this month would be very tough,” said Arbeloa. “But I told my players it will not define our entire season.” Ed Aarons

Match report: Fulham 2-3 Crystal Palace

5 Gakpo delivers creative edge

Several positives for Liverpool in Suffolk on Friday: Bradley Barcola showing off his lightning speed in his cameo, Ronald Araújo solid in the troublesome right-back position and Alexander Isak coming back to the boil with two well-taken goals. Receiving the most plaudits in post-match was Cody Gakpo, who appeared headed for Manchester City or Tottenham in the transfer window but stayed on to supply both Isak goals. “Cody knows how much we value him,” said Andoni Iraola. The confirmed exit of the sporting director, Richard Hughes, on Saturday brought assessments of a mixed legacy. Eventually, Isak repeating the form of his Newcastle days may stamp the decision to pay a record fee for the striker. Florian Wirtz, another expensive Hughes purchase, continues to receive similarly mixed reviews. At Ipswich, attention was drawn to his losing possession 22 times. It was left to Gakpo, whose purchase and sale were deals Hughes did not do, to provide Liverpool’s creative edge. John Brewin

Match report: Ipswich 0-2 Liverpool

View image in fullscreen Liverpool’s Cody Gakpo tries to break clear of Ipswich’s Julio Enciso. Photograph: Paul Childs/Action Images/Reuters

6 Ndiaye could not refuse City’s offer

Iliman Ndiaye enthused about working hard in his Manchester City debut after his £65m transfer from Everton. “I ran my backside off for the team wanting to get the win and you have to do the dirty side sometimes,” said the Senegalese forward, who was removed on 87 minutes, and brushed off how he might have joined Tottenham instead. “It was always going to be City. I wanted Champions League [football] and to play for one of the best teams in the world. I’m not saying Tottenham is not but when Manchester City comes through you don’t say no. It’s been a good week for me and topped off with a win. I was just being patient and when City came through I was buzzing.” Jamie Jackson

Match report: Manchester City 1-0 Coventry

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

7 Brighton find another diamond

There were plenty of questions for Fabian Hürzeler to answer after Brighton’s draw with Leeds, namely why it took them the best part of an hour to wake up. But, for consecutive weekends, the Brighton manager had the pleasure of lauding Malick Yalcouyé’s performance. The 20-year-old was barely known even by his own club’s fans at the start of the campaign, having spent seasons on loan at Sturm Graz and Swansea since joining from Gothenburg for a reported £6m in July 2024. He has since started against Chelsea and Leeds, excelling in an attacking midfield role. Hürzeler said: “He shows a lot of energy, a lot of effort, he is good in possession and out of possession.” The Brighton manager has previously flagged Yalcouyé’s physicality as an area to improve and it is notable just how slight he is at just 5ft 7in. The Ivorian’s confidence, eagerness to enter combat and close control are in no doubt. He could be the next player off the conveyor belt of young talent who Brighton sell for a vast profit. Ben Bloom

Match report: Brighton 1-1 Leeds

8 Tonali duel sums up Tottenham’s spirit

On the eve of Tottenham firing blanks for the third straight game, Roberto De Zerbi joked Allan Dixon’s bodybuilder physique could help them threaten at set pieces. Tottenham’s player liaison, who is Daniel Levy’s brother-in-law, moved up the pecking order again after Spurs failed to score in their first three league games for the first time since 1974-75. The club spent more than £300m this summer, Sandro Tonali the pick of the new signings on a blunt outing at the City Ground. De Zerbi praised Spurs’ spirit in the stalemate, epitomised by Tonali during a first-half duel with Dan Ndoye which culminated in a Forest corner. “I think it will be an advertising clip for the Premier League,” said Forest’s head coach, Oliver Glasner. “This is what the league is famous for and everyone loves.” Ben Fisher

Match report: Nottingham Forest 0-0 Tottenham

9 Sunderland’s agent of chaos

Nilson Angulo, who scored for Ecuador against Germany at the World Cup, remains an enigmatic presence, at once robust and delicate, cunning and naive, deft and clumsy. At times, not obviously related to the game going on around him, he will simply stop, and waggle his legs around as though stirring paint with his feet. One volleyed flick with the back of his ankle to return an overhit cross to the middle was remarkable. He is a master of accelerating and suddenly slowing to create space, control immaculate, then at other times he will simply charge out of play. The only thing harder than marking him, perhaps, is playing alongside him, trying to work out if a cross is ever going to come. He is a magnificent agent of chaos, that is clear; whether he is a high-grade footballer is less obvious. Jonathan Wilson

Match report: Brentford 1-1 Sunderland

View image in fullscreen Sunderland’s Nilson Angulo attempts to keep the ball in play against Brentford. Photograph: David Klein/Reuters

10 Teenage defender coming of age

Not many teenage centre-halves play regularly in the Premier League, but the Australia international Lucas Herrington is quietly establishing himself in Hull’s acclimatisation to the top flight. The summer signing from Colorado Rapids celebrated turning 19 on Saturday by coming off the bench against Aston Villa to help the Tigers keep another clean sheet. Herrington is rated as one of the finest defensive prospects in world football and underlined his promise with a vital block to deny Tyrone Mings. In all three of Hull’s Premier League games this season, Herrington has featured from the bench and the Queenslander’s star should continue to rise throughout the season. The Hull manager, Sergej Jakirovic, said: “Herrington is excellent and has great potential, so all these minutes are invaluable for him. I don’t have any fear when he’s on the pitch and I believe in him 100%. Provided he stays healthy, anything is possible.” Ross Heppenstall

Match report: Hull 0-0 Aston Villa

Sports.title: Karius keeps Kane at bay as Schalke nullify Bayern on Neuer’s return | Andy Brassell
Sports.content:
If one goalkeeper was going to dominate the discussion in this game, it actually felt as if it would be the less busy one. Schalke fans do not take kindly to being dumped and even if Manuel Neuer left the club behind 15 years ago – and even if most of the world associates him with Bayern Munich rather than his home town club – he is still given a rough ride when he returns.

Opposing sporting directors Max Eberl and Frank Baumann had words to say about that after Saturday evening’s latest visit, but it wasn’t Germany’s legendary goalkeeper who took the headlines – or not he alone, at least. It was always going to be a landmark afternoon with Schalke playing a first home game in the top flight since May 2023, but this was way beyond what anyone could have expected. The numbers said it all – with Bayern failing to score for the first time domestically since a goalless draw at Leverkusen more than 18 months ago, meaning they finished the weekend not on top of the table for the first time in almost two years – but told nothing of the story.

For at the end of this goalless draw, the story was Loris Karius. A goalkeeper who, once upon a time, might have hoped to back up Neuer in the national team on the rare occasions that the totem was indisposed, but whose career has become about attrition rather than aspiration. At 33, this was a day in the sun that seemed like it would never come. Little was expected of Miron Muslic’s team here, with damage limitation and a swift moving on to more winnable battles perhaps the realistic aim, with last week’s 3-0 loss at Augsburg (a bright start followed by a frank reality check) indicative of the task facing them back at the top table.

View image in fullscreen Schalke manager Miron Muslic congratulates Loris Karius after his clean sheet.

Photograph: Martin Meissner/AP

Little has been expected of Karius for a long time, going all the way back to what turned out to be his final Liverpool appearance, the error-strewn Champions League final against Real Madrid in Kyiv in 2018. By the time we learned that Karius’s mistakes were likely conditioned by a concussion suffered earlier in the game, the die had been cast and the damage to his reputation done.

You may know some of the tale since. A move to Besiktas which ran aground when he was forced to take action against the club (twice) for unpaid wages. Another loan to Union Berlin which led to just four Bundesliga appearances – the only league games, mind you, that he would play between leaving Istanbul in May 2020 and being drafted in late to Newcastle’s lineup against Arsenal in February 2024 after Martin Dubravka fell ill on the day of the game. A year before he had been brought in to cover for the suspended Nick Pope in the Carabao Cup final, his first first-team game in two years, and performed creditably.

If the journey has been confusing to us, imagine what it was like for Karius. “Even today,” he told Welt this summer, “I don’t know what I should have done differently. I just felt empty. I even considered ending my career, but I was only 25 years old and couldn’t just stay home.” When he joined Schalke in January 2025 it was six months after his Newcastle deal ended, and then-coach Kees van Wonderen made it clear Karius was signing as second choice. Yet by February he had made the starting spot his own – before picking up a calf injury four games in that forced him to miss the rest of the season.

Last season the worm began to turn. Muslic put his faith in him – as the club already had by extending his contract – and Karius started 30 of the 34 games as the coach’s belt-and-braces side conceded a league-low 31 goals and won the 2.Bundesliga. This summer, his deal was extended again, to 2028.

All of these landmarks in Gelsenkirchen have been victories, but it felt like there were limits for Karius, just like there are for this Schalke, the original giants of German football, the Bayern-before-Bayern, who have been living on reduced means for a number of years now. If they had been the high rollers of just a few years ago, there would have been little need or inclination to give Karius his chance.

But he had his chance here, and he took it. There was command, confidence and a string of fine saves, capped by a stunning, flying one-hander to prevent Harry Kane smashing a late winner. It may be pointed out that neither Kane nor Michael Olise started in a game that also saw Jamal Musiala make a comeback from the bench; it should also be noted that when Vincent Kompany rotated his star pair in the latter stages of last season to keep them fresh around Champions League games, it was a cheat code, unleashing the league’s two best players on tiring defences.

Karius had all the answers, and was warmly greeted by Kompany at full-time, who had been a senior when he was a young player at Manchester City about 15 years ago. That amount of time seemed like nothing on an evening when the past loomed large.

View image in fullscreen Manuel Neuer was given his usual rough ride by the Schalke supporters. Photograph: Christopher Neundorf/EPA

For this, “very likely my last game” in Gelsenkirchen before an eventual retirement, every boo, catcall and chant directed at Neuer felt pertinent. He started training at Schalke when he was five, used to watch matches from the same Nordkurve that rained their displeasure down on him and made over 200 appearances for the first team. The reception was not unexpected but, perhaps accentuated by the sense that this season might be Neuer’s victory lap, there were plenty who felt the need to fight his corner. Eberl called the treatment of his goalkeeper “inappropriate”, and Baumann, his opposite number at Schalke, had disapproving words for his own fans. Neuer’s fellow Gelsenkirchner Olaf Thon wrote in his column in Kicker that “Gelsenkirchen should be proud of him”, rather than booing him.

The man himself was a little more sanguine, having invited a cluster of family members. “That’s love,” he said. “Every whistle is a compliment.” Both Neuer and Karius could tell you that the life of a goalkeeper is thus; setbacks inevitable, but comebacks somewhat less so.

Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

Borussia Dortmund have maximum points, thanks to a remarkable comeback at Hoffenheim. Remarkable, because they should have been three or four down rather than just 2-0, before Serhou Guirassy and Fábio Silva brought them level and Ethan Nwaneri, on his debut, engineered an unlikely winning own goal by Albian Hajdari. Credit too to the newly-adventurous Niko Kovac for sending on the Arsenal loanee for the injured centre-back Filippo Mané and Silva for midfielder Konstantinos Karetsas.

View image in fullscreen Ethan Nwaneri celebrates his part in Albian Hajdari’s own goal. Photograph: Heiko Becker/Reuters

BVB are only third, though. Augsburg lead the pack after coming back from a half-time deficit to eventually demolish a woeful Eintracht Frankfurt in Sunday’s late game, and Freiburg sit second after their single-goal win at Paderborn. Meanwhile Elversberg wowed this week too, recovering from 3-1 down at Borussia Mönchengladbach to win via Maurice Krattenmacher’s stoppage-time winner (his second goal) to make them the fourth team with two wins from two.

Cheers also for Jarell Quansah, impressing as a rampaging right-back in Leverkusen’s 4-0 hammering of Union Berlin, their first points of the season, and Niclas Füllkrug scoring (already) header of the season in Werder Bremen’s surprise 3-1 win over Leipzig.

Sports.title: Aubameyang rolls back years as revamped ‘Super Dépor’ return to La Liga in style | Billy Munday
Sports.content:
Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang was already the best player on the pitch when he ran through to score Deportivo A Coruña’s winner on Saturday night. It was certainly not Ilias Akhomach, the Villarreal substitute whose pass on halfway had inadvertently played Aubameyang through, nor Sergi Cardona, the intended target of that pass. After 89 minutes and two assists, the 37-year-old Aubameyang raced the length of the half to slot past Luiz Júnior to make it 3-2.

It had been a similar case the week before, when Aubameyang’s pace left the Valencia defenders behind before he dinked the ball over the goalkeeper. The week before that, he calmly rounded Málaga’s Alfonso Herrero before opening the scoring. The week before that, the former Barcelona striker marked his return to La Liga against Elche with a superb touch and finish from Lorenzo Amatucci’s diagonal pass. Scoring in each of his first four games for Deportivo is a club record, eclipsing Bebeto’s fast start of three in a row from 1992.

Like Aubameyang, Deportivo appear reborn. “Super Dépor” were Spain’s most popular team around the turn of the century, with Bebeto having helped them win the Copa del Rey in 1995. Djalminha, Roy Makaay and the rest inspired them to a first league title in 2000, followed by another Copa del Rey in 2002 and a run to the Champions League semi-finals in 2004. After the money dried up, they were relegated from the top flight in 2011, 2013 and again in 2018, only returning this summer after eight years away.

The former Arsenal striker Lucas Pérez returned for a fourth stint to help Dépor climb out of the third tier two years ago. Aubameyang now has his sights on the club record of scoring in seven consecutive league matches, held by Pérez and Bebeto from different eras. It was another former Arsenal forward in Nicolas Pépé who broke the deadlock for Villarreal at the Estadio de la Cerámica on Saturday, with their new head coach, Iñigo Pérez, still searching for his first victory since leaving Rayo Vallecano.

At the start of the week, Pérez was preparing to face a very different Deportivo squad. By the weekend, it included the deadline-day arrivals of José María Giménez from Atlético Madrid and Marc Casadó from Barcelona. Deportivo’s equaliser at Villarreal came when Giménez stepped out from centre-back and slid the ball into the box for Aubameyang to chase. He clipped it into the middle with the outside of his boot, Luismi Cruz finishing first-time.

The signings of Giménez and Casadó – both on loan, both two-time La Liga winners – are a coup for Deportivo, even after an ambitious window where they spent €26m (£22.3m) on new players – only Barcelona, Real Madrid, Atlético and Real Betis have spent more.

View image in fullscreen Marc Casadó (right) – a loan arrival at Deportivo – tries to curtail Tajon Buchanan’s progress. Photograph: Mateo Villalba/Getty Images

Investment and debt-clearing at the club have gone hand in hand since the Galician bank Abanca became the majority shareholder in 2020, when Dépor were relegated to the third tier during the Covid pandemic. Abanca now owns 99.99% of the club, but the fans still have a voice. Supporters voted this summer to change the team’s name from Deportivo de “La Coruña” to the Galician version “A Coruña”.

The investment in all areas of the club has paid off. When given a guided tour of the training ground alongside Giménez, Casadó was impressed with the facilities. “It’s better than Barça,” he said, deadpan, on camera. “Seriously.”

Adama Traoré has arrived too, after a chat with his former Barcelona teammate Aubameyang, on a free. Antonio Hidalgo, who guided Deportivo back to La Liga in his first season in charge, deployed debutant Traoré as a wing-back off the bench on Saturday. When Gerard Moreno crossed for Tajon Buchanan at the back post, Traoré scrambled to get back into position but comically looped a header over his own goalkeeper to gift Villarreal the lead again on 76 minutes.

The influx of new players has brought with it concerns about the crop that got Dépor promoted in the first place. But where many thought Aubameyang might replace the bustling striker Bil Nsongo, the pair – 16 years apart in age – are now forming a fearsome partnership. Deportivo scouted Nsongo when he was playing for Canon Youandé in his native Cameroon but decided not to extend his contract after his first year with the B team. He was insistent though, having made A Coruña his home, and won the club over. “He was very interested in staying here,” said Deportivo’s academy director, Ismael Arilla.

Deportivo’s second equaliser came from another striker: Zakaria Eddahchouri, whose 18 months in A Coruña have been marked by his significant contribution to promotion and the time he fell over the top of the waterfront while taking a selfie last year. Firefighters had to rescue the Dutchman from the rocks below and he spent the night in hospital with minor injuries. After 12 goals in the second tier last season, his first in the top flight was drilled past Júnior at the near post after Aubameyang found him with a well-weighted pass.

View image in fullscreen Pierre-Emerick Aubameyang has scored in each of Deportivo’s first four games this season – a club record. Photograph: Maria Jose Segovia/DeFodi Images/Shutterstock

There is no overstating the importance of Aubameyang since his €1.5m arrival from Marseille – in goals, ambition and willingness to mentor younger players. “He has a special talent but you should see him train, how involved he is, how it rubs off on his teammates,” said Hidalgo at full-time after the veteran’s late winner. But it’s also the little things: “His smile is infectious.” The front flip celebrations are a sight, too.

The “brutal” victory, as Hidalgo put it, against opponents who begin their Champions League campaign on Tuesday, moves Deportivo into the top five and keeps them unbeaten, but the former Sabadell, Sevilla B and Huesca coach is not getting ahead of himself. “The table that tells you where you’re at is the one on the final day of the season – now it’s just for looking at.”

Thank you for your feedback.

Talking points

José Mourinho congratulated Real Betis for “playing for a draw and then winning the lottery” after his first defeat back as Real Madrid coach. Troy Parrott, given his professional debut by Mourinho at Tottenham, scored his first Betis goal in Friday’s 1-0 win at La Cartuja. Mourinho slumped in his chair as VAR spotted an offside in Carlos Espí’s acrobatic equaliser before Kylian Mbappé had a stoppage-time penalty saved by Álvaro Valles, leaving Barcelona to extend their lead over Madrid to three points with a 5-0 rout of Valencia on Sunday. Luck of the Irish?

Sandwiched between Barça and Madrid are Alavés, who have won three of their first four games. The former Real Madrid striker Mariano Díaz, who spent over a year as a free agent before signing in 2025, scored his third goal in four games during a 5-2 victory against Osasuna on Sunday. He was upstaged by Lucas Boyé, whose hat-trick included an absolute belter from 35 yards out. “I didn’t even think about it,” the Argentinian striker said.

View image in fullscreen Lucas Boyé (left) wheels away after scoring Alavés’ third goal – his second of a hat-trick in a 5-2 win over Osasuna. Photograph: Juan Manuel Serrano Arce/Getty Images

One Argentina striker who is having considerably less fun is Julián Álvarez. Atlético were 2-0 down at Athletic Bilbao on Saturday by the time he entered the field to whistles from the travelling supporters. Nico Williams and Robert Navarro scored two in three minutes after the restart and Oihan Sancet added a late third. Diego Simeone opted not to comment on Álvarez not doing his post-match warm-down with the other substitutes.

Sports.title: Football Daily | Big day for Ødegaard with balaclavas, Basques and a boot to the head
Sports.content:
PERFECT START CONTINUES

Perusing assorted Social Media Disgrace for some Monday inspiration, Football Daily was struck by the amount of scorn and ridicule heaped upon a large group of men dressed in black, many of them wearing balaclavas to hide their identities. Formed with the intention of creating something resembling a matchday atmosphere in and around the Emirates Stadium, the Ashburton Army is a group of wannabe ultras who would almost certainly retreat at the speed of light if confronted by one of the more hardcore continental firms they style themselves after. While many fellow fans view them with utter disdain for their “try-hard” aesthetic, on the same day a large group of identically attired and significantly older men were marching on Portsmouth to intimidate a boat-load of asylum seekers, the feeling persists that on this occasion, those pouring derision on this gang of overenthusiastic Ruperts might have set their sights elsewhere.

Widely billed as The Basque 44-Year-Olds Who Grew Up Together In The Antiguo Locale of San Sebastián and Remain Close Friends To This Day derby, there was atmos aplenty at the Emirates Stadium as Arsenal hosted one of very few teams given a snowball’s chance in hell of challenging them for the title this season. And while Xabi Alonso’s Chelsea took a very early lead courtesy of some uncharacteristically shonky Arsenal defending at a set-piece, the champions ultimately prevailed. Their victory was due in no small part to Martin Ødegaard, who put in the kind of purring performance we simply did not often see from the frequently absent or knack-plagued Norwegian as his teammates ground out victory after victory en route to last season’s title. “I think he is enjoying his football,” whooped Mikel Arteta as he praised his captain after the game. “His personal life is settled. He is available. He is training. He has his routine and if he is intelligent, he can take a lot of benefits from the players around him. I think he was outstanding today.”

Having watched Arsenal play three, win three and score all six of their goals from open play in the Premier League so far, cynics who spent large tracts of last season criticising Arteta’s side’s over-reliance on set-piece goals have had to find new nits to pick. No stranger to controversy last season, on Sunday Gabriel Magalhães prompted a nationwide chorus of grumbles for escaping a red card despite kicking the Chelsea goalkeeper in the head. “Martínez has got the ball in his hands and he boots him in the head,” observed Wayne Rooney with a chuckle on Match of the Day. “I think he’s extremely lucky to stay on the pitch.” And while Football Daily is largely against heads being kicked on the football pitch or elsewhere, the decision not to dismiss Arsenal’s defender was correct because there was no malice aforethought as the Brazilian scrapped for the ball and he did not throw his boot with excessive force. In so many ways this is an Arsenal we are not used to seeing, but one that already looks far better than the one that won the league.

QUOTE OF THE DAY

“Two months after the events, we note that our questions remain unanswered to date. Given the importance of transparency and clarity for all parties involved, we request the necessary explanations and, at the same time, wish to explore where improvements to the current processes are possible, so that similar cases can be handled in a clear, consistent and efficient manner in the future”​ – Pascale Van Damme, president of the Royal Belgian Football Association. Belgium are currently a “nah” to supporting Gianni Infantino’s run for another go at being Fifa president after an unsatisfactory conclusion to inquiries about how USA USA USA’s Folarin Balogun was suddenly available for selection to face them at the World Cup despite a red card.

double quotation mark Re: Kieron Dyer and his MJ press conference (Friday’s Football Daily, full email edition). I wish he’d just beat it” – Marc Meldrum.

double quotation mark ‘Mike’ Hackett? Let’s start a new trend and give every referee the moniker ‘Mike’, going back as far as 1891. Mike Langenus. Mike Horn. Mike Ellis. Mike Taylor. Mike Partridge. Mike Courtney. Mike Collina. Mike Clattenburg. Heck, even Mike ‘Mike’ Dean. Why not, since they’re all miked up theses days anyway” – Ben van Maaren.

double quotation mark I was wondering if the World Cup had taken some players over that threshold between good and great. Thinking about players who had a brilliant competition and have come back men, not boys. No more nerves or inconsistency. Eg Haaland, post-haircut … maybe Ødegaard? Can you think of anyone else transformed? And, conversely, how would a bad WC affect someone? Or, again, what about Cole Palmer? Four years of hurt or dodged a bullet?” – Russell Richardson.

double quotation mark A promoted team like Hull may be in the top four. Chelsea may sell/loan 40 players and still carry a bench worth half a billion GBP. Manchester United may suddenly look like a team that can play 90 minutes without imploding. Nothing is certain, except Spurs staying in the relegation zone until MD 36. Thank you Spurs, for such stability” – Krishna Moorthy.

If you have any, please send letters to the.boss@theguardian.com. Today’s letter o’ the day winner is … Krishna Moorthy, who gets a copy of The Mbappé Project by Philippe Auclair. Copies are available in the Guardian Bookshop if you are not the lucky scribe. Terms and conditions for our competitions, when we run them, are here.
