Sports.title: Audi to appeal stewards’ decision not to penalise Tsunoda over start error | Formula 1
Sports.content:
Audi have informed the FIA they intend to appeal against the stewards’ decision not to penalise Yuki Tsunoda for his error at the restart of the Italian Grand Prix.

Tsunoda lined up in his grid box incorrectly before the restart of the race. The race director therefore abandoned the start and ordered an extra formation lap.

Ordinarily this would result in the driver who caused the delay having to start the race from the pit lane. Tsunoda did not do this.

The stewards took no action against Tsunoda. They ruled it was the race director’s decision to order an extra formation lap (below).

Tsunoda finished the race in 10th place, seven seconds ahead of Audi’s Gabriel Bortoleto, who was a second ahead of his team mate Nico Hulkenberg.

Car 22 [Tsunoda] approached the grid initially heading for the left hand side of the grid, then

realising he was headed for the wrong grid position, the driver changed direction and positioned his car in the correct grid box and in the correct position within the grid box. This was verified by the stewards with video from multiple camera angles.

The race director, in evidence, stated that it was his call, based on the behaviour of the car on the approach to the grid box, to commence an extra formation lap. He stated he was not comfortable starting the race with the car in that position.

The team representative stated that:

(i) The car was not in a “false start” position – referring to Article B5.1.1c of the F1 regulations, because no contact patch of the front tyres was outside the grid box lines (front and side)

(ii) At the drivers meeting, the race director advised that for the start, the track limits were the pit walls and in this case, even though the car was pointed to the right, it had at least four metres of space to move off from the start

(iii) No other driver was impacted by the position of car 22

(iv) The driver of car 22 was not the “cause” of the extra formation lap.

(v) At no time was the team advised that race control considered car 22 to be the cause of the extra formation lap.

The Stewards agree with the points above and consider that the extra formation lap resulted from the Race Director’s assessment of the situation, rather than being directly caused by the driver of car 22.

Further, Article B5.9.4 goes on to specify that if a driver who causes the extra formation lap and is then able to start the extra formation lap, he must enter the pit lane at the end of the lap and start from the pit lane. It is only then, if the driver fails to do this, that the mandatory penalty of a Stop-and-Go penalty is imposed.

In other words, the penalty is for failing to come into the pit lane and start from there. The penalty is not for causing the extra formation lap, if indeed, he caused the extra formation lap in the first place.

A critical issue emerges here, in that in order to comply with the requirement to enter and start from the pit lane, a driver would need to know that he was the cause of the extra formation lap. The team representative quoted situations where extra formation laps have been commenced due to extraneous circumstances such as the position of a photographer etc. In this case, no message was sent to the team or the driver, advising them that they were the cause of the extra formation lap.

The team, based on the fact that the car was positioned within its starting grid box in compliance with the regulations, had, in our determination, no reason to instruct its driver to enter and start from the pit lane.

Accordingly, irrespective of whether or not the driver directly caused the extra formation lap, the team and driver were unaware that they were being considered as the cause, therefore we determine that we are unable to impose a Stop and Go penalty in this case, and decide to take no further action.

We note that the race director acted in good faith and out of an abundance of caution in ordering an extra formation lap.

We further note that the FIA might wish to consider implementing a process to advise teams and drivers if they are considered to be the cause of an extra formation lap, so that they are then able to comply with the requirements of Article B5.9.4

Sports.title: Jack Dempsey Escapes Without A Verdict Against Miske
Sports.content:
At 22 years of age, Dempsey was tearing through the heavyweight division with his aggressive style and crushing left hook. Miske, 24, had the benefit of fighting before his hometown supporters, but he was far more than a protected local attraction.

Dempsey weighed 187½ pounds, while Miske came in at 182.

Known as the “St. Paul Thunderbolt,” Miske was a fast, clever boxer who understood how to block punches, smother attacks, and work at close range. Those skills gave Dempsey one of his hardest tests during his climb toward Jess Willard’s heavyweight championship.

The local favorite supplied a tactical lesson for smaller fighters facing dangerous punchers. Instead of continually backing away, he stepped into Dempsey’s punching range and crowded him. Retreating would have given Dempsey space to drive forward, build speed, and launch his leaping left hook. Miske took away that leverage by getting close, controlling Dempsey’s arms and preventing him from completing his punches.

The rolling movement associated with Dempsey’s attacks depended upon momentum. He bobbed his upper body from side to side, shifted his weight, and sprang forward with hooks from changing angles. An opponent who backed away gave that attack time to gather force.

Meeting Dempsey chest to chest changed the exchanges into an arm wrestle. His long swings lost much of their force as Miske blocked the hook, jammed the punching arm, and answered with short shots before tying him up.

Quick punches inside prevented the younger man from finding a steady rhythm. Dempsey had productive stretches in the second and third rounds, but Miske answered with a hard right cross in the third.

Years later, Dempsey admitted that Miske was landing more punches and building what looked like a lead. He also recalled being hurt during one exchange and struggling to remain upright until the bell.

“Miske had landed more telling blows than I had,” Dempsey recalled. “He suddenly came at me with a volley that nearly put me out.”

It was a revealing admission from a fighter remembered for overwhelming opponents. Raw aggression had run into a boxer who understood distance, timing and leverage. The visiting fighter finally produced his strongest attack in the seventh. A heavy left to the body followed by a right to the jaw troubled Miske and helped Dempsey recover ground. Neither man scored a knockdown, leaving the newspapers to decide which work they valued more.

Miske’s approach was almost the opposite of the one Jess Willard used against Dempsey in Toledo the following year. The 6’6″ champion tried to control the challenger from long range but remained too upright and stationary.

That distance allowed Dempsey to leap forward with hooks and overhand punches. Willard became an easy target once the challenger closed the distance, leading to seven knockdowns during the savage opening round.

Such a runway was never available against Miske. He moved toward the danger, shortened the punches, and forced Dempsey to work without full leverage. Willard waited at the end of Dempsey’s forward rush, while Miske intercepted it before the punches reached full speed.

The St. Paul fight showed that smothering Dempsey was safer than surrendering the ring and waiting for him to attack. Gene Tunney receives credit for solving Dempsey in 1926 and repeating the result one year later. Miske had exposed several of the same weaknesses eight years earlier. Their tactics were not identical. Tunney relied more heavily on footwork, his jab, and movement at long range. Miske was more willing to hold his position, work inside, and smother Dempsey physically.

Both remained composed when Dempsey attacked. They refused to become stationary targets at his preferred distance and punished him when his forward movement became predictable.

Before their first fight, Tunney studied films of Dempsey and brought former opponents and sparring partners into camp. There is no firm evidence that Miske personally supplied Tunney’s plan, but the St. Paul contest had established the central principle: Dempsey became less effective when an opponent denied him momentum and forced him to restart his attacks.

Miske supplied the early evidence that denying Dempsey momentum made him less effective, and Tunney later produced the polished championship version.

The St. Paul Pioneer Press surveyed eight writers at ringside. Four favored Dempsey, one selected Miske and three scored the fight even. The newspaper published the bout as a draw, although other reports awarded Dempsey a narrow newspaper decision based on his aggression and heavier punches.

A later collection drawing upon additional newspaper sources produced seven verdicts for Dempsey, four draws and one for Miske. That broader tally included reports beyond the eight writers questioned in St. Paul.

Such disagreement exposed the weakness of the no decision era. A boxer’s official record remained untouched after a distance fight, even when most observers believed he had lost. Local sports editors became unofficial judges without a uniform scoring system or any requirement to agree.

Reports from St. Paul do not support the claim that hometown writers simply protected Miske. Four of the eight surveyed writers favored the visiting Dempsey, while only one selected Miske. Regional loyalty may have influenced individual accounts, but the split also reflected a genuinely close fight.

Miske landed more often and controlled long portions of the contest, while Dempsey delivered the harder individual blows. Some writers valued activity and craft; others favored aggression and damage.

Promoters benefited from the uncertainty. Dempsey survived a difficult night without receiving an official loss, allowing his handlers to continue selling him as the next threat to Willard. Miske also avoided a formal defeat and remained a leading heavyweight attraction in Minnesota. Jack Kearns wanted knockouts that would sell Dempsey to a national audience. Taking him into Miske’s hometown against a fast, experienced boxer was a serious gamble.

The no decision format reduced the danger because only a knockout placed an official loss on the record. It did not remove the promotional risk. A decisive beating reported across the country still would have damaged Dempsey’s growing reputation.

Kearns learned that clever defensive fighters presented a different challenge from the large, slower heavyweights Dempsey destroyed. His fighter continued facing dangerous opposition, including Fred Fulton, Battling Levinsky, Bill Brennan and Miske himself, but the first fight supplied a warning. Dempsey’s power did not automatically solve every style.

The pair met again in Philadelphia on November 28, 1918, with most newspapers favoring Dempsey after six rounds. By then, the future champion had gained more experience against Miske’s troublesome methods.

Their third fight came on September 6, 1920, after Dempsey had taken the heavyweight championship from Willard. Miske was suffering from Bright’s disease and was knocked out in the third round of Dempsey’s first title defense.

His illness was not common public knowledge, so there is no basis for claiming Kearns selected Miske because he knew the challenger was dying. In hindsight, the physical decline made the title fight far less dangerous than their first meeting had been.

That knockout became the lasting image of their rivalry. Miske is now remembered primarily as the sick challenger who needed money, while Dempsey remains one of boxing’s most recognizable champions.

The familiar family story belongs mainly to the end of Miske’s life, not the 1920 title fight. A gravely ill Miske returned against Bill Brennan in November 1923, scored a fourth-round knockout, and used the money to give his family a memorable Christmas. He died on January 1, 1924.

Remembering only the tragedy reduces Miske to a sympathetic opponent in Dempsey’s championship story. Reports from 1918 present the fuller picture.

At that time, the St. Paul Thunderbolt was one of the sharpest technical boxers in the heavyweight division, possessing the timing, defense, and composure to frustrate Dempsey near his physical peak. He survived 10 rounds and forced the future champion to abandon many of his preferred attacks. The press left St. Paul unable to agree on a winner.

Sports.title: Ryan Garcia Claims Benn Overlooks His Ring Intelligence
Sports.content:
The less flattering side is his habit of retreating in straight lines until his back reaches the ropes. He often relies on a high guard, clinch, or awkward turn instead of circling into open space. Benn will attempt to close those exits, making Ryan’s footwork an immediate test of the boxing depth he is advertising.

Aggression also creates danger for the challenger. Benn was dropped twice by Cedrick Peynaud early in his career, and he can still rush inside without setting up his attacks. Those entries give Ryan opportunities to land his fastest counter.

Charging forward carelessly during the opening three rounds would leave Benn exposed. Ryan is at his most dangerous when an opponent supplies the movement and gives him a stationary target. One poorly timed leap may be all the champion needs.

The body offers Benn his clearest route to slowing Ryan. Gervonta Davis stopped him with a liver shot in 2023, and Benn throws heavy hooks downstairs when he gets within punching range. Sustained body work could reduce Ryan’s movement and take some of the speed from his counters.

Reaching that distance is the difficult part. Ryan owns the faster hands and is more dangerous from the outside, leaving his challenger dependent on close-quarters exchanges and a punishing pace.

Returning to 147 pounds raises another question for Benn. He added size for two fights with Chris Eubank Jr., and camp footage shows a noticeably leaner fighter coming back down to welterweight. If the cut weakens his legs or stamina, trapping Ryan will become increasingly difficult.

This is Ryan’s opportunity to support his claim. Knocking Benn out with another hook would confirm the power everyone already recognizes. Escaping the ropes, controlling distance, working inside, and adjusting to the body attack would demonstrate the boxing IQ he believes Benn has failed to appreciate.

Sports.title: Fury Calls Itauma A Billion-Dollar Loss
Sports.content:
A few soft opponents will not cause supporters to abandon Itauma. The real difficulty is finding fighters who can extend him without beating him.

To support his warning, Fury used his own career as the example Itauma should have followed.

“I did it the traditional route, and it’s done like that for a reason,” Fury said. “I was 27 years old when I fought Wladimir Klitschko; I was a 10-1 underdog [but] I was ready. If I’d have fought him at 21, I’d have got knocked out, too.”

There is some truth in that. Fury spent years fighting domestic and European opposition before receiving his first world title opportunity. He entered the Klitschko fight with a 24-0 record, making the November 2015 contest his 25th professional bout.

What his version leaves out is Klitschko’s condition at the time. The champion was 39 and nearing the end of his career. His reactions, punch output, and willingness to exchange had declined. Fury did not complete a traditional apprenticeship and then defeat a heavyweight champion at his physical peak.

With only 35 professional rounds behind him, Itauma was given a much more dangerous test. Hrgovic was experienced, durable, and able to force a hard pace after absorbing Itauma’s best punches.

The promotional obsession with Itauma breaking Mike Tyson’s record as the youngest heavyweight champion also helped accelerate his development. That age window had already closed by the time he fought Hrgovic, but the rush had shaped his career. Opponents were selected to produce quick knockouts and keep him moving toward a marketing milestone.

Those victories established Itauma’s destructive image without preparing him for the moment a world-class heavyweight refused to disappear.

Stories about Itauma handling leading heavyweights in sparring helped create confidence in his readiness. Fabio Wardley also confirmed that Itauma had completed 12-round sparring sessions despite an earlier interview clip suggesting otherwise.

Completing 12 rounds in a gym is not the same as fighting nine hard rounds under championship pressure. Sparring partners can reduce the pace and stop when instructed. There are no judges, title stakes, or thousands of spectators reacting to every punch.

Once the fight began, Hrgovic presented a psychological test that closed gym sessions could not reproduce. Itauma hit him hard, dropped him in the second round, and continued attacking, yet the older man kept coming. Every unsuccessful attempt to finish Hrgovic increased the physical and mental cost.

Nothing in Itauma’s professional experience had prepared him for an opponent absorbing that much punishment and returning with greater pressure after six rounds.

It would be too simple to blame roadwork or poor cardiovascular conditioning. Itauma exhausted himself through the way he fought.

Nearly every combination was thrown with maximum torque. He remained tense at close range and repeatedly searched for a damaging finish. He lacked a controlling jab that would allow him to maintain distance, score without spending heavily, and recover while remaining offensively active.

After Hrgovic survived the early assault, Itauma had no economical gear. His legs weakened, his punches lost their shape, and he no longer had the energy to defend himself or slow Hrgovic’s advance.

The jump in opposition was considerable, but the matchmaking alone did not cause the defeat. Itauma’s approach made an already difficult test even harder.

Proof that a young heavyweight can recover from a defeat is already available within Queensberry. Frank Warren continued working with Daniel Dubois after losses to Joe Joyce and Oleksandr Usyk.

After both fights, Dubois faced criticism, particularly when he took a knee and allowed the referee to count him out. Those defeats did not destroy his commercial value or end his title ambitions. Queensberry lowered the pressure, found suitable fights, and gave him another opportunity to develop.

Rather than watching a “billion-dollar” future disappear, Itauma may be following a rougher version of the Dubois route. The difference is that Queensberry must use the rebuilding period to correct an identifiable weakness instead of merely restoring his knockout streak.

“I just think that knocking out a low-level man is different to knocking out a world-class man; different power, toughness, everything,” Fury said. “It is totally different. “It’s about getting the balance right. Get him in with somebody who is durable, not that dangerous, who can take punishment and give him the rounds. He needs to get used to getting the rounds in.”

Here, Fury makes his strongest point. Queensberry needs durable opponents who can survive Itauma’s opening attacks, make him think, and force him to regulate his output. He must learn to vary the speed of his punches, take quiet periods, and stop treating every opening as a chance to produce a knockout.

Until he does, the Hrgovic blueprint will remain available. A mobile heavyweight can stay away during the early rounds, while a durable pressure fighter can absorb his power and wait for him to slow down.

Careful matchmaking can restore Itauma’s popularity, but it cannot disguise his stamina forever. If his engine remains suited to six rounds, the same ending will remain possible whenever an opponent lasts long enough to test it.

Sports.title: Hearn Says TKO Gave Joshua 90 Minutes for America
Sports.content:
“Yesterday, TKO went around the back again to try and offer Joshua money to do the fight in America,” Hearn told DAZN. “It’s a dirty, dirty game, mate, to be honest with you. It’s made it even harder for them because Josh just ain’t about that. You’ve got an hour and a half to make your decision. Mate, what don’t you understand? I signed to fight in Britain. I want the fight in Britain.”

The 90-minute demand is the major addition to Hearn’s story. A deadline that short would leave Joshua little time to study revised terms, consult his lawyers, or calculate the financial consequences of moving the event from Britain.

It sounds like an attempt to place a large number in front of AJ and force an immediate decision. No amount has been disclosed, but TKO presumably understood that a modest increase would not persuade him to surrender Wembley Stadium, his home support, and the protection Hearn says was written into the signed agreement.

“You can’t buy everybody,” Hearn continued. “Especially the ones who it means something to.”

Hearn said the approach strengthened Joshua’s determination to keep the Fury fight in Britain. The growing public support has also changed the tone of the venue negotiations. A week earlier, Hearn said there was “zero interest” in London and that New York was being treated as the only destination. He now claims Sela has asked him about contacting London Mayor Sadiq Khan to help make the British event possible.

The conflict with TKO has not ended. When asked if Matchroom would take action over the direct approach, Hearn said his team had already written to the company.

“What are you doing?” Hearn said. “You guys are on the New York Stock Exchange. What is this? Just coming around the back trying to bung someone a few quid. Come on. It doesn’t have to be like that. But it’s pushing the fight further away because of their behavior.”

That is the danger behind TKO’s alleged tactic. The company may have believed a quick financial offer would settle the American venue, but Hearn says it produced the opposite response. Joshua is now more committed to Britain, Matchroom has contacted TKO in writing, and the relationship between the parties has deteriorated.

Hearn placed the likelihood of Fury and Joshua fighting in Britain at 64%. That oddly precise estimate still leaves New York in contention, but it is more optimistic than his position a week ago.

The missing financial figure remains fascinating. If TKO wanted Joshua’s answer within 90 minutes, it must have believed the offer was large enough to make him reconsider everything he had signed for.

Sports.title: Muhammad Ali, Richard Dunn, And The AccuPunch
Sports.content:
Both stood 6’3″, but nearly everything else separated them. Ali traveled with an international promotional circus and commanded million-dollar purses. Dunn was a former paratrooper and working scaffolder who balanced his trade with professional boxing. Their meeting was not part of the original plan.

German promoters anticipated that Bernd August would win the vacant European championship and provide Ali with a German challenger. Dunn ruined the arrangement by stopping August in the third round at London’s Royal Albert Hall seven weeks before the Munich date.

That victory sent Bradford’s working-class champion into a fight with the most famous athlete in the world.

Dunn was Ali’s third championship opponent in barely three months. Ali stopped Jean Pierre Coopman in February, struggled through 15 rounds with Jimmy Young in April, and returned against Dunn only 24 days later.

The champion traveled between Puerto Rico, Maryland, and West Germany while completing three training camps and fulfilling three promotional commitments. Money helped drive the pace. His large entourage, expensive lifestyle, and business obligations required a steady supply of purses.

Ali’s performance against Young showed what the schedule was costing him. He looked slow, poorly conditioned, and frustrated as Young made him miss before leaning through the ropes to escape exchanges.

The judges awarded Ali a unanimous decision, but the scores did not erase the criticism. Young had exposed how much of the champion’s timing and movement had disappeared since his physical peak.

Munich gave Ali an opportunity to look dominant again. Dunn held three respected championships, but his direct, aggressive style offered fewer complications than Young’s movement and defensive tricks.

The promotion struggled before either boxer reached the ring. A dispute involving $225,000 from Ali’s purse and German taxes placed the event in danger only days before the fight.

A late compromise kept the card alive. Ali’s purse was reported at approximately $1.6 million after adjustments, while Dunn received about $100,000, easily the largest payday of his career. Ali also helped cover a shortage in the challenger’s money.

The champion spent another $100,000 purchasing 2,000 tickets for American servicemen stationed near Munich. Even that gesture did not rescue the live gate.

The main event began around 3 a.m. local time to place it on NBC during American primetime. That decision served the television audience but punished German ticket buyers. High prices and the brutal starting hour helped leave thousands of seats unsold.

Roughly 11,000 people were inside the 12,700-seat Olympiahalle, but about 4,000 reportedly attended with complimentary tickets. Estimates placed the promoters’ losses between $300,000 and $500,000. Ali and Dunn received their money. The local backers were left with the bill.

Ali frequently described southpaws as awkward opponents. Karl Mildenberger had given him uncomfortable moments from the left-handed stance during their 1966 championship fight, creating the belief that the alignment itself caused Ali trouble. Dunn demonstrated the limits of that theory. A southpaw stance changes punching angles, but it does not automatically provide timing or defense. Dunn approached Ali upright, followed him instead of cutting off the ring, and often began his attacks with looping punches.

Those wide shots gave Ali time to recognize what was coming. Dunn also advanced without consistent head movement, leaving a direct lane for the champion’s right hand.

A quicker and more deceptive southpaw might have punished Ali’s low left hand and tendency to pull away from punches. Dunn lacked the speed and disguise required to take advantage. His stance altered the angles, but his technical flaws gave Ali the solution.

Ali waited for Dunn to square himself and drove short rights through the opening. The fight showed that his difficulties were not caused by southpaws alone. They came against opponents who knew how to use the stance.

Dunn pressed forward from the opening bell and tried to force a physical contest. His activity kept Ali from treating the bout as an exhibition, but much of his work struck gloves, arms, or empty space.

The challenger’s bravery soon worked against him. He continued marching forward after Ali established his advantages in speed, timing, and power. Instead of changing his approach, Dunn kept presenting the same openings.

Ali was more than 10 pounds lighter than he had been against Young. He remained heavier and less mobile than the dazzling fighter of the 1960s, but the lower weight helped him look sharper.

The champion stayed patient during the early rounds, studied Dunn’s attacks, and gradually began sitting down on his punches. Once he committed to the right hand, Dunn lacked the defensive reactions to protect himself.

Ali dropped him three times in the fourth round. Each knockdown exposed the difference between determination and defensive ability at championship level.

Dunn rose from another knockdown in the fifth, but a short right sent him to the canvas again. Referee Herbert Tomser stopped the fight at 2:05 as Ali theatrically wound up his right arm from a neutral corner.

Ali later credited taekwondo instructor Jhoon Rhee for teaching him the short right used in the finish. Rhee called it the “AccuPunch” and said its quick delivery was based on a technique Bruce Lee had shown him.

The punch was designed to remove the physical warnings that normally precede a power shot. Instead of drawing back the hand or first rotating the shoulder, the boxer sent the fist directly toward the target and brought the rest of the body behind it.

That approach suited the opening against Dunn. The challenger was advancing with his head high and his guard separated. Ali released the right from close range before Dunn recognized the attack.

The exaggerated arm motion came afterward, when Ali knew the contest was finished and began performing for the crowd.

It gave him the 37th knockout of his professional career. Ali never stopped or officially knocked down another opponent.

The Dunn victory was the last time Ali increased the pressure, repeatedly floored an opponent, and ended a fight before the final bell.

His later victories depended more heavily on endurance, clinching, defense, and carefully rationed attacks. Ken Norton forced him through another punishing 15 rounds. Earnie Shavers hurt him badly before Ali rallied in the final round. Leon Spinks outworked him in their first fight and pushed him through 15 more rounds in the rematch.

Ali retained the ability to produce combinations and fight through exhaustion, but he was no longer an offensive finisher. His legs moved less, his punches carried less force, and too many rounds were spent on the ropes while opponents worked.

Dunn became the final opponent Ali was able to erase once he decided to attack.

Ali had little time to recover. Just 33 days after beating Dunn, he faced Japanese professional wrestler Antonio Inoki in a mixed rules exhibition at Tokyo’s Nippon Budokan.

Inoki spent much of the 15-round contest on the canvas, repeatedly kicking Ali’s legs while remaining outside punching range. Ali absorbed more than 100 kicks and left with severe swelling, bleeding, an infection, and two blood clots.

Three months later, he defended his championship against Norton at Yankee Stadium and escaped with a disputed decision after another exhausting 15 rounds.

The sequence captured the reckless pace of Ali’s career. He fought Young in April, Dunn in May, Inoki in June, and Norton in September. His body received little opportunity to recover between major events.

Thousands of people lined the streets of Bradford to welcome Dunn home. They honored a working scaffolder who had risen to challenge the most famous boxer in the world.

His championship run ended five months later when Joe Bugner stopped him in the first round. Dunn retired after a 1977 knockout loss to Kallie Knoetze.

The Munich promotion lost money, but the fight gained historical importance. Dunn became the final opponent Ali stopped, permanently linking the Bradford heavyweight to The Greatest.

Sports.title: Dave Allen’s 40 Fight Plan Gets Bizarre Twist
Sports.content:
Officials had several possible outcomes to consider after watching the replay. Allen could not receive a stoppage victory because the punch was ruled an accidental foul rather than a legal blow. A disqualification would have required the referee to treat the foul as intentional.

Trainer Jamie Moore accepted the no contest despite Allen’s visible unhappiness inside the ring. “He’s gone to hit him in the side of the head. He’s turned his head, he’s hit him in the back of the head, and he’s fallen out of the ring,” Moore told IFL TV. “Dave can’t win on an unintentional foul, but he can’t lose either. So it’s got to be a no contest. By the rules, they’ve done the right thing.”

Under the unified rules commonly used in professional boxing, a fighter knocked out of the ring receives 20 seconds to return without assistance. An injury caused by an accidental foul before four completed rounds generally produces a no contest or technical draw, depending on the governing commission. There were no completed rounds available for a technical decision.

Consequently, neither boxer could be awarded a win from such an unusual sequence. The brief fight was erased competitively, leaving both men without a satisfactory result after completing full training camps.

Falling outside the ring also carried more danger than an ordinary knockdown. Carty dropped from the elevated platform into an area containing chairs and other ringside equipment. Medical personnel therefore had to consider the impact outside the ropes rather than judging his condition solely by the punch.

Before the ending, Carty had used his southpaw jab and attempted to press Allen. Moore was encouraged by how quickly his fighter closed the distance. Allen reached Carty at close range earlier than anticipated and forced the type of physical exchanges that suited him.

“I thought he hurt him a couple of times,” Moore said. “I was over the moon with the way it was going up until that point. It was just over way too quickly to tell anything.” Allen now has one appearance remaining under his 40-fight limit. The Carty contest counts as his 39th professional bout even though it ended without a winner.

A rematch would settle the unfinished business, but it would also require Allen to use his intended last appearance on another meeting with a tricky southpaw. He could instead pursue a larger domestic payday and leave Carty as one of the strangest opponents listed on his record.

Sports.title: Katie Taylor Defeats Flora Pili!
Sports.content:
The two-time undisputed champion controlled the opening rounds with her jab, speed, and movement. Pili made the third round competitive, but Taylor continued landing the cleaner punches as the fight progressed.

The action increased during the seventh, with Taylor getting the better of the exchanges. Pili switched to southpaw in the ninth and remained in that stance during the final round, but Taylor adjusted and finished strongly.

The judges scored the fight 100-90, 100-90, and 98-91. David Irving was the referee.

Paddy “The Real Deal” Donovan (16-2, 12 KOs) stopped Tyrone “The Mighty Celt” McKenna (25-7-1, 8 KOs) at 2:33 of the fourth round in their welterweight contest.

A body shot from Donovan dropped McKenna in the second round, with referee Paul McCullagh administering an eight-count. McKenna suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during the final minute of the fourth, and the ringside physician stopped the fight.

Taylor Bevan (10-0, 9 KOs) stopped Emmet Brennan (6-1, 1 KO) just 36 seconds into the sixth round of their super middleweight bout.

Bevan dropped Brennan near the end of the third round and put him down again with a left to the body at the bell in the fifth. Two more knockdowns followed early in the sixth before referee Padraig O’Reachtagain stopped the contest.

Joe McGrail (14-0, 7 KOs) stopped Matthew “Bam Bam” Boreland (7-1, 2 KOs) at 3:03 of the fifth round in their super bantamweight fight.

McGrail dropped Boreland with a combination in the closing seconds of the round. Boreland failed to beat referee Padraig O’Reachtagain’s count.

The heavyweight fight between Dave “White Rhino” Allen (27-9-2, 20 KOs) and Thomas “No Carty No Party” Carty (11-1, 9 KOs) ended in a first-round no contest.

Allen landed a right hand to the back of Carty’s head, sending him through the ropes and out of the ring. Carty was unable to continue, and the contest was ruled a no contest at 1:22. Emile Tiedt was the referee.

Molly “Meatball” McCann (5-0, 1 KO) defeated Sylwia Doligala by unanimous decision after eight two-minute rounds in their bantamweight bout.

McCann controlled the fight with her pressure and work rate. The judges scored it 80-72, 80-73, and 79-73. Paul McCullagh was the referee.

Paul “Ravishing” Ryan (12-2, 4 KOs) defeated Paddy “Pat-Man” Gallagher (17-7-1, 10 KOs) over six rounds in their middleweight contest.

Gallagher hurt Ryan badly in the fifth and had him leaning halfway through the ropes. Gallagher suffered a cut over his right eyebrow during an action-packed final round, but Ryan had done enough to receive the decision. Referee Paul McCoy scored the fight 58-55.

Heavyweight Adam Olaniyan (4-0, 4 KOs) stopped Matej Hudak (6-3, 6 KOs) at 2:59 of the first round.

Olaniyan landed a right hand to the chin in the closing seconds of the round. Hudak took the count on one knee before referee Emile Tiedt waved off the fight.

Bobby Flood (4-0, 2 KOs) defeated Jack “Mad Dog” Swallow (4-14-1, 1 KO) by decision in their four-round super welterweight bout.

Flood controlled the contest from start to finish. Referee David Irving scored it 40-36.

Mikey Sheehan and David Diamante served as the ring announcers.

Sports.title: Damian Knyba Is Anthony Joshua’s Perfect Fury Test
Sports.content:
He lacks Wladimir’s speed, timing, defense, and destructive power, but the basic construction is similar. That familiarity should benefit Joshua, who spent years studying Wladimir, training alongside him, and eventually fighting him at Wembley in 2017.

Facing Knyba would not reproduce Fury’s movement, feints, stance changes, or ability to invent his way through a difficult fight. It would give Joshua experience against another towering heavyweight who knows how to keep the action at long range and smother opponents once they get inside.

The matchup becomes more appealing because Knyba is not harmless. His power is respectable enough to test the weakness that now defines Joshua’s career.

Joshua’s punch resistance and recovery can no longer be trusted after his fights against Daniel Dubois and Kristian Prenga.

The younger AJ survived a crushing right hand from Wladimir, regained control, and stopped him in the eleventh round. He had the physical resilience and confidence to fight his way through a crisis. That version of Joshua is gone.

Against Dubois, the consequences of catching AJ cleanly and denying him time to recover were obvious. Once hurt, Joshua became rigid, lost track of incoming shots, and struggled to restore order.

His fight with Prenga provided more evidence that Joshua no longer processes hard punches as well as he once did.

Although Knyba does not punch like Dubois, he hits hard enough to stop Joshua. His height allows him to generate leverage on the straight right, particularly when an opponent remains directly in front of him or pulls back without changing angles.

AJ would have to close the distance behind his jab, keep his head moving, and remain defensively responsible after throwing. One lazy exit or mistimed entry might give Knyba the opening needed to wreck the Fury fight.

That danger is precisely what makes Knyba a worthwhile warm up. A harmless opponent would tell Eddie Hearn nothing about Joshua’s readiness.

The blueprint for beating Knyba was supplied by Agit Kabayel, who stopped him inside three rounds in January. Kabayel refused to conduct the fight from the outside, where Knyba’s 86 inch reach gave him the advantage. He applied pressure, shortened the distance, and forced the taller man to work at an uncomfortable pace.

There is little doubt that Joshua possesses the strength and power to follow that approach, but his recent habits create doubts.

Under Ben Davison, AJ has often settled into cautious outside boxing built around the jab and isolated right hands. That approach may suit him against shorter opponents who must cross open space to reach him. It makes less sense against Knyba, who owns the longer reach and wants a slow fight at the end of his jab.

AJ cannot afford to admire Knyba’s size from the outside. He would need to attack the body, force him backward, and make him reset his feet. Knyba becomes much less effective when denied the time and space required to extend his punches.

That would test Joshua’s willingness to take calculated chances. Moving into mid range places him closer to Knyba’s right hand, but remaining outside allows the Polish heavyweight to dictate the pace. Finding the balance between aggression and recklessness has repeatedly escaped AJ.

Reaching Knyba would solve only the first part of the problem. Against Andy Ruiz Jr., he regularly wrapped up and smothered the shorter fighter whenever Ruiz crossed the distance.

Fury uses that tactic even more effectively. He leans his weight across an opponent’s shoulders, forces him to carry the load, and drains his legs during long clinches. It is not glamorous, but it has become a vital part of his heavyweight style.

While Knyba cannot match Fury’s inside craft, he can give Joshua a physical rehearsal for those wrestling exchanges. AJ would have to keep his arms free, create enough room to punch, and avoid wasting energy trying to overpower a taller man in static clinches.

Too much muscular weight has caused Joshua to burn energy unnecessarily in previous fights. Continually wrestling with a heavyweight of Knyba’s size would test both his conditioning and his patience.

Frustration with the holding may tempt Joshua into lunging from too far away. That is where the straight right becomes dangerous.

Knyba’s victory over Andy Ruiz Jr. supplies more than a recognizable name for the promotion. It connects him directly to the most damaging defeat of Joshua’s career.

The loss to Ruiz destroyed Joshua’s aura at Madison Square Garden in 2019. Although AJ comfortably won the rematch, questions about his confidence and punch resistance followed him from that night onward.

By beating Ruiz, dropping him in the seventh round, and controlling much of the fight with his jab and reach, Knyba added a former unified champion to his record. The official scores were 117-110 and 114-113 twice, although the two narrow cards understated his control.

That creates an easy promotional story. Joshua would be fighting the man who just dominated his old conqueror while testing himself against the physical dimensions he will encounter against Fury.

The psychological angle should not be exaggerated. Beating Knyba would not erase what happened against Ruiz. It would still allow Joshua to show that he can dominate the fighter who just reduced Ruiz to a fading former champion.

Hearn cannot treat Knyba as an opponent controlled entirely by Matchroom. The Polish heavyweight signed a multiyear promotional agreement with Bob Arum’s Top Rank in 2023 and remains listed on the company’s roster. That introduces promotional politics.

From Top Rank’s perspective, the money and exposure attached to a Joshua fight may be tempting, especially after Knyba rebuilt himself by beating Ruiz. The company would also know that his size and right hand give him a genuine chance to spoil the larger plan.

Calling Knyba a warm up sacrifice would undersell his value. He has already fought Kabayel for an interim heavyweight title and now owns a win over Ruiz. Top Rank would likely want proper compensation and a favorable arrangement before placing him across the ring from one of Matchroom’s most valuable fighters.

Warren’s connection to Fury adds another consideration, although he does not control Knyba’s contract. Anyone invested in Fury versus Joshua must decide if the preparation value justifies placing AJ in another dangerous fight first. The financial calculation may ultimately kill the idea.

Heavy investment from Turki Alalshikh in both Joshua and Fury has helped keep their fight alive as one of the largest events available in British boxing. Sending Joshua against a towering heavyweight with a hard right hand creates a direct threat to that investment.

If Knyba knocks out AJ, the Fury fight loses much of its commercial power. It may still happen because of the names involved, but it would no longer carry the same sporting value or sense of occasion.

That gives the match its central contradiction. Knyba is the ideal warm up for Fury because he reproduces several of the physical problems Joshua must solve. He is also the wrong warm up from a business perspective because he carries enough power to destroy the entire plan.

On experience and technical development, Joshua should be able to pressure Knyba, attack his body, and exploit the weaknesses Kabayel exposed. But “should” offers little comfort with Joshua now.

Winning would not require Knyba to outbox him for 12 rounds. He would only need to survive long enough to land one clean right hand on a fighter whose recovery has badly deteriorated.

That is why the fight works. Knyba can prepare Joshua for Fury’s dimensions, force him to solve the clinching problem, and test the punch resistance Fury would attack. If AJ cannot safely handle that assignment, he has no business moving directly into the Fury fight.

Ghana News.title: Abu Jinapor demands transparency over GH¢49.72m evacuation cost
Ghana News.content:
Ranking Member on Parliament’s Foreign Affairs Committee, Samuel Abdulai Jinapor, has called for greater transparency over the GH¢49.72 million spent by the government to evacuate 1,900 Ghanaians from South Africa.

Speaking on Joy FM’s Top Story, Mr Jinapor said while the government’s decision to protect Ghanaians caught up in renewed xenophobic attacks was necessary, the expenditure must also be properly accounted for.

He said the Minority in Parliament supported the government and other stakeholders when the crisis emerged, describing the situation as disturbing.

Mr Jinapor stressed, however, that the protection of citizens’ lives should not be reduced to a monetary calculation, while insisting that transparency and value for money remained important principles of public expenditure.

“We cannot begin to quantify monetary expenses or value when it comes to lives of our citizens,” he said on Monday, September 7.

His comments follow Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa’s disclosure that GH¢49.72 million was spent on the evacuation exercise.

Mr Ablakwa said GH¢38.84 million went towards chartered flights, air tickets, ground transportation, feeding, accommodation and medical care for the evacuated Ghanaians.

A further GH¢10.80 million was spent on reintegration support and transportation allowances, while GH¢84,274 was used to repatriate the mortal remains of two Ghanaians.

Mr Jinapor said the figures released by the government suggested an average expenditure of approximately GH¢25,000 per evacuee, equivalent to about US$2,200 per person.

He said the calculation was not meant to place a monetary value on the lives of the citizens rescued, but to demonstrate why the Ministry should provide further details on how the money was spent.

“If you take the figures the government put out, the Ministry is suggesting that they spent close to 50 million cedis to evacuate close to 2,000 Ghanaians,” he said.

Mr Jinapor therefore urged the Foreign Affairs Ministry to publish a detailed account of the expenditure, arguing that such disclosure would serve the interests of transparency, good governance and the nation.

“It will be useful for the Ministry to put out the details,” he added.

Ghana News.title: 4,972 Ghanaians repatriated from 10 countries since 2025 – Ablakwa
Ghana News.content:
The Ministry of Foreign Affairs has repatriated 4,972 Ghanaians from distress situations across the world since 2025, Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa has disclosed.

According to the Minister, the repatriations form part of ongoing interventions by the government, Ghana’s diplomatic missions and international partners to assist citizens stranded or facing difficult circumstances abroad.

Mr Ablakwa said the figure covers Ghanaians repatriated from 10 countries.

"This figure is an accumulation of the following: 3,807 from Libya, 440 from Côte d'Ivoire, 246 from Nigeria, 244 from Cambodia, 201 from Algeria, 18 from Kuwait, 8 from Sierra Leone, 5 from Mauritius, 2 from Morocco and 1 from Iraq," he said during a press briefing on Monday, September 9.

Mr Ablakwa said the recurring evacuation and repatriation exercises had placed a significant financial and logistical burden on the state because many of the situations requiring intervention were unexpected.

He explained that the circumstances have made it necessary for Ghana to establish a dedicated emergency funding mechanism to respond more quickly to crises involving its citizens abroad.

“It is precisely why it has become imperative to establish the Ghanaian Diaspora Consular Fund,” he said.

According to him, the fund will provide a dedicated and sustainable source of emergency financing to enable government to mobilise resources promptly whenever Ghanaians are in distress.

The proposed fund, he said, will help the government safeguard the rights, dignity and welfare of Ghanaian citizens wherever they may find themselves.

He also renewed government’s warning to Ghanaians, particularly the youth, to be cautious of illegal recruitment agencies and human trafficking networks that lure people abroad with promises of better opportunities.

The Minister said such schemes had contributed to some Ghanaians ending up in dangerous situations, including the ongoing Russia-Ukraine conflict.

He disclosed that 62 Ghanaians have lost their lives in the conflict, while another 15 remain missing.

Two other Ghanaians, he added, are currently being held by Ukrainian authorities as prisoners of war, although negotiations for their release are progressing positively.

Mr Ablakwa said government had intensified efforts to clamp down on criminal networks involved in illegal recruitment and trafficking.

He reiterated the government’s commitment to protecting Ghanaians abroad and said the Ministry of Foreign Affairs would continue to take timely and decisive action whenever the safety and security of Ghanaian nationals are at risk.

Ghana News.title: Israeli strikes in southern Lebanese village kill 12
Ghana News.content:
Israeli air strikes on a village in southern Lebanon have killed at least 12 people, the Lebanese health ministry says.

Eleven people, including two children and four women, were killed in a strike that destroyed a residential building in Kfar Roummane overnight. A second strike on a vehicle killed a paramedic.

The Israeli military said it struck infrastructure sites belonging to the Shia Muslim armed group Hezbollah, as well as "several terrorists" transferring weapons, in retaliation for a drone attack on troops in an occupied area of the country.

Israeli attacks across southern Lebanon have killed at least 27 people over the past three days, according to the health ministry.

Lebanese President Joseph Aoun said the "dangerous escalation" was jeopardising June's US-brokered ceasefire, which was meant to end the conflict between Israel and Hezbollah.

He urged the international community to put pressure on Israel to stop the attacks.

They have happened in places near the strip of territory that is occupied by Israeli troops, and large numbers of residents have again been fleeing those areas.

The latest attacks targeted Kfar Roummane, in Nabatieh district, which is only a few hundred metres from what the Israeli military calls its "security zone".

The first air strike destroyed a three-storey residential building near the town's Shuyuiya roundabout shortly after midnight, Lebanon's state-run National News Agency reported.

The Lebanese health ministry said that in addition to the 11 people killed, eight were injured, including three children and a paramedic from the Islamic Health Association, which is an emergency service linked to Hezbollah.

The second strike hit a vehicle carrying paramedics from the Islamic Risala Scout Association, killing one of them and injuring two others, according to the ministry. The Risala Scouts is an emergency service affiliated with the Amal movement, a Shia group allied to Hezbollah.

The health ministry said the death toll "serves as further irrefutable evidence of the grave violations of international humanitarian law committed by the Israeli occupation, targeting medics and children".

A resident of Kfar Roummane, Sara Moallaem, 35, told the BBC that she had been asleep with her five children in their rental home when she heard the explosions.

She immediately grabbed her children and moved them into the home's "safe room" while they waited for the booms and the sirens to stop.

The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) said it struck "several Hezbollah terrorist infrastructure sites across southern Lebanon" overnight after the group's fighters launched two explosive drones towards Israeli troops operating in the Ali al-Taher ridge area, which is just south of Kfar Roummane and inside the Israeli-declared "security zone".

"Additionally, the IDF struck several terrorists who were identified transferring weapons in the area of Kfar Roummane, in order to remove the threat they posed to IDF soldiers."

"The claim that several uninvolved individuals were harmed as a result of the strikes is being reviewed," it added.

The IDF also said it had struck the Nabatieh area and killed several Hezbollah fighters on Sunday following a separate drone attack.

Lebanon's health ministry said 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes across the south of the country on Sunday. They included nine people in Nabatieh al-Fawqa, which is south of Kfar Roummane, and two women in Arab Salim, to the north of the village.

There was no immediate comment from Hezbollah. But on Sunday, one of the group's members of parliament, Ali Ammar, declared that "the language of resistance is the only language that is effective against the Israeli enemy".

The ceasefire agreement between Lebanon, Israel and the US calls for Hezbollah to disarm, Israeli forces to withdraw gradually from southern Lebanon, and the Lebanese army to deploy across the area.

Hezbollah has rejected the framework, saying the provisions linking Israel's withdrawal to the group's disarmament cross "all red lines".

Lebanon was drawn into the war between Israel, the US and Iran on 2 March, when Hezbollah - which is supported by Iran - launched rockets into Israel in retaliation for a strike that killed Iran's supreme leader.

Israel responded by launching a bombing campaign across Lebanon and invading a significant part of the country's south.

At least 4,362 people have been killed in Lebanon during the conflict, including 395 women and 259 children, according to the health ministry, whose figures do not differentiate between combatants and civilians.

Israeli authorities say 40 Israeli soldiers and four civilians have been killed during the conflict.

Ghana News.title: Ghana to launch Diaspora Consular Fund to support citizens in crisis – Ablakwa
Ghana News.content:
Minister for Foreign Affairs, Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa

The Ministry of Foreign Affairs is set to launch a Ghanaian Diaspora Consular Fund to provide emergency support to Ghanaians who find themselves in distress or crisis situations abroad.

Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa announced the initiative during a press briefing on the government’s evacuation of Ghanaian nationals from South Africa on Monday, September 9.

“I wish to announce that the Ministry of Foreign Affairs will soon launch a Ghanaian Diaspora Consular Fund which will serve as an emergency response funding mechanism to swiftly take care of Ghanaians in distress and during crisis situations anywhere in the world,” Mr Ablakwa said.

The announcement follows the government’s evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa amid heightened concerns over the safety of foreign nationals.

According to the Minister, the South Africa evacuation exercise was not anticipated and therefore had not been budgeted for.

Government, he said, was nevertheless compelled to act to protect the lives and welfare of Ghanaian nationals as the situation deteriorated.

Mr Ablakwa reiterated government’s commitment to protecting Ghanaians wherever they may be, saying the state would continue to take “timely and decisive action” whenever the safety and security of its citizens abroad are at risk.

He also commended Ghanaians for the solidarity they demonstrated in defending the rights of compatriots affected by the xenophobic attacks in South Africa.

“We have demonstrated what we can achieve by ourselves when we are united. Our creed is not in doubt: touch one, touch all. Team Ghana is the winner in this entire evacuation exercise,” he said.

The evacuation exercise, which began on May 27 and ended on September 4, was coordinated by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs in collaboration with the Ghana High Commission in Pretoria, the Presidency, National Security Secretariat and other relevant state institutions.

The first evacuation flight prioritised vulnerable groups, including children, the sick, the aged and women.

Mr Ablakwa said the new Diaspora Consular Fund would strengthen Ghana’s capacity to respond to similar emergencies in the future by providing a dedicated mechanism for assisting citizens in distress anywhere in the world.

Ghana News.title: Asiedu Nketiah urges political parties to rebuild public trust at inter-continental dialogue in South Korea
Ghana News.content:
National Chairman of the ruling National Democratic Congress (NDC), Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, has urged political parties to adapt to changing societies, strengthen leadership development and make deliberate efforts to rebuild public trust.

He said political institutions could no longer rely solely on historical identities, ideological traditions or generational loyalties to retain public support, as each generation increasingly expects political parties to demonstrate their relevance to contemporary social and economic realities.

Mr Asiedu Nketiah made the remarks at the inaugural Inter-Continental Dialogue on Political Parties in Seoul, South Korea, where he addressed the gathering on behalf of political parties participating in the African Political Parties Initiative (APPI).

The event brought together the Africa Governance Centre (AGC), through APPI, the International Conference of Asian Political Parties (ICAPP), and the Permanent Conference of Political Parties of Latin America and the Caribbean (COPPPAL).

He commended the Africa Governance Centre for establishing APPI and creating a structured platform for African political parties to engage with one another and political organisations from other regions.

Johnson Asiedu Nketiah, National Chairman of the NDC

Changing political loyalties

A central theme of Mr Asiedu Nketiah’s address was the changing relationship between citizens and political parties.

He argued that political organisations that were once sustained by strong historical identities, ideological traditions or generational attachments could no longer assume that those loyalties would automatically be passed from one generation to another.

He said a party’s history might explain its position in national life but could not guarantee its future.

According to him, every generation encounters politics under different economic and social circumstances and ultimately makes its own assessment of whether existing political institutions remain relevant to the society it wants to build.

The former Parliamentarian said the judgement of citizens was becoming increasingly demanding, particularly among young people who have greater access to information and developments beyond their own countries.

He noted that many young people were simultaneously confronting unemployment, economic insecurity, rising living costs and uncertainty about whether education and hard work still offered a dependable route to economic advancement.

Political parties that failed to appreciate the depth of those changes, he warned, risked continuing to project confidence while gradually losing the public confidence on which their political relevance depended.

Economic hardship and public trust

Mr Asiedu Nketiah also linked public trust in political institutions to citizens’ everyday experiences.

He said dissatisfaction could deepen when people felt they had fulfilled their responsibilities to society—working, obeying the law, raising families and making sacrifices for their children—yet remained unable to see a realistic path towards a better standard of living.

In such circumstances, he argued, frustration could move beyond dissatisfaction with individual policies and develop into broader scepticism about political institutions.

He urged political leaders to treat such developments as an institutional warning rather than dismiss them as temporary public discontent.

Parties must prepare leaders before elections

Another major point of the address was the responsibility of political parties to prepare people for leadership before they gain political power.

Drawing on his experience in grassroots politics, Parliament, government and national political organisation, Mr Asiedu Nketiah said the character of a future government was often shaped within a political party long before an election.

He said decisions about who advances within a party, the qualities it rewards, the seriousness with which it develops policy and the conduct it tolerates eventually influence the character of public administration when the party assumes power.

He cautioned political organisations against confusing electoral effectiveness with readiness to govern.

A party may be highly skilled at mobilisation, campaigning and electoral strategy but still lack the policy, institutional and leadership capacity required to manage the complexities of government.

The gap, he said, might not be obvious during an election campaign but would become more difficult to conceal once a government had to deal with limited resources, competing public demands and decisions with long-term consequences.

He therefore called for greater emphasis on leadership preparation during the period before political opportunities arise.

Political parties, he said, needed sufficient institutional depth to ensure that the quality of government did not depend on a narrow group of personalities.

He also stressed the need for parties to develop successive generations of leaders capable of taking responsibility without every transition becoming an institutional crisis.

Parties must learn from failure

Mr Asiedu Nketiah further urged political parties to examine their own failures instead of focusing exclusively on explaining their successes or blaming opponents for setbacks.

He said electoral defeats, declining membership, public disaffection and difficult leadership transitions could expose weaknesses that prolonged political success might conceal.

Political organisations that were willing to examine why citizens had withdrawn their confidence, he argued, were better positioned to renew themselves than those that attributed every setback to the shortcomings of their opponents.

He said opposition should not be treated as a period of political inactivity but as an opportunity for serious preparation.

Similarly, parties in government needed to remain connected to citizens despite the pressures and demands of governing.

He warned that parties could become insulated from ordinary citizens once they assumed office, while opposition parties could become so focused on criticism that they neglected the development of credible alternatives.

Learning across political systems

Mr Asiedu Nketiah said the Inter-Continental Dialogue could provide an avenue for political parties from different regions to learn from one another.

He noted that participating organisations had different political histories and governing traditions, creating opportunities to examine how parties elsewhere handled leadership renewal, transitions from opposition to government and recovery from electoral defeats.

However, he cautioned against simply importing political models from one country into another.

National politics, he said, remained shaped by individual countries’ histories, cultures, institutions and local circumstances.

The value of international engagement, he argued, was therefore in exposing political leaders to different experiences and perspectives that could help them examine challenges within their own political systems.

Building institutions beyond election cycles

Mr Asiedu Nketiah said political parties needed structures and institutional habits that remained useful whether they were in government or opposition.

Their relevance, he argued, should not depend entirely on the authority of government or the temporary weakness of a political opponent.

Rather, political parties should build their long-term relevance around their ability to produce ideas, develop leaders and maintain public confidence.

He said institutional depth was particularly important because political leaders and governments would change, while strong institutional relationships could survive those changes.

He also welcomed plans for the Inter-Continental Dialogue to develop into a continuing process, with future engagements held in different locations as relationships among participating institutions deepen.

He said the initiative should be judged less by the visibility of individual meetings and more by the quality and usefulness of the relationships developed through them.

A new political environment

Mr Asiedu Nketiah said political parties were operating in a more demanding environment than when many of them were established.

Citizens now have more avenues for organising outside conventional party structures, greater access to competing ideas and less patience with political institutions perceived as unable to adapt to changing circumstances.

For established political parties, he said, the challenge was no longer simply to preserve their organisations but to demonstrate why they continued to deserve a place in the political future.

He said political leadership should ultimately be judged over a period longer than an electoral cycle.

While electoral victories determine which political party has prevailed at a particular point in time, he argued that the more enduring assessment should be based on the quality of leaders produced, institutions strengthened and political culture handed to succeeding generations.

For political parties seeking to regain or retain public confidence, he said, the task was continuous: remaining serious, adaptable and connected to society so that each generation could find its own reason to believe in the political institutions it inherits.

Ghana News.title: Heavy pitch, intense heat made Kotoko draw physically demanding – Eric Tinkler
Ghana News.content:
Asante Kotoko head coach Eric Tinkler believes the heavy pitch and intense heat contributed to the physical demands of his side’s 2-2 draw with newly promoted Debibi United in their Ghana Premier League opener.

Kotoko took an early lead through Yakubu Dogo, who calmly finished after receiving a well-weighted pass from Herbert Gyau.

The Porcupine Warriors carried their advantage into the break, but Debibi United responded strongly in the second half.

Richard Owusu levelled the score with a powerful free-kick before completing his brace in the 73rd minute to put the home side 2-1 ahead.

Kotoko, however, fought back to earn a point, with Gyau finding the equaliser in the 79th minute following a goalmouth scramble.

Speaking after the game, Tinkler said the playing conditions took a toll on both teams.

“I could see their legs were dead. Not only our legs, their legs. And yes, the pitch is heavy, the pitch is thick,” Tinkler said.

The South African coach, who has played on similar surfaces, explained how such pitches can quickly affect players physically.

“I’ve played on pitches like that, and it’s hard, because it starts affecting your calves, your thighs, your hamstrings. They start going very, very quickly.”

Tinkler also expressed concern about the intense heat and the lack of a water break during the match.

“And then the intense heat, the dehydration starts coming in. We didn’t have a water break, but in this weather we should be at least having a water break for the players. That’s the only criticism that I would give.”

Despite the difficult conditions, Tinkler insisted the pitch did not prevent Kotoko from playing their preferred style.

“The pitch didn’t stop us from playing our brand of football.”

Kotoko will now look for their first win of the season when they host Heart of Lions in their next league fixture.

Ghana News.title: Pregnancy School initiative lauded for reducing maternal mortality in Kwabre East
Ghana News.content:
Residents, especially mothers in the Kwabre East Municipality of the Ashanti Region, have lauded the Ghana Health Service's Pregnancy School initiative for its role in improving maternal healthcare delivery.

The initiative provides free, structured education, support and guidance to expectant mothers and their families on prenatal care, nutrition, danger signs in pregnancy and safe childbirth practices.

At the Peace Speciality Hospital at Mamponteng, the facility is using the school to reshape attitudes of pregnant women and their partners while creating a welcoming and informative environment for maternal health education.

Held every first week of the month, the September edition of the school was held on the premises of the hospital, with the session bringing together pregnant women and nursing mothers within and beyond Kwabre East Municipality, who were taken through various maternal health topics aimed at protecting the lives and well-being of mothers and their babies.

A key focus of the session was pre-eclampsia, which was identified as one of the dangerous conditions affecting pregnant women.

Speaking to JoyNews, Dr. Edmund Obeng, an Obstetrician at the Peace Speciality Hospital, said pre-eclampsia is a serious pregnancy-related high blood pressure condition that is increasingly affecting mothers and newborns across Ghana.

He disclosed that the rate of occurrence is rising at an alarming rate, stressing the need for health facilities to intensify education for early symptom recognition and timely medical intervention.

Dr. Obeng cautioned that missing regular antenatal check-ups prevents early detection of rising blood pressure and urged pregnant women to adhere to frequent hospital visits.

A Senior Surgeon and Specialist, Dr. Francis Osei Kofi also encouraged mothers to participate in the monthly health education for safe delivery, noting that regular hospital visits help in early detection of anomalies in pregnancy for prompt medical solutions.

As part of the event, awards were presented to dedicated mothers who regularly attend antenatal care and the pregnancy school.

Husbands who consistently accompany their spouses to the facility were also commended and presented with gifts.

Some beneficiaries shared testimonies about the impact of the initiative.

Assa Assif, a mother of three, testified that the Pregnancy School has been of great help to her, explaining that the education has given her a better understanding of pregnancy and the need to report to the hospital in case of any anomaly. She encouraged other pregnant women to participate for their own safety and that of their babies.

Elizabeth Yeboah, also a beneficiary, said the school helps demystify labour and delivery, which lowers anxiety and helps reduce unnecessary medical interventions such as caesarean sections.

The Kwabre East Municipal Health Director, Mrs. Elsie Kissi-Appiah, during the launch of the Pregnancy School at the hospital in July, underscored its significance across health facilities in the municipality, disclosing that the initiative has helped reduce maternal mortality.

Ghana News.title: Emergency nature of South Africa evacuation justifies GH¢49.7m cost — International relations expert
Ghana News.content:
International relations expert Dr Ishmael Hlovor has defended the government’s expenditure of GH¢49.7 million on the evacuation of 1,964 Ghanaians from South Africa following renewed xenophobic attacks.

According to him, although the amount may appear high, the emergency nature of the operation meant the government could not secure services such as flights at the rates available for planned travel.

Speaking on Joy News, Dr Hlovor said emergency operations often come with higher costs because of the limited time available for preparations.

“While it may appear as a very large sum, you must also understand that this operation is kind of an emergency operation. Naturally, some of the things that you may apply at ordinary prices will have some inflated prices at the time because you are operating under emergency situations,” he said.

He said flight arrangements, for instance, could have been cheaper if authorities had sufficient time to plan and make bookings in advance.

Dr Hlover also urged Ghanaians to assess the expenditure beyond its financial implications, particularly in the context of Ghana’s foreign policy and the government’s responsibility to protect its citizens abroad.

He said the evacuation demonstrated Ghana’s willingness to intervene when the safety of its nationals is threatened.

“Where you are trying to communicate a certain understanding to the international community that Ghana is always ready to defend its citizens wherever they are. Then we may not necessarily be worried about the cost,” he said.

Dr Hlovor added that the expenditure could be justified if documentation supports the amount spent on the evacuees.

“No amount is too huge to be spent on the life of a Ghanaian,” he stated.

Foreign Affairs Minister Samuel Okudzeto Ablakwa, at a press briefing in Accra on Monday, September 7, disclosed that the evacuation cost a total of GH¢49,721,786.

The largest component, GH¢38,835,512, covered chartered flights, tickets, ground transportation, feeding, hotel accommodation, medical care and hospitalisation in South Africa.

Another GH¢10,802,000 was spent on reintegration and transportation allowances, while GH¢84,274 was used to repatriate the remains of two Ghanaian nationals who died during the crisis.

The government funded GH¢33,721,786 of the total cost.

Businessman Ibrahim Mahama, through Engineers and Planners, contributed GH¢16 million towards the exercise.

Mr Ablakwa said the entire cost had been paid, with no outstanding liabilities.

World.title: Trump pleads not guilty to 34 felony counts
World.content:
News outlets will not be allowed to broadcast former President Donald Trump’s arraignment on Tuesday in a New York state court, a judge said Monday night, but he will allow some photographers to take pictures in the courtroom before the proceedings formally begin.

Acting New York Supreme Court Judge Juan Merchan rejected the request by several media organizations, including CNN, for permission to broadcast the historic proceedings. Trump’s arraignment — like most arraignments in the Manhattan courthouse — is a public proceeding, but news cameras are not usually allowed to broadcast from inside the courtroom.

However, the judge is allowing five pool photographers to take still photos at the beginning of the proceedings “until such time as they are directed to vacate the jury box by court personnel.”

Earlier on Monday, Trump’s lawyers urged the judge to reject the media’s request for live cameras in the courtroom. The Manhattan District Attorney’s office told the judge they didn’t have a position.

The media outlets that tried to get cameras into the courtroom argued that “the gravity of this proceeding … and, consequently, the need for the broadest possible public access, cannot be overstated.”

Trump is now in Manhattan ahead of the arraignment. A grand jury indicted the former president last week.

The arraignment is also expected to bring the unsealing of the criminal charges against Trump, which have not yet been seen by his lawyers or the public.

The indictment stems from Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg’s investigation into hush-money payments, made during the 2016 presidential campaign, to women who claimed they had extramarital affairs with Trump, which he denies.

Trump denies all wrongdoing and his lawyers said last week that they’ll fight to get the charges dropped.

World.title: Russian authorities detain suspect over St. Petersburg cafe blast
World.content:
A Ukrainian tank is seen near the frontline area amid the Russia-Ukraine war, in Bakhmut, Ukraine, on April 02. (Muhammed Enes Yildirim/Anadolu Agency/Getty Images)

The Ukrainian military has reported little change to the front lines but heavy fire from Russian forces at various parts of the front line in the Donetsk region.

The General Staff said that more than 45 enemy attacks had been repelled over the past day, with the focus on Lyman, Bakhmut, Avdiivka and Mariinka.

It said there were 17 air strikes and more than 20 strikes by multiple launch rocket systems.

“In the Bakhmut direction, the enemy is trying to take full control over the city of Bakhmut and continues to storm it,” the General Staff said.

West of the city, Ukrainian defense forces repelled about 20 enemy attacks, according to the General Staff.

Oleksandr Syrskyi, commander of Ukrainian Land Forces, posted on Telegram that in Bakhmut he had met with “soldiers and commanders who destroyed the myth of invincibility of the Wagner fighters and Russian paratroopers.”

“The enemy is weakening and trying to cover up its failures with new fakes about the capture of Bakhmut,” Syrskyi said.

Syrskyi referenced the possibility of a future counter-offensive, saying that “the forward movement of our entire army depends on what every soldier is doing right now on their section of the front.”

Some of the most intense fighting is to the northwest and west of the city of Donetsk – as the Russians continue months-long efforts to dislodge Ukrainian defenses in Avdiivka and Mariinka. The General Staff said that some 20 assaults had been repelled.

“There are also some operational successes of our military in the Donetsk area. Our military have taken some positions. They have taken a more strategic and favourable position,” said Oleksii Dmytrashkivskyi, spokesperson for the military in that zone.

He also noted that Russian special forces had been introduced in the area.

“The enemy is trying to attack our positions between Avdiivka and Marinka. These attempts do not stop. It should be noted that the enemy has suffered quite significant losses,” Dmytrashkivskyi said.

He also claimed that the Russians “don’t have the same amount of equipment and, as they themselves say, they are on a ‘diet’ of ammunition for assaults.”

Social media video showed both sides engaged in heavy fire in the Avdiivka area, which the Russians have surrounded on three sides.

Denis Pushilin, the leader of the self-declared Donetsk People’s Republic, claimed that Russian forces were still advancing in the Avdiivka direction.

“It is still premature to speak of encirclement, but the situation is being created, if not critical, then extremely difficult for the enemy… After clearing Kamianka, our units are moving further. There are difficulties both with the terrain, which must also be overcome, and there are also similarities with weather conditions. But these difficulties are mutual — both for the enemy and for us,” Pushilin said.
