World.title: ‘R50 million minimum for Orlando Pirates superstar’
World.content:
Orlando Pirates are reportedly considering an overseas offer for Oswin Appollis. But who’s put a massive price tag on the Bafana star’s head?

Appollis could still leave Orlando Pirates

According to a source via the Citizen, an unnamed European club has tabled an enticing offer for the Bafana Bafana winger, and Pirates are considering it. The 25-year-old featured in every single Betway Premiership match last season for the champions, contributing nine goals and six assists in 30 outings. This term, he’s already got two goals and two assists in five matches. The transfer window closes on 21 September.

“Don’t be surprised to see Oswin leave Pirates before the transfer window closes. There’s serious interest in him, and an offer for him from a European team has been tabled already. I think it’s from France, but it’s not easy to get information from Pirates these days; they protect it,” said the source.



Nkota’s arrival at Orlando Pirates increases competition for places

Bafana Bafana star Mohau Nkota’s 21 Saudi Pro League appearances last term only yielded two goals and three assists. It’s understandable, then, that the 21-year-old is back in South Africa to find his form again on loan. Nkota will vie for a starting role wide in attack alongside Tshepang Moremi and Oswin Appollis. If only two of those players can start regularly, which one of the three is the odd one out?

Pirates fans, what’s your minimum asking price for Oswin Appollis?

World.title: ‘R5000 for pensioners’: SASSA grant recipients rally behind one simple demand
World.content:
Amid a broader discussion about SASSA payment dates on The South African’s Facebook page, some commenters used the moment to raise a different issue entirely: the actual value of the grants themselves.

Elaine Charlotte’s comment was short but direct, simply asking for 5000 for pensioners. Though brief, the comment tapped into an ongoing frustration among grant recipients who say current grant amounts are not keeping pace with the rising cost of living in South Africa.

Ivadene Isabella Bantom shifted the conversation further, arguing that the focus on payment dates was overshadowing a more pressing concern: children who have lost their grants altogether. Her comment struck a noticeably different tone from others in the thread, redirecting attention away from scheduling complaints and toward beneficiaries who have been removed from the system entirely.



The comment did not go unnoticed, with the shift in tone highlighting how deeply personal and varied the impact of SASSA’s processes can be for different households across the country.

Frustration Grows Over Pace Of Change

Roy Subramanian’s comment tied the thread together, stating that changes are needed and that it is taking too long to implement them for the citizens of South Africa.

Taken together, the comments paint a picture of grant recipients who are not only frustrated with logistical issues like payment dates but with deeper structural concerns: grant values, eligibility losses, and the overall pace of reform at SASSA. As these conversations continue to unfold on The South African’s Facebook page, they underscore the scale of what grant recipients hope SASSA and the government will address.

SASSA has not commented on the specific concerns raised regarding grant values or children’s grant losses referenced in the thread.

Win R2 000 in the South African SASSA grant survey

If you receive a SASSA grant and want to share your story, we want to hear from you.

Take part in our survey and stand a chance to win R2 000. Your responses help us tell the stories that matter.

World.title: Orlando Pirates get tempting Oswin Appollis offer – Report
World.content:
Orlando Pirates are reportedly considering an enticing offer for star Bafana Bafana winger Oswin Appollis. Will he leave before the deadline?

Pirates brace for potential Appollis sale

According to a source via the Citizen, an unnamed European club has tabled an enticing offer for the Bafana Bafana winger, and Pirates are considering it.

“Don’t be surprised to see Oswin leave Pirates before the transfer window closes. There’s serious interest in him, and an offer for him from a European team has been tabled already. I think it’s from France, but it’s not easy to get information from Pirates these days; they protect it,” said the source.



Orlando Pirates set a special record

After four consecutive domestic wins with 1-0, 2-0, 3-0 and 4-0 scorelines, the champions have done something that no other Betway Premiership side has done. The sequence started with a 1-0 win over Sekhukhune in the MTN8. It then continued with successes over Sekhukhune in the league, Sekhukhune again in the MTN8 semi-final second leg, and a 4-0 trouncing of Kruger United.

Pirates fans have jokes

Meanwhile, head over to the official Orlando Pirates Facebook account, and there’s usually a laugh or two in store. On a recent image of Yanela Mbuthuma celebrating a goal against Kruger United, one supporter has dropped a pearler. Is there some truth to this analogy?

“Pirates is like the police. It might look like they are not doing their job until they start looking for you.”

World.title: Mokoena welcomes Nkota back to Pirates But…
World.content:
Orlando Pirates legend Lebohang Mokoena has welcomed Mohau Nkota back to the club but has questioned the decision to sign so many wingers during the current transfer window.

The Buccaneers have signed Kabelo Kgositsile, Bohlane Ngwato and Gamphani Lungu, with Nkota now becoming the fourth winger to arrive at the club.

Pirates already have several options in the position, including Oswin Appollis, Tshepang Moremi and Daniel Msendami.



Despite questioning the number of wingers at the club, Mokoena believes Nkota can make an important contribution, particularly because of the experience he gained during his time in Saudi Arabia.

“I think he’s got a big role to play, especially with the experience he has gained over the last season or so. Also remember, he was a big part of that Bafana team, as much as he didn’t make the World Cup squad,” the former Pirates star told Soccerbeat.

Mokoena then added that Nkota could be returning to Pirates with one goal in mind: winning the league title.



“Maybe at the back of his mind, he’s thinking, ‘I left without winning the league. Time for me to collect a league medal because this side, it looks like oil prices have increased in Saudi,'” Mokoena joked.

The former winger also believes Nkota’s ability to play on the left could prove particularly valuable for Pirates.

“Looking at the position he is playing, and being a left-footer, I think Pirates are scarce in that department. They only have Moremi starting,” he added.



Nkota returns to Pirates

Mokoena questioned whether Nkota’s arrival could have an impact on the club’s other new signings, particularly the younger players competing for places on the wings.

Mokoena believes the increased competition could make it difficult for some of Pirates’ recent recruits to establish themselves.

“It will bring stiff competition to the wingers. My question is, what is going to happen with the young left players who just signed with the club?”



Nkota is yet to make an appearance since rejoining Pirates.

What’s your take on Nkota’s signing?

World.title: When will Zimbabwean international Jonah Fabisch make his Golden Arrows debut?
World.content:
Zimbabwe international Jonah Fabisch has provided an update on his injury, revealing when Lamontville Golden Arrows supporters could finally see him make his debut for the club.

Jonah Fabisch explains Golden Arrows absence

Fabisch joined Arrows in July 2026 ahead of the 2026/27 Betway Premiership season after leaving German 3. Liga side Erzgebirge Aue.

The 25-year-old midfielder arrived with expectations of playing an important role for Abafana Bes’thende after the club signed him as a replacement for Ivory Coast star Isaac Cisse, who left for Belgian Pro League side RC Sporting Charleroi.



However, Fabisch is yet to make his competitive debut for Arrows after suffering an injury during training.

The Zimbabwean international explained the situation while speaking to Lamontville Golden Arrows.

“Unfortunately I got injured in about two weeks ago in training. So now I am just in rehab, trying to recover, getting back on the pitch as quick as possible,” Fabisch said.

Zimbabwe international reveals injury setback

His absence has been a frustrating start to his time at the Durban-based club, particularly after he joined during pre-season and attracted interest from several clubs before choosing Arrows.

Fabisch has now given supporters a clearer indication of when they could expect to see him in action.

Asked when he could return to the pitch, the midfielder pointed to the international break as the likely timeframe.



“I will probably say after the international break because I still need a bit of time to get back to 100 percent,” he said.

When will Fabisch make his Golden Arrows debut?

The update means Arrows fans may not have to wait much longer to see their new signing in competitive action, provided he completes his rehabilitation without any setbacks.

Fabisch has already built a reputation as an experienced midfielder despite his relatively young age, having spent much of his career in Germany before making the move to South Africa.

His arrival at Arrows also adds another Zimbabwean international to the South African top-flight scene.

The midfielder will now focus on regaining full fitness before making his first appearance for his new club.

For Arrows, his return could provide a timely boost as the Betway Premiership season gathers momentum.

Fabisch’s first appearance will also be closely watched in Zimbabwe, where supporters will be eager to see how the Warriors international performs in South Africa’s top flight.

World.title: Joburg pensioner wins R2.6m billing battle
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - A two-and-a-half-year fight against a multi-million-rand municipal bill has ended in victory for a Johannesburg pensioner and restaurant owner.

More than R2.6-million has been credited to Jenny-Lee Bot’s account after a Public Protector investigation revealed a faulty water meter.

Bot's billing nightmare began after her water bill rose from just over a thousand rand to hundreds of thousands in just one month.

READ | Cost-of-living squeeze deepens as electricity, water and fuel prices surge

Initially, the city blamed a leak at her three-bedroom Fourways property, which she had been renting out.

But plumbers who were called in to inspect found nothing, and the volumes being billed were staggering.

“One of the reports I looked at said it was the equivalent of 50 Olympic-size pools. And if that volume of water had been leaking, there would be a sinkhole in my property,” Bot detailed

Bot said she paid Joburg Water to have the meter tested, but the test never happened.

READ | Joburg’s debt crisis deepens as R72bn goes unpaid

As she fought the charges for two and a half years, her municipal debt climbed to nearly R3-million.

The mounting bill soon became more than a billing dispute it put her home at risk.

“It’s been so difficult. I have been sick. I have lost weight. When the bank came and said, you’re in arrears with the bond; we’re going to repossess the house, I was like I can’t even sell this house because there isn't enough equity to sell to try and pay back this ludicrous water bill. "It honestly was the toughest two years of my life. It made me want to pack up everything and leave Joburg.”

Her problems came to an end when the Public Protector intervened.

The meter was eventually tested and found to be faulty.

Although Jenny-Lee Bot eventually resolved her dispute, her ordeal highlights deep systemic flaws in how billing errors are managed and the extreme lengths ratepayers must go to for justice.

Managing Director of Joburg Community Action Network (JoburgCAN), Julia Fish such issues have long existed.

“This should have been resolved by the municipal services trading reforms where they took back the billing.”

Johannesburg Water admits Bot was incorrectly billed, but says it never received her initial meter-test application.

It maintains the matter could have been resolved through normal customer-service channels without the Public Protector’s intervention.

World.title: WATCH | Singabalapha residents in limbo as eviction deadline nears
World.content:
CAPE TOWN - For years, the Singabalapha informal settlement in Observatory in Cape Town has been home to about 150 families.

But in just two months, residents will be forced to pack their bags after a Western Cape High Court ordered the site to be vacated by 30 November.

The group had moved to Singabalapha informal settlement after they were evicted in 2019 from the Arcadia Place old age home, a building they had hijacked.

READ | R87m Hospital View housing project abandoned as beneficiaries wait

The City of Cape Town has been trying to move them on ever since and has recently got a court order to do so.

Singabalapha dwellers have urged city officials to accommodate them in town, where their children attend school.

In 2012, the Western Cape High Court ordered the Masonwabe Hostel to be demolished after the building was declared unsafe.

14 years later, the Masonwabe residents are still living in the temporary housing they were moved to.

The City now plans to redevelop the original hostel site into housing to accommodate both the Masonwabe and Singabalapha communities.

World.title: Manhunt launched for escapee who cut burglar-bar of prison cells
World.content:
MAHIKENG - A manhunt is under way for convict Edward Khomotso Madiba.

He escaped from the Rooigrond Maximum Security Correctional Centre near Mahikeng on 6 September.

Madiba is serving a 20-year sentence for robbery, possession of a firearm and ammunition, kidnapping and parole violations.

According to Department of Correctional Services (DCS) spokesperson Singabakho Nxumalo, Madiba, was being detained in the single cells on a further charge relating to a previous escape when he managed to break out of the correctional centre.

"Preliminary information indicates that offender Madiba cut through the burglar-bar door of the single cells," he said.

Eight officials have been served with notices to suspend pending the outcome of investigations into the escape.

World.title: Three talking points from the Italian Grand Prix
World.content:
ROME - Rarely has a race, or a singular drive, stirred the emotions as did Kimi Antonelli's spectacular home triumph in Sunday's stunning and wildly entertaining Italian Grand Prix.

It was a season-defining performance, a display foreseen by his team boss as a "walk on water" demonstration of pure talent.

AFP Sport looks at three talking points from a weekend of the unexpected at Monza where Ferrari fervour turned to Italian joy in celebration of a first home winner for 60 years:

Antonelli: 'Generational genius'

It was less about the history and the statistics, impressive as they are, but much more a show of precocious speed and talent as the boy from Bologna, who turned 20 two weeks ago, won from 19th on the grid.

In becoming the first Italian driver to win at Monza since 1966 -– to move 66 points clear of nearest rival and teammate George Russell in the title race -– he proved Italy still produces winners and champions.

Only a series of catastrophes in the remaining 10 races can prevent Antonelli from becoming the first Italian to win the world title since Alberto Ascari in 1953.

This was Antonelli's seventh win this year, lifting him level with Russell, who was the pre-season favourite, in career victories, despite the Briton having made 128 more race starts.

As he said in the ecstatic aftermath of the race, as thousands of Ferrari fans, in a weekend record crowd of 403,666, thronged below the podium, this win "is great, but the best is yet to come".

World.title: Authorities in Gauteng on standby amid Yellow Level 2 warning
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Authorities in Gauteng remain on standby after severe weather conditions battered parts of the province over the weekend.

The South African Weather Service (SAWS) has already issued a Yellow Level 2 warning for Monday.

The warning is for severe thunderstorms resulting in localised damage to structures, falling trees and lightning over parts of Gauteng, the Highveld of Mpumalanga, North West, Free State and the Northern Cape.

In the City of Tshwane, residents have been urged to stay indoors where possible and avoid flooded roads, open areas and isolated trees.

City of Tshwane Deputy Chief for Public Information and Liaison Services Nana Radebe-Kgiba said to date, they have not attended to a lot of calls.

This, however, was not the case for the weekend, when there were strong winds prompting authorities to be visible on the ground.

Radebe-Kgiba said that while authorities will be on standby, motorists need to be extra careful during this time.

READ | Localised flooding and trapped vehicles in Joburg

The same sentiments were echoed by Johannesburg Metropolitan Police Department (JMPD) spokesperson Xolani Fihle as he detailed the disruptions to parts of the city over the past weekend.

Localised flooding hit Doornfontein, where two vehicles became submerged and got stuck in high water.

One of them, according to Fihla, was a cash-in-transit vehicle.

He said the driver was reportedly warned not to attempt driving through the water but allegedly went ahead and ended up stuck.

But he said that no injuries were reported.

READ | Kruger rebuilds after January floods

Fihla said the extreme weather started on Saturday, when strong winds brought down several trees across Johannesburg, disrupting traffic.

The traffic was eventually cleared.

Fihla said authorities remain on standby and are monitoring all the areas that are prone to flooding, including Witkoppen Road as well as Brynston and Alexandra, where the Jukskei River passes through.

Another hotspot being monitored is Doornfontein as well as parts of Soweto.

World.title: Scholar transport driver shot dead in Westbury
World.content:
WESTBURY - Gauteng police have launched a manhunt for two suspects after a scholar transport driver was shot and killed in Westbury on Monday.

Police say the 53-year-old had just dropped off school pupils and was about to park at a flat when two men approached him and opened fire.

He was shot multiple times and declared dead at the scene.

READ | We can’t lose our children | Westbury mothers take on gang violence

The two suspects then fled in a blue Volkswagen Polo.

The motive for the shooting is unknown at this stage.

Sophiatown police have opened a case of murder, and police investigations are continuing.

World.title: Transport costs becoming barrier to opportunity for millions: Ipsos
World.content:
JOHANNESBURG - Transport affordability is not just an inconvenience. It is a barrier to opportunity.

This is according to the latest IPSOS survey, conducted in June and July, which found that rising transport costs are preventing some people from accessing opportunities to improve their lives.

About 15 percent of people surveyed said they had missed school, university, college or work because they could not afford the transport costs.

“At first glance, 15 percent may not seem large, but when you project it to the population, it is almost seven million people,” said IPSOS’s Natalie Otte.

“Transport affordability is not a cost-of-living issue. For many South Africans, it’s a barrier to opportunity,” she said.

According to the study, the Free State is the most affected province, with residents reporting the greatest difficulty with transport costs.

It is followed by the Northern Cape and Gauteng.

Otte says there are multiple reasons for the differences between provinces, including distances people have to travel, settlement patterns, employment opportunities and transport infrastructure.

“The picture is mixed across the country,” said Otte.

World.title: LIVESTREAM | Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula on the stand
World.content:
PRETORIA - The Gauteng High Court in Pretoria is expected to deliver judgment on Monday on former National Assembly Speaker Nosiviwe Mapisa-Nqakula’s application for a discharge under Section 174 of the Criminal Procedure Act.

Mapisa-Nqakula is facing corruption allegations linked to claims that she solicited millions of rand in bribes while serving as Defence Minister.

She has consistently denied the allegations.

Her legal team has argued that the State has failed to present sufficient evidence to justify putting her on trial on the corruption charges.

A Section 174 application allows an accused person to seek a discharge at the close of the State’s case where there is insufficient evidence on which they could be convicted.

If the court grants Mapisa-Nqakula’s application, she could be acquitted without being required to present her defence.

World.title: Centum taps insider as Mworia exits after nearly two decades
World.content:
Centum Investment Company PLC acting Group Chief Executive Thomas Omondi-Achola. [Courtesy]

Centum Investment Company PLC has appointed Thomas Omondi-Achola as acting group chief executive, tapping an internal candidate to succeed long-serving CEO James Mworia, who is leaving to head Kenya’s newly established National Infrastructure Fund (NIF).

The transition, effective immediately, marks the end of an 18-year tenure during which Mworia transformed Centum from a small investment firm into East Africa’s largest diversified investment platform, the company said in a statement.

World.title: Ruto: Kenya to end raw mineral exports
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County on September 6, 2026. [PCS]

President William Ruto says Kenya will no longer allow its mineral wealth to leave the country in raw form, coming days after the controversial saga surrounding Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi.

Ruto defended the government’s decision to suspend Tata Chemicals’ operations at Lake Magadi, Kajiado County, arguing that Kenya has not been receiving sufficient value from the natural resource and that more investors should be given an opportunity to develop the area.

“We want to give five, six or even 10 companies an opportunity to use the resources there to create jobs, value, create wealth and reduce poverty,” Ruto said.

The President made the remarks during a thanksgiving service in South Horr, Samburu County, on Sunday, where he announced a broader government policy aimed at shifting Kenya from exporting raw materials to processing them locally.

“Going into the future, our position as the government. Whether we are talking about Magadi Soda or oil or all our minerals, we have taken the decision that we will no longer export raw materials,” Ruto said.

“We are going to process all minerals available in Kenya.”

The declaration puts the long-running Lake Magadi dispute at the centre of a much wider economic strategy.

Tata Chemicals has been associated with soda ash production at the lake for more than a century. Its Kenyan operations trace their history to 1911, when the Magadi Soda Company began extracting trona from Lake Magadi.

Operations were suspended on July 28, 2026, following a directive from the Ministry of Mining, Blue Economy and Maritime Affairs over compliance and licensing issues.

Ruto has argued that the resource should generate greater benefits for Kenyans through expanded investment, job creation and local value addition.

He accused the existing model of allowing valuable resources to leave the country while Kenya receives less economic benefit than it could.

The President’s comments reflect a longstanding challenge facing Kenya’s extractive sector: how to turn mineral deposits into manufacturing opportunities rather than simply exporting commodities.

Under the proposed approach, minerals such as gold, limestone, iron ore, graphite, titanium and soda ash would be processed or refined in Kenya before being exported.

The government says this would create industrial jobs, strengthen local supply chains and increase the value of exports.

Ruto cited planned cooperation with Nigerian businessman Aliko Dangote as an example of the investment model the government wants to pursue.

He said talks were underway to establish an oil refinery and petrochemical complex in Lamu, alongside efforts to attract investors into mineral refining.

“It is imprudent for any government to export raw materials, create jobs and value in other countries while we have a big population of young people who need jobs,” Ruto said.

World.title: Sifuna condemns abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Busia County Senator Okiya Omtata, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, Bumula MP Jack Wamboka during the burial service of Mary Gorreti Okiya at Kabula, in Bumula on September 5,2026. [Benjamin Sakwa, Standard]

Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna has declared that the fight to restore democracy, media freedom and the rule of law following the abduction of Standard Group Senior Editor will form the centrepiece of the Linda Mwananchi government vowing to defeat President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election.

Sifuna accused President Ruto’s administration of undermining constitutional freedoms and creating an atmosphere of fear, saying the country must be returned to what he described as “the rail of the six important values” enshrined in the Constitution.

Speaking in Bumula Constituency, Kakamega County during the burial of Mary Goreti, the sister of Busia Senator Okiya Omtatah, Sifuna strongly condemned the abduction and arrest of a Standard Group Associate Editor, Alex Kiprotich, arguing that journalists must be protected if Kenya is to remain a democratic country.

“It is impossible that you are driving on the road and you are taken away the way the way the Standard Group Journaliat and Editor Alex Kiprotich was taken. Kenyans want to live in a free country. We do not want to live in fear,” said Sifuna.

He questioned the circumstances surrounding the incident and accused the Government of failing to protect media freedom, adding that the Linda Mwananchi movement would seek to restore institutions and constitutional safeguards if elected to power, arguing that democracy could not survive where citizens, journalists and political opponents lived in fear.

"You cannot just arrest a senior journalist in the middle of the road with police carrying firearms, then you dump him some 500kilometres near the dam, a country cannot have democracy if media is not being respected and allowed to do it's work as per the constitution," said Sifuna.

He said the movement’s agenda was not merely about removing the current administration from power but it's main plan is rebuilding systems of governance around constitutionalism, democracy, individual freedoms and the rule of law.

“With less than 11 months remaining, we want to tell Kenyans that our entire plan is to return this country to the rails of the six important values contained in our Constitution, including democracy, freedom of citizens and the rule of law,” said Sifuna.

Sifuna also accused the Government of using threats against political opponents, saying leaders should not threaten citizens with arrest, expulsion or other forms of intimidation.

He challenged religious leaders to remind politicians that the power to determine the length of a person's life belongs to God.

Sifuna further linked the rule of law to economic growth, warning that investors would be reluctant to establish businesses in Kenya if government could arbitrarily order them to leave.

He said Kenya could not rely on government alone to create employment for millions of young people, arguing that the country needed both local and foreign investors.

“No investor can bring his project to a country where he can wake up one day and the President tells him, ‘Pack and go.’ It is impossible,” Sifuna said.

He argued that investor confidence was also affected by the possibility of commercial disputes being referred to foreign jurisdictions because investors lacked confidence in Kenya’s legal system.

Sifuna also criticised the government over the ongoing nurses and midwives strike, saying the rule of law required the State to honour agreements signed with workers.

World.title: Murkomen reaffirms IG Kanja's command of National Police Service
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Interior Cabinet Secretary Kipchumba Murkomen has reaffirmed that the Inspector General of Police retains constitutional command of the National Police Service, saying the government will continue to respect the independence of the office.

Speaking during the passing-out parade of new Administration Police recruits in Nairobi, Murkomen said the Inspector General has authority over key operational matters within the service, including investigations, promotions and deployment of officers.

“Your Excellency, the Inspector General of Police retains the command of the National Police Service, especially on matters of investigation, promotion and deployment of officers without interference from anyone, including the Cabinet Secretary. We will continue respecting Article 245 of the Constitution,” Murkomen said.

His remarks come amid public debate over the relationship between the Interior Ministry and the National Police Service, particularly allegations that political leaders sometimes issue direct instructions to police officers.

Murkomen dismissed criticism directed at the office of the Inspector General, describing some of its proponents as tribalists and propagandists. He maintained that the Inspector General is carrying out his responsibilities and said he had confidence in the leadership of the police service.

“I have full faith in the IG and believe that every act that is done by the National Police Service is guided by the Constitution,” he said.

The Cabinet Secretary also addressed concerns over his role in directing the police, saying that his responsibility is primarily to provide policy direction rather than interfere with the operational command of the service.

“When required to give policy direction, I always give it in writing and we will continue to support the independence of the National Police Service from external interference,” Murkomen said.

During the ceremony, Murkomen also cautioned the newly graduated officers against corruption, excessive alcohol consumption and conduct that could undermine the reputation of the police service.

He urged the recruits to uphold discipline and protect the dignity of the police uniform, noting that the respect they receive from members of the public would depend largely on their conduct.

The Cabinet Secretary encouraged the officers to understand the responsibility that comes with joining the National Police Service and to discharge their duties within the confines of the Constitution and the law.

The passing-out ceremony marked the entry of the new recruits into the police service that made the CS use the occasion to emphasize professional conduct and respect for the constitutional framework governing policing in Kenya.

World.title: Ruto assures Kajiado residents of full control of Amboseli National Park
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

President William Ruto inspects the Rombo Clusters Irrigation Development Project in Kajiado County on September 3, 2026. [Peterson Githaiga, Standard]

President William Ruto has assured Kajiado residents that they will soon have full control of the management of Amboseli National Park, following his decision to return the park to the county in November 2025.

However, he said the transfer has been temporarily halted by the court.

The President hit out at those he accused of frustrating the move, saying they will be in for a rude shock.

“They took us to court over the Social Health Authority and the Affordable Housing Programme, but these programmes are progressing well. Similarly, I want to assure the people of Kajiado that, before the end of this year, Amboseli will be fully in the hands of Kajiado County,” he said.

Speaking in Kajiado County on Thursday during his development tour, President Ruto reiterated that he will not relent in his pursuit of equity and inclusive development across Kenya, saying that longstanding inequalities have unduly benefited certain regions at the expense of others.

He revealed that the securitisation of the Road Maintenance Levy Fund and the Sports Fund has enabled the Government to clear pending bills in the roads sector and construct 6,000km of new roads, and accelerate the construction of 32 new stadia across the country.

"The Road Maintenance Levy Fund was misused to only build roads in some parts of the country. Those opposing securitisation are unhappy that we are advancing equity," he said.

The President began his tour at Oloirien in Kajiado South Constituency by inspecting progress of the 67km Illasit-Rombo-Chala-Njukini-Taveta road, which is 48 per cent completed.

The Sh9.4 billion project will cut travel time between Kajiado and Taita-Taveta counties from two hours to just 40 minutes, thus easing the movement of goods and people.

The Head of State announced that eight new roads of 220km are being built across Kajiado County at a cost of Sh13 billion to open up the region and improve transport.

The President commissioned Sh221 million Rombo Clusters Irrigation Development Project, which is expected to enhance livelihoods and boost irrigation in the area.

He also inspected progress of the Sh2.2 billion Loitoktok Affordable Housing Project, and laid the foundation stone for the Sh220 million Loitoktok Kenya Medical Training College student hostels with a 580-bed capacity.

At Kimana, in Kajiado South Constituency, President Ruto commissioned the Sh2.7 billion Sultan Hamud-Loitoktok 132kV Transmission Line and Loitoktok Sub-Station, which will serve the residents of Kajiado South and parts of Makueni County.

He inspected construction of the Kimana modern market, which is aimed at giving traders dignified working environment.

At Namanga, Kajiado Central Constituency, the President commissioned the Namanga Sub-Station, a project of the Kenya Electricity Transmission Company (KETRACO), which is part of the 132KV Machakos- Konza-Isinya-Namanga Transmission Project.

Namanga Modern Market, which is under construction at a cost of Sh50 million, will benefit 120 traders at the border town.

In Kajiado town, the President toured the construction of the Kajiado Affordable Housing Project, a Sh473 million investment that will deliver 196 housing units, as well as the 100-unit police housing project at a cost of Sh137 million.

He also inspected the progress of the 580-bed student hostels at Maasai National Polytechnic, which is being built at a cost of KSh216 million.

Ruto ordered the closer of Tata Chemicals, saying the government will identify a new and responsible investor to take over soda ash mining operations at Lake Magadi.

The President said Tata Chemicals had failed to adequately modernise the plant, create sufficient employment opportunities for residents, and deliver meaningful economic benefits to the people of Kenya.

“It is unfair for one company to dominate the ownership and operations of Magadi Soda for years, yet it has done little to improve the factory or create employment opportunities for our youth,” he said at Rombo in Kajiado South Constituency.

He added: “Because they have been unable to do anything meaningful with the plant for more than 100 years, I have directed them to pack up and go.”

The Ministry of Mining suspended the company’s mining operations in July 2026 over concerns relating to regulatory compliance, value addition and licensing.

The ministry also ordered the closure of the company’s depot in Kajiado Town for contravening environmental regulations.

In addition, the company has been unable to reach an agreement with the Kajiado County Government over a land rates dispute following the expiry of its operating licence in 2023.

The plant produces soda ash, or sodium carbonate, a key industrial mineral used in the manufacture of glass, soap and laundry detergents, among other products.

Despite being Africa’s largest soda ash producer, President Ruto noted that the operation had not delivered commensurate benefits to Kenyans over its more than 100-year history, particularly because much of the soda ash produced is exported for processing and consumption in overseas markets.

The Government, the President said, would therefore prioritise an investor capable of modernising the facility, expanding local value addition, creating jobs for young people, and ensuring that Kenya derives greater economic value from its natural resources.

World.title: IG Kanja orders probe into abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor
World.content:
Audio By Vocalize

Standard Group PLC Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich. [Stafford Ondego, Standard]

The Inspector General of Police Douglas Kanja has ordered immediate and transparent investigations into the alleged abduction of Standard Group Associate Editor Alex Kiprotich in Gilgil.

The National Police Service (NPS) said it had taken note of reports that Kiprotich was allegedly kidnapped on Tuesday and had moved swiftly to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

NPS spokesperson Muchiri Nyaga said the police service treats kidnapping and abduction with the utmost seriousness, describing the offences as a threat to the lives, liberty and security of Kenyans.

“The Inspector General of Police has accordingly ordered immediate investigations to determine what transpired, including the identity of the heavily armed individuals reportedly seen ordering occupants out of their vehicle,” Nyaga said in a statement.

The NPS said its Anti-Abduction Unit, established to investigate abductions and disappearances, had taken up the matter and would work to ensure that those responsible are brought to justice.

“We unequivocally condemn any act of kidnapping, abduction, or intimidation intended to interfere with press freedom or any other constitutional right,” Nyaga said.

The police service assured the public that the investigation into the Gilgil incident would be conducted transparently, stressing that no one was above the law.

The development comes amid growing condemnation of Kiprotich’s alleged abduction, with the Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also calling for an immediate investigation.

CPJ Africa Director Angela Quintal described the incident as a “shameful indictment” of the Kenya Kwanza administration, raising concerns over the safety of journalists and press freedom in the country.

“The attempt to forcibly disappear Alex Kiprotich, three days after President William Ruto railed against The Standard Group, reflects the growing dangers that journalists face in Kenya, despite the president’s earlier promise to allow the press to work freely,” Quintal said.

The New York-based press freedom organisation further expressed concern over what it described as an escalation in cases of abductions and enforced disappearances in Kenya.

World.title: Trumpets of reforms blow louder as Kenya marks 16 years under 2010 Constitution
World.content:
The Constitution, Kenyan flag and the National anthem. [PCS]

On Thursday, August 27, a group of people largely composed of the youth gathered under some trees at Jeevanjee Gardens in Nairobi, carrying Kenyans flag, and banners and placards inscribed with "implement the constitution. Kenyans first" words.

These were in protests against what they believed is deliberate failure of those in authority to fully implement the 2010 Constitution.

World.title: Ruto allies hit back at Gachagua over IEBC tender concerns
World.content:
The Kenya Integrated Elections Management System (KIEMS) kit. [File, Standard]

President William Ruto’s allies led by National Assembly Speaker Moses Wetang’ula have launched a scathing attack on former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and the Opposition over their criticism of the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission (IEBC), citing blackmail by the Opposition.

The leaders warned that attempts by politicians to dictate how the electoral agency procures technology and other election materials could undermine public confidence in the 2027 General Election.

World.title: When is the trial operation for Egypt’s high-speed electric train?
World.content:
The head of the National Authority for Tunnels, Tarek Goweily, told the Extra News TV channel that trial operations for the high-speed electric train project will begin in October on the section from Ain Sokhna to 6th of October City.

He explained that the first line of the project, extending from Ain Sokhna to Marsa Matrouh, has reached completion rates between 85 percent and 88 percent.

The start of trial operations on the first section will be followed by gradual testing of the remaining sections of the line, Goweily added.

The implementation of the operational timeline depends on the completion of testing and obtaining international safety certification, he said, in addition to finalizing the training and qualification of the operating crews, including drivers and technicians

The German company responsible for operating the train began training the operating crews in February and is expected to complete this phase by February or March, thus preparing the crews to manage and operate the system.

The project’s impact extends beyond simply developing transportation, he said, explaining that the high-speed electric train will affect the urban and industrial communities along its route by contributing to the development of new areas and boosting investment and population growth along the line.

Goweily viewed the high-speed electric train project to be one of the most important pillars of modern transportation in Egypt, given its role in supporting the new urban and industrial areas along its route.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: This city is one of the world’s most important AI hubs. It’s not where you’d expect
World.content:
Toronto, Canada — Geoffrey Hinton, a Nobel Prize-winning computer scientist, took a leap in the 1980s — leaving a well-funded post at Carnegie Mellon University to pursue a little-studied area of machine learning research at the University of Toronto.

Four decades later, Hinton and that research paved the way for how modern AI systems function, all while changing the face of the Canadian city.

Silicon Valley is the beating heart of the tech industry, but a thriving AI ecosystem has developed around Hinton in Toronto.

Tech giants including Google, Nvidia, Meta and Microsoft, along with a slew of startups, have opened offices or research labs within miles of the University of Toronto. Even non-tech firms are now eyeing the city for its AI expertise: pharmaceutical company Sanofi this year announced a nearly $300 million investment in a Toronto AI Center of Excellence.

Toronto now boasts the world’s third best tech talent market, ahead of New York City but behind San Francisco and Seattle, according to an annual analysis by commercial real estate firm CBRE. That’s thanks to educational institutions like the University of Toronto, and public-private research institutes like the Vector Institute, which Hinton co-founded to help commercialize AI breakthroughs.

Cohere co-founder Nick Frosst, and Radical Ventures co-founder Jordan Jacobs and Geoffrey Hinton. CNN

“I was lucky because very few people were working on this 20 years ago, and so smart young students would come to Toronto … and they’ve now turned into a whole generation of AI leaders,” Hinton told CNN in an interview in Toronto.

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney is now aiming to boost the local AI ecosystem with a national AI strategy that includes more than $2 billion in spending on AI research, education and efforts to increase adoption, as well as new safety guardrails.

Toronto’s growing AI power comes as trade relations between the United States and Canada have deteriorated. A trade war has exploded in recent weeks, with Canadian officials seeking to protect the country’s industries. It may be yet another reason why the country’s tech investments are important.

“I don’t think we can afford for Canada to get all this technology from the States or from China,” Hinton said.

‘We liked it here’

Among Toronto’s new generation of AI leaders is Nick Frosst, who studied under Hinton at the University of Toronto and was one of the first hires at Hinton’s Google AI lab in Toronto in 2017. Frosst then went on to co-found the $7 billion enterprise AI firm Cohere.

Frosst decided against the traditional route of moving to Silicon Valley to start his company for a simple reason: He likes living in Toronto.

“There’s a great tech ecosystem, there’s also a great arts community, there’s also a great academic community, there’s a great business community,” said Frosst, who also fronts Toronto-based indie rock band Good Kid. “All of it is here.”

Many other founders in the city feel the same.

An aerial view of Toronto on May 27, 2026. Nadtochiy/iStockphoto/Getty Images

Gennady Pekhimenko, who sold his startup CentML to Nvidia last year and now serves as senior director of AI software for the chip giant, said Toronto’s international food scene serves as a useful recruiting tool for out-of-town talent.

Tomi Poutanen, founder and CEO at AI healthcare firm Signal 1, mentioned the benefits of Canada’s healthcare system and Toronto’s famed “Hospital Row.”

Hinton added that, unlike the United States under the Trump administration, Canada welcomes immigration, which tech firms have long relied on as a talent pipeline. One of Pekhimenko’s first hires at CentML was an Amazon engineer who was unable to renew his H1-B visa to stay in the United States. He could, however, get a Canadian work permit.

Friendlier immigration policies make it easier to attract international talent who likely have a knack for thinking about how to serve a global market, said Jordan Jacobs, managing partner at investment firm Radical Ventures.

Toronto also benefits from close proximity to major markets such as New York, Washington, DC and Chicago.

“You can get on a flight that’s 90 minutes long and reach 200 million people,” Jacobs said.

Building outside the Silicon Valley bubble

San Francisco is still the undisputed center of the tech industry, with around 20% more tech workers than Toronto, according to CBRE. Tech firms are also making a big push back into the city center after many dispersed during the Covid-19 pandemic.

Still, builders in Toronto’s AI ecosystem say they benefit from being headquartered outside the Silicon Valley bubble.

The cost of living is generally less expensive in Toronto, thanks in part to lower home prices, socialized healthcare and good public schools, local founders say. That means high-quality talent can come cheaper, too. (Although many Toronto AI firms also have a California presence.)

Toronto also doesn’t struggle with high staff turnover rates in the same way as San Francisco, according to Ray Reddy, a former vice president of Shopify who is building a new startup in stealth.

In Silicon Valley, “even people who are very mission driven are always looking over their shoulder, like, is there something better there?” said Reddy, who previously worked at Google’s Silicon Valley headquarters.

San Francisco is often characterized by its hype and unbridled enthusiasm around AI, but Frosst says there’s an openness to friendly debate in Toronto that feels unique.

Cohere co-founder Nick Frosst. CNN

Frosst offered his own relationship with friend and mentor Hinton as an example: the two have long disagreed on core questions, like whether building AI constitutes creating a new type of being or simply a tool. But they still regularly play chess together, and Frosst will bring up the debate in hopes of throwing Hinton off. (Hinton’s game is normally undeterred, he said.)

“I think it goes back to … Toronto and Canada not being a monoculture,” Frosst said. “It isn’t just tech workers here, it’s a bit of everything, and I think that leads to innovation, it leads to people thinking about what isn’t popular.”

Canada’s AI opportunity

Already, Canada’s digital sector contributes more than $140 billion to the country’s GDP, according to the government. And the local AI ecosystem has other benefits for the country, according to Hinton.

“If AI causes a lot of unemployment, we’ll want the profits that are made by replacing workers to stay within Canada, so they can be taxed within Canada to support the replaced workers,” Hinton said.

Geoffrey Hinton interviewed by CNN’s Clare Duffy in Toronto. CNN

What’s more, governments and companies around the world are increasingly looking to diversify away from buying advanced technology solely from the United States. That’s created an “ongoing advantage” for Canada-based firms, Frosst said.

Cohere received an influx of new customer inquiries after the White House in June put export controls on Anthropic’s advanced AI models.

“The flag of Canada is one that builds trust,” Frosst said. “We’re looking to increase the resiliency and independence of anybody who uses our technology, and broadly I think Canada, as a country, is interested in doing the same for all of our partners.”

And while the most well-known tech investors are in Silicon Valley, being located elsewhere is no longer an obstacle to fundraising.

Raquel Urtasun left her role running Uber’s autonomous driving lab in Toronto to start self-driving semitruck company Waabi five years ago. She founded the company in Toronto, although it’s piloting its trucks mainly in the American southwest. Earlier this year, Waabi raised a more than $1 billion Series C, the largest funding round in Canadian history.

“At the end of the day, what attracts investors is: what is going to be the top company that is leading a massive market,” Urtasun told CNN. “Whether we are in Canada, whether we are in the Silicon Valley, it didn’t really matter.”

World.title: Cubans are coming up with creative ways to generate power when their island has almost none left
World.content:
Havana — How to conserve cellphone battery when recharging options are scarce; how to preserve food when the fridge isn’t working; how to cope with the heat when air-conditioners aren’t an option; how to generate power when the whole country has almost none left.

These are the sort of tutorials that have made the Instagram feed of influencer Dayán Marrero indispensable to many Cubans as they try to adapt to the rolling electricity blackouts and fuel shortages that are increasingly part of everyday life on this Caribbean island.

As the US-imposed oil blockade that is worsening the situation bites ever deeper, Marrero and his compatriots are having to get creative. Farmers pasteurize milk over charcoal fires; commuters ride solar-powered Chinese tricycles; tour guides grind coffee by hand for the vanishingly few visitors that remain.

Like his fellow countrymen, Marrero — a third-year computer science student at the Agrarian University of Havana — has become adept at adapting.

Dayán Marrero shows an improvised cell phone stand. CNN

Previously, the idea that he might become a content creator had “never even crossed my mind,” yet here he is, in the living room of his home in Caraballo, a former sugar town, promoting the latest must-have items, such as a rechargeable fan that also provides light while he records his videos. And he is successful; one of his most popular posts, a tutorial on how to build an antenna to pick up the mobile network’s elusive internet signal, is approaching 800,000 views.

Still, if he is to reach his next goal as an influencer — establishing a presence on TikTok — he will have to get even more creative, as use of the app is restricted by US sanctions.

At his home, Cuban Dayán Marrero explains some of the measures he takes to deal with the blackouts on the island. CNN

Tourism without tourists

Cubans have known for decades what it is like to live without abundance and — while it is true that things have worsened markedly since the US blockade and the subsequent loss of energy imports from both Venezuela and Mexico — people like Marrero are showing there is no scarcity of creativity or resilience on this island.

At 57 years old, Osiris Hernández has spent more than half his life as a tour guide in Viñales, Cuba’s ecotourism mecca. He works at one of Viñales’ main tourist attractions, the Indian Cave, where he operates a boat that carries visitors through waters deep underground and ends its journey with a spectacular view as it emerges from darkness into light.

The streets in Viñales are clean, signs advertising rooms for visitors are everywhere and there is even a market where artisans sell their wares. There’s just one problem: There are almost no tourists.

Tourism on the island fell 62 percent from January to July compared with the same period last year, according to official figures.

When Hernández hears a single Chinese tourist has arrived, a smile crosses his face. He is eager to please the few who, despite it all, still come to visit. He has set up rooms in his own home to accommodate them and cooks their food over charcoal, grinds coffee by hand and passes around the same type of rechargeable, light-providing fan that Marrero advertises on his Instagram.

He tells CNN his goal is to provide quality service, whatever is happening with the electricity. Even when the power is down, he says, he has an inverter that converts energy from solar panels for use in household appliances. It allows him to keep at least one freezer running.

An empty cafe at the Old Square, once one of the most popular tourist spots in Old Havana, as US sanctions have decimated tourism, in Havana, Cuba, on June 8, 2026. Norlys Perez/Reuters

Pasteurizing with charcoal

On the outskirts of Viñales is El Olivo agroecological farm, where Osnel Corrales and his family have installed solar panels and batteries to help them produce dairy.

Although they have an industrial generator, they do not have fuel, or at least not enough. On the day CNN visited, they were producing yogurt — pasteurizing the milk first by heating it over charcoal, then cooling it in vats using electricity generated by solar panels.

The farm has a restaurant specializing in Mediterranean food, but there are no customers. Yet they continue operating — the cows have to be milked no matter what — and produce cheese in addition to their yogurt, which they distribute through a branded store in Viñales and to customers in Havana.

Still, the lack of tourists means demand for their award-winning produce has dropped severely and given the shortage of fuel it’s not easy for the few tourists still arriving in Cuba to visit the farm.

People ride an electric tricycle, one of the few modes of transportation still functioning, in Havana, Cuba, July 14, 2026. Norlys Perez/Reuters

A glimmer of light on the roads

The lack of fuel, however, does have one silver lining: Traffic congestion in Havana feels like a thing of the past.

With buses in short supply, a growing fleet of privately operated solar-powered electric tricycles provide public transportation for the city’s nearly 1.8 million residents.

Augusto operates one of the latest-generation models. Not only does it have a small fuel-powered engine but, more importantly, it has three rechargeable batteries. He can connect these to the power grid — when there is electricity — or charge them via the solar panel that serves as the vehicle’s roof.

Augusto, who has spent years driving taxis, rents the tricycle for about 9,000 Cuban pesos ($15) per day, whether or not he has passengers.

It can carry up to six passengers at a time, in a system in which operators have strategically divided the city into routes that take into account the distance they can travel based on battery range and the available charge level.

With or without fuel, Augusto manages to help his fellow Cubans get around every day by relying on a dynamic that is long familiar on the island. Augusto, Marrero, Hernández and countless others have little choice but to figure things out which, in Cuban parlance, means overcoming whatever obstacle is placed in their way.

World.title: At least 11 killed after avalanche hits climbers in Russia’s North Caucasus
World.content:
Reuters — At least 11 people were killed and six ​others injured after an At least 11 people were killed and six ​others injured after an avalanche ‌struck a group of climbers in Russia’s Kabardino-Balkaria region in the ​North Caucasus, local emergency ​services said.

The avalanche swept down ⁠Mount Mizhirgi, one of the ​highest peaks in Russia’s North ​Caucasus, at around 5 p.m. local time (9 a.m. EST) on Sunday, hitting a ​group of 33 climbers.

As of ​9 a.m. local time on Monday, 10 ‌climbers ⁠had made their own way down the mountain, while the fate of six others ​remained unknown, ​emergency ⁠services said.

More than 50 emergency workers were involved ​in the search and ​rescue ⁠operation, but efforts were being hampered by difficult terrain and ⁠a ​high risk of ​further avalanches, they said.

World.title: Amina Orfi wins London Squash Classic championship
World.content:
Egyptian squash champion Amina Orfi won the London Squash Classic championship on Sunday after defeating England’s Georgina Kennedy in the final.

Orfi defeated Kennedy 3-0 in the final – scoring 11-6, 11-8, and 11-2.

The tournament featured an array of top Egyptian squash players, including world number one Hania al-Hammamy, world number two Amina Orfi (the defending champion), Salma Hany, Farida Mohamed, Sana Ibrahim, Zeina Mekkiwy, Mariam Metwally, Nardine Gerges, Hana Ramadan, and Nour Heikal.

Several Egyptian players also participated in the men’s competition, including Ali Aboul-Enein, Youssef Soliman, Mohamed Abouelghar, Karim al-Torky, and Mostafa el-Sirty, facing stiff competition from some of the world’s best players.

World.title: Amr Adib calls for urgent decision to regulate tree cutting in Egypt
World.content:
TV host Amr Adib proposed issuing an urgent decision to halt tree cutting for one or two months to reorganize the issue and establish clear regulations governing removal operations.

During his program “al-Hekaya” (The Story) on Sunday evening, Adib emphasized that the widespread public opposition to tree cutting necessitates a review of current practices and the exhaustion of alternatives before any tree is removed.

He did not anticipate the issue of tree cutting to become such a significant public concern, noting that the public reaction has transcended being a passing trend and is now clearly a broader stance.

Recent events reflect the deep connection citizens have with green spaces, pointing out that the rejection to tree cutting is not limited to any particular social or educational group, but rather encompasses various segments of society, whether motivated by environmental concerns or the desire to benefit from shade.

Regulations required

Adib therefore called for a temporary freeze on tree cutting operations until a clear framework is established for addressing this issue.

He said that he was unaware of whether the law prohibits tree cutting, but noted that this ongoing issue reveals a need for clearer regulations.

Adib also called for first verifying compelling reasons for tree removal and exploring possible alternatives before any cutting decision is made.

He also expressed surprise at the lack of clear explanations being provided to the public regarding the tree cutting operations, particularly on Arab League Street, which he sees no clear justification for.

The TV host addressed a response about cutting down trees for the purpose of exporting timber, noting that the financial return – however large – does not justify disregarding the value of trees.

Exporting these quantities of timber will not make a significant difference to the national economy, he added.

Abib explained that he had received numerous messages from citizens regarding incidents of tree cutting or pruning in various areas, which he believes reflects the degree of public concern about the issue.

Growing public awareness and rejection of tree cutting necessitates a review of the related decisions, he said, warning that the loss of trees is not easily compensated for.

World.title: Microbus driver arrested for ‘Long Live Israel’ prank in Imbaba
World.content:
Giza security forces revealed the exact circumstances behind controversial videos shared online showing a microbus in the Giza Governorate displaying offensive banners, including “Long Live Israel”.

The security forces successfully identified the vehicle and arrested its driver, a resident of al-Warraq district.

During questioning, the suspect confessed to committing the act on September 4 while on tour in Imbaba district.

He explained that he used flashlights equipped with LED screens, controlled via a mobile phone application, to display the messages, claiming it was a prank on his fellow drivers in the parking lot.

The vehicle was impounded, a report was filed, and the suspect was referred to the Public Prosecution for further investigation.

Edited translation from Al-Masry Al-Youm

World.title: Audio recordings of Muslim Brotherhood leaked on Egyptian TV
World.content:
Egyptian media host Amr Adib and writer Abdel-Rahim Ali broadcasted audio recordings of Muslim Brotherhood leaders during Sunday’s episode of the “al-Hekaya” (The Story) show on MBC Egypt.

The recordings allegedly reveal plans for a new revolution and the formation of a government in exile, RT reported on Sunday.

According to Ali – a writer and researcher specializing in Islamist groups – the leaks document meetings between leaders and members of the Muslim Brotherhood and Egyptian opposition forces abroad.

These meetings reportedly included discussions about instigating political change in Egypt and preparing for what they called a new “revolution,” followed by an agreement on the form of the constitution and the political system of the country.

Ali explained that the obtained recordings total around 30 hours, but could not be broadcast in their entirety for security reasons.

He indicated that these meetings raised the idea of ​​a “civil state” as a formula to avoid early clashes with state institutions and religious movements.

Ali pointed out that the discussions were not limited to preparing a political project.

According to the recordings he presented, they also included discussions about forming a political entity abroad and a government-in-exile that could manage the transitional period should a change occur within Egypt.

According to Ali, these recordings are part of what views to be organized moves to reorganize the ranks of the Muslim Brotherhood and its allies abroad, and to prepare political alternatives that can be used in the event of unrest or a change in the internal Egyptian scene.

World.title: Liberia: Fear At Monrovia City Court As LNP Officer Fires Tear Gas Just Before Ex-VP Taylor’s Expected Appearance
World.content:
Monrovia-Fear and confusion briefly gripped the courtyard of the Monrovia City Court on Monday after a Liberia National Police officer unexpectedly discharged a canister of tear gas as police were lined up in anticipation of the arrival of former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The incident occurred at a particularly sensitive moment, with security personnel positioned at the court and several journalists, lawyers and members of the public gathered in anticipation of Madam Taylor’s expected appearance for a preliminary examination into allegations of money laundering and drug trafficking.

But before the former Vice President arrived, hdefencense lawyers withdrew their request for the preliminary examination, meaning Madam Taylor did not appear at the court before the unexpected tear-gas incident.

The sudden discharge immediately triggered alarm among those within the court’s compound, with questions arising over what prompted the officer to release the chemical agent at a time when heightened security was already in place for the expected arrival of the former Vice President.

A Liberian journalist, Saah Augustine Mbayoh, was nearly hit by the tear gas as the officer discharged it. A FrontPageAfrica Judicial Reporter was also in the immediate vicinity when the incident occurred.

The officer responsible for firing the tear gas has not yet been identified.

What makes the incident particularly concerning is that, moments before the tear gas was discharged, FrontPageAfrica observed the officer dropping his baton and face shield twice while standing in the police formation.

It remains unclear whether the officer was experiencing a medical problem, disorientation or another difficulty at the time. The Liberia National Police has yet to publicly explain what led to the officer’s actions or whether any intervention was made after his apparent difficulty handling his equipment.

There is no evidence at this point linking the tear-gas discharge to Madam Taylor’s case or her expected appearance, but the timing of the incident—while police were awaiting her arrival—heightened fear and uncertainty among those gathered at the court.

The incident has also raised questions about police preparedness, the handling of security personnel assigned to sensitive court proceedings, and the circumstances under which tear gas was deployed inside a crowded judicial compound.

The Liberia National Police is yet to state whether the officer has been identified, whether an investigation has been launched, or whether disciplinary or medical action has been taken.

FrontPageAfrica is continuing to establish the circumstances surrounding the incident.

World.title: Liberia: Taylor Lawyers Withdraw Request for Preliminary Examination in Drug Trafficking, Money Laundering Case
World.content:
Monrovia-Lawyers representing former Vice President Jewel Howard Taylor have withdrawn their request for a preliminary examination of evidence in the State’s alleged money laundering and drug trafficking case against their client.

By Willie N. Tokpah

The decision was made Monday at the Monrovia City Court, where Magistrate Ben Barco granted the defense request and instructed the Clerk of Court to formally communicate the latest development to Criminal Court “C,” where the case is pending.

The defense’s request for a preliminary examination was filed pursuant to Liberia’s Criminal Procedure Law, which provides defendants with the right to seek such an examination.

The law also permits a party to withdraw the request.

The withdrawal comes amid controversy surrounding an audio recording introduced by the prosecution’s first witness, Raphel Wilson.

Defense lawyers objected to the recording being admitted into evidence as part of the State’s case.

The defence has yet to publicly disclose the full reasoning behind its decision to withdraw its request for a preliminary examination.

One of Taylor’s lawyers, Cllr. Finley Kangar, told FrontPageAfrica that the defense team is expected to make its next decision within the hour.

The latest development adds another twist to the closely watched proceedings involving the former Vice President, as both sides continue to contest the audio recording evidence being presented before the court.

FrontPageAfrica is continuing to follow developments from the court and will provide updates as they emerge.

World.title: Guus Kouwenhoven, Dutch Businessman Whose Fortunes Rose and Fell With Charles Taylor’s Liberia, Dies at 84
World.content:
Monrovia – Guus Kouwenhoven, the Dutch entrepreneur whose timber empire made him one of Liberia’s most powerful foreign businessmen — and whose alleged arms-trafficking ties to former President Charles Taylor made him one of its most notorious — died Sunday evening, September 6, surrounded by family, according to a statement released by his relatives. He was 84.

“The Kouwenhoven family lost our father, husband and leader,” the family wrote, adding that he “left surrounded by family and at peace” and asking for prayers and continued kindness “during this time.”

Kouwenhoven, born February 15, 1942, in ‘s-Hertogenbosch, Netherlands, first arrived in Liberia in the late 1980s, taking over management of the Africa Hotel outside Monrovia. He went on to build one of the country’s largest logging operations, heading the Oriental Timber Corporation and later the Royal Timber Corporation, and by the late 1990s was widely regarded as Liberia’s most influential foreign timber trader.

Ties to Charles Taylor

Kouwenhoven’s business rise coincided with the ascent of Charles Taylor, whose 1997–2003 presidency plunged Liberia into renewed civil war. A United Nations Panel of Experts report on Sierra Leone in 2000 placed Kouwenhoven within Taylor’s inner circle, alleging he handled logistics for arms shipments that reached Taylor’s forces and allied militias — weapons investigators linked to atrocities against civilians during the conflict. Kouwenhoven’s timber concessions, according to UN investigators, doubled as cover for weapons imports routed through associates including Soviet-era arms dealer Viktor Bout.

The Sanctions and Legal Saga

The UN placed Kouwenhoven on an international travel ban list in 2001, and in 2003 the Security Council imposed sanctions on Liberian timber exports specifically because revenue from the trade — much of it tied to Kouwenhoven’s companies — was believed to be funding the war.

He was arrested in the Netherlands in March 2005 and tried in The Hague on charges of arms smuggling and complicity in war crimes. A 2006 verdict convicted him of arms smuggling, sentencing him to eight years, though judges stopped short of a war-crimes conviction. An appeals court fully acquitted him in 2008, only for the Dutch Supreme Court to order a retrial in 2010, citing errors in how witness testimony had been handled.

The case dragged on for years amid difficulty securing witnesses. Kouwenhoven fled to South Africa in December 2016 citing medical grounds, but was arrested there within the year. In 2017, Dutch courts convicted him on both arms-smuggling and war-crimes counts, sentencing him to 19 years — a ruling rights group Global Witness called a landmark precedent for holding conflict-resource traders accountable. Taylor himself was convicted separately in 2012 by the Special Court for Sierra Leone and sentenced to 50 years, a sentence he is still serving.

Legacy

To supporters and business associates in Liberia, Kouwenhoven — known widely as “Mr. Gus” — was remembered as a formidable dealmaker who built one of the country’s largest private enterprises. To human rights investigators, he remained emblematic of the “blood timber” trade that helped sustain one of West Africa’s bloodiest conflicts.

He is survived by his wife and children. Funeral arrangements have not yet been announced.

World.title: Liberia: What Comes Next for Jewel Howard-Taylor
World.content:
MONROVIA – Eleven days after she was led into Monrovia Central Prison, Jewel Howard-Taylor went home on Thursday — but not to freedom. Under an order signed by Criminal Court “C” Judge Ousman F. Feika, the woman who once stood a heartbeat from the Liberian presidency now lives under a regime nearly as controlled as the one she left. A single-family caregiver has been designated to look after her. Police are posted at the gate around the clock. A visitor’s log, modeled on the one the Bureau of Corrections keeps at the Central Prison, tracks everyone who comes and goes. She cannot step outside the compound on Tubman Boulevard in Sinkor without the court’s advance approval — and even then, only for a hospital appointment.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

It is not vindication, and Judge Feika was careful to say so. The order releasing Howard-Taylor from pre-trial detention on medical grounds does not touch the case underneath it. Liberia’s first and only female vice president still faces trafficking, money-laundering and conspiracy charges connected to what prosecutors have called the largest cocaine seizure in the country’s history. What changed this week is where she waits for trial, not what she will have to answer when it begins.

HOW THE CASE REACHED THIS POINT

The case traces back to July 21, 2026, when Liberian authorities intercepted nearly four metric tons of cocaine in Duazon, east of Monrovia — a haul officials valued at roughly $317 million and described as one of the largest narcotics seizures in the country’s history. It followed a smaller but still significant bust in June, when 237.6 kilograms of cocaine worth more than $19 million was seized at Roberts International Airport. Taken together, investigators say, the two seizures pointed to a sustained trafficking corridor running through Liberia — consistent with warnings from the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime that West Africa has become a key transit route for South American cocaine bound for European markets. The July bust also implicated senior police and intelligence officials, widening the investigation well beyond the traffickers caught with the drugs.

Howard-Taylor was arrested on August 19 at Roberts International Airport. Her lawyers say she was intercepted while on her way to meet them, despite having agreed to report voluntarily to police headquarters — a procedural grievance that has since become part of her defense. A magistrate at the Monrovia City Court initially handled her first appearance, but on August 26, Stipendiary Magistrate Ben Barco ruled that his court had no authority over charges this serious and denied her request for humanitarian home confinement, finding medical assessments showed her “sufficiently stable” to remain in custody. She was transferred to Monrovia Central Prison. Her defense team then carried the fight to Criminal Court “C”, the tribunal with jurisdiction over major felonies, where a preliminary examination opened in early September — pushed back a day at the defense’s request so she could be seen by her personal physician. Days later, Judge Feika granted the compassionate release that now has her under house arrest rather than behind prison walls.

AT A GLANCE — CONDITIONS OF RELEASE

Travel documents surrendered to the Sheriff of the Court immediately upon release.

Confined to her Tubman Boulevard residence in Sinkor, under a single court-approved family caregiver.

Access limited to Howard-Taylor, her caregiver and her physician or physician’s assistant.

A visitor-logging system modeled on the Bureau of Corrections’ protocol at Monrovia Central Prison.

No movement outside the residence except by court order or for an approved medical appointment.

Round-the-clock security or police protection maintained at the residence, with a full visitor log kept on hand.

WHO IS JEWEL HOWARD-TAYLOR

Long before this case, Howard-Taylor had one of the more unusual résumés in Liberian politics. Born in Zorzor in 1963, she married Charles Taylor in 1997 and served as First Lady during his presidency until 2003. She later earned a law degree from the University of Liberia, was elected to the Senate representing Bong County in 2005 as a member of the National Patriotic Party, and chaired the Senate’s committee on health, gender and children’s affairs. In 2017, George Weah picked her as his running mate on the Coalition for Democratic Change ticket, and when the coalition won that December, she became Liberia’s first female vice president, serving from January 2018 until January 2024. More recently, she has clashed with the NPP’s current leadership over her endorsement choices in Liberian politics — friction her supporters now point to as part of the backdrop for a prosecution she calls politically motivated.

THE CASE PROSECUTORS SAY THEY HAVE

According to the writ of arrest, dated August 25 and signed by Clerk of Court Abel Kalay, the state’s narrative begins in 2021, when a man named Sheikh Bashiru Kante allegedly brought two foreign nationals — Taras Zadereiko, a Ukrainian known as “Tony,” and Mihovil Vrovac, a Croatian known as “Michael” — into Liberia to establish a cocaine pipeline between West Africa and Europe. The following year, Kante is accused of introducing the pair to Howard-Taylor at her residence in Congo Town, after which she was allegedly invited to Dubai to meet Nikola Ivancic, a Croatian the writ describes as the ring’s leader. There, prosecutors allege, she received $45,000 in cash. Investigators say further payments followed — $75,000 funneled through the Jewel Star Fish Foundation, a nonprofit associated with her name, and an additional $15,000 delivered through Kante as recently as this past August. On those allegations, she has been charged with importation and exportation of controlled drugs, unlicensed trafficking, criminal conspiracy, facilitation, solicitation and money laundering. Ivancic, Vrovac and Zadereiko have all been charged in absentia; none is currently in Liberian custody. Howard-Taylor and her attorneys — Laveli Supuwood, Kabineh Ja’neh and Finley Y. Karngar — have denied every allegation.

WHERE THE GOVERNMENT’S CASE LOOKS STRONG

Prosecutors are not starting from an informant’s tip; they are starting from four tons of cocaine physically seized and forensically verifiable, which gives the broader investigation a foundation that does not depend on anyone’s credibility. The alleged financial trail is also, in principle, the kind of evidence that outlasts witnesses: if the $75,000 said to have moved through the Jewel Star Fish Foundation left a documentary record — bank deposits, wire transfers, foundation filings — that evidence can be examined independently of what any single witness says on the stand, and money moved through a registered nonprofit is a classic and traceable laundering pattern once investigators have the paperwork. The case also has genuine international reach: two people were captured at the scene of the July seizure carrying Spanish-Colombian and Serbian passports, and three more suspects tied to the alleged Liberia-to-Europe pipeline are Croatian and Ukrainian nationals — a spread that has already drawn the attention of transnational-crime watchdogs and gives Liberian investigators avenues to seek corroboration, such as banking or travel records, from foreign counterparts that a purely domestic case would not have.

WHERE THE GOVERNMENT’S CASE LOOKS SHAKY

The prosecution’s most serious structural weakness is that its alleged ringleader and two of the alleged cash conduits — Ivancic, Vrovac and Zadereiko — are being charged in absentia and are not in Liberian custody. That means the version of events tying Howard-Taylor to a Dubai cash handoff and a foreign trafficking ring rest, for now, on the writ’s narrative and on Kante as the connecting figure, rather than on live testimony from the men prosecutors say ran the operation and paid her. Her lawyers have already signaled how they intend to attack that gap: they argue that meeting foreign businesspeople and traveling abroad were the ordinary furniture of high office, and that a writ describing contacts made “as part of her constitutional responsibilities” does not, by itself, establish criminal intent.
