The case has also stumbled procedurally in ways that hand the defense real ammunition — an initial prosecution at a court later found to lack jurisdiction, a magistrate’s ruling reversed only after Howard-Taylor was sent to Central Prison, and her lawyers’ still-unresolved claim that she was intercepted en route to meet counsel rather than formally summoned. Her legal team has separately alleged, without offering documentation, that government actors might manipulate audio or video evidence using artificial intelligence — an unproven claim, but one that puts prosecutors on notice that any recorded evidence they introduce will be contested on authenticity, not just content. And the timing lands amid a real rupture between Howard-Taylor and the National Patriotic Party’s current leadership over her recent political endorsements, which gives her camp a ready-made political-persecution narrative that will need to be answered with evidence in a courtroom, not simply asserted in the press.

WHAT HAPPENS NEXT

The house-arrest order is not the end of anything; it is a pause inside a case that is still being built. A grand jury term is expected later this month, and it is the grand jury’s indictment — not Thursday’s ruling — that will determine whether the charges against Howard-Taylor formally proceed to trial. Judge Feika still has a stack of preliminary motions to rule on, including defense requests to quash the arrest writ, a habeas corpus petition, a bail motion despite prosecutors’ argument that the charges are non-bailable, and a motion to suppress evidence. Until those questions are resolved, Howard-Taylor remains, in effect, a prisoner of her own address: watched around the clock, barred from travel, and permitted outside her gate only for the medical care that got her out of Central Prison in the first place.

However, the case resolves, it has already become a test of more than one defendant’s guilt. It is a test of whether Liberia’s judiciary can handle a politically connected defendant the same way it would handle anyone else, at a moment when the underlying seizure has implicated police and intelligence officials of its own. And it is a test, watched well beyond Liberia’s borders, of whether a small West African state sitting astride a major cocaine corridor can make a trafficking case against a former head of the executive branch stick — not just on the strength of a writ, but on evidence that survives cross-examination once the grand jury term begins.

World.title: Liberia: Are The Courts Quietly Stalling The Anti-Corruption Commission’s Cases?
World.content:
A Margibi County corruption case — backed by a paper trail of prosecutors asking, three separate times, for a trial date — is raising hard questions about whether Liberia’s courts are giving the LACC’s cases a fair shot at trial, or letting them run out the clock.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

MONROVIA — Picture a prosecutor who has done everything the law asks. The evidence is gathered, the witnesses are lined up, and three times over as many court terms, someone from the prosecution’s side has written to a judge, on paper, asking for a trial date. And still, no trial happens — not because anyone dropped the ball, but because the docket simply never made room. Then the defendant’s lawyers show up and ask the court to throw the whole case out, because too much time has passed.



That is not hypothetical. It is, according to court filings reviewed for this piece, roughly what has played out in a Margibi County corruption case — and it is the latest in a pattern that has some in Liberia’s anti-corruption community asking a blunter question: is the court system, whether by neglect or by design, making it structurally impossible for the LACC to actually get its cases heard?



Section 18.2 of the Criminal Procedure Law is blunt about what’s supposed to happen when a trial doesn’t start on time. “Unless good cause is shown,” it reads, “a court shall dismiss an indictment if the defendant is not tried during the next succeeding term after the finding of the indictment.” Not “may.” Shall. Once the clock runs out, dismissal is close to automatic.



Nobody serious argues with the principle behind that. A person charged with a crime shouldn’t have to live under that cloud forever while the state drags its feet. But a harder question is creeping into Liberia’s anti-corruption cases: what happens when it isn’t the state dragging its feet at all — when prosecutors keep asking for a court date, in writing, and the court is simply too busy with other matters to give them one?



A paper trail, not just a pattern



This isn’t the first time the question has come up. In Criminal Court “C” of the First Judicial Circuit in Montserrado County, corruption cases against former NOCAL head Rustolyn Suacoco Dennis and former Bureau of State Enterprises head Arthur Massaquoi reportedly sat untouched for terms at a time while the docket was consumed by the Financial Intelligence Agency’s case against Samuel Tweh and the Finda Bondoo matter. Both cases were eventually dismissed.



What makes the Margibi case different is that it doesn’t rest on “reportedly.” It’s in the file.



The defendants — Patrick Tarnue Worzie, former head of the Liberia Refugee Repatriation and Resettlement Commission, along with Alieu Fofana, Joseph Wea and Jeredine Kolleh — were indicted back in the May 2025 term, in Montserrado County, on charges including economic sabotage, theft of property and tampering with public records. The case moved to the 13th Judicial Circuit in Margibi County in February 2026.



From there, the record tells a fairly clear story



– On May 11, 2026, Margibi County Attorney H. Deddeh Jomah Wilson asked the court, in a formal filing, to put the case on the docket for that term. Everyone was ready, the filing said — the witnesses, the evidence, all of it.

– Two weeks later, on May 25, the LACC’s chief prosecutor, Bobby F. W. Livingstone, wrote directly to the presiding judge with the same request.

– When that term came and went too, Livingstone tried again on August 10, this time addressing a new judge who’d since taken over the case, asking that it finally be prioritized.



Three requests. Three different points in the calendar. And on September 3, with the case still untried, the defense filed to have it dismissed — pointing to five straight terms, from May 2025 through August 2026, in which no trial ever happened.



Read those two facts side by side and the dismissal motion looks less like a case of prosecutorial neglect and more like a test of what “good cause” is supposed to mean when the neglect, if there was any, sat somewhere else.



Why “without prejudice” doesn’t make this a non-issue



It’s worth being precise here. When cases like Massaquoi’s or Dennis’ are dismissed under Section 18.2, it’s typically without prejudice — meaning the state can, in theory, refile. Section 18.3 says as much: a dismissal entered before a jury is sworn, or before evidence starts in a bench trial, doesn’t close the door on prosecution for good.



But “the door isn’t closed” is cold comfort when you consider what it actually costs to get a corruption case to the indictment stage in the first place — months of investigators pulling financial records, tracing transactions, interviewing witnesses, building a paper trail solid enough to survive a courtroom. Refiling doesn’t mean starting from a clean slate at no cost. It means doing a lot of that work over again, on an agency that’s already stretched thin.



And there’s a cost that doesn’t show up in any budget line at all: what the public makes of watching case after case vanish before a single witness testifies.



What the Supreme Court has already said about this



Liberia’s own case law hints at how this should be handled. In Judge Ware et al. v. Republic of Liberia, the Supreme Court took up Section 18.2 and made a point that’s easy to lose in the mechanical business of counting terms: not every delay is the state’s fault. Where the delay came from legitimate court processes rather than prosecutorial foot-dragging, the Court found, it couldn’t fairly be pinned on the state.



That’s the crux of it. Section 18.2 isn’t supposed to be a stopwatch that runs blind to who caused the delay. It’s supposed to ask why the trial didn’t happen. In the Margibi case, the “why” is sitting right there in three dated letters asking, plainly, for a hearing.



The question this case actually puts to the court



None of this is a case against Section 18.2, or against defendants having a real right to a timely trial. Nobody’s arguing for indictments to hang over people indefinitely.



The argument is narrower than that: when a prosecutor has done the asking — repeatedly, formally, on the record — should the case still fall on the state’s side of the ledger? Or does that record change what “good cause” means?



Uncomfortable Backdrop

There’s a bigger, uncomfortable backdrop to all of this, too. Liberia’s courts are working through crowded dockets with limited capacity, and when a judge has to choose between a corruption trial and, say, a high-profile drug case — as reportedly happened in Margibi, where proceedings against Quita Dolo Kosso occupied the court’s attention during the relevant period — something has to give. That’s not a problem any one judge created, and it’s not one any single ruling will fix. It’s a conversation the judiciary, the Ministry of Justice, the LACC and the Legislature probably need to be having about how cases get prioritized, and what happens to the ones that lose that competition.



For now, though, the immediate question belongs to the 13th Judicial Circuit: does a prosecution that asked for a trial date three times, and never got one, still lose the case on a technicality built to punish the side that didn’t ask?



There is no evidence in the record reviewed here that any judge deliberately set out to sink these cases — congested dockets and competing priorities are a real and separate problem from bad faith, and the two shouldn’t be conflated without proof. But intent may be the wrong thing to fixate on. Whether the courts are working against the LACC on purpose or simply failing it through inertia, the effect on the ground looks the same: cases investigated for months, indictments secured, and then quietly emptied out before a single witness takes the stand. At some point, a pattern repeated enough times stops needing a motive to be a crisis.



An indictment isn’t accountability. A trial that actually happens is. And a system where prosecutors do their part and the case still disappears — dismissed, not because anyone failed to try, but because nobody made time — is a system that owes the public, and the LACC, some answers.

World.title: Liberia: Gongloe Demands Disclosure of President’s Pay, Questions 40% Salary Cut, Constitutional Compliance
World.content:
Monrovia — Renowned Liberian lawyer Cllr. Tiawan Saye Gongloe has challenged President Joseph Nyuma Boakai to publicly disclose his salary, raising questions about the legal basis, implementation, and transparency surrounding the President’s reported 40 percent voluntary pay reduction.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

President Boakai pledged during his campaign and upon assuming office to reduce his salary by 40 percent as part of his commitment to responsible governance and fiscal discipline. The Executive Mansion has subsequently maintained that the President is honoring that commitment.

However, the actual amount President Boakai receives monthly or annually has not been publicly disclosed, prompting Cllr. Gongloe to demand clarity on what he describes as a fundamental transparency issue.

In his latest “Question for the Weekend” commentary, titled “Mr. President, What Exactly Is Your Salary?”, Gongloe said the reported 40 percent reduction raises a basic question: 40 percent of what?

“Liberians were told that President Joseph Nyuma Boakai voluntarily reduced his salary by 40%. But 40% of what?” Gongloe asked.

He pointed to Article 60 of the Liberian Constitution, which provides that the salaries of the President and Vice President are determined by the Legislature and shall neither be increased nor diminished during the term for which they were elected.

Against that constitutional provision, Gongloe is asking the administration to explain the exact salary legally established for the President and how the announced voluntary reduction is being applied.

He posed four specific questions: What salary did the Legislature legally fix for the President? What was President Boakai’s gross annual salary when he assumed office? How much does he actually receive after the announced 40 percent voluntary reduction? How is the voluntary reduction being implemented consistently with Article 60 of the Constitution?

Gongloe also invoked Article 15(c) of the Constitution, which guarantees citizens the right to be informed about the government and its functionaries.

He argued that disclosure of the President’s compensation should not be viewed through a partisan or personal lens, but rather as an issue of public accountability.

“This is not a personal question. It is not a partisan question. It is a transparency question,” Gongloe stated.

The lawyer stressed that the President’s compensation is ultimately financed by Liberian taxpayers and therefore, in his view, the public has a legitimate interest in knowing precisely how much the country’s chief executive is receiving.

“Mr. President, the Liberian people pay the President’s salary,” Gongloe said. “How much are they paying you?”

The call comes amid broader public debates over government spending, executive accountability and the need for greater transparency in the management of public resources.

Gongloe ran on the presidential ticket of the Liberian People’s Party in the 2023 presidential and legislative elections. He and the LPP subsequently threw their support behind then-presidential candidate Joseph Nyuma Boakai during the 2023 runoff election between Boakai and incumbent President George Manneh Weah.

Although Gongloe was offered a cabinet position in the Boakai-Koung administration, he declined the appointment. His vice-presidential running mate, Dr. Emmanuel Urey Yarkpawolo, was later appointed Executive Director of the Environmental Protection Agency.

Gongloe has, however, maintained an independent public posture toward the administration. While applauding the government for what he considers notable achievements, he has also consistently criticized policies and decisions he believes require greater transparency and accountability.

He said his latest inquiry into President Boakai’s salary should therefore not be viewed through a partisan lens, emphasizing that his concern is rooted in the broader principles of transparency, accountability and the public’s right to know.

According to Gongloe, his past political support for Boakai does not prevent him from questioning the administration when issues of public interest arise. His call for disclosure of the President’s salary, he stressed, is intended to promote openness in government and ensure that public officials remain accountable to the Liberian people.

While the Executive Mansion has maintained that President Boakai has fulfilled his pledge to cut his salary by 40 percent, the renewed challenge from Gongloe puts the spotlight on the actual monetary value of the reduction and the mechanism through which it is being implemented.

The questions now place the administration under pressure to provide a clear public accounting of the President’s legally established compensation, the amount he receives, and how the reported salary reduction squares with the constitutional provisions governing presidential remuneration.

For Gongloe, the issue is straightforward: if the public pays the President’s salary, the public should know exactly how much it is.

World.title: UNIBOA at 35: Reeves Challenges Bassa Diaspora to Build an Enduring Future Beyond Charity
World.content:
At UNIBOA’s 35th convention, Liberia Maritime Deputy Commissioner Emmanuel Nuku Reeves tells the Bassa diaspora that charity built the last thirty-five years — but only an endowed, engineered vision will build the next.

By Rodney D. Sieh, [email protected]

UNIBOA 35th National Convention – “The future is calling. History is watching. Our homeland is expecting. The next generation is waiting.”

Emmanuel Nuku Reeves left those four lines for last, but they were the whole point of the speech that came before them. Delivering the keynote at the 35th National Convention of the United Bassa Organizations in the Americas, the Deputy Commissioner of the Liberia Maritime Authority told delegates that the diaspora group’s history — scholarships for Liberian students, medical supplies for hospitals back home, work to preserve Bassa culture and language — has already answered the question of what a united diaspora can accomplish. Now, he argued, it needs to answer a bigger one: what comes next.

“These contributions are not merely acts of generosity,” Reeves told the gathering, held under the convention’s theme, “Today’s Success is Inspired by Building Tomorrow Milestones.” “They are milestones. They are monuments of service.”

The convention itself carried on a UNIBOA tradition, with the organization receiving a customary $15,000 contribution to support its programs. But Reeves spent much of his address pushing delegates past the fundraising-and-goodwill model that has defined the group for three and a half decades. Change is moving too fast, he argued — from artificial intelligence to climate change — for good intentions alone to carry Liberia’s development forward.

“Sustainable success does not happen by accident,” he said. “It is engineered through foresight, planning, and collective action.”

He tied that call directly to the Liberian government’s current development priorities — agriculture, roads, the rule of law, education, sanitation and tourism — and urged UNIBOA to build what he called “intellectual capital” alongside its charitable giving: institutions, leadership pipelines and partnerships designed to outlast any single donation.

His most concrete proposal was a major scholarship endowment fund, one capable of training Liberian doctors, engineers, lawyers, technologists, educators and business leaders on an ongoing basis — building, in effect, a standing diaspora-backed professional network equipped to take on development challenges not just in Bassa counties, but nationwide.

“Imagine a future where diaspora investments create jobs, support innovation, and stimulate local enterprise,” Reeves told the gathering. “Imagine a future where every child of Bassa heritage knows that there exists a global community committed to their success.”

He closed by asking members to treat the convention as something more than an annual reunion — a working summit for ideas, he called it — and to carry that same energy into the organization’s next thirty-five years.

“The future is calling,” Reeves said. “History is watching. Our homeland is expecting. The next generation is waiting.”

World.title: Liberia: Weah’s Opposition Unity Roundtable Kicks Off As Concerned NPP Partisans, Sen. Kogar Endorse Initiative
World.content:
Monrovia — Former President George Manneh Weah’s push for opposition unity is gaining momentum, with a group identifying itself as the Concerned NPP Partisans endorsing a consultative meeting convened by the Congress for Democratic Change despite National Patriotic Party Chairman George Mulbah’s position that the party will not attend.

By Gerald C. Koinyeneh, [email protected]

The development adds a new layer to an emerging disagreement within the NPP over whether the party should participate in broader opposition consultations ahead of Liberia’s next political cycle.

Former President Weah, following his return from abroad, criticized what he described as the deterioration of democracy under the Boakai-Koung administration and announced plans to bring opposition political forces together for consultations.

Several opposition parties and political figures have since expressed interest in the initiative.

However, NPP Chairman George Mulbah has publicly stated that the party will not honor the invitation.

The NPP’s political leader, former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, served alongside Weah during his administration. Against the backdrop of the party’s leadership dispute, the Concerned NPP Partisans have now publicly thrown their support behind the CDC-led consultations.

In a statement issued Saturday, the group, which describes itself as comprising a majority of members of the NPP’s National Executive Committee, said it supports “genuine unity” among Liberia’s opposition political forces and fully endorses the consultative meeting.

“The opposition cannot afford unnecessary division, personal ambitions, or attempts by individuals to speak as though they alone represent the collective interests of the NPP,” the group said.

‘NPP Is Bigger Than Any Individual’

The Concerned NPP Partisans directly challenged Chairman Mulbah’s position, arguing that no single individual should claim to speak for the entire party.

They also questioned Mulbah’s role in the political negotiations and coalition-building efforts that led to the formation of the Coalition for Democratic Change, which included the NPP and ultimately brought Weah to power in 2017.

The group said Mulbah joined the NPP at a later stage and was subsequently appointed to a government position by then-President Weah.

The statement accused him of attempting to undermine political relationships and forces that, according to the group, contributed to his political resurgence.

“The NPP is bigger than any individual. The opposition movement is bigger than personal interests,” the group declared.

Concerned Partisans Praise CDC

The group also commended the CDC and former President Weah for what it described as solidarity with the NPP and its leadership during what it called an “exceptionally difficult period.”

The Concerned NPP Partisans said Liberia’s political environment requires dialogue, consultation and cooperation among opposition parties.

“No single opposition political party can afford to approach the future in isolation,” the statement said, urging political leaders to sit together, negotiate in good faith and work toward a broad-based opposition platform capable of presenting Liberians with a credible alternative.

The group further expressed appreciation to Weah and the CDC for maintaining their relationship with the NPP despite the challenges confronting the party.

Jewel Howard-Taylor’s Situation

The statement also addressed the current challenges facing former Vice President Jewel Howard-Taylor, who has recently been at the center of a major legal and political controversy.

The Concerned NPP Partisans said some individuals within the NPP had contributed to the difficulties confronting Howard-Taylor and warned that history would judge those involved.

“We will not be distracted by those who have chosen to become the ‘Judas Iscariots’ of this moment,” the group said, while urging NPP partisans and opposition supporters to remain calm and united.

The group concluded by reaffirming its commitment to opposition unity and democratic principles.

Round One of Opposition Talks Held

Meanwhile, the first round of the opposition consultative meeting was held Saturday at Weah’s Jamaica Resort in Paynesville.

Several opposition political figures attended the gathering, which is expected to continue today.

Among the notable participants was Senator Samuel G. Kogar, who was recently expelled from the Movement for Democracy and Reconstruction (MDR).

The MDR was a key member of the Unity Party Alliance during the 2023 presidential election, which brought President Joseph Nyuma Boakai and Vice President Jeremiah Kpan Koung to power after their victory over Weah and his running mate, then VP Taylor, in the runoff.

More opposition leaders are expected to participate as consultations continue, with the talks likely to test the willingness of Liberia’s opposition parties to overcome longstanding political differences and pursue a common strategy.

World.title: Edward Chilufya moves to Israel on loan
World.content:
Chipolopolo midfielder Edward Chilufya has joined Israeli Premier League side Hapoel Jerusalem FC on a season-long loan deal from Danish Superliga club FC Midtjyllan.

Both Hapoel Jerusalem and Chilufya separately confirmed the deal on Monday afternoon.

Chilufya, 26, remains contracted to Midtjylland on a permanent deal that runs until 31 December 2028.

In a statement, Hapoel Jerusalem announced: “Edward Chilufya joins Hapoel. The 26-year-old winger from Zambia has a rich career in top Scandinavian teams. He is coming to us on loan for the season.”

Posting on his Facebook page, Chilufya expressed excitement about the move.

“I’m delighted to join Hapoel Jerusalem on loan and I’m looking forward to embracing this new challenge, working hard, and giving my best for the club,” he wrote.

“Thank you to everyone at FC Midtjylland for their continued support. I’m excited for what lies ahead and ready to get to work. New league. New challenge. Same ambition,” he added.

Chilufya, a product of Mpande Academy in Kasama, has been campaigning in Europe for nearly 10 years.

He started training with Swedish side Djurgården in June 2017 and signed his first professional contract with the club on 15 February 2018.

After Djurgården, he moved to Denmark where he has been with Midtjylland.

World.title: Husband of Tanzania’s president dies
World.content:
President Hakainde Hichilema has conveyed his deepest condolences to Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan following the death of her husband, Hafidh Ameir Hassan.

In a message of sympathy, President Hichilema said Zambia stood in solidarity with the First Family and the people of Tanzania during the period of mourning.

“We convey our deepest condolences to Her Excellency President Samia Suluhu Hassan on the passing of her husband, Hafidh Ameir Hassan. We stand side by side with the First Family, and all citizens of the United Republic of Tanzania during this difficult time,” President Hichilema said.

Hafidh Ameir Hassan, who became Tanzania’s First Gentleman in 2021 when President Samia Suluhu Hassan assumed office, died on Monday while undergoing treatment at a hospital in Zanzibar.

Tanzania’s Vice President, Deogratius Ndejembi, announced the death and extended condolences to the bereaved family. He said Hassan had been receiving treatment for a heart condition.

According to Tanzanian authorities, burial arrangements are underway and Mr Hassan will be laid to rest in Zanzibar, the family’s native home.

President Hichilema joined leaders and citizens across the region in mourning the passing of the Tanzanian First Gentleman.

World.title: MoM urged to expedite processing of artisanal licences
World.content:
Central Province Permanent Secretary, Milner Mwanakampwe has called on the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development to expedite the processing of artisanal licences to enable young people engage in safe and legal mining activities.

Dr Mwanakampwe says the lengthy process of acquiring artisanal mining licences is contributing to challenges faced by young people in the mining sector.

He was speaking when officials from the Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development paid a courtesy call on him in Kabwe.

Dr Mwanakampwe observed that people are losing their lives in mining pits, making it important for artisanal miners to be adequately trained and supported to conduct their activities safely.

He said the ministry should encourage artisanal miners to open bank accounts so that they can receive payments through formal financial channels and contribute more effectively to the economy.

Dr Mwanakampwe said training of artisanal miners is important as it promotes safe mining practices which can help reduce accidents and loss of lives.

Meanwhile, Ministry of Mines and Minerals Development Assistant Director for Policy and Development Cooperation, Mercy Zulu said her team is in the Central Province for 20-days training artisanal miners on safe and responsible mining practices.

Ms Zulu said 400 artisanal miners will be trained to equip them with the knowledge and skills needed to conduct mining activities safely.

She said the ministry is also facilitating access to finance for artisanal miners so that they can increase their contribution to the country’s economy.

World.title: Chisamba Councils calls for 2027 CDF applications
World.content:
Chisamba Town Council is calling for applications from members of the public for the various components under Constituency Development Fund (CDF).

This is according to a public notice dated September 2, 2026, signed by Chisamba District Council Secretary, Chamuka Muwamba and made available to the media in Chisamba.

Mr Muwamba said the call for applications is in respect of the 2027 CDF, stating that Chisamba District is expected to receive slightly over K80 million for both Chisamba and Mwomboshi Constituencies.

“Each constituency will receive an equal share of K40, 032, 549.91 to finance community projects, youth and women empowerment, and skills development bursaries,” Mr Muwamba said.

He urged members of the public in the two constituencies to seize the opportunity and apply for the various components of the CDF.

Mr Muwamba explained that 60 percent of the funds is designated for community projects to facilitate critical infrastructure development in the district.

He stated that the applications should be submitted using the recommended application forms, which are available free of charge from area councillors, constituency offices, or the Civic Centre under the Planning Unit.

Mr Muwamba said the deadline for submitting applications is October 16, 2026.

He has also urged applicants to follow the eligibility criteria for each component of the CDF to avoid having their applications rejected.

Mr Muwamba said one of the eligibility criteria for community projects is that the proposed project must appear in the Integrated Development Plan (IDP) for Chisamba District, which can be viewed through area councillors or the local authority.

“The project must be identified and prioritized by the local authority, must be of benefit to the wider community, should use approved designs by the planning authority and take into account persons with disabilities.

“Proof of a bank account or mobile wallet registered for the group, the proposed project is being undertaken within the constituency, applicants must have been residents in the constituency for over six months,” Mr Muwamba said.

He disclosed that local citizens aged between 16 and below 35 years, who are in possession of a Green National Registration Card, as well as out-of-school entrepreneurs requiring up-skilling and re-skilling, are eligible to apply for skills development bursaries.

“The applicant must be a resident of the constituency for more than six months, and must be in possession of an admission or acceptance letter from any of the public TEVET institutions or the Zambia National Service,” he said.

Mr Muwamba said all application letters must be addressed to his office and submitted not later than October 16, 2026.

World.title: Police apprehend Kalulushi girl over dumped baby’s body
World.content:
Police in Kalulushi have apprehended a 15 year old girl for allegedly dumping the body of a newborn baby at a dump site.

Copperbelt Police Commanding Officer, Rae Hamoonga, who confirmed the development to ZANIS, said the incident occurred between August 27, 2027 at around 17:30 hours and September 05, 2026 at around 17:00 hours at Kafulafuta Lane in Milemu Clinic area.

Mr Hamoonga said the matter was reported to Kalulushi Police Station by a 39 year old woman who discovered the body of a new born baby boy wrapped in a plastic bag lying on top of garbage at the dump site near Milemu clinic.

Mr Hamoonga said the information obtained by Officers who visited the scene led to the apprehension of the girl suspected to be connected to the incident which is being investigated as suspected infanticide.

He said the girl was taken to Kalulushi General Hospital together with the body and during preliminary inquiries, disclosed that she had unexpectedly given birth while using the toilet after which she is alleged to have wrapped the baby in a plastic bag and disposed of the body at the dumpsite.

He said the body has since been deposited at Kalulushi General Hospital Mortuary, awaiting a postmortem examination to establish the circumstances leading to the death of the baby.

Mr Haoongaa disclosed that the girl has been admitted at the same hospital for further medical examination and treatment under Police guard.

He stated that a medical report has been issued and a docket opened.

World.title: RUGBY: Mufulira opens 10-point lead
World.content:
Defending Champions Mufulira Leopards have extended their lead at the top of the National Rugby League to ten points with five games remaining in the 2026 season.

Mufulira at the weekend beat their closest rivals Arrows 19-15 at home in Mufulira to move to 39 points after playing nine games.

Second placed Arrows, who have one un-played game, have 29 points from eight matches played.

On the road to victory, Mufulira posted one try which they converted and later scored three penalties and had one drop goal.

Arrows converted one of the two tries they placed and later scored a penalty.

Nkwazi are third on the table with 29 points as well after edging Buffaloes 26-23 in a tightly contested Lusaka derby.

Buffaloes are fourth on the table just two points behind third placed Nkwazi.

Elsewhere struggling giants Diggers returned to league action after a lengthy absence with a 13-8 away loss to Eagles in Kabwe.

Eagles are fifth on the table with 21 points in nine matches and are placed one slot above Diggers, who are six points behind the Zambia National Service side.

Meanwhile, the bottom two sides KPF and Kansanshi shared the 15-15 spoils to stay in their respective positions.

Seventh placed Kansanshi have six points in nine matches while bottom positioned KPF sits on one point from eight games.

KPF remains the only team without a win so far in the 2026 National Rugby League.

World.title: Findlay Needs Urgent Medical Care, Says Family
World.content:
Findlay’s Health Deteriorating In Detention, Family Says

The family of detained Lusaka businessman Harry Valden Findlay says his health has deteriorated sharply after he was denied access to his prescription medication, with the 63-year-old now on a drip and his whereabouts unknown to relatives for extended periods during his detention. The family has emphasized the urgent need for medical attention for Findlay.

In a statement issued at the weekend, the family said it remained deeply concerned that the State had continued moving Findlay between different detention facilities without informing them, leaving them without knowledge of his location for 12 days at a stretch. They called for immediate action to ensure Findlay receives the care he urgently needs.

“We have waited… we have pleaded for humane treatment… we have asked that the law be followed despite the gravity of the charges, to no avail,” the family said.

The statement described a pattern of repeated transfers that left relatives struggling to track Findlay’s condition. “But we are afraid, Harry keeps getting moved between facilities, for 12 days we did not know his whereabouts, he was denied access to his prescription medication and now he is unwell,” the family said.

According to the statement, Findlay has been on a drip since Wednesday, September 2, but has not been taken to hospital despite the seriousness of his condition. The family said the State was fully aware of his medical history and appealed for that awareness to translate into action.

“He needs specialised medical treatment. The State is aware of his medical condition! Regardless of the charges, every human being has constitutional rights! We are seeing someone we love become weaker day by day!” the family said.

The family stressed that detention should never be allowed to become a form of punishment in itself, insisting that Findlay’s wellbeing could not be treated as secondary to the legal process against him. “His life matters, his health matters! We plead that Harry is treated humanely!” the statement read.

Efforts to have Findlay brought before a court to address the concerns around his detention have similarly stalled. The family said it had applied for a writ of habeas corpus seeking to have him produced before the court, but the process was repeatedly delayed because the State failed to bring him to the scheduled hearings.

After several adjournments linked to Findlay’s continued absence, the court proceeded to hear the application without him present, a development the family said undermined the very purpose of the habeas corpus process, which exists to establish the lawfulness of a person’s detention through direct judicial scrutiny.

“Harry has rights! We appeal that these rights are afforded to him!” the family said, framing their appeal as one rooted in constitutional principle rather than a dispute over the underlying allegations against him.

The family was careful to separate the question of guilt or innocence from the question of humane treatment, stating plainly that whatever the outcome of the case against Findlay, no set of allegations could justify the permanent loss of his life or health while the matter remained before the courts.

“Whatever the allegations against Harry, his life cannot be restored if it is lost!” the family said, closing their statement with a direct appeal for the authorities to act before his condition worsens further.

As of the time of the family’s statement, Findlay had not been transferred to hospital despite being on a drip for several days, and his exact custodial location was not confirmed publicly. The family said they intended to continue pressing for both his medical treatment and his right to appear before a court to challenge the legality of his continued detention.

The case adds to a wider pattern of concern raised by rights groups and opposition figures in recent weeks over the treatment and welfare of individuals held in custody following the disputed August general election period, with families of several detainees separately calling for greater transparency around detention conditions and access to medical care.

World.title: Zambia chase 13th COSAFA U-20 crown
World.content:
‎Zambia will be hoping to extend their record number of COSAFA titles at Under-20 level to

‎13 when they compete in the TotalEnergies CAF Under-20 Africa Cup of Nations | COSAFA

‎Qualifier in Mozambique from September 18-27.

‎They have been remarkably consistent at this level. In the 11 tournaments they have played

‎since 2010, they have won five titles, finished runners-up once and third once, with two

‎fourth-place finishes and two exits in the pool stages.

‎This time around they have been drawn in a pool with old foes Malawi, Comoros and

‎Botswana. Only the top team in each group advances to the semi-finals, along with the best

‎runner-up across the three pools.

‎The two finalists in the competition will qualify for the continental finals next year.

‎Zambia finished third in 2025 after losing to Malawi in the semi-finals, having reached that

‎stage as the best runner-up from the pool phase. They edged Angola on penalties in the

‎bronze-medal match.

‎It was a similar story the year before as they qualified for the semi-finals as the best runner-

‎up, having lost to Angola in the pool stages, and then beat Zimbabwe on penalties following

‎a 2-2 draw in the last four.

‎But they came unstuck against South Africa in the decider, losing 2-0 to the side who would

‎go on to be crowned African champions. Their road to the title in 2022 included group-

‎stage wins over Mauritius (3-0), Eswatini (2-0) and Botswana (1-0), before they edged

‎Angola on penalties in the semi-finals and beat then-holders Mozambique 1-0 in the

‎decider.

‎Prior to 2022, their previous victory came in 2019. It was a commanding performance from

‎the side as they claimed a full haul of nine points in the pool stages before seeing off Angola

‎3-0 in the semi-finals.

‎That was followed by victory against old foes South Africa by the same comprehensive

‎margin in the decider.

‎Zambia were also rampant in 2016 as they stormed through that competition and inflicted a

‎2-1 defeat on hosts South Africa in the decider.

‎

‎

‎They went on to claim the 2017 Africa Under-20 Championship title on home soil and also

‎excelled at the FIFA Under-20 World Cup in South Korea.

‎But the side disappointed in the COSAFA Men’s Under-20 Championship that year, bowing

‎out in the first round after a defeat to East African guest nation Uganda was followed by a

‎draw with Malawi and a win over Eswatini.

‎They did make the semi-finals in 2018 but lost 2-1 to Zimbabwe and were then beaten 2-1

‎by Angola in the bronze-medal match.

‎They reached the semi-finals again in 2020, a competition played in South Africa, winning all

‎three pool matches against Namibia (1-0), Comoros (2-0) and Malawi (2-0).

‎They came unstuck in the semi-finals, though, when they were held 0-0 by Mozambique

‎before losing 5-4 on penalties. They were then beaten 2-1 by Angola in the bronze-medal

‎match.

‎Zambia have also been fairly regular visitors to the Africa Under-20 Championship and have

‎appeared at the continental tournament on 11 previous occasions.

Apart from their gold medal in 2017, they also finished fourth in 1991, 1999 and 2007.
