Colombia’s government named Alejandro Ordóñez as its OAS ambassador on September 4, 2026. The appointment marks a return to the post he held from 2018 to 2022.

Who Is Alejandro Ordóñez

Alejandro Ordóñez is a conservative lawyer who served as Colombia’s inspector general until 2016. His second term ended when the Council of State annulled his re-election due to procedural irregularities.

He is known for religiously conservative views and controversial actions, including burning books he considered immoral. These actions drew criticism from human-rights groups and liberal sectors.

Previous OAS Role

Ordóñez already served as Colombia’s ambassador to the OAS from 2018 to 2022 under President Iván Duque. His new appointment is a second term in the same position.

As OAS ambassador, he will head Colombia’s Permanent Mission in Washington. He will represent the country in the Permanent Council and other OAS bodies.

What Is the OAS

The Organization of American States (OAS) is a hemispheric body based in Washington, D.C. It promotes democracy, human rights, security, and development among its 35 member states.

An ambassador to the OAS is a country’s permanent representative. The ambassador presents government positions, negotiates resolutions, and votes in the Permanent Council.

Appointment Details

President Abelardo de la Espriella signed Decree 1365 on September 4, 2026, appointing Ordóñez. The decree was also signed by the Foreign Ministry and took effect immediately.

The appointment does not require Senate confirmation, according to the decree. It was made directly by the president and the foreign ministry.

Reaction from Gustavo Petro

Former President Gustavo Petro criticized the appointment. He said, ‘He who burned books will end up burning human beings,’ as reported by Infobae on September 7, 2026.

Petro’s comment refers to Ordóñez’s past book-burning incident. It reflects the deep political divide between the two leaders.

Shift in Foreign Policy

The appointment is part of President de la Espriella‘s broader foreign policy shift. He is reversing many of Petro’s decisions, especially regarding Israel.

Colombia has named Tania Gilinski as ambassador to Israel. Israel has named Vivian Aisen as its envoy to Colombia.

Future Plans

The new administration plans to reopen Colombia’s embassy in Jerusalem. It also intends to recognize Israeli sovereignty over the Golan Heights.

These moves signal a sharp pro-Israel turn in Bogotá’s foreign policy. They contrast with Petro’s stance and align with the United States.

The Dates

The government signalled the appointment in early August 2026. The formal decree followed on 4 September.

Ordóñez held the same post under President Iván Duque from September 2018. That is why the appointment is a return rather than a debut.

Frequently Asked Questions

Who is Alejandro Ordóñez?

Alejandro Ordóñez is a conservative Colombian lawyer and former inspector general. He served from 2009 until 2016, when his re-election was annulled.

What does an OAS ambassador do?

An OAS ambassador heads a country’s permanent mission to the Organization of American States. The ambassador represents the government in the Permanent Council and other bodies.

Why is this appointment controversial?

Ordóñez is known for religiously conservative views and actions like book burning. Critics, including former President Petro, have condemned his appointment.

Does the appointment need Senate approval?

No, the appointment was made by presidential decree and does not require Senate confirmation. It took effect immediately.

World.title: Saprissa Ends Three-Year Morera Soto Drought With 2-0 Clásico Win
World.content:
Deportivo Saprissa beat Liga Deportiva Alajuelense 2-0 at the Estadio Alejandro Morera Soto on Saturday night, taking the Clásico Nacional in Alajuela for the first time since 2023 and stretching its lead at the top of the Apertura 2026 to seven points. The win leaves Saprissa on 18 points from seven matches. Alajuelense drops to fifth on 11.

The home side had the better of a scoreless first half, pressing forward and creating the clearer openings without finding a finish. Play was halted around the 43rd minute when two floodlight towers went out, leaving part of the stadium dark before the match resumed. Whatever rhythm Alajuelense had built did not survive the interval. Orlando Sinclair opened the scoring for Saprissa in the opening minutes of the second half, forcing the ball home after a sequence of rebounds inside the area.

Sebastián Acuña doubled the lead moments later, around the 51st minute, capitalizing on an error by Alajuelense goalkeeper Washington Ortega. Two goals in the space of a few minutes settled a match that had been evenly balanced through the first 45. Alajuelense could not find a way back. The home side finished with ten men after young midfielder Kyan McDonald was shown a second yellow card in the 84th minute.

By then, sections of the crowd had turned on their own bench. Chants of “Fuera Rescalvo” rolled around the stadium, directed at Spanish coach Ismael Rescalvo, who has yet to win over a support that has grown impatient with what it sees on the field. For Saprissa and coach Hernán Medford, the result closes a gap that had been open for more than three seasons.

The club had not won at the Morera Soto since April 2, 2023, when Luis Javier Paradela and David Guzmán scored in a 2-0 away victory. Alajuelense had gone eleven clásicos unbeaten at home against its rival before Saturday. Saprissa now carries a seven-point cushion into the second half of the tournament with the one result that had been missing from its record. Alajuelense, twenty-one points behind the leaders at the halfway mark of the group phase, faces a longer set of questions than the scoreline alone suggests.

World.title: National Geographic Germany Devotes 11 Pages to Costa Rica
World.content:
National Geographic Traveler’s German edition has given Costa Rica eleven pages in its September issue, describing Costa Rica as a treasure of nature and taking readers on a route that runs from the Pacuare River to the Osa Peninsula. The photographs reaching German newsstands this month include hummingbirds, beaches, forest canopy, a sloth and rafters on whitewater.

The written feature follows a journey through the Nairi Awari Indigenous Territory, San Gerardo de Dota and Los Quetzales National Park before moving south to Carate Beach, Corcovado National Park and the Gulf of Nicoya. The Costa Rican Tourism Institute (ICT) said the article is the product of a partnership with National Geographic Germany. Under that agreement, Costa Rica covered airfare, lodging and production costs for the assignment.

As of Saturday, the institute did not have figures available on how much it spent on those items. The ICT said that in exchange, Costa Rica appeared in a publication where the equivalent advertising space would have cost €207,900, or about ₡109 million. That works out to roughly $240,000 at today’s exchange rate.

Marcos Borges, executive president of the ICT, said partnerships of this kind let Costa Rica put its attractions in front of thousands of potential travelers and encourage them to turn what they see on the page into a trip. The magazine printed 35,000 copies for distribution across Europe and the feature will also run in National Geographic’s digital edition.

Journalist Amelia Duggan wrote the piece, which is structured as a first-person account of her time here. Her framing is that Costa Rica’s natural wealth is not something to be looked at from a distance but something to be walked into and taken in through all five senses.

The article also spends time on conservation, on seeing wildlife in its own habitat, and on how easily a single trip can cross between sharply different ecosystems. According to the ICT, the report presents Costa Rica as a country that has built the protection of its natural heritage and its sustainability commitments into the tourism product itself, reinforcing a reputation the institute describes as global leadership in sustainable travel.

Beyond landscapes and wildlife, the feature argues that understanding Costa Rica means spending time in local communities and engaging with its culture, food and people. Pura vida is presented as shorthand for that identity, and as a way of valuing simple, unpolished experiences over packaged ones.

Germany remains one of Costa Rica’s more important European source markets. Between January and August 2026, it received 50,000 German visitors by air, part of the roughly 300,000 European arrivals by air over the same stretch. Placements like this one sit at the center of how Costa Rica competes for attention abroad, and they carry a cost the public underwrites.

The value of the exposure will be measured against those European arrival numbers over the coming season, and the price paid for it is a figure the ICT has said it will need to look up.

World.title: Panton questions BZ$40 million HRCU loan to BEL, demands full disclosure
World.content:
Panton questions BZ$40 million HRCU loan to BEL, demands full disclosure

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Leader of the Opposition Tracy Taegar Panton is demanding answers over a reported BZ$40 million unsecured loan from Holy Redeemer Credit Union to Belize Electricity Limited, questioning whether the interests of HRCU members were adequately protected.

In a statement issued Monday, Panton said BEL’s audited financial statements reportedly disclose the loan at an effective interest rate of 5 percent per year, repayable over 60 months.

The Opposition Leader said the transaction raises serious questions about how such a large loan was negotiated, assessed and approved.

Panton wants HRCU and the relevant authorities to explain why the loan was reportedly unsecured, what risk assessment was conducted and what safeguards were established to protect members’ funds.

She also questioned whether ordinary HRCU members would have access to comparable borrowing terms.

“Who is protecting the members of Holy Redeemer Credit Union?” Panton asked.

Panton, who identified herself as a long standing HRCU member, is calling for disclosure of the loan agreement, approval records, repayment terms, risk assessments and details surrounding any security arrangements.

She also wants an independent review to determine whether the transaction complied with applicable laws, regulations, lending limits and internal policies.

Panton stressed that her concerns center on accountability for an institution built on the savings of ordinary Belizeans.

“Working people’s money must never be treated as the Government’s private financing facility,” she said.

The statement represents Panton’s allegations and questions regarding the transaction. It does not, by itself, establish that HRCU, BEL or government officials violated any law or lending requirement.

World.title: Taiwan and Belize launch new project to strengthen disaster preparedness
World.content:
Taiwan and Belize launch new project to strengthen disaster preparedness

By Breaking Belize News Staff (HP): Belize is strengthening its ability to prepare for floods, wildfires and other natural hazards through a new partnership with Taiwan.

The Taiwan International Cooperation and Development Fund, TaiwanICDF, and two Belizean government ministries officially launched the Belize Multi Hazard Risk Management Capacity Building Project on August 27 in Belmopan.

The initiative involves the Ministry of Sustainable Development, Climate Change and Solid Waste Management and the Ministry of the Public Service and Disaster Risk Management.

A major component will be establishing a cross ministerial mechanism for integrated disaster management, improving coordination and Belize’s ability to prepare for and respond to emergencies.

TaiwanICDF project manager Lin Li shan said the project will concentrate on strengthening disaster early warning platforms and coordination, developing more resilient communities and introducing automated technology for detecting wildfires.

Under the initiative, disaster risk maps will be developed for 15 newly selected Belizean communities vulnerable to floods and wildfires. Community based disaster preparedness and multi hazard response training will also be expanded.

The project will install three automated ground based wildfire early warning stations in high risk locations. Remote sensing and ground observation information will also be used to develop wildfire risk assessment models and establish carbon monitoring sites.

Minister of Sustainable Development Orlando Habet said early warning systems supported by Taiwan have already produced results in Belize and that greater cooperation between ministries will help the country adopt a broader multi hazard approach.

Minister of Public Service and Disaster Risk Management Henry Charles Usher noted that Belize faces hurricanes, floods, storm surges, droughts and wildfires on a recurring basis.

While those hazards cannot always be prevented, Usher said preparation and training can significantly improve the ability of Belizean communities to respond when disaster strikes.

World.title: Belize and U.S. seek to expand partnership: MCC, Security and Trade discussed
World.content:
Belize and U.S. seek to expand partnership: MCC, Security and Trade discussed

By Zoila Palma: Today, Francis Fonseca, Minister of Foreign Affairs received Rudolph Andreas Bauer, Ambassador-designate of the United States of America, for the presentation of copies of his Letter of Credence.

Following the presentation, Minister Fonseca and the Ambassador-designate engaged in a constructive bilateral meeting on the longstanding relationship between Belize and the United States.

Discussions focused on key areas of mutual interest, including the Millennium Challenge Corporation Compact and opportunities to advance economic growth and development through strategic investments.

They also discussed security cooperation, expanding trade and investment, and deepening collaboration in areas of shared priority.

Minister Fonseca welcomed the continued partnership between Belize and the United States and extended best wishes to the Ambassador-designate Bauer for a successful and productive tenure.

World.title: Belize welcomes International Golfers for 2026 Tournament
World.content:
Belize welcomes International Golfers for 2026 Tournament

By Zoila Palma: Belize once again welcomed the international golfing community as golfers from Belize, the United States and countries across Latin America gathered for the 2026 International Golf Tournament of Belize.

Sponsored by the Belize Tourism Board, the tournament highlighted Belize’s growing appeal as a destination where sports, tourism and memorable experiences come together.

Beyond the competition on the course, the event provided international participants with an opportunity to experience Belize and its vibrant tourism offerings.

The tournament featured several competitive categories, with Kenroy Smith claiming the Gross Championship, followed by Aydan Lizarraga in second and Rupert Tatum in third. Daniel Mazaheri captured the Net Championship, while Saulito Barrera placed second and Rori Barrera third.

Other notable winners included Glenda Thompson in the Women’s Category and Julian Palma in Category B. Lorne Solis and Kenroy Smith were crowned Partner Gross Champions, while Rori Barrera and Lito Barrera took the Partner Net title. Aydan Lizarraga also secured the Longest Drive award, while several golfers captured Closest to the Pin honors.

The Belize Tourism Board congratulated all winners, participants and organizers for another successful tournament, noting the event’s role in bringing international visitors to Belize through sport.

World.title: Four months later, no arrest in shooting deaths of Cayo Special Constables
World.content:
Four months later, no arrest in shooting deaths of Cayo Special Constables

By Zoila Palma: September 6 made four months after the tragic shooting deaths of well-known Cayo Special Constables Fidy Osgalla and Manuel “CarB” Smith.

CarB and Ms. Fidy were well known for their work alongside the Belize Police Department and in particular the San Ignacio Police.

Their familiar faces would be seen on patrols and walking alongside our September parades.

They firmly believed in dedicating their time and effort and volunteering to make our communities safer but their lives were abruptly cut short by gun violence.

Their loss has been devastating to the San Ignacio and Santa Elena communities where they served volunteering their time in the fight against crime.

Four months have now passed and their family and friends are calling on the Belize Police Department for answers since there has been no arrest or charges levied for the murders.

World.title: Leader of Opposition questions who bears the risk in BEL’s $40 million loan from Holy Redeemer Credit Union
World.content:
Leader of Opposition questions who bears the risk in BEL’s $40 million loan from Holy Redeemer Credit Union

By Zoila Palma: Opposition Leader and UDP Party Leader Tracy Taegar Panton is calling for greater transparency over a reported BZ$40 million unsecured loan from Holy Redeemer Credit Union (HRCU) to Belize Electricity Limited (BEL).

Panton said the matter raises questions about how members’ savings are being managed and whether proper lending and governance safeguards were followed.

Panton noted that credit unions are member-owned institutions funded by the savings of teachers, public officers, small-business owners, pensioners and other working-class Belizeans.

Referring to BEL’s audited financial statements, she said the loan was reportedly issued at an effective interest rate of 5 percent per annum, repayable over 60 months. “Who is protecting the members of Holy Redeemer Credit Union?” Panton questioned.

The Opposition Leader questioned how a government-owned company was able to secure what she described as favourable financing terms and whether ordinary credit union members have access to comparable rates. “How did a government-owned company secure such favourable terms when ordinary members may not have access to comparable rates?” she asked.

Panton also raised concerns about the reported unsecured nature of the loan and called for disclosure of the safeguards used to protect members’ funds. “HRCU members deserve a full accounting of how their money was used, who authorized the transaction, what risks were identified and whether the loan complied with all applicable laws, regulations, lending limits and governance requirements,” she said.

Panton further called on the Briceño Administration, BEL, HRCU compliance officers and relevant regulatory authorities to publicly disclose the loan agreement, approval records, repayment terms, security arrangements, risk assessments and any related-party or preferential-treatment considerations. “As a long-standing member myself, I demand transparency, fairness and responsible stewardship,” Panton said.

World.title: Minister of Tourism calls on Belizeans to celebrate Independence with Pride and Positivity
World.content:
Minister of Tourism calls on Belizeans to celebrate Independence with Pride and Positivity

By Zoila Palma: As Belize prepares to celebrate its 45th year of independence, Minister of Tourism, Youth, Sports and Diaspora Relations Anthony Mahler is encouraging Belizeans at home and abroad to reflect on the traditions, culture and values that make the country unique.

In his Independence message, Mahler highlighted this year’s theme, “Look at Me! I am Belize@45,” calling on Belizeans to share what makes the nation proudly Belizean with the world. “Our timeless traditions and rich cultural heritage are among the many things that make Belize unique,” Mahler said.

The Minister also pointed to Belize’s diversity as one of the country’s greatest strengths, while emphasizing the character of its people. “Across every corner of our country, our diversity is part of our strength,” he said, adding that what truly distinguishes Belize is “the warm spirit of our people that has become known and cherished around the world.”

As September celebrations get underway, Mahler urged Belizeans to look toward the future with optimism while appreciating the country’s journey. “Let us celebrate with pride and positivity,” he said. “Let us honor where we have come from, celebrate who we are today, and look with confidence toward the Belize we are building for tomorrow.”

He extended his best wishes to Belizeans at home and abroad and visitors to the country for a safe, meaningful and enjoyable September Celebrations.

World.title: Stronger schools
World.content:
Education Minster Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon walks with students of Maud McLeod High School in Westmoreland where she filmed her back-to-school message to the nation.

After a school year battered by Hurricane Melissa, particularly in western Jamaica, but capped by improved results in the country’s major examinations, Education Minister Senator Dr Dana Morris Dixon is looking to the new school year with optimism, pointing to increased investment, and stronger infrastructure as Jamaica pushes to transform its education system.

The scale of the challenge facing schools remains stark.

According to Morris Dixon’s back-to-school message, more than 688 schools were damaged by Melissa, 313 of them severely, while almost $26 billion is being spent on repairs and reconstruction. As she has repeatedly done in the past few weeks she acknowledged, however, that the work is not advancing as quickly as the Government would like.

Still, she said preparations were being made to get schools open, including contingency arrangements for institutions where repairs have not yet been completed.

“Thanks to the excellent work of our principals, boards, and the ministry team, we are working to have all schools open tomorrow. I have to thank all who have worked so hard over the summer and who have put in place contingency plans to support reopening even where repairs are not completed,” she said.

For Morris Dixon, however, rebuilding after Melissa is only part of the task.

The Government is entering the new school year with more than $835 million in operational support for schools, representing an average 55 per cent increase in funding. The minister said all schools received the first tranche of the increased funding in June, ahead of the reopening.

More than $1 billion is also being invested in educational resources, including workbooks, readers, textbooks, e-books, virtual learning solutions, and supplementary materials.

The increased spending comes against the backdrop of what Morris Dixon described as a strong finish to the last academic year, despite the disruption caused by the Category 5 storm.

“Despite the historic, once-in- a- 100-year devastation caused by the passage of Hurricane Melissa, we ended the last academic year with improved results across our major exams — PEP, CSEC and CAPE. Jamaica’s children did so well despite so much being thrown at them!” she said.

The minister is now betting on that resilience, alongside new investments, to drive further gains. In her speech she reminded the country of plans already in place.

Among the biggest initiatives is a $400-million investment in technical and vocational education at high schools. Technical high schools are to receive state-of-the-art laboratories in areas including autonomous robotics, renewable energy, virtual welding, electrical engineering, industrial controls, and optoelectronics.

The Government is also retooling science laboratories, while more than 150 satellite systems have been distributed to schools to improve Internet access, with additional devices being procured, particularly for rural institutions.

Morris Dixon said the hurricane recovery programme is similarly being used as an opportunity to improve schools beyond simply repairing the damage.

“Our Melissa reconstruction programme has not only presented an opportunity to make our schools more resilient, but it has also provided an opportunity to upgrade and renovate staffrooms for educators across Jamaica. The Staffroom Renovation Programme covers 74 institutions in the first phase, with work concentrated heavily in the parishes hardest hit by Melissa,” she said.

And while buildings, equipment and technology are central to the push, the minister also highlighted the needs of students outside the classroom.

More than 160,000 students are projected to benefit from the traditional cooked lunch programme, while another 69,000 students in the most challenged schools are expected to receive both breakfast and lunch. Meanwhile, 316 school cooks were trained and received range cook certification over the summer.

Psychosocial and psychological support, including trauma-informed services and Psychological First Aid, will also continue into the new academic year, after being intensified during the previous one.

Morris Dixon said the ambition extends beyond simply getting schools reopened and students back into classrooms.

“The ministry’s commitment is to continue transforming education so that every child, regardless of where they live or their circumstances, has a fair opportunity to learn, grow and succeed,” she said.

World.title: Sykes again makes case for judge-alone trials
World.content:
Chief Justice Bryan Sykes.

MONTEGO BAY, St James — Citing a far-advanced case — during the last circuit within the western end of the country— in which the jury had to be discharged, Chief Justice Bryan Sykes has again called for serious consideration to be given to judge-alone trials.

“After four weeks of trial, that was it. It was just waiting for addresses and the summation to be done [but] the jury had to be discharged,” he said during the 2026 Legal Year Western Region Assize Church Service at the West Jamaica Conference of Seventh-day Adventists in Mount Salem, St James, on Saturday.

In cases where juries are discharged Sykes’s preference is for the judge to then give a final verdict instead of having the matter drag on. He has consistently advocated for judge-alone trials in a bid to reduce case backlog and ensure that everyone accused of a crime is granted their constitutional right to a fair trial within a reasonable time. During the weekend church service he spoke of how a reliance on jury trials has impacted St James, particularly in relation to murder cases.

According to Sykes there were 170 cases before the court last circuit, and the perennial problem of finding individuals willing to serve as jurors persist.

“The judge was endeavouring to be as efficient as she could, actually running two to three trials at a time; and after four weeks of trial, [for] one of them, the jury had to be discharged,” said Sykes.

“The question is now, ‘Are we organising ourselves in a manner that justice can reach these 170 cases?’ Because it’s not just 170 persons because some of the cases have multiple defendants,” he added.

He noted that the numbers represent more than 200 people and impact not only those awaiting trial but also witnesses and relatives of the bereaved who have suffered great loss.

“We have to look again at the question of jury trials,” the chief justice urged.

Under the Criminal Justice (Administration) Act, which was amended by the Jury (Amendment) Act in 2015, the prosecution and the defence must agree, in writing, for an offence to be tried by a judge only.

As he has done in the past, Sykes on Saturday pointed to an opinion handed down by Jamaica’s highest court of final appeal, which he said should be utilised to guide the way forward.

“One of the most intriguing things to me is that the Privy Council has pointed to a solution for nearly four years now when the Adijah Palmer case went there,” he said, referencing the case of the individual widely known as dancehall artiste Vybz Kartel.

In 2024 the Privy Council overturned Kartel’s murder conviction based on its findings that the trial judge erred when, instead of discharging the entire jury, instead allowed the trial to continue with a juror who attempted to bribe others on the jury.

“What did they say? ‘If you’re going to have jury trials you can do it in such a manner that in the event that the jury must be discharged, then the trial can continue with the judge,” Sykes said of the Privy Council’s ruling in the Kartel case.

That would be a much easier approach than attempting to start over with a fresh panel of jurors or even adding alternates. Many individuals, for various reasons, shy away from serving as jurors.

On Saturday the chief justice made a fresh appeal for Jamaicans to do their civic duty and participate in the administration of justice.

“I dare say this is an appropriate place for me to repeat this again, ‘Show up when called to serve.’ So I am looking here at potential jurors who will, no doubt, be the first persons at the court in St James when you get the summons,” he quipped.

“You need to turn up and participate because our citizens — both those who are charged and those who are waiting to give evidence, those who have been the victim of violence — they need justice to be done, and you are a part of that process,” Sykes underscored.

He explained that the situation has become even more challenging given the impact on court facilities following the passage of last October’s Hurricane Melissa.

“A region does not fully recover with new buildings and new roofs, it recovers when it’s people also trust that they will be treated fairly, that their disputes will be heard, and that the law stands with them and not over them,” he told the gathering.

“Access to justice must reach every person in western Jamaica as surely as relief and rebuilding must,” he added.

Sykes pointed to the St James and Westmoreland parish court buildings as structures that have been impacted and are in need of urgent repair and redevelopment to serve the needs of the people. He noted that the St James Parish Court has for years had serious flooding issues. Despite these challenges, he urged members and partners of the legal fraternity who interact with the system to play their part in improving its efficiency.

“Justice restored in this region will not be the achievement of the judiciary alone, it depends on every arm of the profession pulling in the same direction. I ask that we examine our own practices,” he said.

“Too often the delay in our courts are not the faults of the bench. And I am not saying that the bench is never at fault, but what I am saying [is that] in many instances it is not the fault of the bench but documents come too late, incomplete, or not at all,” he lamented, adding that this must change.

World.title: Hot under the collar
World.content:
Airy Castle Primary School in St Thomaskarl mclarty

With intense heat expected to test students’ comfort, Airy Castle Primary Principal Dawn Graham is hoping conditions will not become a trigger for aggression this academic year.

“I’m… looking for a better school year than last year in terms of behaviour [because] that has been a concern, especially amongst our grade six students for last year. I’m hoping that the heat is not going to be a trigger to aggressive behaviour,” she told the Jamaica Observer during a visit to the school last week.

The heat was already severe enough to affect adults during a recent training session at the school. Graham is concerned about what conditions could be like once what she described as poorly ventilated classrooms are filled with children for extended periods.

“I sat in a training session with the teachers and the support staff and it was really hot. It was hot to the point that I know that at least two adults complained of severe headache, including myself… When those students are together in that space… I am [expecting we will be] seeing serious fatigue, especially in the afternoon and when the sun is really up,” she expressed.

The educator is counting on parents to keep students in check, despite the challenging circumstances.

“I’m hoping the parents are ready to give their support. I’m looking forward to an improved year, in especially, parent support,” said Graham.

In addition to keeping students cool, school officials will also have to keep an eye on their water supply.

St Thomas is among the parishes affected by water prohibition measures put in place to ration the commodity, as much of the country remains in the grip of a worrying dry spell. According to Graham, Airy Castle has experienced water problems in the past and they are watching closely to see whether the current conditions will place additional pressure on its supply.

“We will not act as though this is not a concern because the drought is upon us. We have already started to see the effects of the drought on the green areas,” she said.

The school currently has two full tanks, including one holding about 4,000 gallons, giving it a measure of protection as students return. Graham has a lot of confidence that support will be provided by the regional arm of the Ministry of Education if needed.

“What I am particularly impressed by is that in our region, they have been doing their checks and balances. The schools are already checked to see how many tanks are available, whether we are having difficulties with getting water for next week or storage. They have already checked that… so, for now, we are safe for starting,” she told the Observer.

But there is still the possibility of disruptions, and she would love to have more storage capacity.

“Should the piped water be affected, as it usually is sometimes, we are going to have serious problems,” Graham warned.

She explained that even before the current drought conditions, they have had challenges that have forced them to rely on trucked water.

“Water lock-offs are an issue here, mainly if the pump is broken or damaged, and that happens… about 40 per cent of the time. When it does happen, it is prolonged. Might be a month or more where you have to get trucked water sometimes, so it is a concern,” she said.

“I would think that we need to get more tanks in, which the ministry, as I said, they have been doing well at that by doing their checks and trying to put plans in place… We could do with another 2,000-gallon tank to be on the safe side; or another 4,000-gallon would be nice,” she added.

Despite concerns about the water supply and heat, Graham said Airy Castle is largely ready for the new school year, with about 90 to 95 per cent of preparations completed when the

Observer visited last Tuesday.

The remaining work involves basic infrastructure repairs, electrical work, and maintenance, which she said are being funded through grants from the education ministry.

World.title: Koffee makes waves with ‘Ova So’
World.content:
KOFFEE...there’s different energies that you’ll experience on the album, different genres, different feels of the music, and I think overall fans can expect a pretty cool, chill experience

By the time the sun began its descent over Wickie Wackie Beach on Friday, the shoreline had taken on a different kind of rhythm. Waves rolled quietly towards the sand, the evening breeze moved easily through the gathering and, against the picturesque backdrop of sea and sky, a specially invited crowd waited for Koffee to give them a taste of what comes next.

There was no sprawling concert stage or sea of thousands demanding her attention. Instead, the Grammy-winning artiste chose intimacy — a fitting setting for a musical reintroduction that appears to be unfolding on her own terms.

At the centre of Friday’s gathering was Ova So, Koffee’s latest single and another breadcrumb on the road towards her highly anticipated new album, due in October. The track was unveiled as part of a series of mini pop-up shows the reggae star has been using to reconnect with audiences ahead of the project, turning each appearance into both a performance and a preview of the musical chapter she is preparing to open.

For an artiste whose career once moved at whirlwind speed — from breakout sensation to Grammy winner and international stages in just a few short years — this latest chapter feels less like a race back into the spotlight and more like a carefully paced return. At Wickie Wackie, there was room for the music to breathe, for Koffee to meet her audience up close and, for one evening, allow a select few inside the world she has been quietly creating.

For Koffee, Ova So may feel particularly familiar to those who have been following her from the beginning.

“I think this is one of the songs dem weh me original fans dem ago love because I think it has a similar style to some of my earlier work like

Raggamuffin, using oldies samples and stuff like that,” she shared.

That familiarity, however, should not be mistaken for an indication that the forthcoming project will remain in one musical lane.

“There’s different energies that you’ll experience on the album, different genres, different feels of the music, and I think overall fans can expect a pretty cool, chill experience,” Koffee said.

Koffee’s latest musical exploits come after a brief hiatus, but as she readies a new project the entertainer is promising consistency. She outlined that her time away from the music scene allowed her to prepare herself mentally for the re-emergence she’s now experiencing.

“Fans can expect more presence and consistency from me,” she said. “I can definitely say that the time I took off the scene, I rejuvenated myself, refreshed myself, and just made sure my mind was in the right place to take on the road again.”

“I think I’m doing the best I’ve been doing my entire life, and I’m looking forward to experiencing even more and better,” she added.

World.title: Cops confident though traffic snarls expected in MoBay
World.content:
Motorists travelling along the West Green/Catherine Hall area of the under-construction Montego Bay Perimeter Road Project about noon on Saturday had to navigate dusty, uneven surfaces, while keeping an eye out for construction crew and heavy equipment. (Charmaine N Clarke)

MONTEGO BAY, St James — With the massive Western Water Resilience Project added, over the summer break, to the mix of work being done in and around this city, there is concern that there will be major traffic challenges today as thousands of students head out for the start of the new school term. Superintendent Eron Samuels, who leads the St James Police Division, is encouraging commuters to factor delays into their travel time.

“In light of all the work that is being done, we have already identified the areas of concern. For the pipeline project, that has been progressing smoothly [in terms of] how they have set up and organised themselves. What we will ask is that people leave out a little bit earlier so that they can make up time for the delays that they will have in that project. That is the one that we believe will cause a little bit more headache than the others,” he told the Jamaica Observer Friday.

Even as he stressed that he does not anticipate any major delays, he said he will have boots on the ground in that area today. Looking ahead to the evening rush hour, he is hoping commuters will take a staggered approach to road travel.

“If they have somewhere they can go and sit and relax for a little while until the traffic runs off, that will help to ease the congestion and ease the anxiety that they’ll face by being in traffic for extended periods,” said Samuels. “The truth is, we have more vehicles than the network of the roadwork can actually manage, so no matter what, the number of vehicles is just a challenge. So unless persons carpool or take public transportation, we will still see some issues as it relates to traffic… We have seen an increase in public transportation, the JUTC buses… so let us ask them to utilise those,” he encouraged.

Samuels and his team have amassed years of experience handling the back-to-school rush, and past traffic management plans have taken into account everything from protests to pothole-riddled roads.

Some may argue that this year is different.

Phase 1 of the US$450-million Western Water Resilience Project began along the Elegant Corridor in Rose Hall, St James, in June. Pipe-laying between Greenwood and Montego Bay is expected to last two years, with completion anticipated by summer of 2028. Work also continues on the US$354-million Montego Bay Perimeter Road which intersects the North Coast Highway at Ironshore, with its various sub-projects impacting traffic flow in the vicinity of Alice Eldemire Drive and Howard Cooke Highway, along with large residential communities in Bogue, Irwin, Cornwall Courts, and Salt Spring. In the Catherine Hall/West Green area, for example, traffic slowed to a crawl about midday Saturday as motorists navigated dusty, uneven surfaces while keeping an eye out for construction crew and heavy equipment.

The last deadline provided by the works ministry is for work on West Green Avenue to be completed this month. Samuels — who said he expects the bypass to open around the middle to the end of this school term — stressed that this will divert significant traffic away from the heart of the bustling city.

For now, based on how the project has been handled to date, he does not anticipate any issues when schools are once again in session. And even if things do not go as smoothly as he expects, he is confident his team can handle it.

“We will have enough personnel on the ground to monitor those. In the township itself, we’ll be putting police officers at the stop lights, as usual, to keep the traffic moving,” explained Samuels.

While he declined to divulge specific numbers regarding deployment, he acknowledged that there are staffing constraints which may impact how his team prevents and clears traffic snarls.

“There are never enough police officers, based on what we do and things that might happen, but we are flexible and we have shown that we have been managing the traffic situation,” he said.

Samuels noted that the division recently received an influx of additional traffic personnel, which paid off in smoother traffic flow since earlier in the year and positively impacted the previous school term. He said overall policing strategies for the city remain largely unchanged, with cops prepared to pivot as necessary.

He also confirmed that traffic personnel are strongly encouraged to wear body cameras.

“Our direct traffic police officers, most of them will be equipped. If they’re not equipped, it’s probably because we ran out of body cameras or if they have more than one police officer working at the same location. But we have been encouraging and monitoring our traffic police officers to wear their body cameras,” stated Samuels.

Confident that his team is ready for today, the St James divisional head pointed to an area of concern that is beyond their control: potholes. He described them as “major impediments” to smooth traffic flow.

“We have to look and see how the NWA [National Works Agency] or the [St James] Municipal Corporation can assist in ensuring that these holes are filled up or patched before the school year begins to fully flow,” he said.

While not all schools are expected to open today, full operations are anticipated by the end of the week. Samuels assured that police personnel will be out in their numbers to cover critical areas, monitoring the situation on a day-to-day basis to prevent recurring issues.

“All in all, we have made our plans and we’re satisfied that the plans can work,” the superintendent assured.

World.title: Expect ‘a little bit of discomfort’
World.content:
Some of the roofless teachers’ cottages are at the front of Knockalva Technical High School located at Ramble in Hanover is seen on WednesdayAnthony Lewis

RAMBLE, Hanover — Staff and students of Knockalva Technical High School here in this parish should not be surprised when they show up to school this morning and see that there is still work left to do to fix damage inflicted by last year’s Hurricane Melissa. During orientation last Tuesday, Principal Gregory Brown gave members of his team and parents a heads up that they will likely experience “a little bit of discomfort”.

He anticipates that when classes resume for the 800 students enrolled, this will delay work planned for some labs, bathroom facilities and re-installation of air-conditioning units.

“Some of those conversations are being had with the parents, that you’re going to experience… a little bit of displacement here and there. But it is far better than the children staying out. They have stayed out too long in our view. The parents and the staff, we are on board together to find a way to make the best use of the space we have to have all the children come [today] as we work to get back to some normalcy,” Brown told the

Jamaica Observer during a visit to the school last week.

He said that after four missed deadlines, repairs finally began on August 6 and there were mileposts along the way to help move the work along.

“We would have set deadlines for individual sections that they were doing, the different areas. So far, they have met the deadline for covering the roof, for resealing them…They have met the deadline for covering the canteen. I’m hoping they were sourcing material to cover the auditorium. If those things are in place, I think they’ll meet the deadline as well,” he said, his voice full of optimism.

“Overall though, I get the impression that we should be about 80 per cent complete by mid-October or roundabout there,” the educator added.

He explained that the remaining 20 per cent of work — such as cupboard replacement and AC installation — are things that will not have a significant impact on the school’s daily operations.

“Overall, the board and myself, we are kind of pleased at the rate at which they are going. It’s night and day, and the premix trucks are there. They come regularly,” stated Brown, who had high praise for the Ministry of Education and its agency, the National Education Trust (NET).

However, while the ongoing repair work is not a major worry, he is concerned about lingering challenges with staff housing and a shortage of water.

Knockalva Technical High is supplied by piped water from the National Water Commission’s (NWC) facility in Chester Castle. While the region sits in a watershed area, the school normally receives water once or twice a week. Brown noted that drought conditions have further reduced supplies.

“An area that is of even greater concern… is water. It’s really something that is now popping up and we are giving it serious attention,” he said.

Before last year’s Category 5 storm damaged vital equipment, the school used to do rain water harvesting.

“Our science department would treat the water [by using] training that they had with NWC. But even though we’re having rains now, the harvesting facility was damaged and since they have worked on the roof, it takes a little while to get back that up,” stated Brown.

Before the storm, the school’s water harvesting system included 25 metal and black tanks. That number has been reduced to 15 tanks which need up to 5,000 gallons daily to operate effectively. Last Tuesday, the school received 10,400 gallons of trucked water that was expected to last them four days.

“The water now is just as critical a thing as full completion [of the repairs]. It’s concerning to us because it’s expensive to get the water in. [Water trucked by] the Government and NWC alone cannot provide the amount of water that we need because they have to go to the police station, they have to go to other schools, they have to go to so many other places. So we too, through our private contractor, have to stop the gap that exists. We are doing so but I don’t know how long we can do that because it’s an expensive venture,” said a worried Brown.

He also has to grapple with fallout from the damage Hurricane Melissa did to the school cottage. Now, teachers who would have stayed there are forced to commute roughly 40 miles daily.

“It’s not easy to get accommodation in the area because most of the houses and the persons who used to provide these accommodations to our staff members are suffering [hurricane] damage as well. It forces our teachers to travel. I have 15 that were living on plant [the cottage] having to travel from as far as Santa Cruz [in St Elizabeth],” explained Brown.

But even with almost a year of challenges, his teachers have put in the work and that was reflected in students’ performance.

“I can’t commend the teachers enough because this year, the exam passes are 50 per cent better than the year before. Some of the teachers who are travelling from as far as Santa Cruz are getting 100 per cent passes in the CSEC [Caribbean Secondary Education Certificate] exams. The effort and the commitment are beyond all contestation,” Brown said proudly.

World.title: EL NIÑO AT PLAY!
World.content:
Kivann Salmon (right) of Excelsior High School falls after a challenge by Kevon Adlam of Tivoli Gardens High School during the ISSA Manning Cup football match at Excelsior on December 2, 2025. (Photo: Naphtali Junior)

WITH the schoolboy football season underway for the next three months, sports medicine specialist Dr Winston Dawes is urging relevant stakeholders to exercise extreme caution to prevent serious issues among players as it relates to the El Niño phenomenon.

The under-19 competition kicked off on Saturday with the opening games of the ISSA daCosta Cup first round, with the Manning Cup set to begin on Wednesday.

However, the players will have to deal with the higher-than-usual temperatures caused by El Niño, a complex weather pattern that results from variations in winds and sea surface temperatures.

Although it has affected the island over the summer months with temperatures approaching near 40 degrees Celsius, the Meteorological Service of Jamaica says the worst effects could last through to November. After seeing this week’s temperature map, senior meteorologist Romayne Robinson said outdoor activities such as physical education classes should “end before 10 or not take place at all”.

Dawes says dehydration and heat stroke are two of the main threats the players will face, especially with the fields constantly absorbing heat. However, he told the Jamaica Observer that these risks can be reduced by hydrating long in advance.

“You have to start from the evening before, whereby you drink tons of water and electrolytes; have glucose; have a carbohydrate-rich meal, simple carbohydrates; then throughout the morning you would drink tons of fluid so that you enter the match fully hydrated,” Dawes said.

ISSA President Keith Wellington says they have put measures in place to ensure the students are taken care of.

“The competition rules speak to these mitigating factors and what are some of the things we expect. Obviously we’ll have a policy of not playing double-headers where the teams have to be playing at 1 o’clock in the afternoon,” he said.

“We are going to be mindful of the issue of safeguarding of our student athletes. Even from a management perspective, we have said this year that each team must have a safeguarding officer — that is somebody who is not a coach, who is not a part of the technical staff, maybe just a teacher who has no interest at all in football but has interest in the duty of care for our students. So yes, we are mindful of the El Niño effect but [at the same time we are] just generally ensuring that our students are taken care of.”

Football’s world governing body, FIFA, introduced mandatory hydration breaks during this summer’s World Cup to combat the heat in the United States, Mexico and Canada, though it was criticised due to its commercial aspect.

The ISSA Competitions Committee revealed that hydration breaks will be implemented but won’t be mandatory. Instead, their occurrence will depend on the specific conditions on match day.

Dawes, though, says players must be given the chance to hydrate at any given point during the game.

“Even if you don’t have the formal break, they should allow the players to be able to come to the sidelines and drink something. Whether it’s for a throw-in or a kick, they could allow 15 seconds for people to drink,” he said.

“The coaches are going to have to monitor the kids, speak to them about everything, and that if the referees, coaches or medical personnel see something happening, they should have the right to assess the player and also call for rehydration. It means that the adults who are responsible for organising the game have got to be on the alert for anything untoward.”

Dawes, who also served as president of the Jamaica Football Federation, says referees should also exercise some leniency as hydration breaks should not be viewed as a time-wasting tactic.

“It’s not time-wasting to have people come and take a quick drink,” he said. “Time-wasting is something different; we have people who take one minute for a throw-in or a goal kick or kicking away the ball — that’s time-wasting. What you want to do is protect the players from overexertion, which creates problems.”

World.title: How Dis Mek? – Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee
World.content:
Coffee seedlings in a nursery at the Mavis Bank Coffee FactoryPhoto: Gavin Jones

WHETHER you have it instant, in a frappé, mocha, latte, or just plain black, coffee is a staple for many Jamaicans, but the deep brown beans we know and love start out very differently.

Managing director of Mavis Bank Coffee Factory Dr Norman Grant recently shared with the Jamaica Observer the process to create what is, for many people around the world, their favourite beverage.

“Coffee came to Jamaica by our then Governor Sir Nicholas Laws. He brought three coffee plants,

Arabica Typica, to the Blue Mountains in Temple Hall in West Rural St Andrew, and coffee was planted there,” Grant explained.

Since then, speciality or gourmet coffee known as Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee has been grown in specified regions in the Blue Mountain range across St Thomas, St Andrew, and Portland at an altitude of between 2,000 and 5,000 feet.

Discovered in Ethiopia in 1614, coffee starts out as a sapling, grown from seeds in a nursery for six to nine months before plants are moved to coffee ‘plantations’. After being planted, coffee trees need another two to three years before they will produce fruit.

When that fruit grows, it’s in the form of a small green bud that turns into a bright red berry, called cherry berries or coffee cherries.

“What we do once the coffee is ripe, the farmers reap, and we have our trucks that go out to collect it from agents that receive it from the farmers. These agents are called our selectors,” Grant explained.

The coffee is then taken to the factory, remeasured and poured into large containers of water to separate the good ones from the bad.

Bad coffee, which has been bitten by birds, or worms, or the ones that are decayed, will float, while good coffee with heavy intact beans will sink to the bottom of the container.

The good coffee is then upended into large vats that pulp the fruit, separating the flesh from the beans.

“There’s a machine that washes and takes off the sugary substance, which is called the mucilage, and then we get what is called wet parchment,” said Grant.

That is dried on patios, or asphalt barbecues that are strictly controlled, no outside shoes or visitors are allowed to step on or walk across the surface.

Drying on the barbecue removes about 30 per cent of the water from the beans.

“We complete the drying process with a mechanical dryer to get what we call cured parchment, having only between 10 per cent to 12.5 per cent moisture,” said Grant.

The cured or dry parchment is then collected in sacks, and stored in warehouses where it will age for between 12 and 40 weeks.

“Once properly rested, we go to the hulling stage, and there’s a huller that takes off the brown section and then polishes the beans,” Grant explained.

The next stage must be done by human beings, sorting the beans one by one into different grades.

“The beans are listed as grade ones, twos, threes, and pea berries, which are oval-shaped beans. We also have select, which is a rerun of all the different grades,” Grant further explained.

Throughout this process sample beans are routinely taken to a testing lab on the property where they are roasted in small batches and tested for irregularities or impurities.

Once none have been found, the coffee beans move to the roasting stage where the Blue Mountain coffee gets its traditional dark brown colour and rich flavour.

This is done inside a specially built machine which roasts the beans before spitting them out onto a rotating cooler before they are ground and packaged.

Once packaged, the last step is for employees to use a sewing machine to secure the coffee in traditional brown bags before it is exported, or put onto the local market.

“It’s a small, tight operation, but we roast about close to two million pounds of coffee through this plant per annum,” Grant revealed.

The Mavis Bank Coffee Factory produces, Wallenford, Jablum and True Brew brands. Other Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee producers include Old Tavern Estate, Clifton Mount Estate, which supplies Café Blue, and Clydesdale.

The popularity of the coffee and the fact that the majority of it is exported to Jamaica’s largest coffee market, Japan, has spawned imitations.

All genuine brands bear the Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee trademarked seal issued by the Jamaica Agricultural Commodities Regulatory Authority.

For Grant, who is also a certified Q Grader licensed to assess speciality coffee, Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee is more than a speciality; it is without comparison.

“When you taste it, you get this awesome after-taste that lingers, that says you just had the best coffee in the world. Jamaica Blue Mountain Coffee, made by over 5,000 Blue Mountain coffee farmers. Ah so we mek it!” declared Grant.

Think your product could feature on How Dis Mek? Contact (876) 570 3163, jolmalcolmd@gmail.com or editorial@jamaicaobserver.com

World.title: Russia shuts German consulate as drone dispute escalates
World.content:
The German consulate in St. Petersburg, Russia is pictured on Sept. 2, 2026. | Olga Maltseva/AFP via Getty Images

The German consulate in St. Petersburg must close by Sept. 18, in response to Berlin’s recent “unfriendly actions,” Russia’s foreign ministry announced Monday.

While the embassy and consular services in Moscow remain open, the consulate in the northwest of the country must cease all operations and all staff must leave Russia by the specified date.

“It was the German authorities that once again provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations. All responsibility for the consequences lies entirely with the Government of Germany,” the statement reads, referring to Berlin’s announcement last week that Russia was behind a drone attack on German territory.

World.title: Ratko Mladić funeral exposes gap between Serbia’s EU ambitions and political reality
World.content:
The Serbian government officially said that it had no hand in organizing the funeral, yet Mladić’s body was flown on a government plane and members of the Serbian Armed Forces escorted the coffin to its final resting place while the military band played a funeral march. The patriarch of the Serbian Orthodox Church, Porfirije — a close ally of Serbian President Aleksandar Vučić — led the funeral mass, where Mladić’s coffin was draped in the Serbian flag.

Mladić, a general who spearheaded military campaigns across Bosnia and Croatia and was convicted of genocide for the killing of more than 8,000 people in early July 1995 in the eastern Bosnian town of Srebrenica, died in late August aged 84 while serving a life sentence at Scheveningen prison in the Netherlands.

Senior Serbian officials turned out for the service at the Church of Saint Luke on Monday, including Defense Minister Bratislav Gašić and Justice Minister Nenad Vujić. Danilo Vučić, the president’s son, was also in attendance, as was Russian Ambassador Aleksandr Botsan-Kharchenko.

Vučić, a populist nationalist who has been president of Serbia since 2017, himself skipped the funeral to meet with Shavkat Mirziyoyev, president of Uzbekistan, and made no reference to Mladić or the funeral in his public statements.

The president has often positioned himself as a pragmatic technocrat in Brussels, while Serbia continues an EU accession bid that started in 2014. But critics and human rights organizations have accused him of allowing — sometimes encouraging — nationalism to foment domestically.

Vujić, the justice minister, defended the right of Serbian citizens to pay their respects to Mladić on Friday, stressing that “the punishment ends with death.”

World.title: Champagne production halves as scorching summer dents French wine grape harvest
World.content:
In Champagne, growers reaped their earliest harvest on record, racing to pick grapes before rising sugar levels pushed potential alcohol too high. Output there is expected to be roughly halved, with grape bunch weights at their lowest in 20 years.

In southern France’s Languedoc-Roussillon wine region, by contrast, production is forecast to rebound 5 percent from last year’s weak harvest, which was about 13 percent below the five-year average. Even with that recovery, output this year remains 8 percent below average.

Conditions had initially looked promising, with good grape development and low disease pressure. But “the hot and dry conditions of the summer degraded this potential,” Agreste said.

If confirmed, the sub-3.4 billion-liter crop would be France’s smallest since 1957 — a nearly 70-year low.

And wine is only one casualty of Europe’s brutal summer. Farmer group Copa-Cogeca estimated in a report published last week that maize losses reached 50 to 70 percent in Slovenia, 40 percent in France and 20 to 25 percent in Italy, reaching 70 percent in some unirrigated areas. Croatia expects fruit and grape output to fall around 30 percent.

French Environment Minister Monique Barbut has put the summer’s economic damage at €10 billion to €15 billion, or as much as 0.5 percent of GDP.

Paris unveiled more than €1 billion in emergency farm aid Friday, though agricultural groups say the package falls short.

World.title: L’UE veut sévir contre les locations de courte durée pour rendre le logement plus abordable
World.content:
Dan Jørgensen met en avant que la nouvelle législation “donner[ait] aux autorités locales qui souhaitent prendre des mesures, la possibilité de le faire de manière efficace et sans s’exposer à des risques de litige”. Le commissaire conteste les arguments du secteur, qui affirme que ces restrictions pourraient nuire aux économies dépendantes du tourisme et aux propriétaires qui comptent sur leurs revenus locatifs. Il a souligné que “le logement est un droit, pas seulement une marchandise”, et que “les gens doivent passer avant les profits”.

Il balaye également l’objection avancée par le secteur selon laquelle la Commission outrepasserait ses compétences en légiférant sur le logement, un domaine dans lequel l’UE ne dispose que de compétences directes limitées. Dan Jørgensen souligne que, dans le cadre de la future législation, ce sont les autorités nationales, régionales et locales qui détermineront quelles zones seront considérées comme tendues et qui décideront s’il convient d’intervenir et, le cas échéant, de quelle manière.

“L’objectif n’est pas d’imposer des restrictions depuis Bruxelles”, assure-t-il. “Mais l’accès au logement est l’un des défis les plus urgents de l’Europe, et les institutions européennes ne peuvent fermer les yeux sur les problèmes quotidiens très concrets auxquels nos citoyens sont confrontés.”

“Si nous ne parvenons pas à faire face à cette crise, nous risquons de perdre la confiance de nos concitoyens dans les institutions démocratiques, poursuit-il. Et cela conduirait à la montée en puissance des forces politiques extrémistes.”

Cette législation intervient près d’un an après que la présidente de la Commission, Ursula von der Leyen, a qualifié la pénurie de logements dans l’UE de “crise sociale” et s’est engagée à prendre des mesures.

Pour Dan Jørgensen, cette nouvelle loi constitue “une étape décisive pour soutenir les villes, les régions et les pays qui souhaitent apporter des solutions immédiates aux zones et aux populations les plus touchées”, tout en soulignant que ce n’est pas la panacée.

“La crise du logement est un problème complexe”, complète-t-il, et l’UE doit encore “prendre des mesures en matière d’investissement, de simplification des règles, d’offre et de pressions sur le parc immobilier existant”.

Cet article a d’abord été publié par POLITICO en anglais, puis a été édité en français par Jean-Christophe Catalon.

World.title: By-election in Keir Starmer’s old seat expected Oct. 8
World.content:
The former prime minister stood down from the House of Commons last week. He said he wants to devote more time to international affairs, despite previously pledging to remain an MP until the next general election.

In 2024, Starmer held the seat with a 11,572 majority, but faced a strong challenge from a left-wing independent candidate and the Greens.

Green Leader Leader Zack Polanski has put himself forward for the party’s nomination, arguing that under him “voters will have someone who will always fight their corner.”

He is facing a challenge from Hamza Chowdhury, a councilor in the Camden Green ward, who said the constituency doesn’t need an MP who “makes a few promises and disappears once the votes are counted.” The party’s candidate will be announced on Sept. 11.

The election is due to take place less than a week after the Green Party’s annual conference, which takes place in Brighton between Oct. 2 and Oct. 4. Labour’s annual conference takes place in Liverpool from Sept. 27 to Sept. 30.

Labour will choose its candidate on Wednesday.

World.title: Von der Leyen: Greenland is choosing Europe and Europe is choosing Greenland
World.content:
U.S. President Donald Trump has made repeated threats to take over Greenland. In July, he said that “Greenland … should be controlled by the United States, not by Denmark” at the outset of a NATO summit in Turkey.

The Arctic has rapidly climbed up Brussels’ geopolitical agenda. Von der Leyen said the region had become a place “where the tectonic plates of geopolitics collide,” adding that the EU has a direct stake in developments there and is preparing a new Arctic strategy for presentation this fall.

The Arctic is also expected to feature prominently in von der Leyen’s State of the Union speech next week, as Brussels prepares the revamped strategy.

She also reiterated that Greenland’s future is for the people of Greenland and Denmark to decide.

The two-day visit, which began Sunday, was aimed at turning the political message into concrete projects. A Commission official said the trip had been months in the making but was postponed at Frederiksen’s request due to Danish elections in March.

Von der Leyen signed a renewed joint declaration with Greenland and Denmark and unveiled a €200 million EU partnership package for this year and next.

World.title: Ireland hails EU tax agreement on carbon imports and electronic waste
World.content:
The president of the European Council, António Costa, urged national leaders to home in on several potential taxes during their next gathering in Brussels on Oct. 15. Supporters argue that own resources are essential to generate more revenue and reduce national contributions to the EU from 2028 to 2034.

With less than four months to go until the informal deadline, the bloc's governments have shown openness towards a tax on foreign carbon imports, officially known as the Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), and a separate levy on non-collected electronic waste.

“Of the Commission’s proposals for new Own Resources, the most consensual among Member States is CBAM, with many open to increasing the call rate further,” the Irish Council presidency, which is steering discussions, wrote in a note to EU governments seen by POLITICO.

Under current rules, capitals must funnel 75 percent of CBAM revenues to the EU budget, and retain 25 percent for their domestic budgets.

CBAM is expected to generate, on average, €1.644 billion per year, roughly adding up to €11.5 billion for the whole budget cycle, according to an updated estimate by the European Commission seen by POLITICO.

The Irish presidency also noted “a broad degree of support” among governments towards the electronic waste tax, which is expected to generate €17.9 billion per year. They added that criticism towards the levy largely focuses on statistical issues.

World.title: Renew MEPs to press Macron on his political future at Paris meeting
World.content:
A Renew official, granted anonymity to speak candidly about the meeting agenda, said lawmakers are growing particularly concerned about the prospect of far-right parties taking power in Germany and France, where Marine Le Pen has a commanding lead in the polls for the spring 2027 presidential race.

“Pro-Europeans … are worried about what happens after Macron because they recognize his vision and ambition for Europe,” said the official.

The burning question on everyone’s lips is what Macron, who cannot run for a third consecutive term, can and will do next. The 48-year-old has given little indication of his plans after he steps down in May 2027, but he has hinted at once again running for the presidency when he is eligible in 2032.

“Lawmakers will question the president on his political future, many would like to see him play a role at a European level,” said the Renew official.

But Macron has also indicated that he will focus on his role as French president until the very last day, raising fears he is not preparing the future of his centrist movement when he leaves office. Last May, he said he would “think about what comes next” after the end of his mandate.

The talks in Paris will also focus on the upcoming State of the Union speech by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen, the Multiannual Financial Framework, social media bans, European preference measures and Ukraine.

CORRECTION: This story was updated on Sept. 7 to reflect that Wednesday will not be the first visit to the Elysée for Renew’s MEPs.

World.title: Record fuel price rise sparks protests in Portugal
World.content:
Portugal woke up to yet another fuel price rise, which in the case of diesel reached a historic high. This time, the increase in prices, which has been occurring throughout the year, was marked by protests on roads across the country.

 

In the morning, a car horn protest on the 25 de Abril bridge could be heard on the crossing that links Lisbon to the city of Almada, on the south bank of the River Tagus.

At the same time, further south, a go-slow march towards Galp's refinery in Sines, in the district of Setúbal, was getting under way. The protest, organised on WhatsApp and social media, was still ongoing after lunchtime and had no set time to end.

Images on social media showed cars with Portuguese flags on their bonnets, sounding their horns. According to the Lusa news agency, protesters were also carrying placards reading "Enough of fuel price rises" and "Families can't take any more". The GNR told the agency that between 60 and 100 vehicles took part.

Petrol at its highest since the invasion of Ukraine

According to forecasts by theAutomobile Club of Portugal (ACP) (source in Portuguese), diesel rose by 15 cents this Monday (to 2,169 euros per litre) and petrol increased by 12 cents (to 2,142 euros per litre).

These amounts do not take into account the reduction in the Tax on Petroleum Products (ISP), applied by the government on an exceptional basis, which capped the increases at an additional 12 cents for diesel and 9 cents for petrol.

This is the highest diesel price ever, according to Dinheiro Vivo's calculations (source in Portuguese). As for petrol, this is the highest level since the energy crisis triggered by Russia's invasion of Ukraine in 2022.

Portugal among the highest prices

FILE (29.04.2025). Petrol station in Lisbon. AP Photo/Armando Franca

Fuel prices in Europe have been rising throughout the year. In Germany too, Frankfurter Allgemeine (source in Portuguese) reports that fuel prices have reached an all-time high, with petrol surpassing the record of 2.203 euros per litre set in March 2022.

But Portugal is among the countries with the highest fuel prices. Thefuel-prices website (source in Portuguese), which aggregates fuel prices in 21 European countries, showed this Monday that Portugal is the 19th most expensive country for petrol. Only France and Denmark rank higher.

For diesel, the position improves to 17th place, ahead of the United Kingdom, Italy, France and Denmark.

The surge in prices even prompted Portugal's environment and energy minister, Maria da Graça Carvalho, to request a study from the Energy Services Regulatory Authority (ERSE).

But the study, published in mid-August, found "no evidence of profiteering by operators". It also said there was no "rockets and feathers" phenomenon, with prices rising quickly and falling slowly.

"The results do not therefore support the notion that reductions are passed through persistently more slowly or less completely than increases," the study says.

ERSE also justified the difference in prices with Spain by pointing to taxes. But it stressed that in Portugal the tax burden has remained constant, "in line with most countries in the European Union and the eurozone".

Hormuz and refining capacity

The rise in fuel prices in Europe has been linked to the conflict in the Middle East and the blockage in the Strait of Hormuz, which has disrupted trade routes.

But experts also point to limited refining capacity, even when crude oil is available. This situation particularly affects diesel.

On the tax front, an extraordinary tax on oil companies' profits is now on the table. According to AFP, ministers from Portugal, Germany, Italy, Austria, Poland and Spain have sent a letter to Ireland's finance minister asking that the issue be discussed at the next meeting of finance ministers. The meeting is scheduled for 18 and 19 September in Ireland, which holds the rotating presidency of the European Union.

World.title: AfD victory exposes divisions on France’s far right as National Rally stays silent
World.content:
France's National Rally party reacted to the victory of Germany’s far-right Alternative für Deutschland (AfD) party with a noticeable silence on Monday, a move that reflects its complicated ties to the party.

 

Marine Le Pen and Jordan Bardella — who are respectively campaigning to be France's next president and prime minister — made no mention of the AfD after the party took 43.8% of votes in Saxony-Anhalt’s elections, racing ahead of Christian Democratic Union, Chancellor Friedrich Merz’s party, which secured 17.2%.

Meanwhile, the Reconquête party — which is positioned further to the right than the National Rally and sits in the same group as the AfD in the European Parliament — welcomed the victory, reflecting political divergences within France's far-right.

Although the National Rally's leading figures have yet to comment publicly, other MPs from the party have weighed in. Bardella had also addressed the issue before the vote, when reporters at the Ambrosetti Forum — an annual economic and geopolitical conference held in Italy — questioned him about the prospect of the National Rally renewing ties with the AfD on Saturday.

In response, he said that this was not "planned," but underlined that "the electoral pressure exerted by the AfD in Germany has helped shift the political landscape within [Chancellor Friedrich] Merz's government, as Germany reinstated border controls a few months ago."

A campaign to recover the party's image

The silence at the top of the party is not surprising, given that Marine Le Pen has spent over a decade working to normalise the image of the National Rally (formerly known as the National Front), both at home and abroad, as part of a campaign to move away from the overt racism and antisemitism promoted by her father, Jean-Marie Le Pen, the party’s founder.

At present, her party is leading in the polls, with around 34 to 36% of respondents stating they intend to vote for her in the first round of the presidential elections scheduled for April 2027, according to a poll by IPSOS/BVA published by the French newspaper Le Parisien on Saturday.

National Rally politician and Patriots for Europe (PfE) MEP Pierre-Romain Thionnet told Euronews that the AfD's result "should not come as a surprise to anyone", arguing that its victory was vested in issues which mainstream parties have not worked to solve: "mass immigration, loss of national identity, and social and industrial decline."

According to the MEP, the result reflects "the collapse of the mainstream parties in favour of political forces that truly represent the aspirations of the European people."

Despite this, he ensured that the National Rally's decision to "no longer be an ally of the AfD" in the European Parliament would remain "unchanged."

"Several members of that political party continue to hold positions on historical and remembrance issues that we find unacceptable, and because there are very significant differences on other issues, such as foreign policy," said Thionnet.

The National Rally party and AfD were formerly part of the Identity and Democracy group, along with Italy’s League and Austria’s Freedom Party (FPÖ), among others. However, things came to a head ahead of the 2024 European Parliamentary elections, following a series of controversies involving some of the AfD's senior figures.

This included comments made by Maximilian Krah, the AfD's lead candidate in the Parliamentary elections, who stated that membership of the Nazi SS did not automatically make someone a criminal, during an interview with Italian newspaper La Repubblica.

The Identity and Democracy group voted to exclude the AfD in May 2024, just weeks before the European Parliament elections. Following the election, the AfD helped form a new far-right group, Europe of Sovereign Nations (ESN), which was formally established in July 2024.

Echoing these points, another MEP from the Patriots for Europe group told Euronews that "nothing will move before the French election," stating that "no one wants to be associated with the AfD, even though we have some points in common and cooperate on many topics."

Reconquête comes out in support of the AfD

The National Rally party may be keeping quiet, but the Reconquête! party, part of the same political group as the AfD in the European Parliament (Europe of Sovereign Nations), came out in support of the election results.

In an X post shared on Sunday evening, MEP Sarah Knafo described the results as "historic," stating that "the European peoples have shown a great deal of patience. Today, they want to take their destiny back into their own hands. An entire continent is rising up."

Meanwhile, Éric Zemmour, the leader of Reconquête, who has said he will wait until December to announce whether he will run in France's 2027 presidential election, qualified the results as "the hour of truth." In the first round of France's 2022 presidential election, Marine Le Pen took 23.15% of the votes, while the hard-right secured 7.07%.
