World.title: Nikola Šubić Zrinski – The Croat Who Stopped 100,000 Ottomans
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – Turning the clock all the way back to the 7th of September 1566, and we meet the famed Nikola Šubić Zrinski, the Croat who stopped 100,000 Ottomans, but lost his life during the final charge.

Nikola Šubić Zrinski was a Croatian nobleman, ban (viceroy) and soldier who lived during the 16th century and is remembered as a defender of Christianity throughout Europe. Index writes that he is best known for the Battle of Szigetvár, in which the sultan himself also lost his life. In Croatia, he holds additional importance because he elevated the Zrinski noble family to the status of the most powerful Croatian family of all.

he never shied away from battling the fearsome ottoman forces

He was born sometime during 1508. We don’t know exactly where he entered the world, but we know he had five brothers and sisters. His father was Nikola Šubić and his mother Jelena Karlović. Nikola’s political activity did not come only from the fact that he was a nobleman; the Karlović family had a long tradition of state functions. Nikola’s uncle Ivan Karlović later served as ban. The brave Zrinski was primarily a soldier. After finishing military school, Šubić joined the ongoing war and defended Vienna in 1529, at which time he was noticed by many nobles and military officials. After the siege he was rewarded with a golden chain and received a horse.

The conflict with the Ottomans only continued. When he inherited the estate in the Una valley in 1534, he also inherited the obligation to pay tribute to the Ottomans. Nikola truly did not want to pay tribute to the enemy, so he provoked a conflict over the fortress of Dubica in order to justify not paying the taxes.

habsburg or zapolya?

At the same time the Kingdom of Hungary was very unstable. After the death of Vladislav II Jagiellon at Mohács, the whole country split into two camps: one favoured the Habsburgs and wanted to bring them to power in Hungary and Croatia, while the other favoured the local Hungarian nobleman John Zápolya. Nikola Šubić Zrinski considered Ferdinand Habsburg the better and wiser choice, and he had already become acquainted with the Habsburgs during the siege of Vienna. That is why, on his own initiative, he decided to kill the nobleman Johann Katzianer, who had rejected the Habsburgs and sworn loyalty to Zápolya. He captured Katzianer’s fortress of Kostajnica, but soon handed it over to the Ottomans, from whom he expected retaliation for refusing to pay tribute.

the zrinskis head north…

From the 1540s on, he was given administration of the whole of Međimurje. He soon moved there, renovated the castle in Čakovec, and after a few years received the right to collect taxes himself and to settle serfs in the area. At the same time he became Ban of Croatia, a title he held until 1556. He left the “office” of ban because he was dissatisfied that he had failed to raise more funds for the fight against the Ottomans. He wanted someone more capable to take the position while he continued to wage war against the enemy. He immediately received the position of treasurer in Hungary (Hungarian nobles were inclined to give him whatever he wanted because he was highly respected even before Szigetvár) and fought the Ottomans twice. He believed he already knew their strategies well and rushed into war with them whenever possible.

the famous battle of Szigetvár

The next opportunity presented itself in 1566 when he was staying in the fortress of Szigetvár. Szigetvár is located in Hungary on the shortest route to Vienna. Suleiman the Magnificent led 100,000 men to capture Szigetvár and begin a new siege of Vienna. To them Szigetvár was just another miserable Christian fortress; the Ottomans conquered such places every other day. However, Suleiman the Magnificent was not prepared for what was about to happen. Around 2,000 men, mostly ethnic Croats, decided that the Ottomans would not pass here. As soon as Ottoman infantry approached the gates of Szigetvár, the defenders threw everything they could at them and the enemy withdrew. Szigetvár was constantly bombarded with cannonballs for a full month, and one did not walk in the inner courtyard because of the arrows that fell into the fortress without stopping.

The defenders ate all the food they had, then began to eat their own horses. They maintained their morale largely thanks to Nikola Šubić, who in his classic style still saw only victory. Then came 7 September 1566, and it was clear that that morning the Ottomans would break into the town. Nikola put on a hat and noble attire, left his knight’s armour aside, took his father’s sabre and bravely led his men into the final episode of that nightmare. All the defenders died that morning, and the Ottomans achieved their goal.

an extremely costly goal

But the goal was achieved at too great a cost. The Ottoman army should not have lost a fifth of its force on some stupid and unimportant fortress, nor should it have been delayed there for half the summer. To make matters worse, during the siege Suleiman the Magnificent died, so the army’s morale was weak and worthless. The army was soon recalled and headed home. Nothing came of a new siege of Vienna. The heroic defence of Szigetvár was the main topic of conversation throughout Europe in the following months. Everyone spoke about Nikola Šubić: from Roman and Spanish diplomats who claimed that God had sent him to save Vienna from the Muslims, to the French Cardinal Richelieu who called him “the saviour of Europe and the Christian world.”

His descendants continued to act politically and hold various positions in the new state, the Habsburg Monarchy. Nikola elevated the Zrinskis from an ordinary noble family to the most important family in Croatia. Their influence would mark the following period, right up to the Zrinski-Frankopan conspiracy of 1671.

Nikola Šubić Zrinski remains incredibly relevant to this very day. Legends of his defence of Szigetvár were retold to children in the following centuries, and when the awakening of nationalism began in the 19th century, Nikola became even more popular. Then the 1880 earthquake struck Zagreb and the city had to be rebuilt. About a hundred metres southeast of Zagreb’s main square, construction began on the most beautiful park in the city centre. The park would be named Zrinjevac, or Nikola Šubić Zrinski Square, further immortalising him.

World.title: Much More Than Tourism: Croatia’s New Zagreb-Beijing Connection
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – Croatia’s brand new Zagreb-Beijing connection by Air China means much more than just more tourism from Asia, with business and cultural ties implied.

On Friday at 09:47, fire engines stood ready as the “giant” Air China aircraft touched down on the runway of Zagreb’s Franjo Tuđman Airport. The majestic plane of the Chinese carrier completed the first, inaugural flight between Beijing, Bucharest and Zagreb. Katarina Kusec reports for Poslovni that the aircraft was welcomed with a water salute upon landing, while passengers and crew were greeted by a number of high-ranking officials. This flight marked the start of year-round services between the mentioned cities.

a bridge of friendship

Air China’s aircraft landed in Zagreb for the first time and thus began regular operations to Croatia, opening many doors for cooperation and travel. The new route will operate three times a week (Monday, Wednesday and Friday), and flights will continue year-round, including throughout winter. “Good day, welcome (Dobar dan, dobrodosli,” Qi Qianjin, Ambassador of the People’s Republic of China to Croatia, briefly addressed everyone in Croatian. He added that the new route represents much more than an air link between China and Croatia: “It’s a bridge of friendship that connects our peoples and develops potential for further bilateral cooperation in culture, tourism, trade… It will also reduce logistics costs and improve delivery efficiency.”

He emphasised that this is the first such flight in the history of the two countries, while recalling that, despite this, we have a long history of cultural exchanges and economic and trade ties dating back to the time of Marco Polo.

The new route connects Beijing and Zagreb via Bucharest, the capital of Romania. Operations will work as follows: passengers, for example, board in Zagreb and fly to Bucharest as they would to other Schengen countries. There is a three-hour stopover during which border formalities and passport checks are carried out, after which the journey continues to China. The procedure is the same for return flights, while luggage remains on the aircraft. The total flight time is around 14 hours and practically connects two ends of the world.

more opportunities for cooperation

“Today we’re celebrating not only a new air route, but also a new opportunity for cooperation between the two countries in the fields of tourism, business and culture. We look forward to the development of this partnership in the years to come. This new route expands our connections and links Croatia with one of the most dynamic markets,” said Nicolas Duthilleul, CEO and Member of the Board of Zagreb International Airport (MZLZ). He added that more than 4.7 million passengers passed through the airport last year and that he is convinced that with this new route China and Croatia gain more opportunities to grow even closer.

He also noted that travel opportunities have now expanded and that the airport has prepared additional information and signage in Chinese throughout the terminal for Chinese passengers so they can navigate more easily and feel more comfortable.

Air China is using wide-body Airbus A330-200 aircraft on the route. This first arrival brings yet another major global carrier to Zagreb and further expands the flight offer. The A330-200 has a capacity of 265 seats, while around 120 passengers arrived on this inaugural flight from Beijing via Bucharest to Zagreb. The arrival time suits everyone, as morning disembarkation allows them to continue their day normally with other flights or to head into the city very early.

In any case, this is a good foundation for the coming tourist years, and Monika Udovičić, State Secretary at the Ministry of Tourism and Sport, also sees potential in it.

great results for croatian tourism

“Croatian tourism will again finish this year with very good results, but what is more important is that we are significantly investing efforts in sustainable tourism, and I think this is something that will resonate well on the Chinese market. They come to see our natural beauty and cultural landmarks. The main motive is not only sun and sea, but our natural beauty,” she said, adding that Croatia has never been closer to China and that this is not just a route, but a better connection between the two countries that is moving towards strengthening relations, friendship and business.

“On distant markets, presence is built continuously through better transport connectivity, promotion and long-term partnerships, and this route represents an important step in that direction. I believe this route will contribute to an even stronger positioning of Croatia on the Chinese market.”

After the official part and the welcome of the crew and passengers, a cake was cut and champagne was poured, because big and new things need to be celebrated. Six journalists from China also attended the ceremony, as well as representatives of tourist boards. Among the speakers were also State Secretary at the Ministry of the Sea, Transport and Infrastructure Tomislav Mihotić, Director of the Croatian National Tourist Board Kristjan Staničić, and many others.

World.title: The Guardian Names Cres Europe’s Best Hidden Gem
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – The Guardian has spotlighted gorgeous Cres, referring to it as Europe’s best hidden gem.

The influential Guardian was well and truly won over by the wilderness of the beautiful island of Cres and its crystal-clear sea, which we must protect if we want it to remain that way.

Morski reports that the very widely read British newspaper The Guardian published a selection of lesser-known European islands worth visiting. Among suggestions from numerous countries, Cres in the Kvarner archipelago took first place. Reader Rhiannon, whose recommendation was chosen as the best, particularly highlighted the island’s nature and its impressive griffon vultures.

The Guardian describes Cres as the least populated of the four large Kvarner islands. The island features a mix of the Tramuntana forests, rocky terrain, olive groves, lavender and hidden coves – all of which clearly left a strong impression on the British. The island is known for its hiking and cycling trails, as well as traditional gastronomy and, of course, Cres lamb.

A particularly special attraction are the rare griffon vultures, which nest on the cliffs above the sea. In the settlement of Beli, there is also a visitor centre and recovery centre for these special natural “hygienists” that we must carefully protect.

World.title: Australian With Croatian Roots Runs 827 km Along Croatian Coast
World.content:
September the 7th, 2026 – An Australian with Croatian roots has run a staggering 827 km along the Croatian coast in honour of his late grandfather and to raise awareness about a rare disease.

Australian ultra-marathon runner Aydan Marko Papac from Melbourne has completed one of the most demanding sporting feats of his career. It’s one that few would dare attempt: 827 kilometres of the Croatian coastline, from the lighthouse in Savudrija to Punta Oštro on Prevlaka. Morski reports that it was a feat of sheer endurance, Croatian solidarity and humanity, dedicated to his late grandfather Jandro and to raising awareness of the dreadful Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease.

Aydan set off from Savudrija on the 24th of August at 05:00, with the ambitious goal of running the entire Croatian coast in a mere ten days. Ahead of him lay 827 kilometres, which implied over 80 kilometres of running every day. That is almost two marathons daily, in the intense Croatian summer heat, plagued with fatigue, pain and with very minimal recovery time.

As he approached Zadar, Aydan’s body began to show the consequences of effort pushed beyond human limits. Due to severe dehydration and significant sodium loss, he had no choice but to stop and receive medical help before he could safely continue, losing more than a full day of running in the process. For most people, that would have been reason enough to give up. For Aydan, it became just another obstacle he was determined to overcome in order to finish the ten-day challenge.

After passing through Dubrovnik on the final stretch, Aydan reached Prevlaka and finally Punta Oštro, the southernmost tip of Croatia, on Thursday, the 3rd of September. With his own feet, he connected the westernmost and southernmost points of the Croatian coast and completed more than 800 kilometres. At the finish line, emotions, hugs, tears of joy and the Croatian flag best showed how much this journey meant to him, his family and the people who supported him along the way.

raising awareness of the devastating Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD)

Behind the sporting challenge there was a much deeper story from the very beginning. Aydan dedicated the endeavour to the memory of his grandfather Jandro Bilić, who suffered from a rare and severe neurodegenerative prion disease called Creutzfeldt-Jakob disease (CJD). Aydan turned his personal loss into a humanitarian mission: through running, to raise awareness of the disease, support those affected and their families, and connect his Australian homeland with Croatia, the country of his family’s roots. Alongside him throughout this exhausting journey was his wife Georgia, his greatest personal support, as well as family, friends, coaches, cameramen and members of the support team: Jack Colletta (team leader), Ben Cherry (physiotherapist / medical support) and Ramsen Kunda (logistics leader). His journey was also followed by his mother Ana (originally from Tomislavgrad), father Smiljan (originally from Stolac) and sister Mimi. The expedition was filmed by Australian filmmaker Rhidian Scott-Towers of Fourth Lane Media, who will produce a documentary about this brave initiative.

dubrovnik refused to let him run alone

A particularly emotional part of the challenge took place in the Dubrovnik area, where local triathletes and runners joined Aydan. On a stretch of approximately ten kilometres, from Zaton to the viewpoint above Dubrovnik, the following athletes ran with him: Željko Cota, Zoran Ateljević, Davorin Krešić, Igor Krmek, Marin Desnica (all from Triathlon Club Dubrovnik or Hybrid Team Dubrovnik) and Jasmin Husejnović. Zoran Ateljević did not stop there, he rejoined Aydan and ran a full 25 kilometres with him from the Dr. Franjo Tuđman Bridge to Cavtat. Later, Elvis Jelčić and Vasily Belousov also joined the Australian team.

A major role in connecting Aydan’s team with the Dubrovnik running community was played by Alen Bošković, Secretary General of the Dubrovnik Sports Community and Director of Du Motion. After direct communication and a request from the Majestic Film organisational team and ICAN representatives, Bošković helped gather and coordinate local athletes so that Aydan would not be alone in the dark during the final kilometres. It was a moment that best showed what sport can mean, people who may not even have known Aydan beforehand came out onto the road and shared part of his burden with him. Steve Ravić, Director of PR and organisation for all needs in Croatia, said: “When I witnessed it, I felt the emotion like in the film ‘Rocky’, when the city joined him to lift him up. In the last 30 kilometres there were even moments when Aydan could barely walk. It was hard to watch. At the moment he continued, a black dog appeared out of nowhere and followed him all the way to the very end.”

an official reception in dubrovnik

Dubrovnik was the last major city stop before the final stretch through Konavle towards Prevlaka near the Montenegrin border. Dubrovnik Mayor Mato Franković greeted Aydan via video message, supported the organisation of the reception and congratulated him on the achievement. Due to official duties the mayor unfortunately could not attend in person. The City of Dubrovnik was officially represented by Deputy Mayor Velibor Puzović and Ana Hrnić, the official authorised to temporarily perform the duties of Head of the Administrative Department for Tourism and Sport.

Puzović congratulated Aydan, emphasising that such a feat requires not only exceptional physical fitness but also enormous mental strength and perseverance, and particularly highlighted the value of linking a sporting challenge with a humanitarian message and the memory of his late grandfather. The City of Dubrovnik expressed pride that Dubrovnik hosted Aydan on the last major city stage of his journey. Frano Soldo, a friend of Steve Ravić and owner of Hard Rock Cafe Dubrovnik, kindly hosted the team inside the Old Town.

an enormous organisational effort

A challenge of this magnitude was not just about running. Behind Aydan and his immediate support team there was an extensive multi-day organisation process that began even before his arrival in Croatia and before the official start of the project. The Majestic Film team was involved from the very beginning and started organising and coordinating key elements in advance – communication with cities and local authorities, institutions, media and journalists, sports and running clubs, local contacts, and people who needed to provide support along the entire route.

An important organisational, communication and media role was played by the Majestic Film team, led by Steve Ravić, CEO of Majestic Film and President of ICAN – International Croatian Artists Network. Ravić and the team worked before Aydan’s arrival on building the necessary network of contacts and support and coordinated communication with local authorities, cities, institutions, offices, media, journalists and other relevant partners along the route. During the challenge itself this coordination continued day by day, depending on Aydan’s progress and changes to the route, and included the organisation of media activities, support from sports clubs and runners, and official meetings, including the final communication and reception in the City of Dubrovnik.

Vesna Trokter, as part of the Majestic Film organisational team and ICAN representative, was involved in the project even before the start of the run and was responsible for coordination with the media, runners, running and sports clubs and local contacts. It was through her communication in the Dubrovnik area that cooperation was established with Alen Bošković, after which Dubrovnik runners and triathletes joined Aydan on the final kilometres.

Petra Antolić, Head of Sponsorship and Public Relations at Majestic Film, was also involved before the start of the challenge and actively worked on PR, distribution of information and materials, communication with institutions and the media, and coordination of activities related to Aydan’s arrival and his attempt to set a world record.

In this way Majestic Film did not act only as media support during the run, but from the very beginning was one of the main organisational and communication drivers of the project in Croatia, working on preparations even before Aydan’s arrival and continuing coordination until he reached the finish line on Prevlaka.

Support for Aydan’s mission was also provided by the Central State Office for Croats Abroad and the Croatian Heritage Foundation, including their branch in Pula. In Pula, after the first stage of more than 90 kilometres, he was welcomed by Barbara Buršić, head of the Pula branch of the Croatian Heritage Foundation.

more than a record

At the end of this journey the numbers say a lot: 827 kilometres, ten days of almost continuous movement, several times more than 100 kilometres in a single day, and the entire Croatian coast behind his back. But the numbers do not say everything. They do not speak of the pain and fatigue. They do not speak of the kilometres when the body wants to stop and the mind has to find a reason for one more step. They do not speak of the wife waiting by the roadside, nor of the mother who holds her breath every time he gets up, nor of the family members and team, the proud father and sister who hide the tension they feel in difficult moments, nor of the people who run beside him or the strangers who cheer him on as he passes through their town.

They also do not speak of the work behind the scenes – the calls, messages, emails, arrangements, media coordination and the people who, even before his arrival in Croatia, began building the network of support that accompanied him all the way to the south of the country.

And above all, they do not say enough about the reason Aydan set out, and that is for Grandpa Jandro.

World.title: Significant Weather Change Coming to Croatia
World.content:
September the 6th, 2026 – A drastic weather change is on the cards for Croatia, bringing relief from oppressive, scorching temperatures.

Index reports that Croatia is currently under the influence of an anticyclone that is bringing clear, stable and hot weather with an inflow of dry air from northern Africa. It won’t last long, however, as a major change is approaching next week. While three tropical cyclones are currently moving across the Pacific, driven by El Niño, and the Atlantic hurricane season is lagging, a deep cyclone between Iceland and Great Britain is slowly shifting eastwards and will affect the weather in continental Europe.

the genoa cyclone

A ridge of high pressure over Scandinavia, connected to the anticyclone over central Europe, extends all the way to northern Africa and the Black Sea. However, a cyclone from the Atlantic will descend towards the North Sea, and its surge of cold and unstable air over western and central Europe will be blocked by the Alps. The jet stream that will bypass the Alps on the western side will trigger the rapid development of a new cyclone in the Gulf of Genoa. That Genoa cyclone, together with the jet stream and a cold front, will begin to influence the weather in Croatia from the middle of next week.

showers, thunderstorms and a significant pressure drop is looming

Before the front actually arrives, due to southerly and south-westerly flow, a strong jugo (sirocco) will blow. The inflow of moisture will further intensify the feeling of sultriness. According to current forecast models, the cold front will affect the northwestern inland areas as well as the northern and central Adriatic during the night from Wednesday to Thursday. During Thursday it will spread across the whole country. The front will be accompanied by thunderstorms, showers and rain, along with strong, locally stormy winds. After the front passes, a strong, locally stormy bora will start blowing in the northern Adriatic. Air temperatures inland will drop by 12 to 15 degrees, and on the Adriatic and in the coastal areas by 8 to 10 degrees.

there’s still a few more days of heat to go

Before the major weather change, we can still expect a few more days of heat. Moderate heatwave warnings from the DHMZ (Croatian Meteorological and Hydrological Service) have been issued for today, tomorrow and Tuesday. Today it will be sunny and hot with a weak north-westerly wind, while on the Adriatic the maestral will blow. Towards the end of the day and during the night there may be a weak bura in the Velebit coastal area. The DHMZ has issued a heatwave warning for the Adriatic that will last until the middle of the week. Sea temperatures are between 25 and 28 degrees.

On Monday and Tuesday predominantly sunny, warm and hot weather continues. Morning temperatures inland will be around 17°C and on the Adriatic around 23°C. Maximum daytime temperatures inland will range from 30 to 31°C, while on the Adriatic they will reach around 34°C, with a weak to moderate maestral.

On Wednesday the jugo will start blowing, and daytime temperatures will still be high, hovering around 32°C inland and up to 35°C on the Adriatic and islands. In the evening and during the night a gradual increase in cloud cover is expected from the northwest, along with the arrival of the cold front.

World.title: Goodbye Toll Booths: Croatia introducing Crolibertas
World.content:
September the 6th, 2026 – Croatia is set to introduce Crolibertas early next year as the country finally bids farewell to toll booths.

Poslovni reports that as of the beginning of March 2027, Croatia will abandon the system of toll booths and introduce a fully electronic toll collection system called Crolibertas. Croatia is preparing for a “traffic revolution” that should permanently erase the images of kilometre-long queues in front of toll booths during the summer months. With planned implementation starting on the 1st of March 2027, a new, fully electronic toll collection system named Crolibertas is coming into force. This will consign to history the model of stopping, taking a ticket and paying on exit from the motorway, replacing it with a free-flow traffic system.

It is important to emphasise straight away that, despite the digitalisation, Croatia is not introducing vignettes along the lines of Slovenia or Austria. Tolls will continue to be charged according to the distance travelled and the vehicle category, meaning drivers will pay only for the distance they actually travel on the motorway. The main change lies in the technology and method of collection, which will be automated, faster and more efficient, with the aim of reducing congestion, shortening travel times and cutting harmful emissions caused by stop-start driving.

how it will work

The new system will operate on the basis of so-called “Multi-Lane Free Flow” (MLFF) technology. Instead of the existing toll plazas, portals equipped with cameras and sensors will be installed along the entire motorway network. The system will rely on a combination of two proven technologies: Automatic Licence Plate Recognition (ALPR), which will be the primary solution for light vehicles such as passenger cars and motorcycles and DSRC technology, i.e. communication via the existing ENC devices.

Drivers of light vehicles will have a choice: they can register in the system and link their licence plate to a valid payment method (such as a bank card), or they can continue using an ENC device as before. However, for heavy goods vehicles weighing more than 3.5 tonnes, the use of an ENC device will be mandatory. This ensures that all traffic, regardless of vehicle type, can pass without stopping.

what tourists and foreign drivers need to do

For tourists and foreign nationals, who make up a significant portion of summer traffic, advance preparation will be key. In order to use the motorways smoothly, they will need to register their vehicle in the Crolibertas system in advance. This can be done in several ways: via the central internet portal or mobile app (the most recommended option, so everything can be sorted out before setting off). For those who do not do this in advance, rapid registration will be available on special lanes at motorway entrances (at the locations of the current toll plazas), as well as at physical sales points such as HAC offices or petrol stations.

To avoid any delays, drivers are strongly advised to complete registration online. Special attention should be paid to the accuracy of the entered licence plate data and the validity of the linked payment method, as even the smallest error can lead to charging problems and potential fines.

existing enc users

Existing ENC device users will not need to buy new ones. They will be able to continue using their devices, but with one key change: it will be mandatory to link the existing ENC device to the vehicle’s licence plate.

associated costs and coverage

Regarding prices, Croatian Motorways (HAC) say that the introduction of the new system itself should not lead to an increase in tolls. A new tariff study is being prepared that could introduce more flexible charging models, for example lower prices for travel outside peak periods, which would further relieve traffic. The single electronic toll collection system will cover the entire motorway network in Croatia, including the sections managed by the concessionaires Bina-Istra and Autocesta Zagreb-Macelj. This means drivers will need only one single system for the whole country.

World.title: Croatian Government: New Package of Measures Coming Soon
World.content:
September the 6th, 2026 – The Croatian Government is currently preparing to present a new autumn package of measures, with nuclear energy part of the discussion.

Croatia has taken a new step towards the possible construction of a nuclear power plant. Ana Blaskovic reports for Poslovni that on Friday, the Croatian Government tasked the Ministry of Economy with launching a structured information procedure and talks with potential suppliers of nuclear technologies and partner countries. Concrete and comparable information will be requested from them on available technologies, technical characteristics and economic conditions.

The process is currently non-binding and does not represent a decision to build a power plant, the government emphasises. However, among the technologies that will be considered are small modular and advanced modular reactors. After the talks, the Ministry will consolidate the collected data and submit a report to the Government. Prime Minister Andrej Plenković announced that at the next session, the government will present the autumn package of measures to mitigate the consequences of the energy crisis for the general public and the economy. The package comes after inflation accelerated to 4.1 percent in August, primarily due to the rise in energy prices, which increased by 17.4 percent on an annual basis.

The government currently expects the upcoming autumn measures to mitigate the impact of energy price increases caused by the crisis still going on over in the Middle East. In addition, through amendments to the Crafts Act, those with crafts will be somewhat financially relieved as chamber contributions will be reduced from two to 1.5 percent of the basic personal allowance, and a novelty is the introduction of status innovations such as the institute of family crafts.

World.title: Estonia has 5th-highest obesity rate in Europe, data shows
World.content:
Estonia has the fifth‑highest share of obese adults in Europe, with 22.0 percent of the population aged 18 and over classified as obese, according to 2025 Eurostat data.

The EU average stood at 16.3 percent, with the highest rates posted in Malta (26.6 percent), followed by Estonia's immediate neighbors to the south and north: Latvia (which saw 24.6 percent of the population classified as obese) and Finland (at 23.2 percent). Ireland at (22.1 percent was fractionally ahead of Estonia. The lowest proportions were seen in Romania (12.9 percent), Greece (12.8 percent) and Italy (7.0 percent).

In addition, 35.4 percent of Europe's population was classified as overweight, or pre‑obese, with a Body Mass Index (BMI) between 25 and 30. Overall, more than half of Europe's population was either obese or pre‑obese/overweight.

Men were more likely to be overweight than women, on the whole. The obesity rate among men was 17.4 percent, compared with 15.3 percent among women EU-wide. Meanwhile, 41.9 percent of men were pre‑obese, compared with 29.3 percent of women. Also, rates of being underweight were nearly three times higher among women (at 2.9 percent) compared with men (at 1.0 percent).

According to Eurostat, 46.4 percent of European adults were at a normal and healthy weight: 39.8 percent of men and 52.5 percent of women.

In Estonia alone, the situation is even more pronounced. ERR's science portal Novaator reported in July, citing a study by the National Institute for Health Development (TAI), which found more than 60 percent of Estonian adults were overweight as of last year, and with 26 percent classified as obese.

The TAI study also found that excess weight imposes significant additional costs on society, affecting healthcare, productivity and overall economic well‑being.

The obesity rate is calculated using body mass index (BMI), which is determined by dividing body weight in kilograms by the square of height in meters. A BMI of 30 or higher is classified as obese, while a BMI between 25 and 30 is considered pre‑obese.

World.title: Estonia's new defense minister expected to be named next week
World.content:
The name of the new defense minister should be known by next week, says Reform Party secretary‑general Kristo Enn Vaga. The Reform Party will also discuss the topic at Wednesday's board meeting.

"The situation is such that the new defense minister cannot take office before the Riigikogu has convened, and the Riigikogu convenes next week. Within the party, different candidates are currently being screened," Vaga said.

"Next week, when the Riigikogu convenes, it should be known," he added.

Vaga said that the first serious discussion on the topic will take place on Wednesday at the party board meeting. "By the end of the week or the beginning of next week, it will be clear who the next defense minister candidate would be," Vaga said.

Martin Herem Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

Search for suitable candidates ongoing

Last week it became clear that Prime Minister Kristen Michal had also spoken with former commander of the defense forces Martin Herem about the defense minister position.

"He has been spoken to, but no official proposal has been made. The screening process is underway, where defense and security policy experts from both inside and outside the party are being considered, in order to restore credibility in the defense field and work to ensure that Estonia is as well protected as possible. Martin Herem is certainly one of Estonia's most reliable defense experts, and I think he would be a very worthy candidate," Vaga commented.

One option is to choose the new defense minister from among the government's existing ministers. However, according to Vaga, they are rather looking for a new person from outside the government. "Everything is possible, but we are not discussing that right now. Rather, we are looking for a new person who would be strong in this field," he said.

Pevkur may not join the defense committee

Riigikogu Reform Party faction leader Õnne Pillak said that Hanno Pevkur, who resigned as defense minister last week, may not join the Riigikogu national defense committee upon returning, but may instead begin working in another committee.

Hanno Pevkur Autor/allikas: Ken Mürk/ERR

"Considering his previous position — for example, he was justice minister — it could be the constitutional committee or the legal affairs committee. There are different options," Pillak said.

"Yes, his last position was defense minister, but that does not mean he will definitely go to the defense committee because of that. We will discuss these matters next week," Pillak said.

Pevkur said last week that according to the coalition agreement, the chairmanship of the defense committee belongs to Eesti 200.

Defense committee currently without chair

"We will certainly not reopen the coalition agreement because of this change. We'll see. I have not yet discussed this with the faction leadership. But there is time, a wise person does not rush," Pevkur said.

The previous defense committee chair, Kalev Stoicescu, left Eesti 200 at the beginning of August and joined the Parempoolsed party. Therefore, Eesti 200 recalled him from the chairmanship of the defense committee. Toomas Uibo (Eesti 200) moved into the committee as a member instead, but a new chair has not yet been elected.

Hanno Pevkur announced last Wednesday that he is resigning as defense minister. He had served as defense minister since 2022.

World.title: Animal‑style movements build balance and strength
World.content:
Trainer Mihkel Vabrit said that bear walk, penguin walk and monkey walk are just some examples of animal movements people can use in their exercise routines.

According to the trainer, a movement style that imitates animal walking trains balance, endurance and strength.

"It is said that humans evolved from apes. Exercises that imitate an animal's walk or an animal's behavioral patterns train balance, endurance and strength quite well. Body‑weight training has again become very popular," Vabrit said.

Before doing the exercises, the body must be warmed up, and according to the trainer, the best for this is the penguin walk.

"Whenever it's difficult, you can say "mõmm" — it helps," the trainer said.

In Estonian, "mõmm" is a common, cute sound associated with a bear.

World.title: Estonian tennis player Mark Lajal gets death threats after tournament loss
World.content:
Estonia's top tennis player Mark Lajal received abusive messages and death threats, some to his own phone, following a tournament defeat Delfi reported .

The messages came following his semifinals loss at the ATP Challenger 75 tournament in Manacor, Spain, held at the Rafa Nadal Academy on Mallorca, and the player said they were from sports bettors unhappy about losing money.

Lajal, currently ranked 152nd in the world, shared screenshots of messages he had received aftermath of his semi-final defeat, including from those who had obtained his personal phone number.

The screenshots were in English and included the message:"I really but really hope you will get cancer including your family as well. I hope you will see then [sic] suffer."

Another screenshot Lajal posted read "Look, you son of a b*tch, you're a f*cking loser. I hate you and you must die. You must die, you f*cking son of a b*tch. You and your family must die. You b*stard. I want to kill you."

"Know, we are going to talk, you know what you are doing and you are not dumb as you want people to know you, that's why I'm going to kill all your family," a third message stated.

Lajal, 23, said the abusive and threatening messages had come primarily from disgruntled sports bettors who had lost money on the outcome, and added while he would not normally post on the topic, the messages had gone too far.

"Sometimes these days happen, you lose, but then you get on your phone and somehow people have gotten your number and are calling and texting death threats," he explained, noting the threats and abuse had been directed against his family as well as personally against him after losing.

The player noted abuse like this is the lot of many top players, but questioned the trade-off between this and the big money that sports betting involves: "At the end of the day, ATP keeps accepting all this money from betting platforms, but at what cost?" he noted.

"Gambling addiction is a real issue and I hope these people find and get the help they need," Lajal concluded.

Lajal went through qualifying at the Mallorca event, and defeated Nicolai Budkov Kjaer, a Norwegian player with Estonian roots, 6-3, 6-1 The next round, the quarterfinals, saw him defeat Spanish player Alejo Sanchez Quileze again in straight sets, 6-2, 6-3.

The winning streak came to an end however with a 7-6 (7), 5-7 defeat to France's Felix Balshaw (ATP 252) in the semi final, despite the Estonian initially leading the second set 4-1.

The entire encounter lasted two hours and 10 minutes and Balshaw, 20, will face Spanish player Inaki Montes-De La Torre (ATP 274) in the final.

Other top tennis players who have recently reported receiving death threats and abusive messages include Italy's Matteo Berettini and Panna Udvardy of Hungary.

World.title: Five injured in accident at Estonian Defense Forces central training grounds
World.content:
A serious accident occurred Monday at the Estonian Defense Forces' Central Training Area near Tapa, injuring five people, ERR has learned.

According to a press release from the Estonian Defense Forces Headquarters, an accident occurred during test firing of 120 mm mortar ammunition, injuring five active-duty members of the Scouts Battalion.

"During today's test firing of 120 mm mortar ammunition, excess pressure developed inside the weapon, causing the barrel to rupture. Five active-duty service members near the weapon were injured. One of them was more seriously injured," Scouts Battalion commander Lt. Col. Madis Koosa said in the press release.

The injured service members were examined by medics at the scene and taken to a hospital for further evaluation. Their next of kin have been notified.

The Military Police and the Estonian Internal Security Service (ISS) have launched an investigation to establish the details and circumstances of the incident.

World.title: Pärnu Beach House extension aims to create new landmark, architect says
World.content:
Architect Jan Skolimowski, whose entry won the architectural competition for the extension of the Pärnu Beach House (rannahoone), said that this is a building that has, over nearly a hundred years, become a symbol of Pärnu.

According to the vision of Kamp Arhitektid, two architectural masterpieces in Pärnu will be modernized: the beach building created by architect Olev Siinmaa and completed in 1938–1939, and the Villa Andropoff complex built during the Soviet era.

The Pärnu Beach House has long no longer met the needs of holidaymakers. The architectural competition held in autumn 2025 sought a solution for how to give the beach building new life and connect the historical building with a modern hotel and new building volume in such a way that the original style and form would remain. The competition was won by Kamp Arhitektid's project "Alt Pernau." The authors of the work are Jan Skolimowski, Anton Andres and Kaspar Kruuse.

"This building is very special to me. It is a symbol of Pärnu," said architect Jan Skolimowski. "For the architect, the most important thing in the case of the beach building is first and foremost the character of the building itself. It is a very good example of resort architecture, whose most recognizable element has become the so‑called mushroom balcony."

Pärnu beach building (1938-1939), Olev Siinmaa. Source: Arhitektuurimuuseum

Before designing the competition entry, the building was visited several times on site, now with a completely different eye: what to preserve, what to restore and what could be done differently. One of the first observations was that the seaside façade is representative, but the park‑side façade feels more like a backyard or service building. This became one of the starting points of the project — to make the park‑side façade representative as well.

"In a building located so centrally in the city, there is actually no back façade. Both façades must be observable," the architect believes.

In designing the new hotel, the principle was that the building must first function for the user. Only then can one begin to think about form. A hotel is a complex system in which guest movement, service operations and many other functions must work simultaneously. At the same time, the old beach building must be connected with the new volume, which is larger than the original building. This was one of the most difficult questions.

Jan Skolimowski Autor/allikas: Kuvatõmmis

The old and new buildings were not allowed to be connected at street level. Therefore, the connections had to be designed underground and via a gallery to the second‑floor level. The underground connection had to be adapted so that reaching the hotel from the parking area would be convenient. For example, a family arriving with suitcases must reach the hotel reception as quickly and logically as possible. All these movements were played through using different usage scenarios.

Once the functional solution was in place, attention could turn to form. The starting point for the new architecture was not copying the old building, but developing its characteristic lines. Thus, the new solution incorporates the rounded forms characteristic of the existing building, the mushroom balcony motif and small arches at the corners of the building.

"These small details ultimately create the whole. No matter which corner of the building you are in, it speaks the same language," Skolimowski described.

The winning entry in the architectural competition for the redevelopment of Pärnu Beach House. Source: KAMP Arhitektid

To restore the original appearance of the historical building, help was sought from archives and old photographs. The extension built during the Soviet era had damaged part of the original façade, and original drawings had not been preserved for all sides. Based on these, the original part could be restored and only then connected with the new architecture.

Material selection also looked toward the existing building. Today, much is said about the environmental impact of construction and the use of wood as a structural material, but in the case of the beach building a different solution was reached.

"With this building, we realized that it is an authentic example of a house that has stood by the sea for a hundred years and must continue to stand," said the architect.

Therefore, the important material of the new building is also concrete, specifically white concrete. This creates a direct connection with the old building: the mushroom, beams, columns and canopies are all made of white concrete, which is characteristic of the beach building.

An airy canopy is planned for the seaside side of the new building, which protects hotel rooms from the sun and at the same time creates a new entrance. The architect also sees a connection here with the Pärnu beach stadium, where bold suspended canopies have been used. If the earlier architect was able, with the technical possibilities of his time, to create an airy concrete mushroom, then today's technology allows this idea to be further developed.

A modern interpretation of the old mushroom is planned at the other end of the new building volume. It is not a one‑to‑one repetition of the old form, but a slightly more angular element fitted into the new architecture.

The winning entry in the architectural competition for the redevelopment of Pärnu Beach House. Source: KAMP Arhitektid

The goal of the new solution is not to turn the Beach House simply into a hotel, but to make the building more open to townspeople and beach users. A hotel guest should be able to reach the hotel directly from the beach, and when spending time at the beach, one should not always have to use the usual main entrance.

A café and the possibility of bringing back smaller beachside services into the building are also planned.

"The richer the range of services offered, the more interesting the building itself is," the architect believes.

The second‑floor gallery connecting the old and new parts is important. It must be as airy as possible: from the beach one must be able to see the park, and from the park in turn the beach and the sky. Sea views have also been one of the important starting points for the hotel rooms.

The landscaping around the building continues the character of the Pärnu beach landscape. During construction, the existing landscape must inevitably be changed, but the goal is to restore as much as possible of what was there before once the work is completed.

The dominant element planned at the end of the building must work both when viewed from the promenade and from far out at sea. It is precisely the distant view that is important for the architect. The form must work well both up close and when approaching Pärnu from the sea. "It is a landmark. And we are not making it for ourselves, but an important landmark for Pärnu."

Intervening in someone else's creation is not easy, according to Jan Skolimowski, especially when it is a building created by a renowned architect and an important symbol for Pärnu.

"You have to think very carefully about where you respect his work and where you boldly add something of your own that speaks of the time we live in today," he said.

In the architect's view, the time is past when a minimalist black box could simply be placed next to a historical building and declared modern. The new part must also be unique and created specifically for this building and this place.

Finding the new form was a long process. It was sketched, modeled, discussed at home and with colleagues, and changed again and again. The final result must work both up close and when viewed from the sea, because ultimately the question is not only about one new hotel, but about how to give new life to a symbol of Pärnu so that the old does not disappear and the new does not overshadow the old.

In the case of the Beach House, the architects had to relate to one strong and recognizable historical building. In Villa Andropoff, whose modernization project was also prepared by Kamp Arhitektid, the initial situation was much more complicated: there stand side by side two very different buildings whose authors and architectural languages differ.

Villa Andropoff Autor/allikas: Verner Vilgas/ERR

The main building with bold angular forms and a large cantilevered volume was designed by Raine Karp. The cinema building created by architect Meeli Truu is characterized by soft forms. Therefore, it had to be decided whether to base the design of the new building on one existing building or take something from both. At the same time, the buildings had to be connected so that the hotel would function comfortably for both guests and service.

As a solution, it was decided to make the new building with a completely distinct character and connect it with Raine Karp's main building via an underground connection. Thus, at ground level, the sense of two different buildings remains. "You essentially still see two different buildings," the architect noted.

In the case of Andropoff, preserving sea views was considered especially important. According to the detailed plan and earlier plans, a four‑story new hotel building could have been built in the area, but this solution was abandoned.

"In cooperation with the developer, we reached a solution where such a large volume is actually not needed there. The environment requires a different approach," the architect explained.

World.title: Estonian agency fails to demonstrate how €70 million unsuccessful ammo contract reached
World.content:
The Estonian Center for Defense Investments (RKIK) is unable to provide documentation showing how it selected Datasel S.R.L., the company with which it signed an approximately €70 million contract to purchase ammunition.

It is now known that in 2024 and throughout the procurement projects involving Datasel established procedures for conducting procurement processes were not followed. RKIK Director General Elmar Vaher said he does not know how the initial negotiations with Datasel were conducted. "I wasn't working here at the time and neither was my team. So what we can talk about now is how we operate today," he said.

Media reports have said that Datasel copied images of artillery shells from other websites and even used cover art from a computer game. RKIK does not know how the decision was made that Datasel was an appropriate company to work with. There is also no documented account of how contact with the company was established or how RKIK came across the company in the first place.

Nor has RKIK subsequently determined how Datasel's background check was conducted and there is no summary of that check. This is important because procurement procedures generally involve checking first and foremost whether a company actually possesses the technology it is offering and how it can demonstrate its ability to supply that technology. The company's financial capacity is also assessed, including whether it has investors, bank guarantees and other financing options.

Elmar Vaher. Source: Priit Mürk/ERR

Investigative team to travel to Estonia

Speaking at a Monday meeting of the Riigikogu State Budget Control Select Committee, Vaher said the European Commission will send an investigative team to Estonia for three days at the end of September to examine how well RKIK fulfilled its due diligence obligations.

According to Vaher, RKIK is continuing to search for documents related to what happened in 2024 and is speaking with former managers to obtain as complete a picture as possible of how the Datasel contracts came about.

The initial claim made publicly that only one contract had gone wrong has since changed. According to RKIK, seven contracts have been terminated.

Five of them are currently the subject of court or arbitration proceedings, while two contracts have been terminated but remain under negotiation, with preparations underway for possible litigation. RKIK cannot currently comment in greater detail on the latter two contracts because the negotiations are confidential.

The contracts currently before the courts or in arbitration are connected to Datasel.

Datasel, in turn, has filed a counterclaim against RKIK, although its exact contents are not currently being disclosed. RKIK has also not seen the documents on which the claim is based. As the disputes are ongoing, RKIK did not rule out the possibility that the counterclaim could be a tactical move. The center declined to disclose the monetary value of the counterclaim at this time.

Money from the European Peace Facility

Funding for the approximately €70 million procurement involving Datasel did not come from Estonian taxpayers but from the European Peace Facility (EPF). The funding was provided at the European level and includes, among other sources, proceeds generated by frozen Russian assets.

According to Vaher, RKIK currently has around 200 procurement projects underway, handled by approximately 80 people. They include lawyers, project managers and specialists who prepare technical specifications. Procurement decisions are made by RKIK and contracts are signed by RKIK's director general. "That means RKIK is responsible for its own actions," Vaher said.

Asko Kivinuk, RKIK's deputy director general for procurement, said RKIK becomes involved in procurements as early as the planning and pricing stage. Infrastructure and procurement plans are drawn up based on the Ministry of Defense's development plan and procurement plans are then prepared on that basis.

Maria Pihlak, an attorney at law with Sorainen who advises RKIK, stressed that court and arbitration proceedings are closed and that the parties cannot publicly comment on all the circumstances or evidence involved in the proceedings.

In addition, the contracts contain confidentiality clauses that may carry contractual penalties. RKIK must therefore be cautious about what information it discloses regarding ongoing disputes.

It emerged last Wednesday that Estonia sought to buy shells for Ukraine and paid a total of €70 million in advance to Indian businessmen who had reportedly never sold a single shell before. RKIK terminated the contract after the company only delivered an incomplete shipment of low-quality components.

World.title: Should the Estonian people be involved in electing the president?
World.content:
Ülle Madise's first-round election as Estonia's next president brought an unusually swift end to a process that nevertheless revived debate over the transparency and democratic legitimacy of the country's presidential election system.

The 2026 presidential election will go down in history as a rare occasion when the sole candidate nominated in the Riigikogu, Ülle Madise, was elected head of state in the first round of voting.

While parliament may regard this as a success, the election process drew mixed reactions from the public.

"I have gathered from various statistics and opinion polls that people do not understand the current procedure for electing the president and that it seems opaque. As a result, a significant amount of frustration has arisen among the public," said legal scholar and chair of the Constitutional Assembly's expert committee Jüri Raidla.

Jüri Raidla. Source: Ken Mürk/ERR

"There has always been a great deal of discussion surrounding the candidates. There has been confusion and there have been attempts to create confusion, but each time they have ultimately managed to get the job done. And this time, too, the Riigikogu did an excellent job," said public administration expert Külli Taro.

But how did we get there? The search for a president began early in the year when incumbent head of state Alar Karis had yet to give a definite answer on whether he intended to continue in office. Although Karis is popular with the public, the political parties were not united in their support for him. As a result, the process remained at a standstill for a long time.

"There was relative quiet in the spring partly because many politicians simply did not know what Alar Karis was going to do. And that [Karis' decision to run — ed.] would have been a major game changer. Even Ülle Madise, who has now been elected president, said that she would not want to run against Alar Karis if he wanted to continue," said political scientist and journalist Erik Moora.

The picture became clearer on Victory Day.

"As head of state, I wish you a happy Victory Day for the last time," Karis said in his Victory Day speech.

That gave the parties reason to put their heads together again, but they still failed to come up with a common candidate. It was at this point that the Social Democrats put forward the name of Chancellor of Justice Ülle Madise who, because of the impartiality required by her office, could not put herself forward for the presidency.

Mart Helme, proposed by EKRE, did not have the support of other parties. At the same time, several other prominent public figures expressed interest in seeking the presidency, including Maive Rute, Indrek Laul, Hannes Hanso and Tiit Land.

"In Estonia, the president has to be elected on the basis of a cross-party agreement. That means it can only happen through the parties gradually coordinating and sounding each other out to determine which candidate their members might be willing to support," Moora said.

The deadline for nominating candidates, however, was drawing ever closer. Isamaa and the Center Party considered nominating university rector Tiit Land, but in the end only the Center Party backed him, arguing that the country needed multiple candidates and society needed a substantive debate.

"I believe public debate is extremely important and it is what keeps us on track. But public debate is happening all the time. It consists of our everyday conversations, opinion articles and expressions of opinion. If we attach great importance to a staged debate between candidates, line them up somewhere, ask them questions they know in advance and prod them from every direction ... I don't attach much importance to that. It tells you little about people other than whether they are good at that particular format. But that doesn't make them a good president," Moora said.

Erik Moora Source: ERR

No such debate ultimately took place. When signatures began to be collected to nominate Ülle Madise, 75 MPs backed her. Madise thus became the only official candidate.

The situation angered several opposition politicians. They no longer regarded the process as an election, but as an appointment made in backroom deals on Toompea.

"I don't understand those Riigikogu members who said they did not come to vote or who afterward say that the president of the republic is somehow not a legitimate president because there was only one candidate. Every Riigikogu member has the right to nominate a candidate. It is true that they may nominate only one candidate, meaning a Riigikogu member may sign in support of only one candidate. But even after 75 members of parliament had signed in support of Ülle Madise's nomination, there were still enough Riigikogu members left to nominate another candidate. Why they did not do so was up to them, but in my view it is not fair to then say afterward that the problem with the election was that there was only one candidate," Taro said.

Ülle Madise was elected president by secret ballot with 71 votes. She was supported primarily by members of the Social Democrats, Reform Party, Eesti 200 and Isamaa, as well as several unaffiliated MPs. EKRE members did not enter the chamber, while Center Party MPs did not collect their ballots.

"Our main message was and remains that the current process is not actually democratic," Center Party chair Mihhail Kõlvart said.

"In my view, when a party does not allow its members to register, does not allow them to collect ballots and does not allow them to cast a vote if they wish, that is, on the one hand, cowardly, because under the Constitution, a Riigikogu member is independent. An MP must be able to make choices that differ from the party's official line; they have a mandate to do so. They represent their voters, not merely the party's interests or message. Restricting or preventing that is not a very honorable course of action. It is perfectly OK for an individual politician not to vote, not to vote in favor, to spoil their ballot or to shout across the chamber that everything happening there is nonsense. But for a party leadership to decide that those who would like to act differently are not allowed to do so is, in my view, a violation of the Constitution," Moora said.

The situation once again raised the question of whether the current system has run its course and whether the election of the president should instead be entrusted directly to the people.

"Every presidential election to date, including the most recent one, has taken place in full accordance with the Constitution and the law; there is no question about that. Despite the good results and an appealing process, there are clearly pain points that should be addressed in the future," Raidla said.

"So far, the issue of direct elections has always faded away, despite having influential supporters at various times. We have had prime ministers who have said that we really should introduce direct presidential elections and so on. And it cannot be ruled out that at some point such a decision will be made," Moora said.

Raidla also does not consider direct elections necessary, but he has proposals for making the process more transparent. The first would be to give the public, in addition to the Riigikogu, the right to nominate presidential candidates.

"In a legally binding way. I emphasize: in a legally binding way. That means that 10,000, 20,000 or 25,000 citizens — whatever number the law might stipulate in the future — would provide their signatures. And once those signatures have been collected, that person would become a presidential candidate," Raidla said.

President Alar Karis and President-elect Ülle Madise at Kadriorg. September 3, 2026. Source: Raigo Pajula/VPK

A second option, according to Raidla, would be to move the election directly to the Electoral College, made up of MPs and local government electors, bypassing the rounds of voting in the Riigikogu.

"In the Electoral College, the president clearly receives a mandate with a broader base of support while remaining fully compatible with the current Constitution. The president gains significantly greater capacity to act as a counterbalance," Raidla said.

For now, however, the process has run its course and the next president of the Republic of Estonia will be Ülle Madise.

"Given that the rule of law in Estonia has clearly come under strong pressure in recent years, it is fundamentally necessary to have someone in Kadriorg who is a highly credible guardian of the Constitution and the rule of law, and Ülle Madise undoubtedly is that," Raidla said.

World.title: Energy resources do not guarantee resilience: Ex-Minister Luay Al-Khatteeb
World.content:
Abu Dhabi (IraqiNews.com) — Possessing vast hydrocarbon endowments and installed power capacity does not insulate an economy from acute vulnerability without institutional coordination, rapid crisis restoration, and contingency planning, former Iraqi Minister of Electricity Dr. Luay al-Khatteeb warned during the Hili Forum 2026 in Abu Dhabi.

Addressing a high-level panel titled “Gulf Economic Resilience: Energy, Infrastructure, and Influence”—hosted jointly by the Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy (AGDA) and the Trends/ECSSR research complex—Al-Khatteeb highlighted the structural lessons drawn from Iraq’s ongoing grid challenges and wider regional supply disruptions.

Core Tenets of Energy Resilience vs. Resource Abundance

Divergence of Resources and Resilience: Al-Khatteeb underscored that abundant crude reserves, natural gas deposits, and nominal nameplate power-generation capacity do not automatically yield economic resilience.

Institutional Coordination Gaps: Hydrocarbon-rich states remain exposed to macroeconomic shocks and infrastructure paralysis if administrative bodies fail to coordinate cross-sectoral supply chains, anticipate supply interruptions, and restore essential baseload power swiftly.

Stress-Test Benchmark for Systems: The definitive measure of an energy framework’s resilience lies not in standard baseline efficiency on normal operating days, but in its capacity to preserve core economic activity and critical infrastructure under worst-case disruption scenarios.

Panel Profile: “Gulf Economic Resilience: Energy, Infrastructure, and Influence”

Participant Title / Affiliation Core Domain Dr. Luay al-Khatteeb Former Minister of Electricity; Member of Iraq’s Federal Energy Council Energy transition, grid governance and Iraqi infrastructure Hussein Shoukry President, Middle East and Africa, Siemens Energy (UAE) Power generation technology, EPC execution and turbine systems Dr. Karen Young Senior Research Scholar, Center on Global Energy Policy, Columbia SIPA (USA) Gulf political economy, energy finance & regional statecraft Dr. Abdulla Isa Alabbasi Director of Energy and Environmental Studies, Derasat (Bahrain) Regional environmental policy, grid interconnectivity and strategy Dr. Mohamed Al Zarouni (Moderator) Lecturer, Anwar Gargash Diplomatic Academy (AGDA) Strategic diplomacy and infrastructure security

Al-Khatteeb’s intervention touches directly upon Iraq’s persistent structural dilemma: despite producing over 4.4 million barrels of oil per day and spending billions on generation units over the past decade, chronic gas feedstock shortfalls, distribution grid bottlenecks, and reliance on imported fuels leave the power sector vulnerable during seasonal peaks.

Building durable energy resilience, the panel emphasized, requires moving beyond raw generation figures toward decentralized grid architecture, commercial capture of associated flared gas, upgraded transmission grids, and institutional agility capable of withstanding external geopolitical and financial shocks.

World.title: Mbappe embraces Ballon d’Or talk after historic World Cup exploits
World.content:
Madrid – Real Madrid striker Kylian Mbappe said Monday it was natural for people to consider him as a potential Ballon d’Or winner this year after his World Cup exploits.

The France captain scored 10 goals at the tournament this summer to win the Golden Boot, with his country finishing fourth, and has netted 22 in the competition during his career, making him the World Cup’s all-time top scorer.

Mbappe, 27, has not yet won the prestigious trophy given to the world’s best player.

“I think that when you play for Real Madrid, which is the best club in the world, naturally people associate you with that kind of award, they associate you with collective awards, individual awards,” Mbappe told reporters.

“A lot of people, when they see me in the street, talk to me about the Ballon d’Or, a lot of people talk about me as a possible Ballon d’Or winner…

“Of course I made a lot of history this summer in the most important competition in sport, but we’ll see.

“I have the feeling that it’s a good year for that, but there’s still a long time to go and people are free to vote for whoever they think is the best player in the world.”

Since joining Real Madrid in 2024 Mbappe has scored huge quantities of goals but the club has failed to win a major trophy.

On Tuesday the record 15-time European champions host Inter Milan in the Champions League in the first match of the league phase.

During Mbappe’s first two years at Madrid the team has appeared unbalanced, with too many star names, including the Frenchman and Brazilian winger Vinicius Junior, widely considered not to be contributing enough to the team effort — in contrast to Ousmane Dembele at Paris Saint-Germain and Raphinha at Barcelona.

“We have to improve,” admitted Mbappe. “But I could play dumb and tell you that I score more goals than (Dembele and Raphinha), and that they need to score more goals to be like me.

“Everyone is different, but I want to do things intelligently and say that of course I have to improve and all that, but I don’t like comparisons because I think I do a lot of things that others don’t do.”

Real Madrid coach Jose Mourinho recently said he would prefer if Mbappe scored fewer goals but also worked hard to help the team win titles.

Mbappe said he would accept lower numbers if it led to trophies, but noted they were not mutually exclusive.

“I’d take 30 goals with titles, yes, but… for me it’s an absurd debate,” said Mbappe.

“I always want to score goals and win titles… you don’t have to choose, you can do both things.”

– Mourinho faces old friends –

Veteran Portuguese coach Mourinho led Inter to Champions League glory in 2010 at the Santiago Bernabeu before he departed to take over at Real Madrid.

Despite his history with the Italian side, whom he steered to the treble that year, the coach said that only mattered before and after, but not during the match.

“There aren’t many (people) left from my time, but it’ll always be a pleasure to see people, even if I don’t know them, but people who defend Inter, before and after,” said Mourinho.

“During the game I want to win, they want to win, and there won’t be time to think about things from a wonderful past.”

Mourinho wants his Madrid players to bounce back from their first defeat of the season, 1-0 at Real Betis on Friday in La Liga.

“I want to win. I could tell you I want to play well, but I don’t want to play well like we did against Betis and lose,” said Mourinho.

“Obviously we’re in a phase where we play eight games and the objective in these eight games is to qualify, and I think we’re going to do that. But I want to think about this match in isolation from that context.

“I want to think about this match as a one-off game. I don’t want to think that we still have seven more matches to play, and I want to win.”

World.title: Tech firms rally, with eyes on US inflation update
World.content:
London – Technology firms rallied on stock markets Monday, with traders gearing up for key US inflation data this week that could lock in a September interest rate rise from the Federal Reserve.

The share price gains — led by chipmakers in Seoul and Tokyo — came even after a forecast-busting reading on US jobs Friday that ramped up bets that the Fed will tighten monetary policy on September 16.

A fresh bout of tit-for-tat US-Iran strikes at the weekend pushed oil prices higher and added upward pressure to inflation expectations.

Average diesel prices in the United States climbed to a new record Monday, the motorists’ association AAA said, as damage to Gulf refineries during the war against Iran disrupted supplies.

For stock markets, “many of the headlines from the dominant AI theme remain positive”, noted Dan Coatsworth, head of markets at AJ Bell.

“But investors are having to contend with the potential for an interest rate hike at the US Federal Reserve’s meeting later this month.”

After July’s rout of AI-linked firms, dealers have been edging back into the sector, confident that the vast sums invested in recent years will pay off — despite concerns about elevated valuations.

Investors are looking ahead to earnings from tech titan Oracle on Thursday. The release will be pored over for a fresh idea about the outlook for the AI boom.

South Korea’s Samsung added 5.7 percent to its share price Monday and SK hynix jumped 8.3 percent.

Tech investment giant SoftBank soared more than 11 percent.

On broader markets, Seoul ended more than four percent higher and Tokyo added more than two percent, with Taipei up 1.7 percent thanks to a spike in chipmaker TSMC.

However, Hong Kong, Singapore, Wellington, Manila, Jakarta and Mumbai fell.

In the eurozone, whose economy grew more than expected in the second quarter according to official data Monday, the Paris stock market showed a slight gain in early afternoon deals, while Frankfurt slid.

Separate data showed Germany factory output fell more than expected in July, underscoring the economy’s fragility as Chancellor Friedrich Merz comes under mounting pressure to boost growth.

Outside the eurozone, London’s stock market was up 0.2 percent.

“Markets may look calm on the surface, but the combination of central-bank meetings, US inflation, Oracle earnings and flows in China tech suggests the conditions for a more meaningful expansion in volatility are building,” said analyst Chris Weston at Pepperstone.

US consumer prices for August will be released on Friday, with a worsening of core inflation likely to cement investor expecations that the Fed will hike interest rates.

Wall Street is closed for trading on Monday for the US Labor day holiday.

The absence of US investors and traders impacted the currency markets.

“There was a lot going on in FX today, despite, or maybe because of, the US holiday,” said Trade Nation analyst David Morrison.

“The yen made significant gains versus all the majors, raising speculation that perhaps Japan was intervening once again,” added Morrison, who noted that the yen was trading at its highest level against the dollar since Feburary.

While there has been no official confirmation, Morrison said that any intervention Monday would have an outsize impact with less liquidity in the markets due to US traders being off.
