World.title: Australian choristers swap their day jobs for the international stage
World.content:
Do you have to be a professional musician to perform on some of the world's most iconic stages?

Not necessarily.

Community choirs can give amateur singers the opportunity to perform in venues many musicians only dream of visiting.

Groups like the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs help singers develop their skills while opening doors to prestigious performance opportunities.

Hear Sydney Phiharmonia Choirs sing at the BBC Proms Hear Sydney Philharmonia Choirs perform John Adams’s Harmonium at the BBC Proms, alongside Lucas and Arthur Jussen playing Poulenc’s Concerto for Two Pianos.

The Sydney Opera House Concert Hall is their home stage, but the choir recently returned from a 12-day tour of the UK.

One of the tour's highlights was a performance at the Royal Albert Hall as part of the BBC Proms.

This renowned, month-long classical music festival is known for its rich history and tradition of offering affordable standing-room tickets.

The performance, which will be broadcast on ABC Classic today, was a huge financial and musical commitment for the choristers.

But for many, it was the opportunity of a lifetime.

Hitting the ground singing

The Sydney Philharmonia Choirs is made up largely of amateur singers.

Among them are GP and practice owner Kate Clowes, who has been singing with the choir for 20 years, and music teacher Joel Wilkinson, who joined the under-30's choir last year.

After the long-haul flight to the UK, the choir launched straight into an intensive schedule of rehearsals and performances.

According to Wilkinson, the pace was hectic.

"Some of the choristers finished a show in Sydney on Saturday, flew out, landed in London on Monday, rehearsed, and went into a 12-day tour."

And Clowes had another curveball right before she got on the plane: "I actually caught COVID [and recovered], but I was nervous that would interfere with my capacity to sing," she says.

Nearly 150 choristers took part on the recent Sydney Philharmonia Choirs tour. (Sydney Philharmonia Choirs: Vesna Hatezic)

Adding to the challenge was the repertoire itself.

Sydney Philharmonia Choirs Artistic Director Brett Weymark describes John Adams's Harmonium, which the choir performed, as an "extremely difficult piece" that requires "precision".

It calls on "a different level of expertise from what they're used to" according to Weymark.

But the effort paid off.

Weymark shares how walking into the Royal Albert Hall, a venue steeped in over a century of musical performances, is "an extraordinary experience" even for seasoned musicians.

More than 300 performers took part on the night.

Wilkinson says the feeling of being in a massed choir "was like being swept up in a sea of sound".

"The Royal Albert Hall is such a hallowed place," Clowes says.

" To stand on stage and fill the space with incredible sound was a thrill. "

Singers from Sydney travelled across the world to perform at the iconic Royal Albert Hall, the primary venue for the world-famous BBC Proms. (BBC: Chris Christodoulou)

Living the life of a musician

There's a special bond that's often formed by singing together. This is intensified when a group goes on tour.

Amateur groups like the Sydney Philharmonia Choirs operate through members paying to take part in music projects, including self-funding international travels.

Clowes first joined the group in 2006, without having to audition, as part of a Christmas performance in the Sydney Opera House Concert Hall.

Now a seasoned chorister and traveller, she sings in the choir's rigorously auditioned Chamber Singers.

Although Wilkinson has experience tackling complex repertoire through his music studies at university, he needed to save for six months to go on the tour.

For many of these choristers, touring is a significant financial and musical commitment. (Supplied: Sydney Philharmonia Choirs)

"It was quite a big thing to do for me and my girlfriend," Wilkinson says.

"It was a hectic couple of weeks, but the experiences that we were able to have were pretty cool."

During the tour, "they actually become professional musicians for that period," Weymark says.

"They're not going to the office to become accountants or teaching in their schools or working in a hospital.

"For that period, they are there to do one thing only: to sing as a group."

He is "incredibly proud of all the singers" who rose to the challenge of learning music, travelling and performing in new venues most have never been to.

Why community choirs matter

Weymark likens community music groups to sport.

He says it starts with "people who are out kicking a football around in their local park" rather than professional league players.

Similarly, "more people take part in amateur music making than we think," Weymark says.

And although Australia has professional ensembles such as state orchestras and opera companies, Weymark says the sector couldn't exist without "the grassroots music making that happens on an amateur level."

For Clowes, making new memories on tour and strengthening friendships made the commitment worthwhile, despite having to close her practice and "working doubly hard" when she got back.

"My patients are very patient with me, and interestingly have been the most curious ever about our recent choir tour," Clowes says.

Learning from some of the best conductors was valuable professional development for Wilkinson's teaching career.

But the best confidence boost was being able to tell his students that "Mr Wilkinson actually does some cool stuff on tour."

Weymark sums up why being part of a choir or an orchestra is so addictive and valuable:

" We are creating some joy in the community by bringing people together to make music. "

Until you experience it for yourself, Weymark says, "you cannot, even for a second, imagine the camaraderie, support and connection you have with people when you make music together."

Listen to Sydney Philharmonia Choirs perform at the BBC Proms on ABC Classic on Tuesday, September 8 at 8pm.

World.title: Why you need more than trust when lending family money
World.content:
With the Australian dream of owning a home becoming increasingly out of reach for young Australians, the bank of mum and dad is an option many turn to.

It's not just for buying property, with families frequently lending money to help with everyday expenses amid the cost-of-living crisis.

But youth sociologist and senior lecturer at the University of Newcastle Julia Cook says there are legal risks when borrowing from family, and the taboo of talking about money is at the heart of many.

Our experts Dr Julia Cook, youth sociologist and senior lecturer at the University of Newcastle

Elizabeth Shaw, CEO of Relationships NSW

Gabriella Pomare, family lawyer

Firstly, what is the bank of mum and dad?

In short, it's a term for the financial support that parents give to their adult children.

It's estimated to be worth about $35 billion and the Productivity Commission says if it was an actual bank, it would be somewhere between the fifth and ninth biggest mortgage lender.

Dr Cook and her team spoke with 80 older parents and adult children as part of new research into the bank of mum and dad.

Most were from Gadigal Country/Sydney and had either given or received family money to help with buying a home.

Participants of the study had provided or received an average of $75,000, although amounts were as small as $5,000 and in one case, $500,000.

Bank of Mum and Dad branches out to living expenses The typical way the so-called "Bank of Mum and Dad" is used appears to be shifting, according to new figures that show most of the cash passed from parents to children is being used on living expenses, rather than a home deposit.

Dr Cook says while the cohort was mainly middle and upper class, there were parents who weren't "well-to-do" giving whatever they could to help their child get into the property market.

" One father was living in social housing and was a full-time carer for his wife. He had saved money for years to give to his daughter. "

"A single older lady didn't own property and was living rent-free in a friend's house. She was 70 and working part-time as a teacher still.

"She was giving all the money she could afford to her son to help with his mortgage."

The taboo of talking about money

Parents and adult children interviewed for the study said they were often unclear whether the money was a gift or loan, says Dr Cook.

Most of the time, they reported not having even written anything down about the money.

"I would go and speak to someone, then go and speak to their mum. That's how it became apparent … they had very different understandings of the money," Dr Cook says.

She says the financial arrangement could be "fuzzy" because the status of the money changed over time.

For example, it might have started off as a loan, but once the adult child had kids or experienced financial difficulty, the parents effectively wrote it off as a gift.

"There was rarely an explicit conversation," Dr Cook says.

Relationships NSW CEO Elizabeth Shaw says money remains a difficult subject for people to talk about.

"With money, there can be the fear of triggering shame," she says.

Given a parent might want to protect their child from "feeling bad" for needing a loan, the terms of it can remain undiscussed, she adds.

"It can result in a loan that comes with all sorts of unspoken ties that can come back to bite people."

The risks of a family loan

There are many risks that come with this financial arrangement, especially when the terms aren't clear, says Dr Cook.

Even if the money is intended to be a loan, the family might not take steps to protect that with documentation.

"The most people would do is send an email, setting up the terms, or writing on a piece of paper and asking kid to sign it.

"But basically no-one sought professional or legal advice."

And because many banks require written proof that funds from the bank of mum and dad are genuinely a gift, Dr Cook says some participants in her study were asked to sign gift letters for their children, even when they viewed the money as a loan.

"These are important family relationships, and it can put them under strain and also create tension with siblings," Dr Cook says.

She says the financial risk can be great for the parent lending money and "leaves the door open for abuse and coercion".

" In some cases, older adults feel very obliged or pressured to step in and help. "

Spotting elder abuse Older women and people from migrant communities are most likely to experience elder abuse, and the pandemic has only increased that risk.

Dr Cook says the other big risk is when a parent is lending or gifting money to a couple, rather than just their child.

"If that couple parts ways, it's really difficult to try and substantiate 'that gift was just to my daughter.'"

Gabriella Pomare is a family lawyer in Gadigal Country/Sydney and says these loans often operate on trust.

"Nobody is thinking about lawyers or loan agreements because the relationship is good and everybody trusts one another.

"The problem is that family lawyers usually become involved after something has changed — a separation, a falling-out, a death, financial difficulties.

"Courts and lawyers eventually have to operate on evidence."

Ms Pomare says a parent may forget to secure their own future while being focused on helping their child.

"I've seen parents provide substantial sums at a point in their lives when they're approaching retirement.

"If circumstances change and they need that money back, they may discover there is no clear repayment mechanism."

Protecting everyone involved

Ms Shaw says many people spend more time focusing on the benefits than discussing the risks.

"It is worth discussing up front the potential impact on the relationship.

"Where might merging money and relationships be a problem and where does it make sense — and does it feel right for both parties, or only one? Where might a separation of commercial interests be better for longstanding family dynamics?

" Discuss unforeseen circumstances, such as defaulting on the loan, and how to manage that. "

She says families should also consider what other stakeholders, such as siblings, need to be across the agreement. While privacy is important, secrecy can be dangerous.

Ms Pomare says clear documentation can protect the relationship.

"Have the uncomfortable conversation at the beginning rather than the expensive argument at the end.

"If it is genuinely a gift, document that it is a gift. If it is genuinely a loan, treat it like a loan."

She recommends a properly prepared agreement recording things such as:

How much is being lent

Who exactly is borrowing it

Whether interest is payable

When repayment is required

Whether repayments are regular or only triggered by something like the sale of the property

What happens if the borrower separates from their partner

What happens if somebody dies

Whether the loan is secured; and

Whether the arrangement needs to be considered as part of the parents' broader estate planning.

"Where significant money is involved, I'd also strongly encourage independent legal advice, particularly where the child is purchasing property with a spouse or partner," Ms Pomare says.

Ms Shaw says sometimes the best move is not to lend an adult child money, but instead help them get good financial advice and build financial skills.

"There are financial options, and family need not always be one of them."

This article contains general information only. You should consider obtaining independent professional legal advice in relation to your particular circumstances.

World.title: Israel carries out fresh strikes on Lebanon, killing 12
World.content:
Israeli strikes on a southern Lebanese town has killed at least 12 people including two children early, Lebanon's health ministry said, in one of the deadliest days of Israeli bombardment in recent weeks.

Fears of a renewed Israeli military campaign are mounting in Lebanon after days of escalating strikes despite a June ceasefire that was meant to halt fighting between the Israeli military and Lebanese armed group Hezbollah.

A woman who said she was related to at least three of the dead said one attack hit a residential building as children were getting ready for school.

The Israeli military said it struck people seen transferring weapons in the area of the town, Kfar Rumman.

At the site, Reuters reporters saw children's schoolbooks strewn between chunks of concrete where the building once stood. Rescue workers with heavy machinery had worked throughout the morning to pull bodies out from underneath the rubble.

Eight-year-old Mustafa Farhat lost his grandparents and his mother in the strike, locals said. Rescue workers were still searching for his father's body on Monday morning while the boy lay in the hospital being treated for his wounds, they added.

Israel's strikes have fuelled worries about a renewed conflict in southern Lebanon. (Reuters)

One of his relatives, Mona Farhat, told Reuters it was their home that was hit in the run-up to school-time.

"What did they target? What is the goal they are targeting? Do they want us to leave our land? They are mistaken," Ms Farhat said at the hospital.

Lebanon's health ministry said 11 people, including two children and four women, were killed in that attack on a residential building on Monday. State media had earlier said the attack happened after midnight.

A separate Israeli drone strike on a civilian vehicle in the town killed one medic, the health ministry said. Two other medics were wounded in the strike, the ministry said.

The strikes on Kfar Rumman came without an online evacuation warning from the Israeli military.

Israel reviewing reports of civilian casualties

Israel's military said steps had been taken to mitigate harm "to uninvolved individuals, including the use of precise munitions and aerial surveillance."

The military said it was reviewing the report that "uninvolved individuals" were harmed as a result of the strikes.

The Israeli military said Hezbollah had launched two explosive drones overnight towards Israeli troops operating near the Ali al-Taher ridge, a strategic cluster of hills in south-eastern Lebanon where Hezbollah is thought to have built an underground military complex.

Loading...

Israel said last week that it had cleared Hezbollah fighters out of the ridge.

Hezbollah has not commented and Reuters could not independently confirm the military situation at Ali al-Taher.

In the days since, Israel has ramped up deadly strikes on towns to the ridge's north and west where residents had returned after the June ceasefire, Lebanese security officials told Reuters.

The officials said they were anticipating continued escalations in the south in the coming weeks.

On Sunday, at least 11 people were killed in Israeli strikes on three towns near the ridge, Lebanon's health ministry said in an updated toll.

Two of the dead were women killed in strikes on the town of Arab Salim, where Israel's military had issued an online evacuation warning at 6:04 am local time (1:04 pm AEST).

The health ministry said separate Israeli strikes on Sunday had destroyed the Ghandour hospital in the town of Nabatieh al-Fawqa.

Four other people were killed on Friday, including a woman, it added. Those strikes came without evacuation warnings.

Israeli strikes on Lebanon have killed more than 4,300 people since Hezbollah launched rockets at Israel on March 2 — two days after the start of US and Israeli strikes on Iran, triggering an Israeli air and ground offensive.

The dead include more than 250 children, nearly 400 women and more than 130 medics, according to Lebanon's health ministry. The ministry does not otherwise distinguish between civilians and militants, and Hezbollah has not issued a toll for its own fighters.

The ceasefire saw violence decrease dramatically, but Israeli troops occupying swathes of southern Lebanon have continued razing villages in the self-declared security zone. Israel's military has continued carrying out strikes both within the zone and to its north, mostly without evacuation warnings.

UN expert issues warning over Gaza rubble clearing

Growing tensions in southern Lebanon on Monday came on the same day a United Nations expert warned that large-scale rubble removal in parts of Gaza under Israeli control risked erasing traces of "atrocity crimes", and preventing the recovery and identification of human remains.

Francesca Albanese, the United Nations special rapporteur on the Palestinian territories, warned in a statement that the implications of Israel's "ongoing removal, crushing and relocation of rubble in Gaza" were "profound".

"Gaza's rubble contains human remains and physical evidence relevant to the investigation of alleged international crimes, including genocide," she said, pointing to estimates from Palestinian authorities that more than 10,000 people remain buried under the debris in the war-ravaged Palestinian enclave.

Large swathes of Gaza were reduced to rubble during Israel's military response to the October 7, 2023 Hamas attack. (Reuters: Mahmoud Issa)

The Italian-born independent expert has faced harsh criticism from Israel and some of its allies over her long-standing accusations that Israel is committing genocide and other war crimes against Palestinians in Gaza and the occupied West Bank.

Albanese, who was appointed by the UN Human Rights Council in 2022 but who does not speak on behalf of the United Nations, said she had received credible information from multiple sources last month of "deliberate and widespread removal, crushing and transport of rubble".

In the devastated, Israeli-occupied Palestinian territory, "rubble is not just construction waste", the expert insisted.

"It is part of a crime scene, a graveyard, and the material record of what happened during a brutal and senseless bombing campaign that lasted two years."

Reuters

World.title: King clarifies Harry's status to government officials in unusual move
World.content:
The Duke and Duchess of Sussex will not resume royal duties despite returning to the United Kingdom, the King has clarified.

A letter, on behalf of King Charles, has been sent to government and military officials in a bid to "avoid doubt or confusion".

It stated that the couple were no longer working members of the Royal Family and addressing them as His and Her Royal Highness was not to be used.

"The charitable work of the Duke and Duchess is a personal matter for them both and undertaken in their private capacity," Lord Chamberlain, a senior Buckingham Palace official, wrote.

" In short, their position is akin to private citizens with commercial and charitable interests. "

Prince Harry and Meghan made a shock return to the United Kingdom with their children last month, six years after they moved to California.

What's behind Harry and Meghan's UK return While a move to London now brings Meghan and Harry in closer proximity to the royal family, it does not solve the Windsor's complicated dynamics or the deep rift between two brothers.

The pair gave up their royal duties at the start of 2020 and moved to Montecito, near Santa Barbara, as relations with the Royal Family deteriorated.

The prince's relationship with his father, King Charles has said to have improved in recent times, in particular after a visit in July but it has been widely reported that Harry is not on speaking terms with his brother and heir-to-the-throne, Prince William.

Prince Harry told British media last year he would not feel safe returning to the UK with his family after losing his fight for government-funded security protection.

The letter said the couple's position as non-working royals meant any security issues should be directed to the police while any administrative questions regarding the couple should be sent to their office, which operated separately from The Royal Household.

The Duke and Duchess of Sussex take a stroll in Sydney earlier this year. ( Reuters: Hollie Adams)

However, any questions about what reception to give Prince Harry and Meghan, "particularly where recourse to public funds may be required, should be directed to Buckingham Palace".

The ABC has contacted representatives of the Duke and Duchess of Sussex for a response.

World.title: Russia orders German consulate to close in worsening diplomatic spat
World.content:
Russia says it has ordered the closure of Germany's Consulate-General in Saint Petersburg, as a diplomatic spat between the two countries escalates.

The move to close the consulate in Russia's second biggest city comes in retaliation for Berlin's decision to close the Russian consulate in Bonn and a Russian cultural centre in Berlin.

Tensions between the two countries have intensified after Germany accused Moscow of an attempted drone attack at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an allegation Russia called an absurd fabrication.

The Russian foreign ministry said in a statement that the German consulate in Saint Petersburg must cease operations no later than September 18.

It also confirmed that Germany's Goethe-Institut cultural centres in Russia must cease their activities, with staff ordered to leave the country by September 13 at the latest.

"It was the German authorities who, once again, provoked a new round of escalation in bilateral relations. The German government bears full and complete responsibility for the consequences," Russia's Foreign Ministry said.

Authorities found a drone laden with explosives at Leipzig/Halle airport in August. (Reuters: Axel Schmidt)

German leaders and European allies reacted with outrage after intelligence services alleged Russia was behind a drone attack at Leipzig's airport early last month.

Germany is one of Ukraine's main allies and European countries have worried over what what they say are hybrid attacks on their soil.

The EU said the incident at Leipzig airport, which involved an explosive-laden drone, bore all the signs of "state sponsored terrorism".

Russia has dismissed the allegations.

Over the weekend, Russian Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov accused Berlin of "wanting war again".

Finland fences border with Russia

Germany has been rocked by further purported attempts at sabotage on the country's power grid and defence contractors over the past two weeks, although Berlin is yet to directly blame Russia for those incidents.

Russia's alleged use of hybrid warfare has become a concern for European nations since the invasion of Ukraine began in February 2022.

Despite warnings from intelligence agencies, the pro-Russian Alternative for Germany party was the big winner in a regional election in Saxony-Anhalt.

On Germany's support for Ukraine, German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Monday stressed he would "not budge a single millimetre from my fundamental conviction that we must defend our freedom against Russia as well".

Meanwhile, on Monday, local time, Finnish authorities unveiled a 200-kilometre fence erected along its border with Russia.

Finland's interior minister, Mari Rantanen, said the new fence was needed to foil hybrid warfare attacks and to dissuade Moscow from "instrumentalising" migrants to destabilise the Nordic country.

"Today, it is calm but tense, and we really don't know about tomorrow," she said.

"It can change really rapidly, and that is why we need to be very prepared."

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Autonomous drones and AI called out by UN human rights chief
World.content:
UN High Commissioner for Human Rights Volker Turk has warned artificial intelligence could pose a threat to humanity, and pledged to press AI firms to reduce risks that his office said included disruptions to services, communications and democratic systems.

He called for "cast-iron guarantees" to secure AI in a speech ahead of the start of his unprecedented second term, in which he also demanded accountability over deaths in US immigration custody and condemned Russia's reported use of autonomous drones.

The wide-ranging address was his first to the 47-member council since he won the four-year term in July in the face of opposition from Moscow and Washington.

UN rights chief Volker Turk called for "cast-iron guarantees" to secure AI. (via Dado Ruvic)

"I share the concerns of industry insiders that advanced AI could pose an existential risk to humanity," Mr Turk told the body in Geneva.

"I am calling here, today, for an all-out effort to put cast-iron guarantees in place around the safety and security of AI, before it is too late."

Mr Turk did not elaborate on the nature of the risks but a spokesperson for his office said failures involving powerful AI systems could disrupt critical infrastructure and democratic institutions.

'Silicon Valley fascism' is waging war on democracy The author of The Nerd Reich: Silicon Valley Fascism and the War on Democracy, has a warning.

The spokesperson referred to the "dangerous agent-training behaviours" in July's so-called Hugging Face incident where a swarm of OpenAI agents hacked an open-source platform, saying it suggested that frontier AI capabilities are advancing faster than the safeguards.

Mr Turk warned that just a handful of men held "almost unlimited power over AI" without naming any.

Top AI companies include Meta (Facebook's parent company), Anthropic, OpenAI (creator of ChatGPT) and Google.

"At a minimum, we need countries hosting AI and those involved in its supply chains to come together around agreed red lines," he said.

The council will meet again in October 7 when it will discuss the Iran war, Sudan's civil conflict and a string of other crises.

The Trump administration disengaged the US from the council last year, accusing it of anti-Israeli bias.

Mr Turk called for accountability for around 23 deaths he said had taken place in US immigration custody so far this year and added that he was concerned about plans to equip agents with electric shock gloves.

The US Department of Homeland Security has previously said it was committed to ensuring a "safe, secure and humane" environment in detention. Its inspector general is examining deaths in custody since October 2021.

The US State Department did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

'Horror' at autonomous drones in warfare

Mr Turk condemned Russia for its intensified attacks on Ukraine, and Iran for the rising numbers of executions.

He also voiced "horror" at reports that Russia had used fully autonomous drones in Ukraine, allegedly killing three people in August.

"I join calls for the urgent prohibition of weapons that can take lives without human involvement," he said, referring to talks in Geneva.

Reuters has not independently verified these reports. Russia's diplomatic mission did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

With more than 60 wars around the world involving at least one state — the highest since World War Two — Mr Turk set out ideas for ways to promote peace, pledging greater scrutiny of the businesses and economic interests that are fuelling conflicts.

"We will not shy away from exposing the shadow players and calling for accountability," he said.

Later this month, the UN human rights office is due to publish a list of businesses operating in Israeli West Bank settlements the global body deems illegal — a charge dismissed by Israel.

Reuters

World.title: North Korea and Russia open first road bridge, sparking Ukrainian concerns
World.content:
North Korea and Russia have opened the first road bridge over their shared border in a show of deepening ties between the two nations amid the Ukraine war.

The new bridge, which crosses the Tumen river, is designed to accommodate "a projected growth in freight and passenger traffic", according to the Russian government.

The government said up to 300 vehicles will be able to pass through it daily.

The first flag-adorned trucks crossed the one kilometre road on Monday as Russian Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin and North Korea's Premier Pak Thae Song tuned in by video link to address workers and government officials from both countries.

The road bridge connects Russia and North Korea across the Tumen River. (Russia Government via Reuters)

Mr Mishustin said the new route would "further strengthen the connection between our friendly countries".

"I am convinced that the expansion of cross-border transport infrastructure will provide a powerful impetus for the further development of trade, economic, scientific, technological and cultural cooperation," he said.

Mr Mishustin also said ties between Moscow and Pyongyang were "at an unprecedented high level" and called the opening of the bridge "a genuinely historic event".

While the two countries already share rail and air links, a road bridge had been under discussion for years.

Construction began in April last year after a deal was reached during Russian President Vladimir Putin's visit to North Korea in 2024.

Vladimir Putin has not visited North Korea in 24 years. (Reuters: Kremlin.ru/Handout)

Russia and North Korea have heavily boosted military and economic ties since Moscow launched its Ukraine offensive.

North Korea has dispatched thousands of troops to Russia since 2024 to help ward off a Ukrainian incursion into the Kursk region.

Meanwhile, Ukraine has accused Moscow of using North Korean missiles in its nightly barrages.

North Korea benefits from Russia alliance Almost two weeks ago, what is believed to be a North Korean missile was fired in an attack that killed a Ukrainian family. It could be part of a major escalation in North Korea's involvement in the war in Ukraine.

Last month, Ukraine's President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said up to 50,000 North Korean soldiers would be deployed to fight for Russia.

"It is absolutely clear that North Korea will continue to build its experience in modern warfare, receive licenses from Russia, and receive all kinds of military tools from them," he said.

Ukrainian human rights organisation Truth Hounds has said the bridge, which connects the Russian town of Khasan with the North Korean town of Tumangang, could be used as "a covert military logistics corridor rather than to facilitate trade".

"The bridge could be used to transport North Korean military personnel, construction workers and senior military officials directly to Russia," it said in a recent statement.

"It would also enable the flow of Russian technology and resources in the opposite direction."

North Korea and Russia signed a defence treaty in 2024 that provided mutual support if either country were to be attacked.

Russia said trucks would begin to use the bridge immediately to transport cargo, and would be fully operational for passenger traffic by the end of the year.

One of the world's most isolated and repressive countries, North Korea bars most its citizens from leaving and heavily monitors incoming travellers.

Russian tourism to the hermit state has also increased in recent years, although Pyongyang sometimes closes its border at short notice.

AFP/Reuters

World.title: Behind the $10m project poised to transform Perth’s forgotten late-night favourite
World.content:
NationalWAPlanning and development Behind the $10m project poised to transform Perth’s forgotten late-night favourite Indigo Lemay-Conway September 8, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fast Eddys was once an institution for a late night bite to eat in Perth’s CBD before it closed its doors in 2019. But that history could soon be wiped away, with a planning panel poised to wave through a $10 million tourist development in the long-dormant building’s place. Artist impression of the seven-storey development proposed for the former Fast Eddys site. Urbanista Town Planning The eatery’s former home on Murray Street has laid dormant for the past seven years, but any remainder of its existence is likely to be demolished if state planners approve a new tourist accommodation project next week. The Metro Joint Development Assessment Panel has been recommended to approve a seven-storey mixed-use development containing 68 tourist and visitor accommodation units and a ground floor café at 454 Murray Street.



The panel’s meeting on September 15 will determine whether to allow the development to be built with height variations of about 9 metres and completely knock down the former 24-hour kebab and fast food eatery in the process. The former Fast Eddys restaurant is located at 454 Murray Street. Indigo Lemay-Conway The development proposal says the building would typically accommodate 12 rooms per floor with each room containing a bed, kitchenette and bathroom. The ground floor would contain the reception area, lobby, cafe tenancy and dining areas while level one would have eight one-bed rooms alongside a gym and staff office areas. Levels two to six would have 12 one-bed rooms per floor and level seven would contain two two-bedroom units.



Of the 64 rooms, 14 rooms would have access to a balcony or outdoor terrace. The applicant – Urbanista Town Planning – said the proposal would reinvigorate the former two-storey Fast Eddys site and bring much-needed accommodation to the area. “The proposal will facilitate the redevelopment of a currently underutilised site while delivering a high-quality architectural outcome that responds to the site’s prominent corner location and provides an active and engaging street interface,” Urbanista said in the proposal. “The design of the proposed development has been carefully considered to ensure compatibility with the surrounding Perth CBD commercial environment, while incorporating contemporary architectural design that enhances the character and functionality of Murray Street and the broader Citiplace precinct. “The proposal seeks to deliver a development that contributes positively to the surrounding urban environment and provides a high-quality experience for visitors and patrons while reinforcing the activity and vibrancy of the city centre.”



It is understood no structural or design elements of the former site will be incorporated into the new development. The development is worth $10 million and would demolish the former Fast Eddys building. Urbanista Town Planning The report says the proposed apartment use will provide “specialised accommodation, which will have access to public transport, be in close proximity to additional retail and entertainment uses and assist in stimulating the weekend and nighttime economy of the city.” The proposal seeks to vary the height of the building from 14 metres to 23.5 metres along Murray Street and 21 metres to 24.5 metres along Milligan Street. According to the responsible authority recommendation, there are little concerns around the additional height requests.



“While the proposed development includes variations to the street building height and setback requirements for the site … it is considered that if approval were to be granted, the development would be consistent with the orderly and proper planning of the locality,” the recommendation to the panel states. “Furthermore, it has been assessed that the non-compliances would not have any undue adverse effect on the properties in the locality or the likely future development of the locality and can therefore be supported.” If the development proposal is granted, it will only be valid for a period of four years until September 15, 2030.

World.title: ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRenewables ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment James Hall September 8, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The abandonment of Queensland’s clean energy target and delayed closure of coal-fired power is driving away investment in renewable energy, the industry peak body will warn in a speech revealing of the increasingly hostile relationship between the sector and the Crisafulli government. Smart Energy Council chief executive David McElrea’s keynote address to the body’s conference on Tuesday will accuse the LNP administration’s energy policy of contradicting the shift towards solar, batteries and clean energy in the business sector and households. The Queensland government has been accused of driving away investments into renewables. Damian White “The Queensland government is moving in the opposite direction,” his speech will say. “The Crisafulli government has repealed the legislated renewable energy targets, abandoned a firm coal timetable, committed to running state-owned stations to their technical lives and left open further extensions.”



Last year, Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki scrapped the former Labor government’s plan to end the state’s reliance on coal-fired power by 2035, delaying the closure of the publicly owned assets to at least 2046. Related Article Energy Queensland to burn coal for decades as LNP tears up Labor energy target The LNP’s energy plan included a five-year spend of $1.8 billion to upgrade the state-owned coal-powered assets. The government retained the net zero emissions by 2050 goal but repealed the renewable energy target, while the state’s energy policy shift included new laws to seek greater community consultation to approve major clean energy projects. Last month, Premier David Crisafulli successfully secured an exemption from national cabinet to enable Queensland to power AI data centres with coal and gas, despite the Albanese government’s insistence they be exclusively fuelled by new renewable energy sources.



McElrea’s wide-ranging critique claimed the “most damaging” impact of the state’s energy policy was a deterioration in investment certainty. “Without firm closure dates, renewable investors cannot confidently price future output or reach financial close,” he will say. David Crisafulli puts Queensland’s case to the prime minister and other state and territory leaders over data centres. Dominic Lorrimer “The overall strategy of the LNP government is clear: remove targets, erase closure dates, protect coal, make renewable investment harder and let the project pipeline thin – then point to the shortage you created as proof renewables cannot do the job. “That is a self-fulfilling strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable. It is ideology, not economics or engineering.”



But Janetzki refuted the claims, noting the Clean Energy Council’s latest quarterly investment report which showed Queensland has the largest volume of large-scale renewable generation financially committed or under construction. Related Article Opinion

Renewables Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build David McElrea Contributor The treasurer also pointed to last week’s green light of a $1.7 billion Gawara Baya wind farm in North Queensland by Danish investment giant Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners – the eastern seaboard’s largest wind farm in more than two years. “Queensland leads all states in large-scale wind and solar projects financially committed or under construction and the Crisafulli government continues to encourage private sector investment in new generation and storage under our open for business approach,” Janetzki told this masthead in response to questions. Grattan Institute energy policy expert Tony Wood said there were broader market and political sentiment issues that had contributed to an investment drought in the sector.



But he said the state government’s suite of policies “certainly created a significant barrier” to investments. “All these announcements that have happened [since forming government in 2024] – keeping coal running longer, having less aggressive renewable projects and effectively, from a planning perspective, throwing a lot of the renewable projects into at least doubt. Janetzki says investments in Queensland’s renewable energy sector remains strong. Jamila Filippone “The end result is it creates significant unpredictability for investment.” The industry body will also use the Smart Energy Queensland Conference to call for coal-fired power stations to be brought properly into the Safeguard Mechanism, which would impose costly carbon credit demands on assets operating beyond previously proposed closure dates.



This would apply to previously announced closures of Queensland assets, including Callide B (2028), Tarong (phased from 2032), Tarong North (2033), and Stanwell (2033). Related Article Energy Why Queensland will splash hundreds of millions on complex spinning machines “Renewable energy, storage and transmission projects require billions of dollars of long-term investment,” McElrea said. “Investors and lenders need to know when replacement power will be required. Every time a coal closure date is pushed back, that investment becomes harder to finance. “That delays new generation, delays jobs and creates worker uncertainty, and leaves consumers exposed to the cost and unreliability risks of ageing coal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRenewables Opinion Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build David McElrea Contributor September 8, 2026 — 12:01am

September 8, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland households, businesses and industry are racing toward solar, wind and batteries, but the state government is driving in reverse. By scrapping renewable energy targets, abandoning coal closure schedules and running state-owned coal stations past their shelf life, the government has injected massive risk into the market. Queensland’s ill-fated Callide coal power station. Paul Harris Investors can no longer predict when replacement power will be needed, choking off finance for new clean energy projects. This reliance on coal actively punishes investment in clean energy. Because coal stations cannot quickly cycle on and off, they idle at minimum output during bright, sunny afternoons – flooding an oversupplied grid.



To prevent blackouts, the grid operator curtails or disconnects rooftop solar and wind. Related Article Renewables ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment Families that have invested in solar lose the electricity they generated, drawing power back from a coal-heavy grid instead. They pay twice: once for their own solar, and again to keep ageing coal on life support. The political playbook is clear: cancel targets, erase end dates, protect old assets and starve new renewables of capital. When the clean-energy pipeline inevitably dries up, manufacture outrage over the energy shortage you created to justify keeping coal online even longer.



It is a deliberate strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable. Now, the same flawed logic threatens public transportation and the AI and data centre boom. These facilities require massive amounts of power. That incoming demand should bankroll fresh generation, storage, and transmission grid infrastructure – not breathe artificial life into obsolete coal plants. The concept model of a large-scale data centre project in Queensland’s Western Downs. Queensland could leverage data centres for high-tech jobs and regional growth.



Instead, current policy guarantees higher power bills, weaker reliability, and stalled investment. Fixing this requires closing a glaring federal loophole. The federal government is currently reviewing the Safeguard Mechanism – Australia’s primary tool for cutting industrial emissions. Treasurer David Janetzki (left) and Premier David Crisafulli. Jamila Filippone Yet coal-fired power stations remain mysteriously exempt, letting the country’s biggest polluters dodge responsibility for their actual costs. The Safeguard Mechanism must apply to all coal-fired generators based on their original closure dates.



If a plant operates past its deadline, the owner must use Australian Carbon Credit Units to cover the pollution. Related Article Queensland government Queensland premier secures data centre power victory over PM This is not a sudden shutdown. It is a clear market signal to finance and build replacement power before we need it. Queensland deserves an energy policy designed to succeed, not one engineered to fail. World.title: ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach Matthew Knott Updated September 7, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale will move to fast-track a sweeping new $1 billion treaty after a push to overthrow Wale’s pro-Australia government imploded in a blow to Beijing’s ambitions to expand its influence in the Pacific. Wale’s success at fending off the attempt to overthrow him came as an immense relief to Albanese and foreign affairs officials in Canberra, who see him as one of Australia’s most important allies in the region. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen A leaked message from Australia’s High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to Deputy Solomons Prime Minister Francis Sade, seen by this masthead, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities. A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests.



“I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity, and lock this in ahead of the November budget session,” Roach wrote last week, as Wale was facing a no-confidence motion. The $980 million in funding by 2028, first reported by the ABC, is similar to the $1 billion pledged to support a recent set of treaties with Fiji over a 10-year timeframe. In Beijing, Xi Jinping’s foot soldiers will be lamenting a lost opportunity to install a pro-China leader in Honiara, just 2000 kilometres from the Australian mainland. The start of last week’s Pacific Islands Forum in Palau was rocked by the news that Wale had to race home to respond to a non-confidence motion lodged while he was en route to the event. As three of his cabinet ministers stepped down, Wale’s hold on power looked precarious just four months after his surprise election victory. But instead of gaining momentum, the amateurish putsch effort sputtered and flamed out. Manasseh Maelanga, the former cabinet minister who led the charge against Wale, announced on Sunday afternoon that he was withdrawing his no-confidence motion after failing to secure the numbers to bring the government down. Wale remains in power, his stature enhanced.



Related Article Pacific diplomacy The Solomons’ surprise new leader is a win for Australia, but the China challenge remains This matters to Australia because of the remarkable turnaround in foreign affairs Wale has spearheaded since coming to power in May. For most of the decade leading up to 2024, the Solomons were led by the mercurial Manasseh Sogavare, who was openly hostile towards Australia and signed a far-reaching security pact with China. That deal shocked Canberra and dominated days of the 2022 election campaign, with then opposition frontbencher Penny Wong branding it the nation’s worst foreign policy blunder since World War II. Successor Jeremiah Manele was less adversarial, but remained determined to play Canberra and Beijing off against each other. By contrast, Wale – a long-time critic of China who railed against politicians “sleazing up to Beijing” – has made clear his priority is deepening ties with Australia. Just weeks after coming to office, Wale declared he would review the China security pact and negotiate a comprehensive new treaty with Australia. He also announced he wanted to achieve an ambitious regional security pact – a move that would limit China’s ability to pick off individual countries.



When China test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile across the region in July, Wale showed no compunction in criticising the superpower, labelling it “not the act of a friend”. One of his top ministers, Peter Kenilorea Jr, has called for security and policing co-operation with China to be sidelined. This is why, despite no firm proof of meddling, Australian officials were convinced Beijing was helping to orchestrate the move against Wale. “It is just speculation, but I imagine they would have been very active,” says James Batley, a former Australian ambassador in Honiara. “They certainly have the motive.” There was even a chance Sogavare could have returned to power in a nightmare scenario for Canberra and a dream come true for Beijing. The Chinese government, for its part, angrily denies it seeks to interfere in Pacific nations’ internal affairs. The Solomons have long been known for its cycle of “grasshopper politics” in which MPs jump from one side of the aisle to another, driven less by ideology than personal advancement. Wale’s rapid attempts to drive domestic reforms and overhaul foreign relations undoubtedly rankled some of his cabinet colleagues, who found him high-handed and accused him of failing to consult on key decisions. Unlike Kevin Rudd, who faced similar accusations as prime minister, Wale has been given a chance to improve and grow in the job.



Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy China’s policing plans should be sidelined, says top Solomons minister Wale and Albanese will look to lock in their comprehensive treaty, which has largely been completed by officials. Initially slated to be struck by the end of the year, a deal could come ahead of schedule, with an Albanese-Wale meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this month the next opportunity to make progress on the pact. Wale’s proposal for a Pacific-wide security agreement will prove far more difficult, and perhaps impossible, to achieve given the diverging views within the region. Even so, Wale’s willingness to propose bold ideas that challenge Beijing shows why Albanese is delighted the push to oust him failed — at least for now. At times, it was difficult to pick the prince from the groomsmen. Notably, there were two of the prince’s favourite carriage horses, plus an empty carriage, in his funeral procession.”

“Karin Viles (C8), before any fellow readers pun me out of town, know this,” declares Mike Fogarty of Weston (ACT). “Spaghetti bolognaise, lasagne and pizza supplement our national diet. The absence of these magnificent three staples, from any cafe menu or home kitchen, is long pasta joke.”

“Has anyone else noticed an abundance of the most efficient killers of the animal world suddenly swarming?” asks Dermot Perry of Mount Keira. “I’m referring to the dragonflies which have appeared in large numbers here in the Illawarra.”

“One wonders if anybody could have a legitimate reason for wearing camera glasses (C8) but now there’s the camera toothbrush!” observes Paul Duncan of Leura. “Could there be a more useless object and what will come next, the hairbrush camera?”

World.title: Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy
World.content:
PoliticsFederalFederal budget Joyce says he’s ‘not Jesus Christ’ when pushed on controversial superannuation policy Daniel Lo Surdo September 7, 2026 — 8:51pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Barnaby Joyce’s latest interview on ABC’s 7.30 program devolved into chaos when he shouted that he was One Nation’s treasury spokesman – “not Jesus Christ” – when pressed on modelling central to his party’s controversial superannuation policy unveiled on Monday. Loading Joyce was facing a grilling on Monday’s edition of 7.30 when host Sarah Ferguson challenged the One Nation MP to model the lifetime losses different Australians would incur from the policy, which would allow renters and mortgage holders to dip into a quarter of their superannuation contributions over three years. Joyce railed against the question, upset that he wasn’t provided the examples before the interview, as Ferguson pushed him for an answer. “Well, here we go folks, I’ll try and answer something which we’ll need an annuity table and will also need a sort of lineal regression, but I’ll do it for you, straight down the barrel,” Joyce said.



Ferguson responded: “Barnaby Joyce, if I may, obviously this is a policy that your party has come up with, so we would expect you as the Treasury spokesman for that party to be across it, just try it.” Joyce: “The Treasury spokesman [yes], not Jesus Christ.” Ferguson continued, listing the forecast superannuation losses for Australians aged 30, 40 and 50, earning a range of incomes. Joyce refused to engage with the question, though did say he was “happy to come back tomorrow” and give informed answers provided Ferguson was “prepared to pay my accountancy fees”. Less than two months ago, Joyce unleashed at his dog, Stella, while being interviewed by Ferguson, creating a video clip that quickly went viral across the country. One Nation capitalised on the attention by selling custom dog leads following the interview, as part of a wider push of products under the “Sit Down! Barnaby’s Dog Leads” merchandise umbrella. Barnaby Joyce yells at his dog, Stella, during a live interview on the ABC current affairs program 7.30 in July. ABC



Joyce announced the superannuation policy alongside party leader Pauline Hanson at a rare Canberra press conference on Monday, dismissing suggestions the proposed reform would raise inflation and discourage real pay rises. Chalmers said One Nation’s policy was a “recipe to make Australian workers tens of thousands of dollars worse off in retirement”, and argued that compound interest losses would negatively outweigh the short-term financial benefit of the new policy. Hanson promptly called Chalmers “hysterical” in a post on social media and blamed him for the state of the economy. “Perhaps if you hadn’t so thoroughly buggered the economy, Jim, they wouldn’t need to [access superannuation],” she wrote.



One Nation leader Pauline Hanson and treasury spokesman Barnaby Joyce hold their press conference in Canberra on Monday. Alex Ellinghausen Hanson and Joyce said there would be no threshold of financial difficulty for access to the scheme, meaning all renters and mortgage holders – about two-thirds of the population – could benefit. Joyce said he anticipated that “overwhelmingly” people would only access the scheme if they were in financial hardship, and would need to make applications to their superannuation funds claiming support to make rent and mortgage payments. He acknowledged that “a couple” of people may attempt to flout the system. World.title: Behind the $10m project poised to transform Perth’s forgotten late-night favourite
World.content:
NationalWAPlanning and development Behind the $10m project poised to transform Perth’s forgotten late-night favourite Indigo Lemay-Conway September 8, 2026 — 3:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Fast Eddys was once an institution for a late night bite to eat in Perth’s CBD before it closed its doors in 2019. But that history could soon be wiped away, with a planning panel poised to wave through a $10 million tourist development in the long-dormant building’s place. Artist impression of the seven-storey development proposed for the former Fast Eddys site. Urbanista Town Planning The eatery’s former home on Murray Street has laid dormant for the past seven years, but any remainder of its existence is likely to be demolished if state planners approve a new tourist accommodation project next week. The Metro Joint Development Assessment Panel has been recommended to approve a seven-storey mixed-use development containing 68 tourist and visitor accommodation units and a ground floor café at 454 Murray Street.



The panel’s meeting on September 15 will determine whether to allow the development to be built with height variations of about 9 metres and completely knock down the former 24-hour kebab and fast food eatery in the process. The former Fast Eddys restaurant is located at 454 Murray Street. Indigo Lemay-Conway The development proposal says the building would typically accommodate 12 rooms per floor with each room containing a bed, kitchenette and bathroom. The ground floor would contain the reception area, lobby, cafe tenancy and dining areas while level one would have eight one-bed rooms alongside a gym and staff office areas. Levels two to six would have 12 one-bed rooms per floor and level seven would contain two two-bedroom units.



Of the 64 rooms, 14 rooms would have access to a balcony or outdoor terrace. The applicant – Urbanista Town Planning – said the proposal would reinvigorate the former two-storey Fast Eddys site and bring much-needed accommodation to the area. “The proposal will facilitate the redevelopment of a currently underutilised site while delivering a high-quality architectural outcome that responds to the site’s prominent corner location and provides an active and engaging street interface,” Urbanista said in the proposal. “The design of the proposed development has been carefully considered to ensure compatibility with the surrounding Perth CBD commercial environment, while incorporating contemporary architectural design that enhances the character and functionality of Murray Street and the broader Citiplace precinct. “The proposal seeks to deliver a development that contributes positively to the surrounding urban environment and provides a high-quality experience for visitors and patrons while reinforcing the activity and vibrancy of the city centre.”



It is understood no structural or design elements of the former site will be incorporated into the new development. The development is worth $10 million and would demolish the former Fast Eddys building. Urbanista Town Planning The report says the proposed apartment use will provide “specialised accommodation, which will have access to public transport, be in close proximity to additional retail and entertainment uses and assist in stimulating the weekend and nighttime economy of the city.” The proposal seeks to vary the height of the building from 14 metres to 23.5 metres along Murray Street and 21 metres to 24.5 metres along Milligan Street. According to the responsible authority recommendation, there are little concerns around the additional height requests.



“While the proposed development includes variations to the street building height and setback requirements for the site … it is considered that if approval were to be granted, the development would be consistent with the orderly and proper planning of the locality,” the recommendation to the panel states. “Furthermore, it has been assessed that the non-compliances would not have any undue adverse effect on the properties in the locality or the likely future development of the locality and can therefore be supported.” If the development proposal is granted, it will only be valid for a period of four years until September 15, 2030.

World.title: ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRenewables ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment James Hall September 8, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The abandonment of Queensland’s clean energy target and delayed closure of coal-fired power is driving away investment in renewable energy, the industry peak body will warn in a speech revealing of the increasingly hostile relationship between the sector and the Crisafulli government. Smart Energy Council chief executive David McElrea’s keynote address to the body’s conference on Tuesday will accuse the LNP administration’s energy policy of contradicting the shift towards solar, batteries and clean energy in the business sector and households. The Queensland government has been accused of driving away investments into renewables. Damian White “The Queensland government is moving in the opposite direction,” his speech will say. “The Crisafulli government has repealed the legislated renewable energy targets, abandoned a firm coal timetable, committed to running state-owned stations to their technical lives and left open further extensions.”



Last year, Treasurer and Energy Minister David Janetzki scrapped the former Labor government’s plan to end the state’s reliance on coal-fired power by 2035, delaying the closure of the publicly owned assets to at least 2046. Related Article Energy Queensland to burn coal for decades as LNP tears up Labor energy target The LNP’s energy plan included a five-year spend of $1.8 billion to upgrade the state-owned coal-powered assets. The government retained the net zero emissions by 2050 goal but repealed the renewable energy target, while the state’s energy policy shift included new laws to seek greater community consultation to approve major clean energy projects. Last month, Premier David Crisafulli successfully secured an exemption from national cabinet to enable Queensland to power AI data centres with coal and gas, despite the Albanese government’s insistence they be exclusively fuelled by new renewable energy sources.



McElrea’s wide-ranging critique claimed the “most damaging” impact of the state’s energy policy was a deterioration in investment certainty. “Without firm closure dates, renewable investors cannot confidently price future output or reach financial close,” he will say. David Crisafulli puts Queensland’s case to the prime minister and other state and territory leaders over data centres. Dominic Lorrimer “The overall strategy of the LNP government is clear: remove targets, erase closure dates, protect coal, make renewable investment harder and let the project pipeline thin – then point to the shortage you created as proof renewables cannot do the job. “That is a self-fulfilling strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable. It is ideology, not economics or engineering.”



But Janetzki refuted the claims, noting the Clean Energy Council’s latest quarterly investment report which showed Queensland has the largest volume of large-scale renewable generation financially committed or under construction. Related Article Opinion

Renewables Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build David McElrea Contributor The treasurer also pointed to last week’s green light of a $1.7 billion Gawara Baya wind farm in North Queensland by Danish investment giant Copenhagen Infrastructure Partners – the eastern seaboard’s largest wind farm in more than two years. “Queensland leads all states in large-scale wind and solar projects financially committed or under construction and the Crisafulli government continues to encourage private sector investment in new generation and storage under our open for business approach,” Janetzki told this masthead in response to questions. Grattan Institute energy policy expert Tony Wood said there were broader market and political sentiment issues that had contributed to an investment drought in the sector.



But he said the state government’s suite of policies “certainly created a significant barrier” to investments. “All these announcements that have happened [since forming government in 2024] – keeping coal running longer, having less aggressive renewable projects and effectively, from a planning perspective, throwing a lot of the renewable projects into at least doubt. Janetzki says investments in Queensland’s renewable energy sector remains strong. Jamila Filippone “The end result is it creates significant unpredictability for investment.” The industry body will also use the Smart Energy Queensland Conference to call for coal-fired power stations to be brought properly into the Safeguard Mechanism, which would impose costly carbon credit demands on assets operating beyond previously proposed closure dates.



This would apply to previously announced closures of Queensland assets, including Callide B (2028), Tarong (phased from 2032), Tarong North (2033), and Stanwell (2033). Related Article Energy Why Queensland will splash hundreds of millions on complex spinning machines “Renewable energy, storage and transmission projects require billions of dollars of long-term investment,” McElrea said. “Investors and lenders need to know when replacement power will be required. Every time a coal closure date is pushed back, that investment becomes harder to finance. “That delays new generation, delays jobs and creates worker uncertainty, and leaves consumers exposed to the cost and unreliability risks of ageing coal.” Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build
World.content:
NationalQueenslandRenewables Opinion Queensland is making cheaper power harder to build David McElrea Contributor September 8, 2026 — 12:01am

September 8, 2026 — 12:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Queensland households, businesses and industry are racing toward solar, wind and batteries, but the state government is driving in reverse. By scrapping renewable energy targets, abandoning coal closure schedules and running state-owned coal stations past their shelf life, the government has injected massive risk into the market. Queensland’s ill-fated Callide coal power station. Paul Harris Investors can no longer predict when replacement power will be needed, choking off finance for new clean energy projects. This reliance on coal actively punishes investment in clean energy. Because coal stations cannot quickly cycle on and off, they idle at minimum output during bright, sunny afternoons – flooding an oversupplied grid.



To prevent blackouts, the grid operator curtails or disconnects rooftop solar and wind. Related Article Renewables ‘It is ideology, not economics’: Queensland accused of driving away renewables investment Families that have invested in solar lose the electricity they generated, drawing power back from a coal-heavy grid instead. They pay twice: once for their own solar, and again to keep ageing coal on life support. The political playbook is clear: cancel targets, erase end dates, protect old assets and starve new renewables of capital. When the clean-energy pipeline inevitably dries up, manufacture outrage over the energy shortage you created to justify keeping coal online even longer.



It is a deliberate strategy to make renewable energy uninvestable. Now, the same flawed logic threatens public transportation and the AI and data centre boom. These facilities require massive amounts of power. That incoming demand should bankroll fresh generation, storage, and transmission grid infrastructure – not breathe artificial life into obsolete coal plants. The concept model of a large-scale data centre project in Queensland’s Western Downs. Queensland could leverage data centres for high-tech jobs and regional growth.



Instead, current policy guarantees higher power bills, weaker reliability, and stalled investment. Fixing this requires closing a glaring federal loophole. The federal government is currently reviewing the Safeguard Mechanism – Australia’s primary tool for cutting industrial emissions. Treasurer David Janetzki (left) and Premier David Crisafulli. Jamila Filippone Yet coal-fired power stations remain mysteriously exempt, letting the country’s biggest polluters dodge responsibility for their actual costs. The Safeguard Mechanism must apply to all coal-fired generators based on their original closure dates.



If a plant operates past its deadline, the owner must use Australian Carbon Credit Units to cover the pollution. Related Article Queensland government Queensland premier secures data centre power victory over PM This is not a sudden shutdown. It is a clear market signal to finance and build replacement power before we need it. Queensland deserves an energy policy designed to succeed, not one engineered to fail. World.title: ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach
World.content:
Analysis PoliticsFederalPacific diplomacy ‘Seize this opportunity’: Leaks reveal $1b pledge to counter Beijing’s Pacific reach Matthew Knott Updated September 7, 2026 — 10:09pm ,first published 5:29pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Solomon Islands counterpart Matthew Wale will move to fast-track a sweeping new $1 billion treaty after a push to overthrow Wale’s pro-Australia government imploded in a blow to Beijing’s ambitions to expand its influence in the Pacific. Wale’s success at fending off the attempt to overthrow him came as an immense relief to Albanese and foreign affairs officials in Canberra, who see him as one of Australia’s most important allies in the region. Solomon Islands Prime Minister Matthew Wale with Prime Minister Anthony Albanese earlier this year. Alex Ellinghausen A leaked message from Australia’s High Commissioner to Solomon Islands, Jeffrey Roach, to Deputy Solomons Prime Minister Francis Sade, seen by this masthead, shows that each Solomon Islands constituency would be granted an estimated $1.9 million over three years in funding for community priorities. A further $142 million would be provided over two years to help fund Wale’s free school education policy plus funding for visa improvements and security requests.



“I very much hope both countries can hold steady to seize this opportunity, and lock this in ahead of the November budget session,” Roach wrote last week, as Wale was facing a no-confidence motion. The $980 million in funding by 2028, first reported by the ABC, is similar to the $1 billion pledged to support a recent set of treaties with Fiji over a 10-year timeframe. In Beijing, Xi Jinping’s foot soldiers will be lamenting a lost opportunity to install a pro-China leader in Honiara, just 2000 kilometres from the Australian mainland. The start of last week’s Pacific Islands Forum in Palau was rocked by the news that Wale had to race home to respond to a non-confidence motion lodged while he was en route to the event. As three of his cabinet ministers stepped down, Wale’s hold on power looked precarious just four months after his surprise election victory. But instead of gaining momentum, the amateurish putsch effort sputtered and flamed out. Manasseh Maelanga, the former cabinet minister who led the charge against Wale, announced on Sunday afternoon that he was withdrawing his no-confidence motion after failing to secure the numbers to bring the government down. Wale remains in power, his stature enhanced.



Related Article Pacific diplomacy The Solomons’ surprise new leader is a win for Australia, but the China challenge remains This matters to Australia because of the remarkable turnaround in foreign affairs Wale has spearheaded since coming to power in May. For most of the decade leading up to 2024, the Solomons were led by the mercurial Manasseh Sogavare, who was openly hostile towards Australia and signed a far-reaching security pact with China. That deal shocked Canberra and dominated days of the 2022 election campaign, with then opposition frontbencher Penny Wong branding it the nation’s worst foreign policy blunder since World War II. Successor Jeremiah Manele was less adversarial, but remained determined to play Canberra and Beijing off against each other. By contrast, Wale – a long-time critic of China who railed against politicians “sleazing up to Beijing” – has made clear his priority is deepening ties with Australia. Just weeks after coming to office, Wale declared he would review the China security pact and negotiate a comprehensive new treaty with Australia. He also announced he wanted to achieve an ambitious regional security pact – a move that would limit China’s ability to pick off individual countries.



When China test-fired an intercontinental ballistic missile across the region in July, Wale showed no compunction in criticising the superpower, labelling it “not the act of a friend”. One of his top ministers, Peter Kenilorea Jr, has called for security and policing co-operation with China to be sidelined. This is why, despite no firm proof of meddling, Australian officials were convinced Beijing was helping to orchestrate the move against Wale. “It is just speculation, but I imagine they would have been very active,” says James Batley, a former Australian ambassador in Honiara. “They certainly have the motive.” There was even a chance Sogavare could have returned to power in a nightmare scenario for Canberra and a dream come true for Beijing. The Chinese government, for its part, angrily denies it seeks to interfere in Pacific nations’ internal affairs. The Solomons have long been known for its cycle of “grasshopper politics” in which MPs jump from one side of the aisle to another, driven less by ideology than personal advancement. Wale’s rapid attempts to drive domestic reforms and overhaul foreign relations undoubtedly rankled some of his cabinet colleagues, who found him high-handed and accused him of failing to consult on key decisions. Unlike Kevin Rudd, who faced similar accusations as prime minister, Wale has been given a chance to improve and grow in the job.



Related Article Exclusive

Pacific diplomacy China’s policing plans should be sidelined, says top Solomons minister Wale and Albanese will look to lock in their comprehensive treaty, which has largely been completed by officials. Initially slated to be struck by the end of the year, a deal could come ahead of schedule, with an Albanese-Wale meeting on the sidelines of the United Nations General Assembly in New York this month the next opportunity to make progress on the pact. Wale’s proposal for a Pacific-wide security agreement will prove far more difficult, and perhaps impossible, to achieve given the diverging views within the region. Even so, Wale’s willingness to propose bold ideas that challenge Beijing shows why Albanese is delighted the push to oust him failed — at least for now. World.title: West Papuan group urges Jakarta to put words into action on UN visit
World.content:
A leading West Papua pro-independence group has questioned Indonesia's assertion that a proposed visit by the United Nations High Commissioner for Human Rights to West Papua is on track.

The West Papua National Committee (KNPB) is urging Indonesia to put its words into action on the proposed visit with a clear date, genuine access and meaningful engagement.

This comes after Melanesian countries last week urged Jakarta to facilitate the long-requested visit or have Indonesia's status as an associate member of the Melanesian Spearhead Group reviewed.

A request for the visit was made by Pacific Islands Forum countries back in 2019, but it has still not gone ahead, despite ongoing armed conflict and human rights violations in Indonesian-ruled Papua region, known internationally as West Papua.

In the intervening years, frustration has built up among the Melanesian countries in particular that Indonesia has not yet allowed the visit to take place.

In response to last week's statement from the MSG, the Indonesian government told RNZ Pacific that the visit was on track, without elaborating on details.

"We are always in constructive discussion on the issues deemed important by other members of the MSG, and we can also confirm that the said proposed visit is on the right path," an Indonesian spokesperson said.

West Papuans protested in numerous cities and towns on 15 August 2026 to mark the anniversary of 1962's New York Agreement. Supplied

The KNPB's international spokesperson, Victor Yeimo, said that for the Papuan people, Indonesia's statement about the visit being on track must now translate into concrete, verifiable action.

"If the visit is genuinely on track, we respectfully ask: What is the timeline? What practical arrangements are being made? And when will the High Commissioner be able to visit West Papua and engage directly with the Papuan people?

"The question is whether the United Nations' highest human rights official will now be given meaningful and independent access to assess the wider human rights situation."

Yeimo said that in Papua the High Commissioner should be allowed to engage freely with Indigenous communities, victims of human rights violations, displaced persons, civil society, churches, human rights defenders and other affected communities.
